items.title: Optimized Matrix-Product State Simulations of Quantum Error Correction Circuits
items.authors: Asier Piñeiro Orioli, Chen Zhao, Guido Masella, Tommaso Macrì, Hengyun Zhou, Shannon Whitlock
items.matched: Power of data in quantum machine learning
items.result: Matrix product state (MPS) optimizations simulate a 15-to-1 magic-state distillation circuit on 187 physical qubits (11 logical qubits, distance d=3, 15 logical T gates, hundreds of QEC rounds) with maximal bond dimension 64 in under 40 seconds on 4 CPU cores.
items.question: Can matrix product states efficiently simulate intermediate-scale quantum error correction circuits with non-Clifford gates in an exact regime?
items.prior: Near-Clifford simulators PPVM and CAMPS run the same 15-to-1 distillation circuit in 7.9 ms and 47 ms, respectively (~1000 times faster than bare optimized MPS).
items.limits: Pure state simulation (no non-Clifford noise modeled). Simulation runtime scales exponentially with logical qubit count due to bond dimension χ_max = 2^(lfloorN_L/2 rfloor+ d + 1).
items.tools: matrix product states (MPS) · qubit reordering heuristics · gate scheduling optimization · ancilla reuse · rotated surface codes
items.caption: Simulation runtime versus number of T gates n_T for random circuits on N_L ∈3, 5, 7 logical qubits in a d=3 rotated surface code. Runtime scales linearly with n_T at constant logical qubit count.
items.abstract: Simulating quantum error correction (QEC) circuits including non-Clifford gates at scale is important to accelerate progress toward fault-tolerant quantum computing. Here we demonstrate that matrix product state (MPS) techniques can handle many QEC circuits exactly and without restriction on gate types. Crucially, we find that MPS efficiency depends sensitively on implementation choices, and we introduce a series of targeted optimizations that reduce bond dimensions and simulation time by several orders of magnitude compared to naive approaches. We illustrate this with examples including: (a) a rotated surface code quantum memory up to distance 11, (b) logical Bell-state preparation up to distance 9, (c) a 15-to-1 magic-state distillation circuit including hundreds of QEC rounds that we optimize to be simulated with only 11 logical qubits (187 physical qubits) and a maximal bond dimension of 64 in under 40 seconds, and (d) a narrow, deep random circuit that scales linearly with the number of T gates. These results demonstrate the importance of circuit-level optimizations and position MPS as a valuable complement to near-Clifford simulators for QEC circuits.

items.title: Discretization-Aware Fine-Tuning for Quantum Machine Learning with Chemical Foundation Models
items.authors: Shunji Matsuura, Sonika Johri
items.matched: Power of data in quantum machine learning
items.result: Discretization-aware fine-tuning (DAFT) reduces BBBP cross-class bit collisions from 11544 to ≈1, raising 10-qubit quantum classifier accuracy by +12.2 pp to 0.883 and beating an identically-discretized classical logistic regression by +2.8 pp (p=0.026).
items.question: How can continuous representations from classical foundation models be adapted to prevent label-destroying collisions when discretized into small quantum registers for bit-bit QML?
items.prior: Without DAFT, frozen ChemBERTa-77M embeddings produced 11544 collisions and 10-qubit quantum circuits trailed the matched classical bit-string baseline by -6.0 pp (0.762 vs 0.822).
items.limits: Evaluated on BBBP binary molecular classification dataset up to n_q=10 qubits; quantum simulation setting.
items.tools: ChemBERTa-77M foundation model · differentiable soft collision loss · bit-bit basis encoding · parameterized quantum circuits · mutual-information bit allocation
items.caption: End-to-end pipeline mapping SMILES strings via ChemBERTa-77M and DAFT fine-tuning, standardized/quantized to bit-strings, and fed into quantum and classical baselines.
items.abstract: A key challenge in practical quantum machine learning (QML), particularly for discriminative tasks such as classification, is the limited capacity of near-term quantum devices to encode high-dimensional classical data into small quantum registers. In optimized basis-encoded (bit-bit) settings, this constraint leads to cross-class collisions, where samples with different labels are mapped to the same discrete bit-string and thus become indistinguishable to any downstream model. In this work, we investigate how data representation affects QML performance under such severe information bottlenecks. We introduce discretization-aware fine-tuning (DAFT), a method that adapts a pre-trained chemical foundation model to produce representations that remain informative after quantization. DAFT reduces collision probability through a differentiable soft collision loss. We evaluate both quantum and classical models under a controlled setting in which they receive identical discretized bit-string inputs, isolating the effect of representation from model architecture. On the blood-brain barrier penetration (BBBP) molecular property prediction benchmark using ChemBERTa-77M, DAFT reduces collision counts by several orders of magnitude and improves quantum classification accuracy by more than 12 percentage points compared to a frozen backbone. Importantly, without DAFT, classical models outperform QML under the same input constraints. With DAFT, however, this comparison reverses at higher qubit counts. At 10 qubits, the quantum model surpasses a matched classical baseline trained on identical bit-strings (0.883 vs. 0.855, p = 0.026). These results show that, in information-constrained regimes, achieving a quantum advantage critically depends on aligning continuous representations with discrete quantum encodings.

items.title: Quantum communication and Bell nonlocality require infinite classical communication to simulate
items.authors: Carlos de Gois, Thyago S. R. Santos, Carlos Vieira
items.matched: Power of data in quantum machine learning
items.result: No finite classical communication can exactly simulate quantum communication or entangled-pair Bell correlations for dimension d_Q ≥4. For qutrits (d_Q = 3), an explicit protocol simulates all states and measurements using 357 classical bits.
items.question: Can the statistics of d-dimensional quantum communication and Bell correlations across all measurements be exactly simulated with a finite amount of classical communication and shared randomness?
items.prior: Qubits (d_Q = 2) were known to require and suffice with 2 classical bits (Toner and Bacon 2003). For d_Q ≥3, only lower bounds were known: C_cl(3) ≥5 and C_cl(4) ≥10.
items.limits: Exact classical simulation with unlimited shared randomness; single-round classical communication; exact reproduction of all POVMs and quantum states.
items.tools: complex projective space CP³ and CP² geometric analysis · binary projective measurement embedding · fallback protocol and acceptance rejection sampling · spherical covering bounds
items.caption: Schematic setup for classically simulating single-party d_Q-dimensional quantum state transmission (a) and bipartite entangled Bell nonlocality (b) via classical message c and shared randomness λ.
items.abstract: A quantum system of any fixed dimension can be prepared in a continuum of states, yet it cannot be used to transmit an unlimited amount of classical information. Similarly, the correlations observed between measurement outcomes on separate parts of a shared quantum system can be stronger than classical correlations, but they cannot transmit information. These fundamental limitations suggest that the statistics observed from quantum communication and quantum correlations may admit a simulation using a finite amount of classical communication. This expectation is confirmed in the smallest nontrivial quantum dimension, with two classical bits being necessary and sufficient to exactly simulate qubit communication and all correlations between qubits. Despite significant efforts during the previous decades, this remained the only solved case. Here we resolve both problems for every quantum dimension. The solution reveals an unexpected qualitative transition starting at dimension four: no finite amount of classical communication can exactly simulate ququart communication nor all quantum correlations of two entangled ququarts, even with unlimited shared randomness. One might have expected this transition, if it existed, to appear already for qutrits. Instead, we construct an explicit protocol that exactly simulates qutrit communication using 357 classical bits, and consequently, all correlations of two entangled qutrits.

For qutrits (<math xmlns="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML"><mrow><msub><mi>d</mi><mi>Q</mi></msub><mo>=</mo><mn>3</mn></mrow></math>), an explicit protocol simulates all states and measurements using <math xmlns="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML"><mn>357</mn></math> classical bits.

items.title: Approximate cubic phase states in a trapped ion
items.authors: C. Ventura-Velázquez, Juan Mauricio Torres
items.matched: Quantum Machine Learning in Feature Hilbert Spaces
items.result: Native nonlinear Jaynes-Cummings interaction generates an approximate cubic phase state in a trapped-ion vibrational mode, reducing nonlinear squeezing σ₍₃₎(λ) below the Gaussian threshold σ_G=(3/2)^(5/3)|λ|^(2/3).
items.question: How can an approximate cubic phase state be generated directly in the vibrational mode of a single trapped ion?
items.limits: Requires initial coherent vibrational state with large occupation number (N = |α|² ≫1) and vanishing second derivative of eigenfrequencies ((2η)² N ≈9.95160559).
items.tools: nonlinear Jaynes-Cummings model · nonlinear squeezing parameter · Wigner function phase-space analysis · Taylor expansion around inflection point of Bessel function
items.caption: Nonlinear squeezing σ₍₃₎(λ) plotted against parameter λ for different initial coherent amplitudes α at time τ=π/|ω₁|, dipping below the Gaussian boundary into the quantum non-Gaussian region.
items.abstract: Universal quantum computation with continuous variables cannot be attained solely with a set of Gaussian operations, it requires the addition of a non-Gaussian element, at least of third order in the quadrature operators, such as the cubic phase state. In this work, we present a method to generate a quantum state in the vibrational mode of a trapped ion that exhibits characteristics compatible with the cubic phase state, such as the distinctive oscillating pattern in its Wigner function. This state emerges from the nonlinear Jaynes-Cummings interaction native to the trapped-ion model, and under the assumption of an initial coherent vibrational state with a large occupation number. Consequently, the evolved vibrational state approximates the cubic phase state with high fidelity, and we use the variance of a nonlinear combination of the quadratures to characterize it. Finally, we provide an analytical expression for its cubicity that shows the high performance of the approximate vibrational cubic phase state.

items.title: Low-Frequency Charge Noise in Bilayer Graphene Quantum Dots
items.authors: Jessica Richter, Max J. Ruckriegel, Jonas D. Gerber, Tijl Degroote, Christoph Adam, Markus Niese, Lara Ostertag, Clara Galante, Kenji Watanabe, Takashi Taniguchi, Petar Tomic, Artem O. Denisov, Hadrien Duprez, Klaus Ensslin, Thomas Ihn

items.result: Extracted median charge-noise amplitude of S_μ^(1/2)(1Hz) = 1.16~μeV/√Hz in gate-defined bilayer graphene quantum dots, with a 10-90 percentile range of 0.41~μeV/√Hz to 2.24~μeV/√Hz.
items.question: How low-frequency charge noise in bilayer graphene quantum dots compares to established semiconductor qubit platforms and how it behaves across tuning and material variations.
items.prior: Established semiconductor platforms span 0.1~μeV/√Hz to 10~μeV/√Hz across GaAs, Si MOS, Si/SiGe, and Ge/SiGe quantum dots.
items.limits: Measured at 20mK. Charge-qubit coherence estimates assume S₁/f^γ scaling extrapolates from 1mHz to 5GHz. Quantitative charge-noise dephasing bounds do not directly translate to spin or valley qubits.
items.tools: hBN-encapsulated bilayer graphene van-der-Waals heterostructures · transport-based noise spectroscopy (Coulomb blockade flank method) · superconducting resonator-based dispersive readout · WSe2/BLG heterostructures
items.caption: Charge-noise amplitude S_μ^(1/2) at 1 Hz across bilayer graphene single dots, double dots, resonator readout, and TMD proximitized devices, benchmarked alongside literature values for GaAs, Si MOS, Si/SiGe, and Ge/SiGe.
items.abstract: Bilayer graphene (BLG) quantum dots (QDs) are a promising platform for semiconductor qubits. However, the low-frequency charge noise that may ultimately limit coherence has remained largely unexplored. Here, we systematically characterize charge noise in gate-defined BLG QDs using transport-based noise spectroscopy. We extract a median amplitude of S_μ^(1/2) (1~Hz) = 1.16~μeV/√Hz, placing BLG well within the range reported for established semiconductor quantum-dot platforms. Across variations in charge occupation, confinement, source-drain bias, and charge-sensor operating conditions, neither the noise amplitude nor the spectral dependence shows a reproducible trend in electrostatic tuning, indicating that we extracted the intrinsic semiconductor noise. Consistent noise levels are further observed in double QDs and confirmed using an independent superconducting resonator-based dispersive readout. Extending the study to BLG devices incorporating transition metal dichalcogenide layers reveals no measurable charge noise increase in weakly proximitized QDs. These results validate BLG as a viable platform for coherent quantum information processing.

items.title: Spin-to-polarization mapping with a coherent quantum dot-cavity receiver
items.authors: Adrià Medeiros, Vincent Vinel, Eliott Rambeau, Petr Steindl, Elham Mehdi, Manuel Gundín, Clément Millet, Petr Stepanov, Niccolo Somaschi, Aristide Lemaître, Isabelle Sagnes, Olivier Krebs, Pascale Senellart, Dario A. Fioretto, Loïc Lanco
items.matched: Single-shot read-out of an individual electron spin in a quantum dot
items.result: Single-photon reflection projects quantum dot electron spin to an eigenstate with 95±2% fidelity, producing orthogonal reflected polarization states with relative Stokes angle α/π= 0.95±0.02 (171^∘±4^∘).
items.question: Can spin-induced Kerr rotation in a quantum dot-cavity system realize a bijective one-to-one mapping between spin eigenstates and orthogonal reflected photon polarization states?
items.limits: Liquid Helium cryostat at 4 K; limited by competition between trion radiative lifetime T₁^((rad))=200±20ps and spin relaxation time T₁^((spin))=1.9±0.2ns.
items.tools: negatively charged InGaAs quantum dot · AlGaAs micropillar cavity · time-resolved conditional polarization tomography · continuous-wave laser reflection
items.caption: Angle α/π and Stokes vector purities as a function of delay τ between two reflected photons, showing near-antiparallel polarization states (α≈π) after the transient regime.
items.abstract: Coherent light-matter interfaces controllably modifying the state of a photon upon interaction with a stationary qubit are a key resource for implementing deterministic entangling gates for optical quantum technologies. This requires a one-to-one mapping between the state of the scattered photon and that of the embedded qubit. Here, we present an experimental signature of such a bijection by leveraging the spin-induced Kerr rotation present in a low-noise charged quantum dot-micropillar cavity device. Through time-resolved polarization measurements, we project the electron spin to one of its eigenstates with 95±2% fidelity with a single reflected photon detection, and follow the subsequent spin relaxation through the detection of a second reflected photon. We demonstrate that, after a transient regime governed by the trion radiative lifetime, two orthogonal polarization states can be produced, each associated to a given spin eigenstate. While the current results are limited by a timescale competition between electron spin relaxation and trion radiative lifetime, they could be improved using hole spins displaying increased relaxation times. Our work paves the way towards deterministic logic gates exploiting this one-to-one mapping between a spin and the polarization of a scattered photon.

items.title: Extrinsic orbital Edelstein effect from asymmetric scattering
items.authors: Sankar Sarkar, Koushik Ghorai, Amit Agarwal
items.matched: Spins in few-electron quantum dots
items.result: Disorder-induced asymmetric scattering produces side-jump and skew-scattering orbital Edelstein responses in systems with broken time-reversal symmetry. In a magnetized Rashba 2DEG with Rashba coupling of 1 eV Å, orbital magnetization is about one order of magnitude larger than spin magnetization.
items.question: How do side-jump and skew-scattering mechanisms modify the orbital Edelstein effect?
items.limits: Weak electric field and disorder treated perturbatively, elastic impurity scattering, intraband small-momentum-transfer approximation, Gaussian noncrossing disorder.
items.tools: semiclassical Boltzmann transport theory · first and higher-order Born approximations · magnetized Rashba 2DEG model · magnetic point-group symmetry analysis
items.caption: Orbital Edelstein susceptibility χ^(z,x) components plotted versus chemical potential and exchange-field orientation angle θ.
items.abstract: The generation and manipulation of orbital angular momentum (OAM) by an external electric field constitute one of the central themes of orbitronics. In particular, the electrically induced nonequilibrium OAM polarization, known as the orbital Edelstein effect (OEE), has attracted considerable attention in recent years. While the intrinsic band-geometric mechanism and the role of conventional symmetric impurity scattering in the OEE are well understood, the contribution from disorder-induced asymmetric scattering remains unclear. Here, we develop a semiclassical theory that separates the OEE into intrinsic, Drude, side-jump, and third- and fourth-order skew-scattering channels. Unlike the Drude channel, the intrinsic, side-jump, and skew-scattering responses survive only in systems with broken time-reversal symmetry. We find that in a magnetized Rashba two-dimensional electron gas (2DEG), these disorder-induced mechanisms can substantially exceed the intrinsic contribution. Remarkably, we find that for a system with Rashba coupling of 1 $eV Å$, the orbital magnetization is about one order of magnitude larger than the spin magnetization for the chosen parameters, highlighting the crucial role of orbital degrees of freedom in the Edelstein effect.

items.title: Nanoscale magnetometry via collective many-body dynamics in diamond
items.authors: Haoyang Gao, Piotr Put, Nathaniel T. Leitao, Nazli U. Köylüouglu, Andrew Maccabe, Mathew Mammen, Siddharth Dandavate, Lillian B. Hughes Wyatt, Leigh S. Martin, Ania C. Bleszynski Jayich, Hongkun Park, Mikhail D. Lukin
items.matched: Spins in few-electron quantum dots
items.result: Collective one-axis-twisting dynamics driven by pulsed magnetic-field gradients and dressed-state encoding achieve metrological gains of up to 7.9(2) dB for magnetic signal detection and 8.8(3) dB for magnetic noise sensing.
items.question: Can dipolar interactions in a solid-state spin ensemble be coherently controlled to provide practical metrological enhancement in nanoscale magnetic sensing accounting for experimental overheads?
items.prior: Prior NV-ensemble experiments demonstrated ~0.5 dB spin squeezing in sub-ensembles and a 1.067x (0.56 dB) signal enhancement under idealized conditions.
items.limits: Demonstrated with ~8000 spins in bulk diamond; decoherence during gradient winding increases exponentially with wavevector magnitude.
items.tools: 3D dipolar nitrogen-vacancy center ensemble in bulk diamond · pulsed magnetic field gradients from on-chip microwires · perpendicular bias field dressed-state qubit encoding · one-axis-twisting (OAT) spin-spiral dynamics · Fourier magnetic imaging
items.caption: Measured spin polarization dynamics, twisting/decay rates, and separation distance showing up to 5.4x signal amplification via multi-stage collective one-axis twisting.
items.abstract: Many-body dynamics constitutes a promising approach for creating correlations between quantum particles which can be used for applications in sensing and metrology. However, utilizing this potential for substantial gains in practical settings is a challenging task with only a very few applications realized to date. Here, we demonstrate an approach to nanoscale magnetic sensing enabled by strongly interacting electronic spins in a room temperature solid. By coherently controlling collective many-body dynamics of a dipolar ensemble of ∼10⁴ nitrogen-vacancy (NV) centres in diamond with pulsed magnetic field gradients, we demonstrate practical metrological gain up to 7.9(2) dB for magnetic signal detection and 8.8(3) dB for magnetic noise sensing, fully accounting for experimental overheads. Finally, we combine these methods to demonstrate a momentum-space-resolved sensing modality that enables detection of spatially correlated magnetic noise at continuously tunable length scales down to 50 nanometers. These observations open the door toward practical applications of interaction-enhanced quantum sensors for nanoscale biological imaging and material characterization.

items.title: Deterministic nanofabrication for engineering nanowire quantum dot devices
items.authors: Tarun Patel, Matteo Pennacchietti, Greg Holloway, Stephen R. Harrigan, Sayan Gangopadhyay, Anthony Drouin, Megha Jain, Dan Dalacu, Philip J. Poole, Sasan Vosoogh-Grayli, Michael E. Reimer
items.matched: Single-shot read-out of an individual electron spin in a quantum dot
items.result: Deterministic vertical-to-vertical transfer of InAsP/InP nanowire quantum dots via electron-beam-induced deposition of SiO_x nano-glue onto pre-fabricated templates. Yields 75% photon extraction efficiency on an Au/SiO₂ mirror substrate and 3.6 GHz electrostatic Stark tuning between quadrupolar gates while maintaining g⁽²⁾(0) = 0.002.
items.question: Can vertical nanowire quantum dots be deterministically transferred to pre-patterned templates without losing their upright geometry, optical quality, or single-photon purity?
items.prior: Nanowire quantum dot pick-and-place transfer relied on van der Waals forces limited to lying-down geometries, while as-grown upright nanowires had a maximum top extraction efficiency limit of 50%.
items.limits: Demonstrated across 8 transferred nanowire devices on mirror templates; Stark tuning tested up to 120 V across a 600 nm gap; spectral shift is reduced compared to theory likely due to screening from background doping in the nanowire.
items.tools: dual-beam SEM/FIB with GIS · electron-beam-induced deposition (EBID) · tungsten nanoprobe · InAsP/InP site-selected nanowire quantum dots
items.caption: Electron microscopy frames showing the vertical nanowire transfer sequence: mechanical detachment by a tungsten probe at the base (a), followed by EBID SiO_x nano-gluing to pick up and secure the nanowire upright onto a target template (b).
items.abstract: Semiconductor quantum dots (QDs) are a leading platform for realising bright, wavelength-tunable sources of single and entangled photon pairs for photonic quantum technologies. Site-selected nanowire quantum dots (NWQDs) are a promising platform for fabricating such photonic devices in a scalable manner. However, implementing additional structures around the photonic nanowire while maintaining its vertical growth geometry has remained a challenge. In this work, we develop a deterministic pick-and-place technique to conduct a vertical-to-vertical transfer of NWQDs from the growth substrate to arbitrary templates. Using this transfer technique, we enhance the photon extraction efficiency to 75% by implementing a bottom gold mirror and tune the emission wavelength by 3.6 GHz via implementing electrostatic gates around the QD. Importantly, we measure low-multiphoton probability (g^(2)(0) = 0.002) and high indistinguishability (>80% for +/-100 ps) of the QD emission after the transfer process, yielding high-quality devices. These results demonstrate the repeatability and versatility of the developed transfer technique, which is an enabling step towards scalable single and entangled photon sources.

items.title: Analog quantum simulation of bosonic and anyonic models with flux-driven transmons
items.authors: Isak Lyngfelt, Jorge Fernández-Pendás, Göran Johansson, Laura Garciá-Álvarez
items.matched: Quantum computation with quantum dots
items.result: Alternating sinusoidal flux modulation on capacitively coupled transmons enables analog simulation of Bose-Hubbard models with up to three bosons per site without total particle number limits, and provides the first analog transmon protocol for the 1D anyon-Hubbard model with tunable on-site interaction U and statistical phase θ.
items.question: Can capacitively coupled flux-tunable transmons perform analog quantum simulation of Bose-Hubbard and anyon-Hubbard models with tunable interactions beyond the two-particle limit?
items.prior: Parametrically tunable interaction Bose-Hubbard transmon simulations were limited to two particles in total, and anyon models were only simulated digitally.
items.limits: Hilbert space truncated to at most three excitations per site for Bose-Hubbard and two for anyon-Hubbard; decoherence and higher-order flux harmonics neglected.
items.tools: flux-tunable transmons · sinusoidal frequency modulation · QuTiP state-vector simulations · rotating wave approximation
items.caption: Particle asymmetry Δn at time t=5/J as a function of anyonic statistical phase θ for interaction strengths U/J ∈1, 3, 5, 7. Driven transmons (markers) reproduce the exact anyon-Hubbard model curves (solid lines).
items.abstract: When quantum particles interact, many-body phenomena that are hard to simulate classically emerge. Quantum analog simulation offers an alternative in which the target system's dynamics is directly realized in controllable quantum hardware. Here, we give a general protocol for simulating the Bose-Hubbard and anyon-Hubbard models using lattices of capacitively coupled flux-tunable transmons. By modulating the transmon frequencies in an alternating pattern, we resonantly drive multiple many-body transitions and can tune the on-site interaction and density-dependent hopping amplitudes for up to three bosons per site, with no additional restriction on the total particle number. By adding phases to the modulation, which renders the transition amplitudes complex-valued, we propose the first simulation protocol for the anyon-Hubbard model with transmons. Numerical simulations of the driven transmon arrays with experimentally realistic parameters reproduce the characteristic dynamics of the target models across a range of interaction strengths and statistical phases, including the interaction-dependent localization and the statistics-dependent asymmetry of the anyonic quantum walk.

items.title: Stabilization of dark states in emitter arrays coupled to a half-waveguide
items.authors: Oriol Rubies-Bigorda, Susanne F. Yelin, Ana Asenjo-Garcia, Stuart J. Masson
items.matched: Single-shot read-out of an individual electron spin in a quantum dot
items.result: Applying optimal relative frequency detunings Δ_j between emitters in a half-waveguide cancels coherent coupling to bright modes, producing exact single-excitation dark states with zero decay rate (γ_φ=0) and near-perfect multi-excitation dark states in small arrays.
items.question: How can stable, addressable single- and multi-excitation dark states be prepared in small arrays of quantum emitters coupled to a half-waveguide?
items.limits: Markovian approximation (travel time between emitters and mirror is negligible relative to emitter lifetimes), 1D waveguide, two-level emitters.
items.tools: Markovian master equation · non-Hermitian Hamiltonian diagonalisation · interference via mirror boundary conditions · engineered emitter detuning profiles
items.caption: Level diagrams and decay mechanisms for two emitters in a half-waveguide. Non-zero detuning eliminates coherent cross-coupling between bright and dark Lindbladian eigenstates, isolating the dark state with zero decay rate.
items.abstract: The radiative properties of quantum emitters are profoundly influenced by their electromagnetic environment. When coupled to a waveguide terminated at one end by a mirror, distant emitters interact strongly via virtual photon exchange, leading to collective superradiant and subradiant states with enhanced or suppressed decay rates. We demonstrate that applying optimal frequency shifts to each emitter enables the formation of perfect single-excitation dark states (i.e. states with zero decay rate) and near-perfect multi-excitation dark states in small ensembles. These collective states can be deterministically prepared with high fidelity using classical driving fields or few-photon pulses propagating along the waveguide. These results, readily implementable in superconducting qubit platforms, open new avenues for quantum information storage, networking and control of light.

items.title: Tuning Andreev reflection and conductance in proximitized nanowires through the spin-orbit field direction
items.authors: Leonardo Musca, Fabrizio Dolcini
items.matched: Charge Noise Spectroscopy Using Coherent Exchange Oscillations in a Singlet-Tri…
items.result: In the topologically trivial phase of a proximitized nanowire junction, varying the spin-orbit field misalignment angle φ_SO from 0 to π tunes the finite-energy Andreev reflection coefficient from R_he ≃0.87 down to complete suppression R_he ≃4·10⁻⁴, and conductance at eV = 0.1Δ₀ from ≈1.74 e²/h to ≈10⁻³ e²/h. Zero-energy values remain fixed by the topological invariant.
items.question: How do spatial inhomogeneities in the direction of the Rashba spin-orbit field across a normal-superconductor nanowire junction affect Andreev reflection and conductance?
items.limits: Single-channel nanowire model with axial Zeeman field b = (b_x,0,0) and transverse spin-orbit fields lying purely in the y-z plane; no inelastic scattering.
items.tools: Bogoliubov-de Gennes Hamiltonian · Scattering matrix method · Effective mass model
items.caption: Plots show the bulk excitation spectra (a), the energy-dependent Andreev reflection coefficient R_he(E) (b), and the nonlinear differential conductance G(V) (c) in the trivial phase (E_Z = 0.8Δ₀) for spin-orbit misalignment angles φ_SO = 0, π/2, π. Tuning φ_SO strongly suppresses both R_he and G(V) at finite energy/bias while leaving zero-bias values at zero.
items.abstract: We investigate the Andreev reflection (AR) and the nonlinear conductance in a normal-superconductor junction realized with a proximitized semiconductor nanowire exposed to a magnetic field along its axis. We show that, while at zero energy the AR coefficient is determined by the topological phase of the superconducting side of the junction, at finite energy the AR is strongly affected by the directions of the Rashba spin-orbit field characterizing the normal and the proximitized sides. The tunability of the AR and the nonlinear conductance as a function of the spin-orbit misalignment angle is particularly pronounced when the proximitized side is in the topologically trivial phase. The spin-orbit field direction is revealed to be an efficient knob to control the electron transport through the hybrid junction, realizing an electrically widely tunable device. The implementation in realistic setups is discussed.

items.title: Development of quantum technologies for optical/infrared interferometry
items.authors: John D. Monnier (University of Michigan)
items.matched: cavity QED, atom-photon interfaces and quantum networks
items.result: Quantum-assisted interferometers retain direct-detection weak-light sensitivity SNR∝|V|√η_q Moverlinen while avoiding physical optical delay lines across baselines >1km, but cannot beat direct detection on ground arrays up to a few kilometers.
items.question: Can quantum networking and quantum memory architectures overcome classical beam-transport limits in optical and infrared astronomical interferometry?
items.prior: Classical direct detection spans baselines up to 330 m but is limited by optical transport losses, while HBT and heterodyne detection scale unfavorably as SNR∝overlinen when overlinen≪1.
items.limits: Broadband astronomical light is photon-starved (overlinen≪1), single-mode, and degraded by atmospheric turbulence; no on-sky stellar fringe verification yet reported.
items.tools: entangled-reference photon pairs · quantum memories (diamond color centers and cold atoms) · single-photon avalanche diodes (SPADs) · superconducting nanowire single-photon detectors (SNSPDs)
items.caption: Schematic comparison of direct transport, local-oscillator (heterodyne), and nonlocal quantum-assisted phase-sensitive detection with their respective signal-to-noise scaling in the weak-source limit.
items.abstract: Quantum technologies may revolutionize optical interferometry through new means to distribute and preserve electric-field amplitude and phase correlations between widely separated telescopes. After reviewing existing techniques, I survey proposed quantum-sensing and quantum-networking applications and highlight recent laboratory demonstrations of key building blocks. By easing field-transport demands for baselines beyond ∼1 km, quantum-enhanced interferometry could enable sub-milliarcsecond imaging and microarcsecond-class differential astrometry. That said, "going quantum" is not a magic shortcut to sensitivity because many of the most compelling science cases remain photon- and turbulence-limited. I therefore emphasize the practical constraints -- loss, bandwidth, coherence time, synchronization, and wavelength limits of quantum interfaces -- that must also be overcome to make these capabilities useful for astronomy, whether deployed on the ground or from space.

items.title: DPRQ: A Dynamic Programming-based Qubit Routing Algorithm for Collective Communication in Distributed Quantum Computing
items.authors: Dhaval Vaidya (North Carolina State University, Raleigh, NC, USA), Ruozhou Yu (North Carolina State University, Raleigh, NC, USA)
items.matched: Demonstration of a small programmable quantum computer with atomic qubits
items.result: Dynamic programming qubit routing reduces inter-node EPR pair consumption by an average of 24.40% and up to 85.06% across 80 circuit configurations.
items.question: How to minimize inter-node communication across collective communication blocks in distributed quantum circuits by accounting for global inter-block dependencies?
items.prior: QuComm compiler, which uses greedy block-level routing.
items.limits: Evaluated on 4 benchmark circuits (QAOA, RCA, BV, VQE) up to 200 qubits in simulation across 3 network topologies (mesh-grid, ring, fully-connected).
items.tools: dynamic programming · collective quantum communication · TP-Comm protocol · communication fusion · shortest-path early execution
items.caption: EPR cost plotted against total circuit qubits (50 to 200) for DPRQ versus QuComm across four benchmark circuits. DPRQ maintains lower communication cost as network size increases.
items.abstract: Distributed quantum computing (DQC) offers a promising approach to scale quantum computing by overcoming the resource limitations of a single quantum processor. However, inter-node communication remains a major bottleneck of DQC due to inefficient and error-prone entanglement distribution. Optimizing inter-node communication can not only reduce the amount of entanglement resource needed to execute a quantum circuit but also improve execution speed and accuracy of the results. This paper proposes DPRQ, a qubit routing algorithm for minimizing inter-node communication in distributed quantum circuits divided into collective communication blocks. Unlike current approaches that utilize greedy block-level qubit routing strategies, DPRQ employs a dynamic programming-based technique focused on global circuit-level optimization, while capturing inter-block dependencies. We evaluated DPRQ on four sets of quantum circuits and a variety of DQC configurations. The results demonstrate that DPRQ's innovative routing strategy achieves an average of 24.40% reduction with a maximum of 85.06% reduction in inter-node communication, when compared to the state-of-the-art collective communication-based DQC compiler QuComm.

items.title: Three-Photon and Hybrid Coherent-Fock Interference in a Two-Phase Six-Port Mach-Zehnder Interferometer
items.authors: P. O. Amadi, P. Pewkhom, N. Sitpathom, R. Endut, N. Ali, S. A. Aljunid, S. Suryadi, P. Kalasuwan
items.matched: photonic qubits, linear-optical computing and boson sampling
items.result: Analytic transfer matrix for two-phase six-port Mach-Zehnder interferometer collapses into three symmetry triplets. In hybrid |α⟩₁|α⟩₂|1⟩₃ regime, the dark-to-bright threshold drops from |α|² = 2 at φ₂ = 0 to |α|² = 1/2 along φ₂ = φ₁.
items.question: How do two independent relative phase modulators govern three-photon coincidence statistics and hybrid coherent-Fock interference in a six-port Mach-Zehnder interferometer?
items.prior:
was |
α|² = 2 dark-to-bright threshold in single-phase CCF regime (Ref. [30])
items.limits: Assumes ideal lossless symmetric tritters and fully indistinguishable photons with zero spectral or temporal mismatch.
items.tools: discrete Fourier transform tritter matrix · composite transfer matrix derivation · density matrix and displacement operator formalism · quantum bosonic interference calculation
items.caption: Density maps of port-1 photon number ⟨n₁ ⟩ versus independent phases φ₁ and φ₂ in [0, 2π]². Shows bright ridge parallel to φ₁ = φ₂ below threshold (|α|² = 0.3) reorganizing into single lobe above threshold (|α|² = 1.0).
items.abstract: We present a unified theoretical analysis of three-photon quantum interference in a Six-Port Mach-Zehnder Interferometer (6p-MZI) constructed from two cascaded tritters, with two independent phase modulators placed between the tritter arms. We analytically derive the transfer matrix of the 6p-MZI and show how they organize into three symmetry classes, governed by the discrete Fourier transform (DFT) structure of the tritter and the conjugate relations. Furthermore, we analyze two input regimes: First, three indistinguishable single photons are injected into the tritter, and the output probability distributions P_([111]), P_([300]), and P_([210]) are derived as functions of the two relative phases (φ₁, φ₂). At φ₂ = 0, the single-phase limit is recovered, which confirms 100% visibility of the even-distribution fringe. Second, a hybrid coherent-Fock input |α⟩₁|α⟩₂|1⟩₃ is analyzed via the density matrix formalism. The average photon number at each output port exhibits amplitude-dependent phase shifts. Our results establish the 6p-MZI as a programmable platform for tripartite quantum state manipulation and coherent amplitude sensing.

items.title: Learning unknown stabilizer codes using product measurements
items.authors: Heather Leitch, Sowmya Tirukkovalluri, Yingkai Ouyang
items.matched: High-threshold and low-overhead fault-tolerant quantum memory
items.result: Stabilizer generators of an unknown stabilizer code can be reconstructed from N ≥Alng + Aln(1/δ) states using single-qubit product measurements, requiring polylogarithmically many copies in physical qubit count n for qLDPC codes.
items.question: Can stabilizer generators of an unknown quantum error-correcting code be learned using only local single-qubit measurements on codewords without prior structural knowledge?
items.limits: Bounded stabilizer generator weight w, code defined in stabilizer formalism, failure probability δ, bit-flip error rate per qubit p.
items.tools: randomized product Pauli measurements · parity checks on qubit subsets · multiplicative Chernoff bounds
items.caption: Step-by-step schematic for measuring random bases on N codewords, recording bit outcomes, evaluating subset parities, and filtering stabilizer generators via thresholding.
items.abstract: Efficiently characterizing quantum error correcting codes is a key challenge on the path to fault-tolerant quantum computation. Stabilizer codes, a central class of such codes, are defined by a set of stabilizer generators. Here, we present an algorithm that uses random single-qubit measurements to learn the stabilizer generators of any stabilizer code from N copies of stabilizer states in its codespace, requiring no prior knowledge of the code's structure. This also enables verification that a device implements its intended code. We derive a lower bound on N needed to recover the stabilizer generators with high probability, together with a bound on the algorithm's overall probability of success. When applied to quantum low-density parity-check (qLDPC) codes, a leading candidate for practical fault-tolerant architectures, our approach requires a number of states that scales polylogarithmically with n, the number of qubits.

items.title: Efficient Quantum Error Correction from Three Dimensional Qubit Control
items.authors: Kevin Yipu Wu, Ohik Kwon, Maxwell F. Parsons
items.matched: Surface codes: Towards practical large-scale quantum computation
items.result: 3D neutral-atom embedding of the [[144,12,12]] bivariate bicycle code achieves approximately 4× higher areal logical-qubit density than planar layout and 42× higher than distance-11 surface codes, while halving syndrome-extraction round duration.
items.question: How does native 3D qubit control affect the routing overhead, footprint, and temporal execution cost of nonlocal qLDPC syndrome extraction?
items.prior: Planar 2D atom-array embeddings of the [[144,12,12]] code.
items.limits: Numerical simulation rather than physical hardware implementation. Assumes single-shot multi-layer readout and collision-free parallel 3D transport.
items.tools: 3D optical tweezer arrays · Rydberg blockade routing · Bivariate bicycle code · Collective check-register transport scheduling
items.caption: Syndrome-extraction round cycle time broken down by operation (readout, transport, transfer, and gates) across surface-code, systolic planar, LR-planar, and LR-triangular 3D architectures, showing total time halved in 3D relative to the planar baseline.
items.abstract: High-rate quantum low-density parity-check (qLDPC) codes can substantially reduce qubit overhead relative to surface codes, but their advantage depends on efficiently realizing nonlocal syndrome extraction. We study the \([[144,12,12]]\) bivariate bicycle code on a neutral-atom architecture with native three-dimensional (3D) geometry, comparing planar and 3D embeddings while holding the code fixed. We characterize spatial efficiency using the logical-qubit density, defined as the number of encoded logical qubits per unit spatial footprint. Because the optical controller's field of view limits the transverse extent of an array, this metric estimates the number of logical qubits that can be accommodated within a fixed optical field of view. The 3D embedding achieves approximately \(4×\) greater areal logical-qubit density than the planar layout and \(42×\) greater than a surface-code baseline. It also reduces the bivariate bicycle syndrome-extraction time by roughly \(2×\) compared to a planar baseline, with fewer movement operations and substantially shorter atom-transport distance. Native 3D geometry can improve both the packing density and executable realization of nonlocal qLDPC codes, making practical performance depend jointly on code structure, optical geometry, transport scheduling, and hardware-level noise. This motivates further development of control techniques in 3D.

items.title: TETRIS-Q: Tiling-based Effective Transient-fault Reduction on Interleaved Superconducting Qubits
items.authors: Marzio Vallero, Gioele Casagranda, Flavio Vella, Paolo Rech
items.matched: High-threshold and low-overhead fault-tolerant quantum memory
items.result: Combining substrate phonon barrier tiling with QEC interleaving reduces peak logical error rate by over 99.8% and shortens transient duration by 80% under simulated radiation strikes. Sparser multi-qubit tiling cuts barrier fabrication perimeter cost by up to 87% with minimal performance loss.
items.question: Can substrate-level phonon barrier tiling and quantum error correction code interleaving mitigate radiation-induced spatially correlated faults in superconducting quantum chips without execution overhead?
items.limits: Numerical simulation only (51 million circuit simulations) using rotated surface codes under a parametrizable barrier permeability model (b_p).
items.tools: TETRIS-Q planar-mesh tiling algorithm · rotated surface code simulation · substrate-level phonon barrier model · QEC code interleaving
items.caption: Heatmap of average logical error rate for a distance-7 rotated surface code across tile sizes (1 to 16 qubits) and numbers of interleaved codes (1 to 9) at barrier permeability b_p = 0.1.
items.abstract: The struggle of the hour in quantum computing research is achieving effective suppression of the error mechanisms induced by the interaction of external radiation with superconducting quantum devices. Despite the rapid advancements in quantum error correction (QEC) of recent years, radiation-induced faults are yet to be fully addressed. These events are known to be the cause of simultaneous correlated defects in qubits that lie onto a single substrate, ultimately jeopardising QEC code effectiveness. In this paper, we propose to selectively combine substrate-level phonon barriers and QEC interleaving via a planar-mesh tiling algorithm, TETRIS-Q, reaching efficient and effective suppression of radiation events. Our cross-layer solution comes at no extra cost in terms of QEC code execution or decoding time. We model and simulate radiation-induced transient faults over a plethora of barrier and QEC interleaving configurations. Through more than 51 million quantum circuit simulations, we show peak logical error reductions of more than 99.8 %, together with an 80% reduction of the observable transient duration with permeable barriers. We find that sparser tiling can reach comparable performance to single qubit tiling, prompting cost reductions of upwards of 87 % in barrier tracing. By leveraging independent QEC code interleaving, we measure up to one order of magnitude average logical error rate reductions without the use of permeable barriers, and up to three orders of magnitude with the joint usage of barriers.

Sparser multi-qubit tiling cuts barrier fabrication perimeter cost by up to <math xmlns="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML"><mrow><mn>87</mn><mi>%</mi></mrow></math> with minimal performance loss.

items.title: Compiling the 2D Fermi-Hubbard ground-state energy estimation algorithm for active volume quantum architectures
items.authors: Harriet Apel, Athena Caesura, Carys Harvey, Sam Heavey, Angus Kan, Jessica Lemieux, Ryan Levy, Sam Pallister, Joseph Peetz, William Pol, Sukin Sim, William A. Simon, Mark Steudtner, Gideon Uchehara
items.matched: High-threshold and low-overhead fault-tolerant quantum memory
items.result: Active-volume-aware compilation cuts the active volume of 2D Fermi-Hubbard ground-state energy estimation by up to 3.9× across L×L square lattices with L=4 to 20. Also cuts Toffoli count by ∼2× at L=20.
items.question: How much can the execution cost and runtime of quantum phase estimation for 2D Fermi-Hubbard ground-state energy be reduced by compiling directly for active-volume architectures instead of non-Clifford proxies?
items.prior: Baseline compilation optimized for non-Clifford cost, as analyzed by Campbell (2022) and Kan et al. (2024).
items.limits: Evaluated for t=1, u=8 with periodic boundary conditions and extensive energy error budget 0.0051t L_x L_y.
items.tools: active-volume-aware compilation · second-order Suzuki-Trotter evolution · sine-window quantum phase estimation · batched Hamming weight phasing · oriented ZX calculus
items.caption: Active volume and conventional computational spacetime volume plotted against logical qubit count across square lattice sizes L=4 to 20, comparing baseline against improved compilation.
items.abstract: As quantum computing enters the early fault-tolerant era, circuit compilation choices will increasingly depend on details of the underlying architecture rather than solely optimizing for generic proxies such as non-Clifford count. We present an active-volume-aware compilation of the ground-state energy estimation algorithm for the two-dimensional Fermi-Hubbard model using quantum phase estimation and Trotterized time evolution. The proposed compilation reduces the active volume across L×L square lattices with L=4 to 20, achieving up to a 3.9× reduction over prior work optimized for non-Clifford cost. As a by-product of these compilation improvements, the resulting circuits also achieve state-of-the-art Toffoli counts, with a ~2× reduction for the L=20 case. Lastly, the active volume architecture and recent execution scheduling advances provide a means of translating these reduction trends into runtime. This demonstrates the increasing importance of architecture-aware compilation for practical early fault-tolerant quantum computing.

items.title: DPRQ: A Dynamic Programming-based Qubit Routing Algorithm for Collective Communication in Distributed Quantum Computing
items.authors: Dhaval Vaidya (North Carolina State University, Raleigh, NC, USA), Ruozhou Yu (North Carolina State University, Raleigh, NC, USA)
items.matched: Fault-tolerant quantum computation by anyons
items.result: Dynamic programming qubit routing reduces inter-node EPR pair consumption by an average of 24.40% and up to 85.06% across 80 circuit configurations.
items.question: How to minimize inter-node communication across collective communication blocks in distributed quantum circuits by accounting for global inter-block dependencies?
items.prior: QuComm compiler, which uses greedy block-level routing.
items.limits: Evaluated on 4 benchmark circuits (QAOA, RCA, BV, VQE) up to 200 qubits in simulation across 3 network topologies (mesh-grid, ring, fully-connected).
items.tools: dynamic programming · collective quantum communication · TP-Comm protocol · communication fusion · shortest-path early execution
items.caption: EPR cost plotted against total circuit qubits (50 to 200) for DPRQ versus QuComm across four benchmark circuits. DPRQ maintains lower communication cost as network size increases.
items.abstract: Distributed quantum computing (DQC) offers a promising approach to scale quantum computing by overcoming the resource limitations of a single quantum processor. However, inter-node communication remains a major bottleneck of DQC due to inefficient and error-prone entanglement distribution. Optimizing inter-node communication can not only reduce the amount of entanglement resource needed to execute a quantum circuit but also improve execution speed and accuracy of the results. This paper proposes DPRQ, a qubit routing algorithm for minimizing inter-node communication in distributed quantum circuits divided into collective communication blocks. Unlike current approaches that utilize greedy block-level qubit routing strategies, DPRQ employs a dynamic programming-based technique focused on global circuit-level optimization, while capturing inter-block dependencies. We evaluated DPRQ on four sets of quantum circuits and a variety of DQC configurations. The results demonstrate that DPRQ's innovative routing strategy achieves an average of 24.40% reduction with a maximum of 85.06% reduction in inter-node communication, when compared to the state-of-the-art collective communication-based DQC compiler QuComm.

items.title: Thermal lifetime of the centralized repetition code: From quantum annealing to social dynamics
items.authors: Ari Mizel, Van Molino
items.matched: High-threshold and low-overhead fault-tolerant quantum memory
items.result: Centralized repetition code storage lifetime scales exponentially with qubit count n at any finite temperature T < ∞, avoiding the thermal instability of a 1D Ising chain despite having only 1 Ising bond per qubit.
items.question: Does a star-graph centralized repetition code behave thermodynamically like an unstable 1D Ising chain or a stable complete-graph repetition code under thermal noise?
items.limits: Local bit-flip error model only (does not suppress phase errors). Assumes Born-Markov bath coupling and odd physical qubit number n.
items.tools: Lindblad master equation · spectral analysis · variational eigenvalue bounds · Gershgorin circle theorem
items.caption: Upper bound on the transition rate eigenvalue λ₁ plotted against qubit number n at inverse temperature βJ = 0.8. The decay toward zero illustrates exponentially increasing stability with system size even when thermal energy k_B T exceeds coupling J.
items.abstract: There is an extensive body of research probing the potential of adiabatic quantum computation and quantum annealing to solve hard computational problems. This research endeavor is complicated by noise afflicting hardware during the computational process. An error-correcting approach called quantum annealing correction (QAC) was suggested to mitigate this noise. The QAC approach employs a centralized version of the repetition code in which the qubits are configured in a star-graph pattern with one special qubit playing the role of the hub. In this paper, we explore the thermal physics of the centralized repetition code, using a Lindblad equation framework to analyze its lifetime when coupled to a thermal bath. We show that its centralized configuration leads to thermal stability, enabling the robust storage of a logical bit of information, despite the fact that there is only 1 ferromagnetic Ising interaction per qubit like a 1-dimensional Ising chain.

items.title: Optimal inequalities for completely bounded polynomials and the limitations of quantum query algorithms
items.authors: Francisco Escudero Gutiérrez, Miquel Saucedo, Carlos Palazuelos
items.matched: quantum algorithms with provable speedup, query and gate complexity bounds
items.result: Proves optimal root-influence inequality |p|_cb≥∑_i √Inf_i[p]/t for degree-t block-multilinear polynomials, and tight top-level Fourier growth |widehatp_2t|_(ℓ₁) ≤(en/(2t-1))^((2t-1)/2) |p|_cb for degree-2t polynomials.
items.question: Can inequalities for completely bounded polynomials establish improved upper limits on the computational power and Fourier growth of quantum query algorithms?
items.prior: Root-influence bound was |p|_cb≥∑_i √Inf_i[p]/t² (Bansal, Sinha, and de Wolf 2022).
items.limits: Applies to quantum query algorithms whose acceptance probabilities or amplitudes map to completely bounded polynomials (e.g. block-multilinear architectures, parallel query models).
items.tools: completely bounded polynomial method · Fourier analysis on the Boolean cube · operator norm bounds on tensor forms · non-adaptive classical sampling
items.caption: Quantum circuit schematic with t sequential queries applied to disjoint input blocks x₁, …, x_t, interleaved with unitary operations.
items.abstract: We consider the problem of establishing limitations on the power of quantum query algorithms via the completely bounded polynomial method. In particular, we prove several optimal functional inequalities involving different notions of completely bounded polynomials. These inequalities lead to limiting theorems for the power of quantum query algorithms that improve on prior works. 1. An optimal root-influence bound for block-multilinear polynomials. Prior work showed that block-multilinear polynomials p of degree t satisfy a root-influence bound, |p|_cb≥∑_i √Inf_i[p]/t², which is stronger than the bound appearing in the Aaronson-Ambainis conjecture. We find the optimal constant in that inequality: |p|_cb≥∑_i √Inf_i[p]/t. Since the amplitudes of quantum algorithms that query disjoint blocks of inputs-such as t-fold forrelation- are block-multilinear polynomials with |p|_cb≤1, our inequality shows that they satisfy t≥∑_i√Inf_i[p]. We prove that this inequality yields both a more efficient classical simulation than prior results based on the Aaronson-Ambainis argument, and a qualitative improvement: all classical queries are nonadaptive. 2. Optimal Fourier growth of the highest level of quantum query algorithms. We show that for every polynomial p defined on -1,1ⁿ of degree 2t, the Fourier Growth at the level 2t, namely |widehatp_2t|_(ℓ₁), satisfies |widehatp_2t|_(ℓ₁)≤(en/(2t-1))^((2t-1)/2)|p|_cb. This is optimal up to the factor e, as witnessed by 2t-fold forrelation. As quantum query algorithms that make t queries (to the whole input) satisfy |p|_cb≤1, this yields a Fourier growth bound for these algorithms, partially resolving a question by Girish (STOC, 2026).

items.title: DPRQ: A Dynamic Programming-based Qubit Routing Algorithm for Collective Communication in Distributed Quantum Computing
items.authors: Dhaval Vaidya (North Carolina State University, Raleigh, NC, USA), Ruozhou Yu (North Carolina State University, Raleigh, NC, USA)
items.matched: Toward the first quantum simulation with quantum speedup
items.result: Dynamic programming qubit routing reduces inter-node EPR pair consumption by an average of 24.40% and up to 85.06% across 80 circuit configurations.
items.question: How to minimize inter-node communication across collective communication blocks in distributed quantum circuits by accounting for global inter-block dependencies?
items.prior: QuComm compiler, which uses greedy block-level routing.
items.limits: Evaluated on 4 benchmark circuits (QAOA, RCA, BV, VQE) up to 200 qubits in simulation across 3 network topologies (mesh-grid, ring, fully-connected).
items.tools: dynamic programming · collective quantum communication · TP-Comm protocol · communication fusion · shortest-path early execution

items.abstract: Distributed quantum computing (DQC) offers a promising approach to scale quantum computing by overcoming the resource limitations of a single quantum processor. However, inter-node communication remains a major bottleneck of DQC due to inefficient and error-prone entanglement distribution. Optimizing inter-node communication can not only reduce the amount of entanglement resource needed to execute a quantum circuit but also improve execution speed and accuracy of the results. This paper proposes DPRQ, a qubit routing algorithm for minimizing inter-node communication in distributed quantum circuits divided into collective communication blocks. Unlike current approaches that utilize greedy block-level qubit routing strategies, DPRQ employs a dynamic programming-based technique focused on global circuit-level optimization, while capturing inter-block dependencies. We evaluated DPRQ on four sets of quantum circuits and a variety of DQC configurations. The results demonstrate that DPRQ's innovative routing strategy achieves an average of 24.40% reduction with a maximum of 85.06% reduction in inter-node communication, when compared to the state-of-the-art collective communication-based DQC compiler QuComm.

items.title: State-Based Quantum Operations: Chameleon Gates
items.authors: S. Alipour, A. T. Rezakhani
items.matched: Toward the first quantum simulation with quantum speedup
items.result: Introduced chameleon gates C_ρ parametrized by a quantum state knob ρ, constructible via a controlled-swap and partial trace to implement state-based quantum computation and simulate nonlinear Hamiltonians.
items.question: How can quantum controlled-gates be generalized to adapt their transformations dynamically based on arbitrary input quantum states without prior knowledge of those states?
items.limits: Requires ancilla control qubit initialized with small parameter |δ| ≪1; valid up to O(δ²) error; requires post-selection on the |+⟩ measurement outcome.
items.tools: Controlled-swap (Fredkin) gate · Partial trace · Post-selection · Trotter-Suzuki expansion
items.caption: Circuit schematic for the chameleon gate C_ρ and its implementation using an ancilla in state ψ_δ, a state knob ρ, target state σ, controlled-swap, and partial tracing over the first target.
items.abstract: We introduce chameleon gates as a natural generalization of conventional quantum controlled-gates. Chameleon gates are state-based quantum controlled-operations that retain standard elements such as control and target systems, while introducing a new feature: the quantum knob. This knob is a quantum signal (state) that determines the operation performed by the gate. Consequently, the action and form of a chameleon gate depend dynamically on the quantum knob, allowing the gate to adapt its operation and implement transformations that are not necessarily unitary. This shapeshifting property is in stark contrast to conventional quantum controlled-gates, whose actions are fixed and cannot be modified. We also propose how chameleon gates can be realized using conventional quantum gates available in current quantum technologies. We then employ chameleon gates as a useful building block within the recently proposed state-based quantum computation (SBQC) framework. Using this approach, we demonstrate the simulation of state-dependent (nonlinear) quantum evolutions.

items.title: Lindblad Multiproduct Formulas
items.authors: Niall F. Robertson, Andrea D'Urbano, Anton Dekusar, Max Rossmannek, Eric D. Switzer, James R. Garrison, Nicolas Lorente, Igor Pasichnyk, Paolo D'Alberto, Muhammad Osama, Zachary Streeter, Yasuko Eckert, Constantinos Evangelinos, Sergiy Zhuk
items.matched: Theory of Trotter Error with Commutator Scaling
items.result: Lindblad Multiproduct Formulas (L-MPF) combine classically computed linear coefficients with noisy quantum expectation values to outperform low-bond-dimension classical tensor network simulations and unmitigated quantum results on 65 qubits, achieving classical GPU speedups up to 5.6×.
items.question: Can high-dimensional tensor network contractions be integrated directly into a quantum error mitigation workflow to estimate noiseless expectation values with rigorous error bars?
items.limits: Demonstrated on a 2D discrete time crystal model on a 3×3 heavy-hexagonal lattice up to 10 Floquet cycles; non-ergodic amplification settings require PEA and higher sample counts to prevent large error bars.
items.tools: Lindblad Multiproduct Formulas (L-MPF) · Loop-corrected belief propagation · 2D tensor networks · Ergodic amplification / Probabilistic error amplification · ibm_basquecountry quantum processor (65 qubits)
items.caption: Expectation value vs. Floquet cycle number, comparing purely classical low-bond simulations, unmitigated hardware measurements, and L-MPF error-mitigated results against high-bond-dimension classical ground truth.
items.abstract: We introduce Lindblad Multiproduct Formulas: a quantum error mitigation technique that uses two-dimensional tensor networks contracted with loop-corrected belief propagation. The quantities required to implement the error mitigation scheme that are evaluated with tensor networks can be less computationally expensive to calculate than the expectation values themselves, thus allowing for the possibility of applying our method to certain systems for which tensor network methods may struggle to calculate the observable quantities of interest. The workflow incorporates Clifford rescaling techniques and outputs an estimated error bar. We apply our method to a model of two-dimensional discrete time crystals studied previously and implement it on 65 qubits arranged in a 3 ×3 heavy-hexagonal topology on the quantum computer ibm_basquecountry. We show that a GPU implementation of the classical part of our workflow achieves a speedup of up to 5.6×.

items.title: Thermal lifetime of the centralized repetition code: From quantum annealing to social dynamics
items.authors: Ari Mizel, Van Molino
items.matched: Evidence for the utility of quantum computing before fault tolerance
items.result: Centralized repetition code storage lifetime scales exponentially with qubit count n at any finite temperature T < ∞, avoiding the thermal instability of a 1D Ising chain despite having only 1 Ising bond per qubit.
items.question: Does a star-graph centralized repetition code behave thermodynamically like an unstable 1D Ising chain or a stable complete-graph repetition code under thermal noise?
items.limits: Local bit-flip error model only (does not suppress phase errors). Assumes Born-Markov bath coupling and odd physical qubit number n.
items.tools: Lindblad master equation · spectral analysis · variational eigenvalue bounds · Gershgorin circle theorem
items.caption: Upper bound on the transition rate eigenvalue λ₁ plotted against qubit number n at inverse temperature βJ = 0.8. The decay toward zero illustrates exponentially increasing stability with system size even when thermal energy k_B T exceeds coupling J.
items.abstract: There is an extensive body of research probing the potential of adiabatic quantum computation and quantum annealing to solve hard computational problems. This research endeavor is complicated by noise afflicting hardware during the computational process. An error-correcting approach called quantum annealing correction (QAC) was suggested to mitigate this noise. The QAC approach employs a centralized version of the repetition code in which the qubits are configured in a star-graph pattern with one special qubit playing the role of the hub. In this paper, we explore the thermal physics of the centralized repetition code, using a Lindblad equation framework to analyze its lifetime when coupled to a thermal bath. We show that its centralized configuration leads to thermal stability, enabling the robust storage of a logical bit of information, despite the fact that there is only 1 ferromagnetic Ising interaction per qubit like a 1-dimensional Ising chain.

items.title: Toward Resilient Many-Body Formulations under Incomplete Correlation Models: A Dual-Space Variational Formulation
items.authors: Vibin Abraham, Bhumika Jayee, Bo Peng, Nicholas P. Bauman, Karol Kowalski
items.matched: Probing many-body dynamics on a 51-atom quantum simulator
items.result: Dual-space NOCI variationally couples a parent reference manifold to generated correlated quantum states, bounding the Rayleigh–Ritz energy at or below both reference-only NOCI and correlated-only NOQE while reducing sensitivity to amplitude and matrix-element noise.
items.question: How can quantum subspace eigensolvers augment a classical nonorthogonal configuration interaction reference without degrading variational flexibility when correlated quantum states are incomplete or noisy?
items.limits: Simulated benchmarks on small molecules (H₂, H₄, H₆, N₂, cyclobutadiene); noisy matrix elements degrade the strict variational bound without metric regularization.
items.tools: Dual-space nonorthogonal configuration interaction (DS-NOCI) · Nonorthogonal quantum eigensolver (NOQE) · Rayleigh–Ritz variational diagonalization · Schur metric conditioning
items.caption: Energy error relative to FCI for linear H₄ plotted against amplitude noise variance σ. DS-NOCI retains stable accuracy while correlated-only NOQE error degrades rapidly.
items.abstract: Quantum simulations of correlated many-body systems will inevitably operate with imperfect information: the prepared states may arise from incomplete or approximate ansatze, while their measured Hamiltonian and overlap matrix elements are additionally affected by hardware and statistical noise. Robust quantum algorithms will be those that can improve upon reliable lower-level descriptions in spite of these imperfections. We introduce a dual-space nonorthogonal configuration-interaction (DS-NOCI) framework built around this principle. Rather than replacing a classically accessible NOCI reference manifold with correlated quantum states, DS-NOCI retains both spaces and couples them variationally. The reference sector provides a stable many-body backbone, while the quantum states contribute whatever additional correlation directions they contain. With exact matrix elements, the enlarged dual space gives a ground-state energy no higher than either the reference-only NOCI or correlated-only quantum-NOCI spaces, ensuring that an incomplete correlation model cannot degrade the underlying variational description. The additional reference--correlated matrix elements require only one correlated state preparation and are therefore less demanding than the correlated--correlated block already required by quantum variant of NOCI. Molecular benchmarks further show enhanced resilience to imperfect amplitudes and noisy matrix elements. DS-NOCI thus provides a general strategy for building quantum many-body formulations that remain useful when both correlation models and quantum computations are necessarily incomplete and noisy.

items.title: Compiling the 2D Fermi-Hubbard ground-state energy estimation algorithm for active volume quantum architectures
items.authors: Harriet Apel, Athena Caesura, Carys Harvey, Sam Heavey, Angus Kan, Jessica Lemieux, Ryan Levy, Sam Pallister, Joseph Peetz, William Pol, Sukin Sim, William A. Simon, Mark Steudtner, Gideon Uchehara
items.matched: Evidence for the utility of quantum computing before fault tolerance
items.result: Active-volume-aware compilation cuts the active volume of 2D Fermi-Hubbard ground-state energy estimation by up to 3.9× across L×L square lattices with L=4 to 20. Also cuts Toffoli count by ∼2× at L=20.
items.question: How much can the execution cost and runtime of quantum phase estimation for 2D Fermi-Hubbard ground-state energy be reduced by compiling directly for active-volume architectures instead of non-Clifford proxies?
items.prior: Baseline compilation optimized for non-Clifford cost, as analyzed by Campbell (2022) and Kan et al. (2024).
items.limits: Evaluated for t=1, u=8 with periodic boundary conditions and extensive energy error budget 0.0051t L_x L_y.
items.tools: active-volume-aware compilation · second-order Suzuki-Trotter evolution · sine-window quantum phase estimation · batched Hamming weight phasing · oriented ZX calculus
items.caption: Active volume and conventional computational spacetime volume plotted against logical qubit count across square lattice sizes L=4 to 20, comparing baseline against improved compilation.
items.abstract: As quantum computing enters the early fault-tolerant era, circuit compilation choices will increasingly depend on details of the underlying architecture rather than solely optimizing for generic proxies such as non-Clifford count. We present an active-volume-aware compilation of the ground-state energy estimation algorithm for the two-dimensional Fermi-Hubbard model using quantum phase estimation and Trotterized time evolution. The proposed compilation reduces the active volume across L×L square lattices with L=4 to 20, achieving up to a 3.9× reduction over prior work optimized for non-Clifford cost. As a by-product of these compilation improvements, the resulting circuits also achieve state-of-the-art Toffoli counts, with a ~2× reduction for the L=20 case. Lastly, the active volume architecture and recent execution scheduling advances provide a means of translating these reduction trends into runtime. This demonstrates the increasing importance of architecture-aware compilation for practical early fault-tolerant quantum computing.

items.question: Can an ancilla qubit be used to engineer tunable system-reservoir coupling and reservoir temperature to achieve anti-thermalization and non-equilibrium steady states?
items.limits: Natural ¹³C abundance Type IIa diamond at room temperature; NV-nuclear spin correlations assumed weak and ignored across cycle boundaries.
items.tools: single NV center electron spin (ancilla) · proximal ¹³C nuclear spin (target system) · shaped Gaussian microwave pulses · 532 nm optical polarization and readout
items.caption: Excited-state population dynamics and energetics of the nuclear spin system qubit undergoing collisions under engineered interaction channels.
items.abstract: Engineering the properties of a reservoir and its coupling to a quantum system is a powerful tool for simulating quantum thermodynamic processes and for generating otherwise inaccessible steady states. Yet tailoring both the reservoir and its coupling within a single platform remains challenging. Here we introduce a platform, in which an ancilla qubit mediates the coupling of a target system to a reservoir, providing independent control over the interaction form, coupling strength, and effective reservoir temperature. Our implementation uses the electron spin of a single nitrogen-vacancy center in diamond as the ancilla and a proximal ¹³C nuclear spin as the target. By alternating engineered unitary interactions with dissipative ancilla resets, we realize dynamics naturally described by a collision model, enabling straight-forward tracking of the work, heat, coherence, and entropy generated at every collision. We experimentally demonstrate conventional thermalization and also realize anti-thermalization: the stabilization of the target system in a temperature opposite to that of its reservoir. Finally, harnessing this steady-state engineering, we utilize the nuclear spin as a quantum battery, achieving a steady-state ergotropy exceeding 70% of the theoretical maximum.

items.title: TETRIS-Q: Tiling-based Effective Transient-fault Reduction on Interleaved Superconducting Qubits
items.authors: Marzio Vallero, Gioele Casagranda, Flavio Vella, Paolo Rech
items.matched: analog quantum simulation of lattice models on cold atoms or superconducting ar…
items.result: Combining substrate phonon barrier tiling with QEC interleaving reduces peak logical error rate by over 99.8% and shortens transient duration by 80% under simulated radiation strikes. Sparser multi-qubit tiling cuts barrier fabrication perimeter cost by up to 87% with minimal performance loss.
items.question: Can substrate-level phonon barrier tiling and quantum error correction code interleaving mitigate radiation-induced spatially correlated faults in superconducting quantum chips without execution overhead?
items.limits: Numerical simulation only (51 million circuit simulations) using rotated surface codes under a parametrizable barrier permeability model (b_p).
items.tools: TETRIS-Q planar-mesh tiling algorithm · rotated surface code simulation · substrate-level phonon barrier model · QEC code interleaving

items.abstract: The struggle of the hour in quantum computing research is achieving effective suppression of the error mechanisms induced by the interaction of external radiation with superconducting quantum devices. Despite the rapid advancements in quantum error correction (QEC) of recent years, radiation-induced faults are yet to be fully addressed. These events are known to be the cause of simultaneous correlated defects in qubits that lie onto a single substrate, ultimately jeopardising QEC code effectiveness. In this paper, we propose to selectively combine substrate-level phonon barriers and QEC interleaving via a planar-mesh tiling algorithm, TETRIS-Q, reaching efficient and effective suppression of radiation events. Our cross-layer solution comes at no extra cost in terms of QEC code execution or decoding time. We model and simulate radiation-induced transient faults over a plethora of barrier and QEC interleaving configurations. Through more than 51 million quantum circuit simulations, we show peak logical error reductions of more than 99.8 %, together with an 80% reduction of the observable transient duration with permeable barriers. We find that sparser tiling can reach comparable performance to single qubit tiling, prompting cost reductions of upwards of 87 % in barrier tracing. By leveraging independent QEC code interleaving, we measure up to one order of magnitude average logical error rate reductions without the use of permeable barriers, and up to three orders of magnitude with the joint usage of barriers.

items.title: A double-resonator coupler for high-fidelity two-qubit gates between superconducting qubits
items.authors: Seunghyeon Jin, Seungha Woo, Shinyoung Hwang, June-Young M. Lee, Jeongmin Shim, Sunje Kim, Dae Seok Han, Jaeho Shin, Eunjong Kim

items.question: How to completely suppress residual ZZ interactions across flexible qubit-qubit frequency detunings without requiring multi-junction couplers or direct capacitive layout constraints?
items.prior: Single-transmon couplers require qubit detuning within straddling regime and direct qubit capacitance balancing; double-transmon and fluxonium couplers require multiple Josephson junctions.
items.limits: Numerical simulation only. Evaluated using a 20-state basis with perturbative leakage corrections; dephasing assumes 1/f flux-noise amplitude A_(φ_ex)=2π×10⁻⁶.
items.tools: circuit quantization · instantaneous dressed-state time evolution · CMA-ES pulse optimization · Slepian-like flux pulse · quasi-static noise model
items.caption: Circuit and layout of transmon qubits coupled via the double-resonator coupler (a, b), mode coupling and flux-dependent single-excitation spectra (c, d), differential-mode potential wells (e), and mechanism of virtual-exchange path cancellation (f).
items.abstract: Tunable couplers have enabled two-qubit gate fidelities in superconducting quantum processors to approach 99.9%, yet simultaneously suppressing residual interactions and maintaining flexible qubit-frequency allocation remain central challenges for scaling. Here, we propose a double-resonator coupler (DRC) consisting of two resonators interconnected by a single Josephson junction and a capacitor. The hybridized resonator modes provide two mediated exchange paths whose interference controls the qubit-qubit interaction. The DRC enables complete cancellation of residual ZZ interaction for qubit-qubit detunings well outside the straddling regime, even in the absence of direct qubit-qubit coupling, thereby relaxing constraints on frequency allocation and qubit placement. Away from the idle point, the same circuit provides a strong ZZ interaction of approximately 70 MHz, enabling a 20 ns controlled-Z gate with simulated coherent infidelity below 10⁻⁵. These results establish the DRC as a flexible single-junction coupler architecture for high-fidelity superconducting quantum processors.

items.authors: Sloän Kouamé, Elric Frigerio, Giacomo Rebora, Suvankar Purkait, Yong Jin, Ulf Gennser, Antonella Cavanna, Jean-Marc Berroir, Emmanuel Baudin, Pascal Degiovanni, Franccois D. Parmentier, Gwendal Fève, Gerbold C. Ménard
