items.result: Electrostatic splitting of an edge magnetoplasmon resonator yields RF transmission signatures for integer (ν=1, 2) and fractional (ν=4/3, 2/3) quantum Hall states, with cavity perimeter dropping to 17.5μm past QPC pinch-off.
items.question: How does polarizing an embedded quantum point contact influence edge magnetoplasmon modes and cavity geometry in a quantum Hall resonator?
items.limits: Aharonov-Bohm interference oscillations not observed due to small expected period; ν=2/3 center field was beyond maximum accessible magnetic field (B > 8T).
items.tools: AlGaAs/GaAs 2DEG · RF lock-in reflectometry and transmission · electrostatic quantum point contacts · cryogenic dilution refrigerator (30 mK)
items.caption: Averaged RF transmission amplitude ⟨|Z|²⟩ plotted against QPC gate voltage V_QPC and perpendicular magnetic field B. Peaks trace resonance trajectories for integer ν=1, 2 and fractional ν=4/3, 2/3 Hall plateaus across the QPC pinch-off transition.
items.abstract: Edge-magnetoplasmon resonators have been proposed as a powerful tool to detect anyons by introducing a quantum point contact into an isolated quantum Hall system probed via radiofrequency radiation. In this paper, we study the effect of a quantum point contact embedded within an edge-magnetoplasmon resonator and how its polarization influences the propagating magnetoplasmonic mode. Combining dc and rf measurements, we unambiguously evidence the signature of both integer (ν= 1 and 2) and fractional quantum Hall states (ν= 4/3 and 2/3) within the radiofrequency transmission signal. Using electrostatic gating, we determine the physical parameters characterizing the electrostatic edge of an AlGaAs/GaAs based two-dimensional electron gas. We extract the dependence of the cavity perimeter with the gate voltage of the quantum point contact and fully characterize the path followed by edge magnetoplasmons in this system. Finally, we provide a geometric model in good agreement with experimental results.

items.title: Single- and Two-Qubit Gates Driven by an Integrated Photonic Laser
items.authors: Chris Caron, Zhenyu Wei, Andrei Isichenko, David Heim, Meiting Song, Nick Montifiore, Kaikai Liu, Josiah Dill, Daniel J. Blumenthal, Robert J. Niffenegger
items.matched: Quantum information with Rydberg atoms
items.result: Single-qubit average Clifford fidelity reaches 99.61% ±0.03% and two-qubit Mølmer-Sørensen Bell-state fidelity reaches 92.35% ±1.50% using a chip-scale Brillouin laser locked to an integrated coil resonator.
items.question: Can an integrated visible-wavelength narrow-linewidth photonic laser meet the phase-noise and coherence requirements to drive coherent single- and two-qubit gates on trapped-ion optical qubits?
items.limits: Coherence limited by residual laser drift and AC mains magnetic-field fluctuations; separate chips connected via fibers/free-space optics rather than full monolithic integration.
items.tools: integrated Si₃N₄ Brillouin laser · integrated coil resonator reference · surface electrode trap with ⁸⁸Sr⁺ ions · active fiber noise cancellation · adaptive Bayesian fluorescence detection
items.caption: Resolved sideband cooling, Rabi oscillations, and randomized benchmarking curve showing sequence survival fidelity as a function of Clifford gate depth d.
items.abstract: Trapped ions are a leading technology for quantum computing, but their reliance on bespoke tabletop laser and optical systems remains a major obstacle to scaling and robustness. Integrated silicon nitride lasers, compatible with future monolithic integration with surface electrode ion traps, have recently demonstrated frequency-selective qubit state preparation and measurement as well as interrogation of an optical clock transition. However, coherent qubit gates driven by integrated laser sources have not yet been demonstrated because coherent quantum logic imposes substantially more stringent performance requirements on the laser. Here, we use a visible-wavelength integrated Brillouin laser stabilized to an integrated coil resonator to drive coherent single- and two-qubit gates with ⁸⁸Sr⁺ optical qubits. We measure an average single-qubit fidelity of 99.61% ± 0.03% per Clifford gate with randomized benchmarking and use a two-qubit Mølmer-Sørensen interaction to generate an entangled Bell state with a fidelity of 92.35% ± 1.50%. The qubit exhibits a bare Ramsey coherence time of 660 ± 9 μs, extended to 1.750 ± 0.033 ms by spin echo. These results demonstrate that integrated visible-wavelength narrow-linewidth photonic lasers can meet the phase-noise requirements for coherent trapped ion quantum logic, providing a path for scalable optical systems integrated within trapped ion quantum processors.

items.title: Telecom-Integrated Photonic Memory Operating Near the Mechanical Ground State
items.authors: Jindao Tang, Bo Jing, Liping Zeng, Peiqin Chen, Hengrui Liang, Yifei Zhang, Xinyao Xu, Qizhi Cai, Xueying Zhang, Qiang Zhou, You Wang, Haizhi Song, Guangcan Guo, Guangwei Deng
items.matched: cavity QED, atom-photon interfaces and quantum networks
items.result: On-chip absorptive optomechanical memory stores telecom-band photons with on-demand retrieval at mechanical phonon occupancy of 0.32.
items.question: Can an on-chip, telecom-compatible optomechanical memory operate near its mechanical ground state with on-demand retrieval for few-photon inputs?
items.limits: Operated in a dilution refrigerator at 20 mK under tailored control field pulses to suppress optical heating; demonstrated at few-photon input levels.
items.tools: Optomechanically induced transparency (OMIT) · Nanofabricated mechanical resonator · Dilution refrigerator at 20 mK · Pulsed control field engineering
items.abstract: Scalable quantum networks require quantum memories that are chip-integrated, telecom-band compatible, and capable of flexible retrieval. Nanofabricated mechanical resonators meet these criteria. They offer independent tunability of optical and mechanical modes, long-lived phonon states, and design flexibility beyond atomic systems, making them strong candidates for practical integrated quantum memory. Here, we demonstrate an on-chip, absorptive optomechanical memory for telecom-band photons, based on optomechanically induced transparency (OMIT) and operating near the mechanical ground state. The device stores telecom-band photons, demonstrating compatibility with external photon sources at the few-photon level, while enabling on-demand retrieval. By placing the device in a dilution refrigerator at 20 mK and tailoring the control field to suppress optical heating, we achieve a remarkably low phonon occupancy of just 0.32 during the storage process. Our results lay the groundwork for scalable, phonon-based quantum memory devices and open new avenues for integrating mechanical systems into practical quantum network architectures.

items.title: From Bits to Qubits: The Theory and Practice of Quantum Data Encoding
items.authors: Xiao-Ming Zhang, Arthur G. Rattew, Bujiao Wu, Georgios Styliaris, Xiaoming Sun, Bálint Koczor, Xiao Yuan
items.matched: photonic qubits, linear-optical computing and boson sampling
items.result: Surveys quantum data encoding methods across state preparation, unitary synthesis, QRAM, and block-encoding, synthesizing circuit size, depth, and fault-tolerant gate counts.
items.question: How can deterministic classical data be compiled into quantum representations under minimal circuit depth, gate counts, and non-Clifford resources?
items.limits: Restricted to deterministic, fully known classical data in the standard qubit circuit model with all-to-all or binary-tree connectivity; excludes sampled distributions and continuous variables.
items.tools: uniformly controlled rotations (UCR) · Schmidt decomposition · QRAM bucket-brigade architecture · linear combination of unitaries (LCU) · block-encoding
items.caption: Three core access models mapping classical vectors and matrices to quantum operations: quantum state preparation, QRAM, and block-encoding.
items.abstract: Encoding classical data into quantum systems is a foundational step in the execution of nearly all quantum algorithms, and a critical bottleneck in realizing practical quantum advantage. This review provides a comprehensive account of the concepts, algorithms, and practical considerations associated with quantum data encoding. We trace the development from its early conceptual foundations to recent advances, considering commonly used access models, such as quantum state preparation, unitary synthesis, QRAM and block encoding. We survey the circuit size, depth, space-time tradeoffs, as well as non-Clifford resources required for fault-tolerant implementation. We also discuss the roles of different access models in quantum algorithms. Special attention is given to structured data, such as sparse data, Boolean functions and data represented by tensor networks. This review bridges theory and applications, serving both as a pedagogical guide for newcomers and as a reference for active researchers. We also highlight the pivotal role of quantum data encoding in quantum computing and provide insights into future directions that will enable quantum advantage.

items.question: How do interactions between different orders of exceptional points affect entanglement dynamics and generation speed in non-reciprocally coupled quantum systems?

items.abstract: The exploration of the effect of non-Hermitian (NH) in quantum systems is gaining renewed momentum as a result of the recent progress in experiments. It has been indicated that the ability to engineer the orders of exceptional points (EPs) can be fundamental to its applications in quantum control, such as accelerating entanglement generation; however, an initial survey of the interactions between different orders of EPs is still missing. In this work, we try to partially address this issue by employing a non-reciprocally coupled cavity system which can be experimentally realizable with a two-dimensional reconfigurable NH gauged laser array. With deliberate design, our systems display both second and third orders of EPs. The sign of a novel, purely quantum continuous entanglement phase transition is observed, which reveals how multi-EP interactions alter entanglement dynamics across different regimes while maintaining accelerated generation. Our findings reveil the genuinely quantum NH physics of higher-order EPs, which has opened up a new avenue for future investigations of the higher-order degeneracy application and the dynamic phase transitions of quantum systems.

items.abstract: We introduce Propaq, a performant and flexible Python package implementing Heisenberg propagation techniques for classically simulating quantum circuits. Propaq is compatible with major quantum software packages like Qiskit and Cirq, and matches or outperforms similar state-of-the-art packages for Heisenberg propagation. Beyond this, Propaq has multiple distinguishing features for simulation and research. These include Heisenberg propagation in any basis, hybrid Schrödinger-Heisenberg simulation, custom truncation and noisy simulation methods, and detailed logging information for analyzing simulation accuracy, runtime, and memory usage. We describe these features, how to use Propaq for research, and its backend implementation.

items.authors: Debsuvra Mukhopadhyay, Jayakrishnan M. P. Nair, Girish S. Agarwal
items.matched: Quantum information with Rydberg atoms
items.result: Cavity magnonics can be driven into non-Hermitian and quantum regimes via reservoir-mediated dissipative coupling, Floquet frequency modulation, and parametric squeezing transfer. Long-lived subradiant modes near anti-PT exceptional points lower the bistability threshold as |Ω_th|²∝(γ-Γ)³/K, scaling quantum Fisher information as F_Q∝ε⁻⁴.
items.question: How do engineered dissipative coupling, Floquet modulation, and parametric driving enable quantum state generation, nonreciprocal transport, and enhanced sensing in cavity magnonics?

items.abstract: Cavity magnonics is moving beyond the conventional paradigm of coherent spin--photon hybridization toward the controlled engineering of dissipative and coherent interactions, Floquet dynamics, and quantum fluctuations. This Perspective examines how these ingredients reshape collective dynamics and open new avenues for quantum state engineering, transport, and sensing. We discuss the role of dissipative coupling and anti-PT symmetry in enabling long-lived collective modes and enhanced spectral response, and highlight Floquet engineering as a means of engineering nonreciprocal transport and phase-controlled interactions. We then review recent progress in quantum magnonics, ranging from squeezed and entangled magnon states, including the squeezing of thermal magnons, to prospective schemes for preparing magnonic Schrödinger-cat states. We also discuss how parametric driving and active gain strongly modify hybrid susceptibilities and amplify magnon--photon response. These advances expand the scope of cavity magnonics beyond conventional polariton physics, establishing it as a versatile platform for sensing, transduction, spin transport, and hybrid quantum technologies.

items.title: Single-tone drive-enhanced CROT gate for bosonic quantum error correction
items.authors: Shushen Qin, Long D. H. My, Adrian Copetudo, Amon M. Kasper, Yvonne Y. Gao, Hui Khoon Ng
items.matched: Quantum information with Rydberg atoms
items.result: Amplifies cross-Kerr interaction between two microwave cavity modes via single-frequency transmon drive near intermediate-state divergences, achieving on-demand textsccrot gate for rotation-symmetric bosonic error correction without requiring multiple frequencies or frequency-tunable elements.
items.question: How can a direct, code-agnostic textsccrot gate between bosonic cavity modes be implemented in circuit QED without multi-tone driving or gigahertz frequency tuning?
items.prior: Prior direct implementations required >1 GHz frequency tunability or multi-tone drives scaling with logical state size.
items.limits: Numerical and analytical modeling. Assumes perfect cancellation of self-Kerr from auxiliary side transmons, neglecting higher-order mode distortions and unmodeled side-transmon Hilbert spaces.
items.tools: circuit QED · transmon-mediated cross-Kerr enhancement · fourth-order perturbation theory · side-transmon self-Kerr cancellation · teleportation-based bosonic error correction
items.caption: Effective self- and cross-Kerr nonlinearities plotted against drive detuning at fixed drive strength |Ω_d/δ_d|=1, showing resonant divergences that enhance cross-Kerr interaction while distinguishing two-cavity from single-cavity resonances.
items.abstract: Bosonic error correction provides a hardware-efficient route to protected qubits for accurate quantum information processing. A critical component for error correction of rotation-symmetric bosonic (RSB) codes, like the well-known cat codes, is the two-mode controlled-rotation (CROT) operation. The CROT gate is useful because of its code-agnostic generality and its error-propagation properties. While the CROT gate can in principle be composed from existing bosonic physical primitives, the desirable properties are typically lost when composed as a sequence of imperfect primitive operations. Past work has focused on direct implementations that rely on features of specific codes. Here, we present a direct route to CROT within the circuit-QED architecture that retains its code-agnostic and error-propagation characteristics. By driving a transmon simultaneously coupled to two microwave cavities, we controllably enhance the effective nonlinearities between the microwave cavities and thus engineer the necessary two-mode interaction underlying the CROT gate. Using only a single drive frequency, we can achieve an on-off ratio sufficient for gate implementation, while minimizing mode distortions. We provide simple analytical formulas that permit the identification of potential working regimes, further refined by exact numerics, and illustrate the efficacy of our CROT approach in an error-correction example involving different RSB codes within the same circuit. Our CROT gate adds to the arsenal of direct two-mode gates available for general bosonic information processing.

items.title: Matrix Holography on an Optical Lattice
items.authors: Robin Löwenberg, Julian Sonner
items.matched: photonic qubits, linear-optical computing and boson sampling
items.result: Constructs bosonic four-body matrix-quantum-mechanics potentials via Floquet-engineered oscillating two-body spin interactions with a constant number of unitaries per cycle. Control-frequency bandwidth scales as O(N³) with matrix size N, reaching non-perturbative couplings λ∼O(1) at driving frequencies ω∼O(MHz).
items.question: Can four-body potentials of bosonic matrix quantum mechanics be simulated on an analog optical-lattice platform without the deep circuits of digital implementations?
items.limits: Requires non-spin-conserving spin-spin interactions and large-spin ferromagnetic regime (m ∼j). Bosonic Hilbert space must be truncated.
items.tools: Holstein-Primakoff transformation · Floquet engineering · Magnus expansion · James' effective Hamiltonian method · optical lattice of atomic ensembles
items.caption: Ground-state energy convergence as a function of spin size j comparing the large-spin model against the truncated SU(2) ×SO(2) bosonic matrix model with λ=2 and cutoff Λ=6. Relative error is 0.5 % at j=3 and drops to 0.007 %.
items.abstract: We propose an analog quantum-simulation protocol based on a lattice of atomic ensembles and time-averaged Floquet dynamics to construct the four-body potentials that typically appear in bosonic BFSS-like matrix quantum mechanics. In contrast to gate-based digital implementations requiring deep circuits, our approach generates the target model through a fixed set of control stages per Floquet cycle, keeping the number of consecutive unitaries constant with respect to the matrix size N. The principal scaling cost in our construction is given by the frequency range required to control the growing lattice. We show that this cost grows at most as O(N³), giving a polynomial scaling route to large-N, attractive to experimental implementation. Additionally, we demonstrate that the coupling parameter can be tuned beyond O(1), enabling the simulation of strong-coupling physics necessary for holographic phases.

items.title: Transversal Fanout for Fault Tolerant Distributed Quantum Computing: Analysis and Application
items.authors: Seng W. Loke
items.matched: Surface codes: Towards practical large-scale quantum computation
items.result: Constructs transversal distributed logical fanout and global controlled-Z (GCZ) operations across encoded code blocks to minimize non-local communication and entanglement overhead.
items.question: How can logical fanout operations across remote nodes in distributed quantum computers be implemented fault-tolerantly with reduced non-local communication overhead?
items.limits: Theoretical and architectural analysis; illustrated specifically on Bivariate Bicycle code blocks.
items.tools: transversal logical operations · Bivariate Bicycle (BB) codes · distributed quantum circuit construction · resource-cost analysis
items.abstract: We study a resource-efficient approach for implementing logical fanout operations in fault-tolerant distributed quantum computing using transversal operations on quantum error-correcting code blocks. Logical fanout, comprising multiple controlled-NOT operations from a common control qubit to target qubits located at remote nodes, is an important primitive for distributed quantum computation but can require substantial non-local communication when implemented directly between encoded blocks. We exploit the structure of encoded blocks and the availability of transversal logical operations to construct distributed fanout circuits that reduce the required non-local operations while preserving the logical action of the fanout operation. The construction is developed for encoded quantum information and illustrated using Bivariate Bicycle (BB)-code blocks. We analyze the resulting physical gate, entanglement, circuit-depth, and ancilla requirements. The approach provides a systematic method for implementing large logical fanout operations across distributed error-corrected quantum processors. Also, we study a distributed implementation of the global gate GCZ involving logical qubits (encoded using BB-code blocks), exploiting the concurrency in transversal distributed fanouts.

items.title: First fault-tolerant quantum memory demonstration for a generalized superfast encoding
items.authors: James Brown, Kenny Heitritter
items.matched: High-threshold and low-overhead fault-tolerant quantum memory
items.result: Even-distance Generalized Superfast Encoding maintains constant stabilizer weights of 4 or 6, exhibiting a quantum memory pseudo-threshold crossing near physical depolarizing error rate p ≈4×10⁻³.
items.question: Can a fermion-to-qubit mapping achieve fault-tolerant quantum memory with threshold-like error suppression under circuit-level noise?
items.prior: Generalized Superfast Encoding was restricted to error detection or odd-distance constructions with weight-6 stabilizers (Brown et al. 2024), with no fault-tolerant quantum memory threshold observed.
items.limits: Circuit-level depolarizing noise simulations only; evaluated on two code instances ([[48,8,6]] and [[64,8,8]]); requires N > d.
items.tools: Generalized Superfast Encoding (GSE) · AlphaSyndrome circuit scheduling · Relay-BP message-passing decoder · Stim Monte Carlo simulation · Bare-ancilla syndrome extraction
items.caption: Logical error rate per round per logical qubit versus physical error rate p. The [[64,8,8]] code suppresses errors faster than the [[48,8,6]] code below their projected crossing point near p ≈4×10⁻³.
items.abstract: The Generalized Superfast Encoding (GSE) is a fermion-to-qubit mapping that has error-correcting/detecting properties. To this point, all demonstrations have been relegated to error-detection only, as no fault-tolerance under circuit-level noise has been observed. Here, we introduce an even-distance d constant stabilizer-weight GSE where each of N modes is assigned a d-qubit block arranged on a ring. The resulting stabilizer generators have constant weight 4 or 6 for any even distance d. Furthermore, the full stabilizer set of this construction can always be partitioned into four qubit-wise commuting groups, which enables compact syndrome-extraction scheduling. We simulate quantum memory experiments under circuit-level depolarizing noise for two instances of this code, [[48,8,6]] and [[64,8,8]] and the threshold is observed to be ≈4×10⁻³. This is, to our knowledge, the first fault-tolerant quantum-memory characterization of a fermion-mapping with threshold-like scaling.

items.title: Asymmetric quantum error correction efficiently tackles application-specific noise effects
items.authors: Abhishek Yadav, Peter K. Schuhmacher, Michael Epping
items.matched: High-threshold and low-overhead fault-tolerant quantum memory
items.result: Asymmetric (5,3) quantum parity code with 15 physical qubits matches the optimization performance of the symmetric (5,5) code requiring 25 qubits because QAOA objective degrades significantly more under bit flips than phase flips.
items.question: How do asymmetric bit-flip and phase-flip Pauli noise channels affect QAOA performance across different circuit decompositions, and can asymmetric quantum error correction exploit this asymmetry?
items.limits: Simulated on a 6-qubit flight-gate assignment problem; syndrome extraction circuit noise and gate-level QEC fault-tolerance overhead not directly modeled in the QEC evaluation.
items.tools: Quantum Approximate Optimization Algorithm (QAOA) · Quantum Parity Code (QPC) · Exact density-matrix simulation · Layer-level and gate-level Pauli noise models
items.caption: Residual cost deviation Δ plotted against physical error probability p under d=2 layer-level noise for uncoded QAOA and various quantum parity code configurations (n₁,n₂).
items.abstract: Noise is a major challenge for current quantum computers. It can be broadly categorized into bit-flip and phase-flip errors. These two types do not necessarily affect the executed algorithm, thus also the application, in the same way. We illustrate this general effect for the example of the quantum approximate optimization algorithm (QAOA) applied to a small instance of the flight-gate assignment (FGA) problem. We compare bit-flip and phase-flip Pauli noise under both layer-level and gate-level noise models, using two circuit decompositions of the same ideal QAOA unitary: a CNOT-based decomposition and a native-R_ZZ decomposition. In the simulations, bit-flip noise produces the larger degradation in the performance of the quantum optimization. The asymmetry is most visible in the layer-level and native-R_ZZ simulations. We explain this by how the errors affect mixing, final measurements, and how they propagate inside the circuit. We then exploit these insights to tackle noise particularly efficiently using asymmetric error-correcting codes. As an illustration, we use the quantum parity code (QPC), a generalization of the 9-qubit Shor code, and show that a smaller asymmetric code can achieve nearly the same improvement as a larger symmetric choice. This demonstrates that error-correction resources should be assigned not only according to physical error rates, but also according to how strongly each error channel affects the application. As a result, asymmetric quantum error correction proves useful even in cases where the noise model is symmetric. Finally, we discuss how information about the noise obtained through calibration can be exploited in our approach.

items.title: Computing 256-bit elliptic curve discrete logarithms in 26 days on a fault-tolerant trapped-ion quantum computer with 20,000 qubits
items.authors: Thomas Häner, Felix Tripier, Jacob Young, Michael Naehrig, Andrii Maksymov, Safwan Alam, Dmitri Maslov, Matthew Parrott, Yvette de Sereville, Jordan Sullivan, Mark Webster, Nicolas Delfosse, John Gamble, Martin Roetteler
items.matched: How to factor 2048 bit RSA integers in 8 hours using 20 million noisy qubits
items.result: Solving the ECDLP on secp256k1 requires 19,397 physical trapped-ion qubits and 25.7 days for a 63% success probability per attempt, executing 40·10⁶ Toffoli gates over 1457 logical qubits.
items.question: How many physical qubits and how much runtime does a fault-tolerant trapped-ion quantum computer need to compute 256-bit elliptic curve discrete logarithms under realistic noise, transport, and loss constraints?
items.prior: Prior trapped-ion estimates required 1.2 million to 9.4 million physical qubits; recent generic-architecture estimates needed 60·10⁶ Toffolis (Schrottenloher 2026).
items.limits: Assumes physical two-qubit gate error rate p = 10⁻⁴, single-qubit error rate 10⁻⁵, swap-loss with p_leak = p/10 and p_loss = p/1000. Success probability lower-bounded assuming all 69 memory blocks remain active throughout full runtime.
items.tools: Walking Cat architecture · quantum LDPC codes ([[102,22,9]] and [[66,4,10]]) · Eastinthillation CCZ factory · depth-one CCZ injection · logical CliNR frame clearing
items.caption: Physical layout of the 19,397-qubit secp256k1 processor, showing 69 memory blocks, 4 CCZ magic-state factories, edge-packed cat-state factories, and Bell-state routing channels.
items.abstract: One of the strengths of our recently proposed Walking Cat Architecture for a trapped-ion quantum computer is that it is straightforward to extend and optimize for a specific application. As a proof-of-concept, here we present such optimizations for solving the 256-bit elliptic curve discrete logarithm problem (ECDLP) on secp256k1, which is the elliptic curve used by blockchain technologies such as Bitcoin, using Shor's algorithm. We optimize the circuits from Schrottenloher's recent work and arrive at a logical quantum circuit for solving the ECDLP using about 1450 qubits and 40·10⁶ Toffoli gates, with a rigorous lower bound on the logical-level success probability that holds with confidence at least 1-2⁻¹²⁸. Using our compilation toolchain with manual optimization of the logical layout and integrated routing, we produce estimates for the logical measurement depth and the required number of physical qubits by compiling all components to measurement schedules that obey the architectural constraints. A key ingredient is a fast CCZ magic-state factory and a depth-one CCZ state injection, reducing the execution time of CCZ gates by a factor of 31. We increase the logical-measurement parallelism using non-overlapping cat-based measurements in parallel, and we leverage the recently proposed logical CliNR protocol to speed up Clifford operations. To reduce the qubit overhead, we introduce a more efficient loss correction protocol, design a layout that allows us to recycle the CliNR ancilla qubits, and provision reusable cat-state resources according to the circuit's peak measurement parallelism. All results and optimizations combined, we conclude that a trapped-ion quantum computer based on our architecture can solve the ECDLP on secp256k1 in approximately 25.7 days using 19,397 physical qubits with an estimated success probability of 63%.

items.title: From Bits to Qubits: The Theory and Practice of Quantum Data Encoding
items.authors: Xiao-Ming Zhang, Arthur G. Rattew, Bujiao Wu, Georgios Styliaris, Xiaoming Sun, Bálint Koczor, Xiao Yuan
items.matched: High-threshold and low-overhead fault-tolerant quantum memory
items.result: Surveys quantum data encoding methods across state preparation, unitary synthesis, QRAM, and block-encoding, synthesizing circuit size, depth, and fault-tolerant gate counts.
items.question: How can deterministic classical data be compiled into quantum representations under minimal circuit depth, gate counts, and non-Clifford resources?
items.limits: Restricted to deterministic, fully known classical data in the standard qubit circuit model with all-to-all or binary-tree connectivity; excludes sampled distributions and continuous variables.
items.tools: uniformly controlled rotations (UCR) · Schmidt decomposition · QRAM bucket-brigade architecture · linear combination of unitaries (LCU) · block-encoding
items.caption: Three core access models mapping classical vectors and matrices to quantum operations: quantum state preparation, QRAM, and block-encoding.
items.abstract: Encoding classical data into quantum systems is a foundational step in the execution of nearly all quantum algorithms, and a critical bottleneck in realizing practical quantum advantage. This review provides a comprehensive account of the concepts, algorithms, and practical considerations associated with quantum data encoding. We trace the development from its early conceptual foundations to recent advances, considering commonly used access models, such as quantum state preparation, unitary synthesis, QRAM and block encoding. We survey the circuit size, depth, space-time tradeoffs, as well as non-Clifford resources required for fault-tolerant implementation. We also discuss the roles of different access models in quantum algorithms. Special attention is given to structured data, such as sparse data, Boolean functions and data represented by tensor networks. This review bridges theory and applications, serving both as a pedagogical guide for newcomers and as a reference for active researchers. We also highlight the pivotal role of quantum data encoding in quantum computing and provide insights into future directions that will enable quantum advantage.

items.title: From NISQ to Fault-Tolerance: Applications and Algorithmic Benchmarks for Spin Qubits
items.authors: Frederik Lohof, Florian Ginzel, Wolfgang Lechner
items.matched: High-threshold and low-overhead fault-tolerant quantum memory
items.result: Compiling Parity Twine to exchange-only (EO) spin qubits reduces the physical exchange-pulse count by more than 22% for QFT and up to 34% for QAOA compared to baseline compilation schemes.
items.question: How do algorithmic benchmarks and simulation routines scale from NISQ to fault-tolerance when mapped directly to physical exchange-pulse sequences on exchange-only spin qubit QPUs?

items.abstract: Motivated by recent breakthroughs in the development of spin-based quantum processing units based on exchange-only (EO) spin qubits, we provide a roadmap for the implementation of quantum algorithms on the EO platform, ranging from the NISQ to the fault-tolerant era. To provide an algorithm-driven perspective on the scaling of quantum chips, we consider a range of applications targeting different stages of hardware maturity and formulate requirements for a successful realization. We show that the compilation method Parity Twine perfectly complements the hardware's capabilities to perform tasks such as the quantum Fourier transform or QAOA. Furthermore, we describe an error detection technique native to Parity Twine, which EO qubits can leverage in a unique and advantageous way to improve algorithm performance. Finally, since both near-term algorithmic benchmarks and a long-term perspective can be found in digital quantum simulation, we specifically discuss the fermionic fast Fourier transform and the simulation of Fermi-Hubbard models. The latter is explicitly discussed in the context of quantum error correction and a partially fault-tolerant realization. By providing detailed resource estimates and identifying scaling bottlenecks on each level, our work offers a quantitative perspective on EO-based quantum computing and will inform future hardware design choices.

items.result: Ancilla-mediated inter-block logical R_ZZ gate enables multi-block [[4,2,2]] error detection for QAOA Max-Cut. Encoded circuits maintain higher ground-state probability than unencoded baselines up to noise rate p = 0.03 under grid-routed two-qubit depolarizing noise and up to p = 0.04 with all-to-all connectivity.
items.question: How can multi-block [[4,2,2]] error detection be implemented for QAOA Max-Cut circuits using non-transversal inter-block two-qubit rotations?

items.abstract: We present a partially fault-tolerant implementation of QAOA based on the [[4,2,2]] error-detection code, targeting the Max-Cut problem on a square graph. Our main contribution is a novel ancilla-mediated logical R_ZZ gate enabling interactions between qubits in different [[4,2,2]] blocks. We evaluate unencoded and encoded circuits under five noise models, with both all-to-all and grid-routed connectivity, using the Cirq and qsimcirq frameworks with parallel CPU execution. Post-selection on stabilizer measurements consistently improves the probability of sampling optimal bitstrings, with five measurements providing the strongest benefit. These results support error-detection as a practical near-term strategy for improving the quality of variational quantum algorithms.

items.title: Quantum bivariate bicycle codes with weight-8 checks surpassing the BB benchmark
items.authors: Liangdong Lu, Ruipan Yang, Guanmin Guo
items.matched: Surface code quantum computing by lattice surgery
items.result: Weight-8 bivariate bicycle codes yield [[144,6,d≥15]], [[144,10,12]], [[144,16,10]], and [[72,14,8]] with kd²/n=12.44. All have exact even dimension k=2dimR/(A,B) and d_X=d_Z.
items.question: Can bivariate bicycle codes with weight-8 checks be constructed and certified systematically to surpass the (n,k,d) performance of standard weight-6 bivariate bicycle codes?
items.prior: Flagship weight-6 bivariate bicycle code reached [[144,12,12]] with kd²/n=12, and length-72 reference was [[72,12,6]] with kd²/n=6 (Bravyi et al. 2024).
items.limits: Circuit-level memory simulations assume gate-level bit-flip noise over 6 rounds without flag fault-tolerance, incurring deeper depth-10 syndrome circuits and thickness 3 embeddings.
items.tools: Algebraic structure theory of 2BGA codes · Bit-mask exhaustive verifier · BP-OSD decoding · Circuit-level stabilizer extraction simulation
items.caption: Logical error rate p_L versus physical error rate p in a 6-round circuit-level memory experiment with BP-OSD decoding. Weight-8 codes exhibit a pseudo-threshold of ≈0.1%, compared to ≈0.4% and ≈0.2% for weight-6 reference codes.
items.abstract: Bivariate bicycle (BB) codes of Bravyi emphet al.~citeBravyi2024 are quantum low-density parity-check codes with weight-6 checks, exemplified by [[144,12,12]] with kd²/n=12. We develop the algebraic structure theory of BB-type codes with weight-8 checks (weight-4 generator polynomials) and use it, together with an exactly validated search pipeline, to construct and certify new codes. We prove an exact dimension formula k=2dimR/(A,B) (forcing even k), a 4ℓm-element symmetry group on generator pairs, an X/Z distance equality d_X=d_Z, and a family of subgroup-coset kernel vectors giving rigorous distance upper bounds and a design rule for high-distance constructions; all distances are computed exhaustively by a cross-validated bit-mask verifier. At n=144 the pipeline returns a census of 53 codes whose strongest members surpass the BB benchmark: [[144,6,d≥15]] exceeds the benchmark distance 12 (certified d≥15), [[144,10,12]] reaches it with weight-8 checks, and [[144,16,10]] encodes a third more logical qubits at kd²/n=11.11 (7.4% below benchmark) while decoding no worse. At n=72, [[72,14,8]] attains kd²/n=12.44---more than twice the same-length BB code---and decodes better; a circuit-level memory experiment places our weight-8 codes at ≈0.1% pseudo-threshold versus ≈0.4% for the BB reference under an identical model, quantifying the threshold cost of the heavier checks. All structural statements are verified numerically on the whole census.

items.title: Experimental realization of quantum-computing-enhanced sensing
items.authors: Yifang Xu, Hongwei Huang, Yilong Zhou, Yunlai Zhu, Chuanlong Ma, Lida Sun, Lintao Xiao, Ziyue Hua, Weiting Wang, Zijie Chen, Weizhou Cai, Hekang Li, Haohua Wang, Xiaoting Wang, Ming Li, Chang-Ling Zou, Luyan Sun

items.result: Grover search implemented in a bosonic mode resolves 11 frequency candidates with 2.40 bits of extracted mutual information at m=2 sensing iterations across a Hilbert space exceeding 128 photons.
items.question: Can the computational advantage of quantum algorithms be directly converted into an advantage for quantum frequency sensing using an unknown physical signal as an oracle?
items.prior: Classical sequential search resolves N=3 candidates with 1.58 bits of mutual information for m=2 iterations.
items.limits: Known signal amplitude and duration; non-uniform Fock distribution in initial coherent states causing over- or under-rotation; cavity and qubit dissipation; cavity nonlinearities.
items.tools: 3D superconducting microwave cavity · transmon qubit sensor/ancilla · signal-driven geometric phase oracle · Grover amplitude amplification · selective number-dependent arbitrary phase (SNAP) gates

items.abstract: Quantum algorithms offer computational advantages, yet incorporating them into quantum sensing and converting these advantages into enhanced information acquisition remains challenging. Here, we realize quantum-computing-enhanced sensing in a spin-oscillator architecture, where a microwave cavity provides a high-dimensional quantum register and a coupled superconducting qubit serves as the sensor. The unknown signal directly generates the phase oracle operation, establishing a natural physical interface between quantum computation and sensing. We experimentally demonstrate the first Grover search in a bosonic mode and observe quantum amplitude amplification in a Hilbert space spanning more than 128 photons. For the same number of sensing iterations, our protocol extracts more information and resolves more frequency candidates than classical sequential search. Our results establish signal-driven oracles as a route for harnessing oracle-based quantum algorithms and realizing quantum-computing-enhanced sensing.

items.title: Saving resources through repeat-until-success positive-operator-valued-measure measurements in quantum computation
items.authors: Hefeng Wang, Sixia Yu, Hua Xiang
items.matched: quantum algorithms with provable speedup, query and gate complexity bounds
items.result: Multistep repeat-until-success computation guided by intermediate ancillary POVM measurements reduces qubit count and unitary operations polynomially compared to deferred end-of-circuit measurements, achieving total success probability P_succ > 1/2(1 + 1/e).
items.question: Can intermediate ancillary measurements be leveraged in a multistep state-evolution path to reduce quantum computing resources relative to deferred-measurement circuits?
items.prior: Deferred measurement requires m control qubits and scales runtime as ∏_(k=1)^m 1/p_k, leading to an exponential decrease in success probability over m steps.
items.limits: Requires state overlap d_k = |⟨φ^((k-1))|φ^((k))⟩| and spectral gap Δ to be polynomially large, with evolution parameter t₀ = π/ (2c d).
items.tools: repeat-until-success (RUS) protocol · positive-operator-valued measure (POVM) · quantum resonant transitions (QRTs) · single-ancilla intermediate projective measurement
items.caption: Quantum circuit schematic for an m-step repeat-until-success POVM computation on n working qubits with one ancillary qubit, showing the repeated unit loop.
items.abstract: We present a quantum computation approach in which computation is guided by positive-operator-valuedmeasure (POVM) measurements following a given computation path in multisteps. In this approach, one ancillary qubit is coupled to a register of working qubits, and a POVM measurement is implemented effectively on the working qubits by applying a unitary operation on the whole system followed by a projective measurement performed on the ancillary qubit. Each step of the computation is a repeat-until-success procedure such that the desired state of the step is obtained deterministically on the working qubits via POVM measurements. The principle of deferred measurement states that measurements can always be moved from an intermediate stage of a quantum circuit to the end of the circuit without affecting the efficiency of the computation.We demonstrate that in our approach, by introducing intermediate measurements on the ancillary qubit in the computation process, both the number of qubits and unitary operations can be reduced polynomially, compared to the case where the intermediate measurements are deferred to the end of the computation. We also provide a method for implementation of the approach.

items.title: Asymmetric quantum error correction efficiently tackles application-specific noise effects
items.authors: Abhishek Yadav, Peter K. Schuhmacher, Michael Epping
items.matched: Toward the first quantum simulation with quantum speedup
items.result: Asymmetric (5,3) quantum parity code with 15 physical qubits matches the optimization performance of the symmetric (5,5) code requiring 25 qubits because QAOA objective degrades significantly more under bit flips than phase flips.
items.question: How do asymmetric bit-flip and phase-flip Pauli noise channels affect QAOA performance across different circuit decompositions, and can asymmetric quantum error correction exploit this asymmetry?
items.limits: Simulated on a 6-qubit flight-gate assignment problem; syndrome extraction circuit noise and gate-level QEC fault-tolerance overhead not directly modeled in the QEC evaluation.
items.tools: Quantum Approximate Optimization Algorithm (QAOA) · Quantum Parity Code (QPC) · Exact density-matrix simulation · Layer-level and gate-level Pauli noise models
items.caption: Residual cost deviation Δ plotted against physical error probability p under d=2 layer-level noise for uncoded QAOA and various quantum parity code configurations (n₁,n₂).
items.abstract: Noise is a major challenge for current quantum computers. It can be broadly categorized into bit-flip and phase-flip errors. These two types do not necessarily affect the executed algorithm, thus also the application, in the same way. We illustrate this general effect for the example of the quantum approximate optimization algorithm (QAOA) applied to a small instance of the flight-gate assignment (FGA) problem. We compare bit-flip and phase-flip Pauli noise under both layer-level and gate-level noise models, using two circuit decompositions of the same ideal QAOA unitary: a CNOT-based decomposition and a native-R_ZZ decomposition. In the simulations, bit-flip noise produces the larger degradation in the performance of the quantum optimization. The asymmetry is most visible in the layer-level and native-R_ZZ simulations. We explain this by how the errors affect mixing, final measurements, and how they propagate inside the circuit. We then exploit these insights to tackle noise particularly efficiently using asymmetric error-correcting codes. As an illustration, we use the quantum parity code (QPC), a generalization of the 9-qubit Shor code, and show that a smaller asymmetric code can achieve nearly the same improvement as a larger symmetric choice. This demonstrates that error-correction resources should be assigned not only according to physical error rates, but also according to how strongly each error channel affects the application. As a result, asymmetric quantum error correction proves useful even in cases where the noise model is symmetric. Finally, we discuss how information about the noise obtained through calibration can be exploited in our approach.

items.title: Near-optimal synthesis of non-Gaussian phase gates via qubit-oscillator Rabi control
items.authors: Zhen Yang, Shan Jin, Zi-Wen Liu, Xiaoting Wang
items.matched: Toward the first quantum simulation with quantum speedup
items.result: Analytic Rabi sequence approximates degree-R continuous-variable polynomial phase gates e^(iTp(hatX)) over Fock subspace H_n with total interaction time T_tot = O(log^((R-1)/2+o(1))(1/ε)), matching the proven lower bound Ω(log^((R-1)/2)(1/ε)).
items.question: Can continuous-variable non-Gaussian polynomial phase gates be synthesized via linear qubit-oscillator Rabi control with polylogarithmic total interaction time in the inverse target error 1/ε?
items.prior: Fourier-Trotter approaches require sequence length O(1/ε) to achieve target error ε.
items.limits: Applies to input states within fixed finite Fock subspace H_n = span|0⟩,…,|n⟩; exact synthesis is impossible for finite same-quadrature Rabi sequences.
items.tools: generalized quantum signal processing (GQSP) · qubit-oscillator linear Rabi coupling · qubit postselection · polarization decomposition
items.caption: Approximation error as a function of total Rabi interaction time T_tot for representative continuous-variable phase evolutions.
items.abstract: Non-Gaussian gates remain a key bottleneck for universal continuous-variable (CV) quantum computation because the nonlinearities they require are difficult to engineer. To address this challenge, we develop an efficient qubit-oscillator Rabi synthesis scheme for polynomial phase gates, with a total interaction time that scales polylogarithmically with the inverse target error \(ε\). Specifically, for a class of readily preparable initial states, we show that a degree-\(R\) phase gate can be approximated by an analytically constructed Rabi sequence with total time \(O(log^(R-1)/2+o(1)(1/ε))\). This construction requires no numerical optimization and therefore extends naturally to arbitrarily large multimode systems. We further establish a total-time lower bound of \(Ω(log^(R-1)/2(1/ε))\), showing that the synthesis is near optimal. As applications, we use this scheme to simulate representative CV quantum dynamics and implement a CV quantum algorithm for solving linear partial differential equations. These results establish qubit-oscillator Rabi control as an efficient, analytically compilable, and near-optimal primitive for CV quantum information processing.

items.title: Wavelength-Uniform Quantum Algorithms for Quantum Dynamics
items.authors: Shi Jin, Chuwen Ma
items.matched: A variational eigenvalue solver on a photonic quantum processor
items.result: Constructed an end-to-end quantum algorithm for the von Neumann equation with polynomial complexity in dimension d and resource bounds containing no negative powers of the semiclassical parameter ε. Evaluated physical observables uniformly across ε∈[10⁻⁴, 1] with observable error E_obs ≤6.8126 ×10⁻⁷ under fixed grid parameters.
items.question: How can quantum dynamics in the semiclassical regime ε≪1 be simulated on a quantum computer without spatial mesh and query constraints scaling inversely with ε?
items.prior: Standard spatial spectral methods and wave-function representations require spatial mesh h = O(ε) and O(ε^(-d)) spatial unknowns due to the Nyquist–Shannon sampling theorem; Gaussian wave-packet methods require h = O(√ε) and cost O(ε^(-d/2)) per step.
items.limits: Applies to smooth physical observables (pairing with L²_(x,y) windows) rather than full density matrix state reconstruction; requires uniform regularity of the density operator in Weyl variables.
items.tools: Weyl variables · Hermite-Galerkin projection · Quantum Singular Value Transformation (QSVT) · Linear Combination of Unitaries (LCU) · Qubitized Hamiltonian simulation
items.caption: Observable error E_obs as a function of grid refinement parameters and across nine values of ε from 10⁻⁴ to 1, demonstrating ε-uniform convergence below the 10⁻⁵ tolerance with fixed (M,K,Q)=(256,36,16).
items.abstract: One of the main challenges in quantum simulation is the prohibitive cost of computing its solutions in the semi-classical regime, in which the de Broglie wavelength is small compared with the characteristic length scale and the solution is highly oscillatory. This difficulty is overcome by using the Weyl variable, under which the solution is not oscillatory. Furthermore, we use the exact Hermite moments and quantum singular value transformation to treat the polynomial and Fourier components of the potential, resulting in a quantum algorithm efficient for all ranges of wavelengths. Specifically, it has a polynomial complexity in spatial dimension, and discretization and query bounds without negative powers of possibly small wavelength, thus enabling it to capture the correct physical observables even if the spatial grid does not resolve the frequency, hence defying the Nyquist-Shannon sampling theorem.

items.title: Reducing quantum and classical resources for quantum-centric supercomputing workloads on near-term hardware
items.authors: Maxence Grandadam, Vladyslav Bohun, Dikshant Dulal, Maciej Koch-Janusz
items.matched: Toward the first quantum simulation with quantum speedup
items.result: Approximate compilation reduces the largest 40-qubit Krylov circuit depth from 2413 to 26 and two-qubit gates from 6840 to 74 with 0.941 fidelity, overcoming depolarizing noise stagnation to restore monotonic ground-state energy convergence in Sample-based Krylov Quantum Diagonalization.
items.question: How does hardware noise affect sample-based Krylov quantum diagonalization support recovery, and can approximate circuit compilation mitigate the resulting exponential depth penalty?
items.prior: Uncompressed Qiskit circuits stagnate at an energy error ΔE ≈9 ×10⁻² t due to noise accumulation across increasing Krylov depth.
items.limits: One-dimensional single-impurity Anderson model with bounded entanglement allowing single-block Trotter compression, evaluated on 20 sites (40 qubits) with 1000 shots per state.
items.tools: Sample-based Krylov quantum diagonalization (SKQD) · Tensor-network approximate circuit compilation · ibm_fez superconducting quantum processor · Single-impurity Anderson model (SIAM)
items.caption: Energy error ΔE (top) and classical subspace dimension (bottom) plotted against Krylov dimension d. Uncompressed circuits stagnate near ΔE ≈9 ×10⁻² t, while compressed circuits achieve monotonic convergence with smaller classical subspaces.
items.abstract: Sample-based Krylov quantum diagonalization (SKQD) is a paradigmatic example of a quantum-centric supercomputing workflow that combines the convergence structure of Krylov quantum diagonalization with classical sampling-based post-processing. It provides convergence guarantees assuming that the important computational-basis configurations can be sampled from a set of Krylov states with sufficient probability. We analyze this assumption under depolarizing noise, deriving shot-count resource estimates that expose an exponential depth penalty, and perform experiments on current noisy hardware with the one-dimensional single-impurity Anderson model on a 20-site (40-qubit) instance. Device noise breaks the practical convergence predicted by the noiseless SKQD analysis, but approximate compilation techniques can compress the Krylov time-evolution circuits before execution. The compressed circuits accumulate less hardware noise, recover the expected energy convergence, and reduce both the quantum shot budget and the classical subspace dimension, remaining beneficial even when classical configuration recovery is applied.

items.abstract: Motivated by recent breakthroughs in the development of spin-based quantum processing units based on exchange-only (EO) spin qubits, we provide a roadmap for the implementation of quantum algorithms on the EO platform, ranging from the NISQ to the fault-tolerant era. To provide an algorithm-driven perspective on the scaling of quantum chips, we consider a range of applications targeting different stages of hardware maturity and formulate requirements for a successful realization. We show that the compilation method Parity Twine perfectly complements the hardware's capabilities to perform tasks such as the quantum Fourier transform or QAOA. Furthermore, we describe an error detection technique native to Parity Twine, which EO qubits can leverage in a unique and advantageous way to improve algorithm performance. Finally, since both near-term algorithmic benchmarks and a long-term perspective can be found in digital quantum simulation, we specifically discuss the fermionic fast Fourier transform and the simulation of Fermi-Hubbard models. The latter is explicitly discussed in the context of quantum error correction and a partially fault-tolerant realization. By providing detailed resource estimates and identifying scaling bottlenecks on each level, our work offers a quantitative perspective on EO-based quantum computing and will inform future hardware design choices.

items.authors: Hrishikesh Belagali, Ryan LaRose

items.abstract: We introduce Propaq, a performant and flexible Python package implementing Heisenberg propagation techniques for classically simulating quantum circuits. Propaq is compatible with major quantum software packages like Qiskit and Cirq, and matches or outperforms similar state-of-the-art packages for Heisenberg propagation. Beyond this, Propaq has multiple distinguishing features for simulation and research. These include Heisenberg propagation in any basis, hybrid Schrödinger-Heisenberg simulation, custom truncation and noisy simulation methods, and detailed logging information for analyzing simulation accuracy, runtime, and memory usage. We describe these features, how to use Propaq for research, and its backend implementation.

items.title: Matrix Holography on an Optical Lattice
items.authors: Robin Löwenberg, Julian Sonner
items.matched: analog quantum simulation of lattice models on cold atoms or superconducting ar…
items.result: Constructs bosonic four-body matrix-quantum-mechanics potentials via Floquet-engineered oscillating two-body spin interactions with a constant number of unitaries per cycle. Control-frequency bandwidth scales as O(N³) with matrix size N, reaching non-perturbative couplings λ∼O(1) at driving frequencies ω∼O(MHz).
items.question: Can four-body potentials of bosonic matrix quantum mechanics be simulated on an analog optical-lattice platform without the deep circuits of digital implementations?
items.limits: Requires non-spin-conserving spin-spin interactions and large-spin ferromagnetic regime (m ∼j). Bosonic Hilbert space must be truncated.
items.tools: Holstein-Primakoff transformation · Floquet engineering · Magnus expansion · James' effective Hamiltonian method · optical lattice of atomic ensembles
items.caption: Ground-state energy convergence as a function of spin size j comparing the large-spin model against the truncated SU(2) ×SO(2) bosonic matrix model with λ=2 and cutoff Λ=6. Relative error is 0.5 % at j=3 and drops to 0.007 %.
items.abstract: We propose an analog quantum-simulation protocol based on a lattice of atomic ensembles and time-averaged Floquet dynamics to construct the four-body potentials that typically appear in bosonic BFSS-like matrix quantum mechanics. In contrast to gate-based digital implementations requiring deep circuits, our approach generates the target model through a fixed set of control stages per Floquet cycle, keeping the number of consecutive unitaries constant with respect to the matrix size N. The principal scaling cost in our construction is given by the frequency range required to control the growing lattice. We show that this cost grows at most as O(N³), giving a polynomial scaling route to large-N, attractive to experimental implementation. Additionally, we demonstrate that the coupling parameter can be tuned beyond O(1), enabling the simulation of strong-coupling physics necessary for holographic phases.

items.title: Wavelength-Uniform Quantum Algorithms for Quantum Dynamics
items.authors: Shi Jin, Chuwen Ma
items.matched: Probing many-body dynamics on a 51-atom quantum simulator
items.result: Constructed an end-to-end quantum algorithm for the von Neumann equation with polynomial complexity in dimension d and resource bounds containing no negative powers of the semiclassical parameter ε. Evaluated physical observables uniformly across ε∈[10⁻⁴, 1] with observable error E_obs ≤6.8126 ×10⁻⁷ under fixed grid parameters.
items.question: How can quantum dynamics in the semiclassical regime ε≪1 be simulated on a quantum computer without spatial mesh and query constraints scaling inversely with ε?
items.prior: Standard spatial spectral methods and wave-function representations require spatial mesh h = O(ε) and O(ε^(-d)) spatial unknowns due to the Nyquist–Shannon sampling theorem; Gaussian wave-packet methods require h = O(√ε) and cost O(ε^(-d/2)) per step.
items.limits: Applies to smooth physical observables (pairing with L²_(x,y) windows) rather than full density matrix state reconstruction; requires uniform regularity of the density operator in Weyl variables.
items.tools: Weyl variables · Hermite-Galerkin projection · Quantum Singular Value Transformation (QSVT) · Linear Combination of Unitaries (LCU) · Qubitized Hamiltonian simulation
items.caption: Observable error E_obs as a function of grid refinement parameters and across nine values of ε from 10⁻⁴ to 1, demonstrating ε-uniform convergence below the 10⁻⁵ tolerance with fixed (M,K,Q)=(256,36,16).
items.abstract: One of the main challenges in quantum simulation is the prohibitive cost of computing its solutions in the semi-classical regime, in which the de Broglie wavelength is small compared with the characteristic length scale and the solution is highly oscillatory. This difficulty is overcome by using the Weyl variable, under which the solution is not oscillatory. Furthermore, we use the exact Hermite moments and quantum singular value transformation to treat the polynomial and Fourier components of the potential, resulting in a quantum algorithm efficient for all ranges of wavelengths. Specifically, it has a polynomial complexity in spatial dimension, and discretization and query bounds without negative powers of possibly small wavelength, thus enabling it to capture the correct physical observables even if the spatial grid does not resolve the frequency, hence defying the Nyquist-Shannon sampling theorem.

items.title: A Platform-aware Compilation Framework for Fault-tolerant Quantum Computation
items.authors: Srushti Patil, Susan X. Chen, Andreas Juul Bay-Smidt, Stefan Alaric Schäffer, Peter Krogstrup, Stefano Paesani, Gemma C. Solomon
items.matched: Evidence for the utility of quantum computing before fault tolerance
items.result: Unified compilation pipeline produces hardware-tailored FTQC resource estimates across three connectivity classes, showing that small-molecule chemistry (trimethylenemethane) requires ∼10⁴ physical qubits with runtimes of 10²ms (photonic, superconducting) to 10⁵ms (neutral atoms).
items.question: How can quantum circuits and fault-tolerant architectures be compiled to enable accurate, platform-aware end-to-end resource estimation across distinct physical hardware modalities?
items.limits: Trotterized phase estimation and simulation; surface-code Clifford + T gate model; physical error rates p = 10⁻³ and p = 10⁻⁴.
items.tools: Transversal active volume (t-AV) architecture · ZX-diagram logical blocks · Pauli product rotation compiler · Lattice surgery · Surface code
items.caption: Physical qubit count versus runtime for the Stat-QPE-gap TMM benchmark across multiple compiler-hardware architectures at error rates p=10⁻³ and p=10⁻⁴.
items.abstract: The compilation of an algorithm can vary significantly with the choice of physical hardware platform and error correction model. Yet, current compilation frameworks typically commit to a single architecture-hardware configuration, making it difficult to assess resource estimates across platforms. We present a platform-aware compilation framework that re-compiles a quantum circuit into a hardware-compatible instruction set as well as fault-tolerant operations and provides end-to-end resource estimates in terms of physical-qubit count, time-to-solution, and classical processing time. We benchmark the framework by obtaining end-to-end resource estimates for different compilers, each tailored to the functionalities of specific hardware modalities: connectivity, clock speed, and noise model. As part of this framework, we introduce a transversal active volume (t-AV) compilation architecture designed for the efficient execution of fault-tolerant operations in platforms supporting long-range logical connectivity. We benchmark the framework for Hamiltonian simulation of the 2D Fermi Hubbard model as well as for eigenenergy estimation of a small molecule (trimethylenemethane) as a candidate for early fault-tolerant demonstration of quantum chemistry. For the latter, we show that end-to-end quantum simulations can be achieved with ∼10⁴ physical qubits and runtimes ranging from 10² ms (photonics, superconducting) to 10⁵ ms (neutral atoms).

items.title: Efficient Quantum Circuits for Electronic Hamiltonian Simulation without Pauli Expansion
items.authors: Tamiya Onodera, Takeshi Sato
items.matched: Probing many-body dynamics on a 51-atom quantum simulator
items.result: Diagonalizing ladder-string-pair (Lasp) operators directly avoids Pauli expansion for electronic Hamiltonian simulation, reducing CX-gate count from 36 to 12 in a 4-index triad and from O(n²) to O(n) across O(n) ordered triads without introducing Trotter error at the triad level.
items.question: How can electronic Hamiltonian simulation circuits be constructed and optimized directly from fermionic ladder operators without Pauli expansion?
items.prior: Standard simulation expands fermionic ladder products into Pauli strings, producing 16 Pauli strings per two-body Lasp operator and O(n²) CX scaling.
items.limits: Theoretical circuit construction and gate-count optimization. Systematic optimization for global triad ordering and composition across all index groups left for future work.
items.tools: ladder-string-pair (Lasp) diagonalization · Jordan–Wigner transformation · GHZ state preparation circuits · parity encoding circuits · multi-controlled Z rotations (C3RZ/C4RZ)
items.caption: High-level quantum circuits for time evolution of a fermionic triad before and after CX cancellation, showing reduction from 36 CX gates to 12 CX gates alongside three C3RZ gates.
items.abstract: Electronic Hamiltonian simulation is commonly formulated by mapping fermionic operators to qubit operators and subsequently expanding the resulting ladder-operator products into Pauli strings. While general, this procedure obscures the higher-level fermionic structure and can hide opportunities for circuit optimization. Building on ladder-string-pair (Lasp) diagonalization originally developed for Hamiltonian simulation of partial differential equations, we construct time-evolution circuits for the second-quantized electronic Hamiltonian without performing a Pauli expansion. For the most general case of complex-valued coefficients, we present a time-evolution circuit for a two-body fermionic Lasp operator that corresponds to 16 Pauli strings in the Pauli-expansion approach but does not suffer from Trotter error at this stage. Expanding the optimization scope from a single operator to a triad of three fermionic Lasp operators sharing the same four spin-orbital indices enables systematic cancellation of CX gates, reducing the CX-gate count from 36 to 12 in the example considered, still without introducing Trotter error at this stage. For n spin orbitals, further expanding the optimization scope to a sequence of O(n) suitably ordered triads enables a cascade of CX-gate reductions across triad boundaries, reducing the CX-gate count from O(n²) to O(n). The Lasp-based approach also naturally accommodates controlled time evolution and yields further optimizations for real-valued Hamiltonians. These results demonstrate that the Lasp-based approach enables more efficient time-evolution circuits by preserving high-level circuit structures and thereby expanding the scope of optimization, providing a systematic route toward more efficient electronic Hamiltonian simulation.

items.title: Benchmarking dynamical-structure-factor protocols in programmable neutral-atom geometries
items.authors: Matteo Grotti, Sergi Julià-Farré, Elisa Ercolessi, Alexandre Dauphin
items.matched: Probing many-body dynamics on a 51-atom quantum simulator
items.result: Emulation of Raman-spectroscopy dynamical structure factor protocol on neutral-atom quantum processors successfully reconstructs magnon excitation dispersions for 1D and 2D transverse-field Ising models with N up to 36 atoms, remaining robust under realistic laser noise and positional disorder.
items.question: Can programmable neutral-atom quantum processors accurately measure dynamical structure factors in 1D dimerized and 2D non-integrable transverse-field Ising models under realistic experimental noise?
items.limits: Numerical emulation rather than physical hardware. Assumes paramagnetic regime h_x/J ≫1; classical validation accuracy degrades near quantum phase transition (J/h_x = 0.4). Noise averaging performed over 50 trajectories before Fourier transformation.
items.tools: Pulser neutral-atom emulator · Matrix product states (emu-mps) · State-vector emulation (emu-sv) · Rydberg tweezer Hamiltonian dynamics
items.caption: Reconstructed dynamical structure factor S^zz(k_x, k_y=π, ω) plotted against momentum k_x (horizontal axis) and frequency ω/h_x (vertical axis) for 2D square lattices (4 ×4 with periodic boundaries, 6 ×6 with open boundaries) at J/h_x = 0.1 and 0.2.
items.abstract: The dynamical structure factor is a central observable in condensed-matter physics, providing direct insight into the excitation spectrum and dynamical response of quantum materials. While it is traditionally accessed in real materials through inelastic neutron scattering, recent works have shown that analogous information can be extracted in quantum simulators using suitable dynamical protocols. So far, these approaches have been demonstrated mainly in paradigmatic integrable one-dimensional models. In this work, we use numerical emulations of a neutral-atom quantum processing unit to assess the feasibility of measuring the dynamical structure factor in a broader class of Ising-like spin systems. Beyond the standard one-dimensional transverse-field Ising chain, we benchmark the protocol in chains with dimerized interactions and in the two-dimensional transverse-field Ising model, where spectral properties are difficult to access with classical numerical methods at large scales. We further analyze the robustness of the protocol under realistic experimental conditions, including finite simulation times, pulse modulation, positional disorder, and laser noise. Our results show that neutral-atom quantum simulators can provide a practical route to probing dynamical response functions in regimes where classical simulations become increasingly demanding, paving the way toward experimental implementation.

items.title: From Bits to Qubits: The Theory and Practice of Quantum Data Encoding
items.authors: Xiao-Ming Zhang, Arthur G. Rattew, Bujiao Wu, Georgios Styliaris, Xiaoming Sun, Bálint Koczor, Xiao Yuan
items.matched: Evidence for the utility of quantum computing before fault tolerance
items.result: Surveys quantum data encoding methods across state preparation, unitary synthesis, QRAM, and block-encoding, synthesizing circuit size, depth, and fault-tolerant gate counts.
items.question: How can deterministic classical data be compiled into quantum representations under minimal circuit depth, gate counts, and non-Clifford resources?
items.limits: Restricted to deterministic, fully known classical data in the standard qubit circuit model with all-to-all or binary-tree connectivity; excludes sampled distributions and continuous variables.
items.tools: uniformly controlled rotations (UCR) · Schmidt decomposition · QRAM bucket-brigade architecture · linear combination of unitaries (LCU) · block-encoding
items.caption: Three core access models mapping classical vectors and matrices to quantum operations: quantum state preparation, QRAM, and block-encoding.
items.abstract: Encoding classical data into quantum systems is a foundational step in the execution of nearly all quantum algorithms, and a critical bottleneck in realizing practical quantum advantage. This review provides a comprehensive account of the concepts, algorithms, and practical considerations associated with quantum data encoding. We trace the development from its early conceptual foundations to recent advances, considering commonly used access models, such as quantum state preparation, unitary synthesis, QRAM and block encoding. We survey the circuit size, depth, space-time tradeoffs, as well as non-Clifford resources required for fault-tolerant implementation. We also discuss the roles of different access models in quantum algorithms. Special attention is given to structured data, such as sparse data, Boolean functions and data represented by tensor networks. This review bridges theory and applications, serving both as a pedagogical guide for newcomers and as a reference for active researchers. We also highlight the pivotal role of quantum data encoding in quantum computing and provide insights into future directions that will enable quantum advantage.

items.title: Trion-mediated quantum operations on a double-dot charge qubit
items.authors: Alexander Tsukanov
items.matched: exchange gates and two-qubit operations in semiconductor double quantum dots
items.result: Optical pulses to trion states restore resonant tunneling in asymmetric double quantum dots via Coulomb compensation, enabling ultrafast orthogonal single-qubit rotations despite suppressed single-electron tunneling.
items.question: Can optical excitation to trion states enable fast single-qubit operations in semiconductor double quantum dots with suppressed baseline tunneling?
items.limits: Theoretical model in two dimensions; relies on specific Coulomb compensation of structural asymmetry.
items.tools: semiconductor asymmetric double quantum dots · resonant trion state excitation · laser pulse control · dissipative master equation modeling
items.abstract: A scheme for controlling a charge qubit on a semiconductor asymmetric double quantum dot with suppressed tunnel coupling between individual quantum dots is proposed. Laser pulses convert the logical single-electron states of the qubit into auxiliary trion states, for which the resonant tunneling condition is restored due to the compensation of structural asymmetry by the Coulomb interaction of the particles. The conditions for performing orthogonal single-qubit rotations are formulated. For a two-dimensional structure, the parameters of the qubit are calculated, and the dependence of the fidelity of the inversion operation on the parameters of the laser field and the rates of dissipative processes is obtained. It is shown that the considered algorithm is characterized by high speed and reliability.

items.title: From NISQ to Fault-Tolerance: Applications and Algorithmic Benchmarks for Spin Qubits
items.authors: Frederik Lohof, Florian Ginzel, Wolfgang Lechner
items.matched: Superconducting Qubits: Current State of Play
items.result: Compiling Parity Twine to exchange-only (EO) spin qubits reduces the physical exchange-pulse count by more than 22% for QFT and up to 34% for QAOA compared to baseline compilation schemes.
items.question: How do algorithmic benchmarks and simulation routines scale from NISQ to fault-tolerance when mapped directly to physical exchange-pulse sequences on exchange-only spin qubit QPUs?
items.limits: Analytical and numerical compilation models; assumes single-pulse error rates p ≈1.5 ×10⁻⁴, readout error p_m ≈0.01, and T₂ ≈19.3 μs.
items.tools: Parity Twine compilation · exchange-only (EO) spin qubits · pulse-level scheduling with exclusion radius · surface code QEC / lattice surgery error modeling
items.caption: Physical exchange-pulse count and Twine/Fowler pulse count ratio as a function of device length L for the quantum Fourier transform.
items.abstract: Motivated by recent breakthroughs in the development of spin-based quantum processing units based on exchange-only (EO) spin qubits, we provide a roadmap for the implementation of quantum algorithms on the EO platform, ranging from the NISQ to the fault-tolerant era. To provide an algorithm-driven perspective on the scaling of quantum chips, we consider a range of applications targeting different stages of hardware maturity and formulate requirements for a successful realization. We show that the compilation method Parity Twine perfectly complements the hardware's capabilities to perform tasks such as the quantum Fourier transform or QAOA. Furthermore, we describe an error detection technique native to Parity Twine, which EO qubits can leverage in a unique and advantageous way to improve algorithm performance. Finally, since both near-term algorithmic benchmarks and a long-term perspective can be found in digital quantum simulation, we specifically discuss the fermionic fast Fourier transform and the simulation of Fermi-Hubbard models. The latter is explicitly discussed in the context of quantum error correction and a partially fault-tolerant realization. By providing detailed resource estimates and identifying scaling bottlenecks on each level, our work offers a quantitative perspective on EO-based quantum computing and will inform future hardware design choices.

items.title: Fast universal parametric spin control in an acoustically modulated quantum dot
items.authors: Mateusz Kuniej, Michał Gawełczyk
items.matched: Semiconductor spin qubits
items.result: Parametric spin control achieves a ∼155 ps Pauli-X gate with average gate fidelity ≥99.9% under uncooled GaAs/InAs nuclear-spin noise and trion lifetime τ≥1.25 ns using ∼44 GHz acoustic driving.
items.question: How to achieve fast, universal single-electron spin control in a quantum dot using an acoustic field without being constrained by bare Zeeman resonance and limited rotation axes?
items.prior: Acousto-optical spin control required resonance with bare Zeeman splitting, was ∼290× slower for noise-mitigating gates, and restricted rotation axes (Ref. 31); all-optical Faraday control was ∼14× slower.
items.limits: Numerical simulations; requires ∼43.88 GHz acoustic driving with 2 meV modulation amplitude ( ∼2--3×10⁻⁴ strain) and trion lifetime τ≥1.25 ns for fidelity ≥99.9%.
items.tools: Optically dressed Λ-system in Voigt geometry · Parametric surface acoustic wave modulation · Rotating wave approximation Hamiltonian modeling · Quasi-static Overhauser noise averaging
items.caption: Average gate infidelity of the Pauli-X gate plotted against Overhauser noise root-mean-square energy ℏσ_δ (and dephasing time T₂^*) across different acoustic frequencies, trion lifetimes, and harmonic resonances.
items.abstract: Quantum communication, distributed computing, and hybrid architectures rely on nodes enabling coherent control of qubits and coupling to propagating quantum modes. While semiconductor quantum-dot (QD) spins couple to microwave and optical photons, weak interaction with mechanical waves has limited the integration of single-QD spin qubits into on-chip, acoustically coupled hybrid systems. The existing theory of acoustic QD spin control suffers from a limited range of rotation-axis angles, enforcing complex realizations of gate primitives and long gate times, leaving little margin against decoherence from trion decay and quasi-static nuclear-spin noise. We propose parametric control that overcomes these problems. We use far-detuned optical coupling to a trion state to dress and thus mix spin states, combined with acoustic modulation of the optical transition energy. Instead of relying on direct acoustic resonance with the spin splitting that leads to significant bottlenecks, we induce spin rotations parametrically via resonance with the dressed-spin splitting. We thus develop a spin analog of the ``swing-up'' charge-state excitation. Our scheme provides fast universal qubit control with nearly arbitrary rotation axes. Our ∼155 ps Pauli-X gate duration is ∼290× faster than in the previous acousto-optical formulation and ∼14× faster than optical Faraday-geometry spin rotation. The parametric scheme naturally enables higher-harmonic processes. Numerical simulations for ∼44 GHz acoustic driving show average gate fidelity ≥99.9% even for uncooled nuclear-spin environments of GaAs and InAs QDs for trion lifetime gtrsim1.25 ns. These metrics suggest practically usable control and may introduce a spin-phonon interface with high interaction rates, versatility, and multi-phonon processes, essential for future acoustically coupled hybrid architectures.
