items.title: Low-cost algorithm-to-execution framework for surface-code quantum computing
items.authors: Yunxin Tang, Zixuan Huo, Junxiang Huang, Zhou You, Zhirao Wang, Zhenai Ding, Yumeng Zeng, Yangyu Lu, Yiming Huang, Zongkang Zhang, Haipeng Xie, Ying Li, Jinzhao Sun, Xiao Yuan, Yuan Yao
items.matched: resource estimation: physical qubit and runtime budgets for useful algorithms
items.result: Unified algorithm-to-execution framework reduces fault-tolerant space-time volume up to 241.5× via non-Clifford supply co-design and cuts routed latency across twenty benchmark circuits.
items.question: How can circuit scheduling, spatial patch layout, and non-Clifford resource supply be coordinated to minimize physical execution overhead in surface-code quantum computing?
items.limits: Modeled on surface-code simulations with fixed physical error rate p_phys=10⁻³ or 10⁻⁴ and 500~ns stabilizer rounds; excludes repetitions for algorithmic success probability.
items.tools: surface code lattice surgery · executable workload extraction · direct-rotation state preparation · magic state distillation and cultivation
items.caption: Space-time volume and latency variations across twenty benchmark circuits comparing standard baseline layouts and synthesis against circuit-specific layouts and optimized non-Clifford allocations.
items.abstract: The execution of useful quantum algorithms on fault-tolerant processors requires more than a mapping from logical gates to encoded operations: the spatial organization, non-Clifford resource supply, and execution schedule must also be determined while keeping physical overhead within practical limits. Although the theoretical hierarchy from logical circuits to fault-tolerant operations is well established, these implementation choices are often specified and optimized separately. Here we develop a low-cost algorithm-to-execution framework for surface-code quantum computing. From hierarchical algorithm descriptions, it constructs dependency-preserving logical schedules and an executable workload capturing logical interactions, operation parallelism, and time-resolved non-Clifford demand, thereby linking logical computation to surface-code organization, resource-state preparation, and fault-tolerant execution in a traceable workflow. We apply the framework to twenty benchmark circuits across seven algorithm families and a hierarchically composed application-scale elliptic-curve discrete-logarithm workload. Physical costs vary substantially even for circuits with similar logical resource counts. Under our direct-rotation calibration, non-Clifford implementation selection reduces space-time volume by up to 241.5 times versus an all-synthesis baseline for the QAOA amplitude-amplification workload. Circuit-specific surface-code layouts reduce routed-latency estimates for all twenty benchmarks; thirteen also reduce space-time volume because communication savings outweigh added spatial overhead. These results show that low-cost fault-tolerant execution depends on computation scheduling and organization, not aggregate logical resource counts alone.

items.title: Walking Floquet code circuits for zero-overhead leakage reduction
items.authors: Hanna Westerheim, Kaavya Sahay, Shruti Puri
items.matched: Quantum error correction below the surface code threshold
items.result: Two zero-overhead walking honeycomb Floquet code circuits remove leakage periodically while maintaining code distance to Pauli errors. They correct as many leakage errors as Pauli errors for two noise models and outperform the same-distance walking surface code in the finite-error-rate waterfall regime.
items.question: Can leakage reduction units be integrated into honeycomb Floquet code syndrome extraction circuits with zero gate and depth overhead while preserving code distance?
items.limits: Simulated on toric honeycomb lattices with periodic boundary conditions using minimum-weight perfect matching decoders, uniform leakage probability p, and idealized Clifford/leakage channels.
items.tools: swirling and sliding honeycomb Floquet code circuits · zero-overhead SWAP compilation · two-body check measurements · Monte Carlo circuit simulation
items.caption: Logical error rate versus physical error rate across code distances for swirling and sliding honeycomb Floquet codes compared against the walking surface code under four leakage noise models.
items.abstract: Leakage, occurring when a qubit undetectably exits the computational subspace, poses a significant challenge for quantum error correction by inducing correlated errors in space and time. These correlations reduce both the code threshold and the effective code distance. To address this challenge, we introduce two zero-overhead walking circuits for the honeycomb Floquet code (hFC), termed the swirling and sliding circuits, which periodically remove leakage while dynamically protecting logical qubits via a schedule of anticommuting two-body measurements. Unlike previous dynamic circuits for the hFC, ours preserves the distance to Pauli errors. We further study their performance under leakage and find that, for two leakage noise models, they may correct as many leakage errors as Pauli errors, improving on the more widely known walking surface code. Through numerical simulation, we observe that finite-error-rate performance under leakage is strongly influenced by entropic effects, producing a pronounced waterfall regime in which the logical error rate decreases much more rapidly with physical error rate than the expected distance-limited scaling. In this regime, even when asymptotic predictions suggest otherwise, the hFC can outperform the same-distance walking surface code in error rates and sub-threshold logical error scaling.

html.limits: Simulated on toric honeycomb lattices with periodic boundary conditions using minimum-weight perfect matching decoders, uniform leakage probability <math xmlns="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML"><mi>p</mi></math>, and idealized Clifford/leakage channels.

items.title: The generalised semi-Clifford conjecture is false
items.authors: Nadish de Silva, Oscar Lautsch
items.matched: Fault-tolerant quantum computation by anyons
items.result: Zeng–Chen–Chuang generalised semi-Clifford conjecture is false: an explicit five-qubit gate in C₅setminusC₄ is not generalised semi-Clifford, and its inverse lies outside the entire Clifford hierarchy.
items.question: Are all quantum gates in the Clifford hierarchy generalised semi-Clifford gates of the form C₁ ΠD C₂?
items.prior: Held for all third-level gates C₃ for arbitrarily many qubits (Beigi–Shor 2008).
items.limits: Counterexample constructed at five qubits (n=5) and level k=5; extends to all n≥5 and k≥5 via identity tensors.
items.tools: multiplexed-Clifford gate ansatz · symplectic linear algebra · Lagrangian subspaces over Z₂ · Pauli commutation constraints
items.caption: Five-qubit quantum circuit counterexample composed of two-control multiplexed Clifford operations: ctrl_d(A) followed by ctrl_c(B).
items.abstract: The Clifford hierarchy is a nested sequence of sets of quantum gates that can be fault-tolerantly performed using gate teleportation within standard quantum error correction schemes. The importance of these gates has motivated numerous studies of their structure. Zeng-Chen-Chuang conjectured in 2007 that all hierarchy gates are generalised semi-Clifford, i.e. take the form C₁ ΠD C₂ for Clifford gates C₁, C₂, a permutation gate Π, and a diagonal gate D; Beigi-Shor proved in 2008 that this holds for all third-level gates. We construct a five-qubit gate that is in the fifth level of the Clifford hierarchy but is not generalised semi-Clifford. Rather than simply present and verify our counterexample to the generalised semi-Clifford conjecture, we show how its form can be deduced. Our counterexample also demonstrates that the Clifford hierarchy is not closed under inverses.

items.title: The cost of simulating classically tractable quantum circuits and dynamics
items.authors: Su Yeon Chang, Supanut Thanasilp, Zoë Holmes, M. Cerezo
items.matched: Toward the first quantum simulation with quantum speedup
items.result: Polynomial-time classical simulations of quantum dynamics are often outpaced by direct quantum hardware execution due to high one-time quantum sampling and shadow post-processing overheads when preparing unknown input states.
items.question: Whether classically simulable quantum evolutions are in practice more resource-efficient to simulate classically or to execute directly on quantum hardware.
items.limits: Independent unentangled input copies only (no multi-copy quantum memory); unitaries and observables restricted to efficient classical representations.
items.tools: classical shadows · Lie-algebraic simulation (g-sim) · Pauli Propagation · Majorana Propagation · hardware pricing models
items.caption: Estimated total wall-clock time versus qubit count n for direct quantum simulation and classical simulation across IonQ Forte, Google Sycamore, and IBM Heron architectures.
items.abstract: Determining whether a quantum evolution can be efficiently simulated classically is central to understanding the boundary between classical and quantum computation. However, polynomial-time simulability is an asymptotic statement, and does not by itself determine whether the (quantum-inspired) classical simulation is actually practical. Indeed, different polynomial scalings can lead to vastly different computational costs, particularly when expensive preprocessing or quantum data acquisition is required. In this work, we ask whether classically simulable quantum dynamics are in practice more resource-efficient to simulate classically than to execute directly on quantum hardware. We analyze this question using three resource metrics, quantum sample, quantum time, and classical time complexity, for several widely studied classically simulable circuit families. Using representative hardware-level estimates, we identify regimes in which quantum simulation can be faster despite the existence of a polynomial-time classical algorithm, as well as regimes in which classical simulation remains more efficient. At the same time, the large quantum sampling cost needed to characterize unknown input states can make this polynomial-time classical simulation prohibitively expensive with current cloud-based hardware access prices. Ultimately, our work indicates that guarantees of classical simulability with polynomial resources alone are insufficient to determine the preferred implementation.

items.abstract: Quantum-inspired classical algorithms have dequantized several quantum machine learning routines by replacing quantum linear-algebra subroutines with classical counterparts. However, the sampler based on quantum singular value transformation (QSVT) for learning with optimized random features is not covered by existing dequantization frameworks, because the matrix to be inverted is not itself available through sampling access. In this work, we develop a classical algorithm to address this type of quantum-advantage candidate. Our method samples heavy indices, reduces the transformation to a small principal block, and outputs a sparse classical representation with operator-norm guarantees. Applying this method dequantizes the sampler for optimized random features, giving a classical sampler with prescribed accuracy and polynomially related runtime. These results show that the factorization underlying a quantum block encoding can itself provide sufficient classical structure even when sampling-and-query access to the composite matrix is unavailable.

items.title: Distributed variational quantum computing with deterministic entanglement tuning
items.authors: Ilhwan Kim, Yong-Su Kim, Kwang Jo Lee, Hyukjoon Kwon, Yosep Kim, Hyang-Tag Lim
items.matched: A variational eigenvalue solver on a photonic quantum processor
items.result: Distributed variational quantum computing protocol deterministically tunes shared Bell-pair entanglement via LOCC with unit success probability (p_M=1) and concurrence C_M(θ)=cosθ, keeping state infidelity below 0.05 across full range.
items.question: How can entanglement between distributed quantum processing units be tuned continuously and deterministically without the probabilistic losses of filtering or the high Bell-pair consumption of gate teleportation?
items.limits: Demonstrated on bipartite single-qubit photonic processors; feed-forward conditional operations performed offline rather than in real time; pure-state majorization requires initial entanglement to be equal to or greater than target.
items.tools: spontaneous parametric down-conversion (SPDC) · displaced Sagnac interferometer · POVM with path-mode ancilla · COBYLA optimization · quantum state tomography
items.caption: Concurrence (top) and state infidelity (bottom) plotted against the tuning angle θ, demonstrating deterministic modulation of entanglement from 1 down to 0 while keeping state infidelity below 0.05.
items.abstract: Distributed quantum computing offers a scalable route to quantum information processing by entangling spatially separated processors. Although gate teleportation enables universal computation across distributed nodes, it requires repeated consumption of high-fidelity Bell pairs, ancillary qubits, and real-time feedforward, which imposes significant overhead and reduces fidelity. However, many variational quantum algorithms do not demand full universality; rather, they rely on sufficient expressibility to explore solution spaces effectively. Building on this, we propose a distributed variational quantum computing protocol based on deterministic entanglement tuning. In contrast to probabilistic filtering, our approach deterministically modulates pre-shared entanglement using only local operations and classical communication. We validate the protocol through a proof-of-principle experiment by estimating ground-state energies of the He-H⁺ molecule and the Schwinger model, showing that diverse entanglement levels can be engineered to match problem-specific requirements. Our results suggest a practical alternative for near-term distributed quantum applications.

items.title: Optimal T-Count for Block Encodings of Fermionic and Spin Hamiltonians
items.authors: Jiaxin Ma, Kevin J. Joven, Yuan Liu
items.matched: Hamiltonian Simulation by Qubitization
items.result: Worst-case block-encoding T-count scales as Θ(n²√log(n⁴/ε)) for general second-quantized fermionic Hamiltonians and Θ(n+log(1/ε)) for bond-dependent Kitaev honeycomb spin Hamiltonians.
items.question: What is the asymptotically optimal worst-case T-count required to construct an ε-approximate block encoding of structured fermionic and spin Hamiltonians?
items.prior: For fermionic Hamiltonians, upper bound was O(n²√log(n⁴/ε)) (Liu 2024), but matching lower bounds and spin-Hamiltonian optimal scalings were unknown.
items.limits: Unitary Clifford+T model without mid-circuit measurements or classical feed-forward. Bounds are worst-case over the full coefficient family and do not exploit specific molecular structure.
items.tools: ancilla compression theorem · volume-covering and circuit counting · stabilizer nullity monotonicity · linear combination of unitaries (LCU)
items.caption: Plots T-gate count versus number of spin orbitals n for molecular electronic Hamiltonians in STO-3G basis, comparing the theoretical lower bound against existing block-encoding implementations.
items.abstract: We determine the non-Clifford T-gate cost of constructing block encodings of structured fermionic and spin Hamiltonians in a unitary Clifford+T model, when arbitrarily many clean ancillas and unrestricted block-encoding subnormalization are allowed, but without mid-circuit measurements or classical feed-forward. Our main technical tool is an ancilla-compression theorem: any block encoding of an n-qubit operator with a clean ancillas and at most s T gates can be compressed to use at most mina,n+2s ancillas, without increasing the absolute error or T-count. For general second-quantized Hamiltonians with bounded one- and two-body coefficients, at operator-norm block-encoding error ε, a volume-covering argument combined with circuit counting gives the worst-case lower bound Ω(n²√log(n⁴/ε)), matching the existing upper bound at fixed precision. For the bond-dependent Kitaev honeycomb family on n spins, we obtain independent lower bounds Ω(n) from stabilizer nullity and Ω(log(1/ε)) from one-qubit state preparation, established using different Hamiltonian instances. Together with an explicit LCU construction, they give the tight worst-case scaling Θ(n+log(1/ε)). As an application, we evaluate the T-count of a Hamiltonian simulation circuit based on quantum singular value transformation, with each block-encoding query compiled separately. When phase synthesis and controlled queries add at most constant-factor overhead, the simulation T-count scales as the query count times the optimal T-count per query.

items.title: Virtual quantum neural networks
items.authors: Benchi Zhao, Xuanqiang Zhao, Yinan Li, Yingzhou Li, Giulio Chiribella
items.matched: Quantum singular value transformation and beyond: exponential improvements for…
items.result: Extending quantum neural networks to linear combinations of completely positive trace-preserving maps via sampling and classical post-processing mitigates hardware noise and recovers ground-state energy curves under depolarizing noise.
items.question: Can quantum neural networks enlarge their optimization space beyond completely positive trace-preserving maps using randomized sampling and classical post-processing to boost expressivity and noise robustness?
items.prior: Standard QNNs and VQEs are restricted to a single parametric completely positive map (|c|₁=1), yielding inaccurate energies under circuit noise.
items.limits: Demonstrated in numerical simulations under depolarizing noise (p=0.01 single-qubit, p=0.02 two-qubit), depth d=5, and Chebyshev truncation K=100.
items.tools: Virtual quantum neural networks (VQNN) · Virtual variational quantum eigensolver (VVQE) · Truncated Chebyshev polynomial negativity approximation · Probabilistic circuit sampling
items.caption: Calculated ground state energy of HeH⁺ plotted against nuclear separation. Increasing the sampling budget from standard VQE (γ=1) to VVQE with γ=1.5 and γ=2.5 pulls noisy estimates back to the exact error-free curve.
items.abstract: Quantum neural networks are a prominent model of quantum machine learning. Their training consists in the minimization of a given loss function over a parametrized family of quantum circuits, mathematically described by unitary operators, or, more generally, completely positive linear maps. In this work, we extend the notion of quantum neural network, using random sampling and classical data processing to enlarge the optimization space in a way that includes linear combinations of completely positive maps. Our extended model, called virtual quantum neural networks, leverages its enlarged optimization space to achieve increased expressivity and improved noise robustness. These benefits are illustrated in three representative tasks: quantum error mitigation, binary classification, and estimation of ground-state energies. Overall, virtual quantum neural networks offer a flexible learning paradigm that expands the space of achievable computations and strengthens the applications of near-term quantum hardware.

items.title: The cost of simulating classically tractable quantum circuits and dynamics
items.authors: Su Yeon Chang, Supanut Thanasilp, Zoë Holmes, M. Cerezo
items.matched: Practical quantum advantage in quantum simulation
items.result: Polynomial-time classical simulations of quantum dynamics are often outpaced by direct quantum hardware execution due to high one-time quantum sampling and shadow post-processing overheads when preparing unknown input states.
items.question: Whether classically simulable quantum evolutions are in practice more resource-efficient to simulate classically or to execute directly on quantum hardware.
items.limits: Independent unentangled input copies only (no multi-copy quantum memory); unitaries and observables restricted to efficient classical representations.
items.tools: classical shadows · Lie-algebraic simulation (g-sim) · Pauli Propagation · Majorana Propagation · hardware pricing models
items.caption: Estimated total wall-clock time versus qubit count n for direct quantum simulation and classical simulation across IonQ Forte, Google Sycamore, and IBM Heron architectures.
items.abstract: Determining whether a quantum evolution can be efficiently simulated classically is central to understanding the boundary between classical and quantum computation. However, polynomial-time simulability is an asymptotic statement, and does not by itself determine whether the (quantum-inspired) classical simulation is actually practical. Indeed, different polynomial scalings can lead to vastly different computational costs, particularly when expensive preprocessing or quantum data acquisition is required. In this work, we ask whether classically simulable quantum dynamics are in practice more resource-efficient to simulate classically than to execute directly on quantum hardware. We analyze this question using three resource metrics, quantum sample, quantum time, and classical time complexity, for several widely studied classically simulable circuit families. Using representative hardware-level estimates, we identify regimes in which quantum simulation can be faster despite the existence of a polynomial-time classical algorithm, as well as regimes in which classical simulation remains more efficient. At the same time, the large quantum sampling cost needed to characterize unknown input states can make this polynomial-time classical simulation prohibitively expensive with current cloud-based hardware access prices. Ultimately, our work indicates that guarantees of classical simulability with polynomial resources alone are insufficient to determine the preferred implementation.

items.title: One-clean-qubit spectroscopy of simulated Kitaev chains
items.authors: Z. M. McIntyre, Daniel Loss
items.matched: Theory of Trotter Error with Commutator Scaling
items.result: Extracts full 2^N eigenenergies of an N-site transverse-field Ising model and the N single-particle energies of its mapped Kitaev chain via stroboscopic DQC1 readout on a single control spin.
items.question: How can the full spectrum and topological crossover of a simulated Kitaev chain be extracted in quantum-dot spin qubit arrays lacking multi-qubit simultaneous readout?
items.limits: Requires simulation time T_tot > 2π/ δε_min and gate infidelity ε_gate < min[1 / (N(J+h)T_tot), δε_min² / (N h²)]; demonstrated numerically for N=6.
items.tools: Digital-analog quantum simulation · One-clean-qubit (DQC1) model · Jordan-Wigner transformation · Repetition-code control qubit · Drive-engineered Floquet Hamiltonian
items.caption: Stroboscopic control-qubit expectation value vs time, showing resolution of single-particle Kitaev spectrum across trivial and topological regimes under 1/f noise.
items.abstract: Spin qubits in gate-defined quantum dots provide a highly programmable platform for simulating condensed-matter phenomena. In this work, we introduce a digital-analog quantum simulation protocol for extracting the single-particle spectrum of a Kitaev chain. The Kitaev chain is mapped onto qubits via the standard Jordan-Wigner transformation and implemented as a drive-engineered, N-site transverse-field Ising model (TFIM) in a linear array of quantum dots. We show that periodically toggling the analog-simulation parameters conditioned on the state of a control qubit causes the dynamics of this control qubit to stroboscopically match the output of the one-clean-qubit (DQC1) model of computation, thereby yielding the full spectrum of the TFIM from measurements of a single spin. Classical postprocessing can then be used to isolate the N single-particle energies of the Kitaev chain from the 2^N eigenenergies of the TFIM. By varying the strength of the Rabi drive used to engineer the synthetic transverse field, the spectral signature of the crossover from the trivial to the topological regime of the Kitaev chain could then be mapped out with measurements of just one spin.

items.title: Joint Mitigation of Algorithmic and Physical Errors in Noisy Hamiltonian Simulation
items.authors: Shuo Zhou, Xinzhao Wang, Ruiqi Zhang, Xiaoyang Wang, Yi-Cong Zheng, Tongang Li, Shengyu Zhang
items.matched: Theory of Trotter Error with Commutator Scaling
items.result: Tying physical-noise strength to Trotter step size as λ(s)=c(sT)^(p+1) aligns physical and algorithmic errors at order s^p, letting a single 1D Richardson extrapolation replace 2D grid extrapolation with provable commutator-scaling resource overhead.
items.question: Can joint extrapolation along a single coupled path simultaneously eliminate algorithmic Trotter bias and hardware noise while preserving provable commutator scaling?
items.prior: Sequential/2D extrapolation requiring an m ×m' grid of circuit evaluations with independent Trotter and zero-noise fits.
items.limits: Requires noise strengths above the intrinsic device-noise floor; assumes local Hamiltonians with local Lindbladian noise.
items.tools: finite-order Baker-Campbell-Hausdorff truncation · Richardson extrapolation · learned sparse Pauli-Lindblad noise amplification · Sparse Pauli Dynamics
items.caption: Comparison of error-mitigation paths on the step size s vs noise strength λ plane: 2D rectangular Richardson grid needing independent zero-noise and Trotter extrapolations versus coupled 1D path λ(s)=c(sT)^(p+1) reaching (0,0) in a single fit.
items.abstract: Product-formula Hamiltonian simulation is naturally suited to near-term quantum processors, but its accuracy is set by two competing errors: finite-step Trotter bias and physical hardware noise. We introduce a joint extrapolation strategy that ties the tunable per-layer noise strength to the Trotter step size, λ(s)=c(sT)^(p+1) for a p-th order product formula. Along this one-dimensional path, the leading physical-noise and Trotter corrections over the full evolution both enter at order s^p and can be canceled by a single Richardson extrapolation. Building on a previously established finite-order Baker--Campbell--Hausdorff truncation bound, we derive a provably commutator-scaling resource guarantee for the joint extrapolation. For local Hamiltonians with local Lindbladian noise, the protocol mitigates physical noise together with Trotter error with only a constant asymptotic overhead relative to noiseless Trotter extrapolation, provided the required noise strengths lie above the intrinsic device-noise floor. We experimentally demonstrate the protocol for Ising dynamics on a superconducting quantum computer using learned noise amplification. Complementary 100-qubit Sparse Pauli Dynamics (SPD) simulations achieve comparable accuracy to two-dimensional Richardson extrapolation with fewer circuit settings.

items.title: Distributed variational quantum computing with deterministic entanglement tuning
items.authors: Ilhwan Kim, Yong-Su Kim, Kwang Jo Lee, Hyukjoon Kwon, Yosep Kim, Hyang-Tag Lim
items.matched: Practical quantum advantage in quantum simulation
items.result: Distributed variational quantum computing protocol deterministically tunes shared Bell-pair entanglement via LOCC with unit success probability (p_M=1) and concurrence C_M(θ)=cosθ, keeping state infidelity below 0.05 across full range.
items.question: How can entanglement between distributed quantum processing units be tuned continuously and deterministically without the probabilistic losses of filtering or the high Bell-pair consumption of gate teleportation?
items.limits: Demonstrated on bipartite single-qubit photonic processors; feed-forward conditional operations performed offline rather than in real time; pure-state majorization requires initial entanglement to be equal to or greater than target.
items.tools: spontaneous parametric down-conversion (SPDC) · displaced Sagnac interferometer · POVM with path-mode ancilla · COBYLA optimization · quantum state tomography
items.caption: Concurrence (top) and state infidelity (bottom) plotted against the tuning angle θ, demonstrating deterministic modulation of entanglement from 1 down to 0 while keeping state infidelity below 0.05.
items.abstract: Distributed quantum computing offers a scalable route to quantum information processing by entangling spatially separated processors. Although gate teleportation enables universal computation across distributed nodes, it requires repeated consumption of high-fidelity Bell pairs, ancillary qubits, and real-time feedforward, which imposes significant overhead and reduces fidelity. However, many variational quantum algorithms do not demand full universality; rather, they rely on sufficient expressibility to explore solution spaces effectively. Building on this, we propose a distributed variational quantum computing protocol based on deterministic entanglement tuning. In contrast to probabilistic filtering, our approach deterministically modulates pre-shared entanglement using only local operations and classical communication. We validate the protocol through a proof-of-principle experiment by estimating ground-state energies of the He-H⁺ molecule and the Schwinger model, showing that diverse entanglement levels can be engineered to match problem-specific requirements. Our results suggest a practical alternative for near-term distributed quantum applications.

items.title: Quantum transport along a tight-binding chain connected to Markovian reservoirs
items.authors: P. S. Muraev, A. R. Kolovsky, D. N. Maksimov
items.matched: thermalization, many-body localization and quantum scars in driven systems
items.result: Stationary current across a tight-binding chain coupled to boundary Markovian reservoirs is derived analytically for arbitrary on-site dephasing κ. At κ= 0, inter-site currents follow an asymmetric Laplace distribution with covariance cov(hatI_ℓ, hatI_(ℓ+1)) = I_st² / 2 and zero covariance for separation |ℓ- ℓ'| ≥2.
items.question: What are the exact stationary current, site populations, and current fluctuation distributions in a boundary-driven tight-binding chain with dephasing?
items.limits: Non-interacting particles (bosons or fermions). Full many-body characteristic function and current distributions derived specifically for bosons in the absence of dephasing (κ= 0).
items.tools: Lindblad master equation · Single-particle density matrix (SPDM) · Phase-space / characteristic function formalism · Itô stochastic drift-diffusion simulations
items.caption: Probability distribution of bond and boundary currents plotted against analytical predictions (red curves) from stochastic simulations (bins) for κ=0.
items.abstract: We consider quantum transport of non-interacting particles in a tight-binding chain coupled to Markovian reservoirs at its boundaries and subject to uniform on-site dephasing. Using the masterequation approach, we derived the exact analytic solution for the mean current along the chain. This analytic solution is obtained in the framework of single-particle quantum mechanics and, thus, equally applies for transport of non-interacting bosons and fermions. In the absence of phase damping, the results are extended to the complete many-body solution for bosonic problem in the form of anti-normally ordered characteristic function. This function allows us to calculate the distribution function for the current at each bond in the chain as well as the inter-bond current correlation functions.

items.title: Instabilities in self-consistent diagrammatic approaches and how to cure them
items.authors: Marcel Gievers, Herbert Eßl, Stefan Rohshap, Anna Kauch, Alessandro Toschi
items.matched: Probing many-body dynamics on a 51-atom quantum simulator
items.result: Misleading convergence in self-consistent boson-exchange schemes (TRILEX, SBE, MBE) is caused solely by algorithmic iteration instability—where Jacobian eigenvalues exceed unity—rather than fundamental multivaluedness of the Luttinger–Ward functional. Inverting the unstable Jacobian eigendirections stabilizes convergence to exact physical solutions across strong-coupling regimes and through vertex divergences.
items.question: What causes self-consistent diagrammatic boson-exchange algorithms to converge to unphysical fixed points at intermediate-to-strong electronic coupling, and how can they be stabilized?
items.limits: Demonstrated on exactly solvable local models (Hubbard atom and zero-point model) without spatial momentum dependence.
items.tools: Boson-exchange formalism (TRILEX, SBE, MBE) · Jacobian eigenspectrum inversion · Hubbard atom model · Zero-point model
items.caption: Phase space of coupling βU versus chemical potential shift βδμ. Shaded regions mark where standard iteration fails (|j_α| > 1), defining the threshold mixing parameter p(c=1) required for stability across TRILEX, SBE, and MBE.
items.abstract: While self-consistent diagrammatic approaches are widely used to compute the physical properties of correlated quantum materials, their applicability may get severely hindered precisely in the parameter regions, where the most exciting physics is observed. One of the major issues, referred to as "misleading convergence", is the tendency of iterative schemes to converge to unphysical fixed points for intermediate-to-strong electronic interactions, regardless of numerical accuracy of the computation. Here, we explicitly verify that the origin of this problem in several established self-consistent many-electron approaches, defined in the general diagrammatic framework of the boson-exchange formalism, resides exclusively in the stability condition of the respective iteration schemes, and not in an intrinsic breakdown of their self-consistent diagrammatic description. This insight enables a simple and general remedy, as recently proposed in Phys. Rev. Lett. 137, 016502 (2026): The redefinition of the iterative procedure, by inverting the unstable eigendirections of the Jacobian associated to the fixed point of the self-consistent algorithm. We illustrate the successful outcome of this procedure by means of systematic calculations performed on testbed, exactly solvable, models. Our results demonstrate that the physical fixed point of the diagrammatic schemes we considered can be stabilized, de facto, across the entire parameter range, including the most challenging nonperturbative/strong-coupling regimes.

Shaded regions mark where standard iteration fails (<math xmlns="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML"><mrow><mi>|</mi><msub><mi>j</mi><mi>α</mi></msub><mi>|</mi><mo>></mo><mn>1</mn></mrow></math>), defining the threshold mixing parameter <math xmlns="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML"><mrow><mi>p</mi><mrow><mo fence="true" form="prefix" stretchy="false">(</mo><mi>c</mi><mo>=</mo><mn>1</mn><mo fence="true" form="postfix" stretchy="false">)</mo></mrow></mrow></math> required for stability across TRILEX, SBE, and MBE.

items.title: Local decoders for fault-tolerant quantum computation and translation-invariant stabilizer codes
items.authors: Nathaniel Selub, Aditya Bhardwaj, Ethan Lake
items.matched: Evidence for the utility of quantum computing before fault tolerance
items.result: Every translation-invariant topological Pauli stabilizer code is locally decodable under phenomenological noise with a non-zero threshold, and a 2D fault-tolerant quantum computer can operate using strictly local operations and constant quantum and classical resource density.
items.question: Can scalable fault-tolerant quantum computation based on topological codes in fewer than four dimensions be implemented using strictly local operations, bounded communication speeds, and constant resource density?
items.prior: All prior local decoders for two-dimensional topological codes required per-site classical resources scaling at least polylogarithmically with system size, and prior fault-tolerant architectures in <4 spatial dimensions required non-local classical computation or communication.
items.limits: Classical computation and communication components are assumed to be noiseless; phenomenological noise assumes p-bounded Pauli and bit-flip errors on data qubits and syndrome measurements.
items.tools: cellular-automaton (CA) decoder · spacetime multiscale clustering · folded surface code · lattice surgery · hierarchical slice architecture
items.caption: Schematic of the 2D local fault-tolerant quantum architecture, showing a 1D array of folded surface-code patches decoded on-chip by constant-density classical cellular automata alongside a local 2D classical program-control computer.
items.abstract: We construct the first fully spatially local fault-tolerant quantum computer based on topological codes in fewer than four spatial dimensions. Our construction is a two-dimensional architecture that uses only geometrically local quantum and classical operations, bounded-speed classical communication and computation, and a constant density of quantum and classical resources. The core component is a new time-translation-invariant cellular-automaton decoder for the surface code. This decoder preserves logical information for a time stretched-exponential in the code distance and operates continuously during state injection, stabilizer-state preparation, lattice surgery, and transversal readout. We also prove that every translation-invariant topological Pauli stabilizer code is locally decodable under phenomenological noise.

items.title: Engineered two-photon dissipative confinement of a Kerr-cat qubit using SISIS quantum circuit refrigerator
items.authors: Shumpei Masuda, Tsuyoshi Yamamoto, Shuji Nakamura, Daichi Sugiyama, Akiyoshi Tomonaga
items.matched: Charge-insensitive qubit design derived from the Cooper pair box
items.result: Superconductor–insulator–superconductor–insulator–superconductor (SISIS) quantum circuit refrigerator selectively activates two-photon absorption near eV/h ≃82.8GHz, cooling dephasing-induced leakage states back into Kerr parametric oscillator qubit subspace while avoiding single-photon parity-flipping errors.
items.question: Can a quantum circuit refrigerator suppress pure-dephasing leakage in Kerr-cat qubits without driving parity-changing single-photon phase-flip errors?
items.prior: SINIS-based QCR suppresses dephasing leakage via single-photon absorption but broad normal-metal density of states accelerates intra-qubit phase-flip errors.
items.limits: Theoretical and numerical simulation; assumes second-order perturbative Born–Markov coupling, zero magnetic field, and specific Dynes subgap density of states parameter γD.
items.tools: SISIS junction QCR · Kerr parametric oscillator (KPO) · Born–Markov master equation · quasiparticle tunneling rate via Fermi's golden rule
items.caption: Excited leakage state populations (A) and qubit state population (B) over time under dephasing and loss. SISIS QCR suppresses leakage nearly as effectively as SINIS while maintaining much higher logical state population against phase flips.
items.abstract: Kerr-cat qubits realized in periodically driven superconducting nonlinear resonators are a promising platform for quantum information processing with biased noise. Pure dephasing in such systems induces leakage out of the qubit subspace, motivating the use of quantum circuit refrigeration (QCR) to remove excess excitations. While conventional superconductor--insulator--normal-metal--insulator--superconductor (SINIS)-based QCRs can suppress leakage via single-photon absorption, they also enhance QCR-induced phase-flip errors. Here we investigate a QCR based on a superconductor--insulator--superconductor--insulator--superconductor (SISIS) junction coupled to a Kerr parametric oscillator (KPO). We show that a SISIS-based QCR can operate in a regime where single-photon processes are suppressed while two-photon absorption dominates. As a result, the proposed SISIS-based QCR achieves strong suppression of dephasing-induced leakage while substantially reducing the increase in phase-flip errors associated with QCR operation. These results demonstrate that the proposed SISIS-based QCR provides an effective approach for mitigating leakage while limiting QCR-induced phase-flip errors in Kerr-cat qubits.

items.title: One-clean-qubit spectroscopy of simulated Kitaev chains
items.authors: Z. M. McIntyre, Daniel Loss
items.matched: Semiconductor spin qubits
items.result: Extracts full 2^N eigenenergies of an N-site transverse-field Ising model and the N single-particle energies of its mapped Kitaev chain via stroboscopic DQC1 readout on a single control spin.
items.question: How can the full spectrum and topological crossover of a simulated Kitaev chain be extracted in quantum-dot spin qubit arrays lacking multi-qubit simultaneous readout?
items.limits: Requires simulation time T_tot > 2π/ δε_min and gate infidelity ε_gate < min[1 / (N(J+h)T_tot), δε_min² / (N h²)]; demonstrated numerically for N=6.
items.tools: Digital-analog quantum simulation · One-clean-qubit (DQC1) model · Jordan-Wigner transformation · Repetition-code control qubit · Drive-engineered Floquet Hamiltonian
items.caption: Stroboscopic control-qubit expectation value vs time, showing resolution of single-particle Kitaev spectrum across trivial and topological regimes under 1/f noise.
items.abstract: Spin qubits in gate-defined quantum dots provide a highly programmable platform for simulating condensed-matter phenomena. In this work, we introduce a digital-analog quantum simulation protocol for extracting the single-particle spectrum of a Kitaev chain. The Kitaev chain is mapped onto qubits via the standard Jordan-Wigner transformation and implemented as a drive-engineered, N-site transverse-field Ising model (TFIM) in a linear array of quantum dots. We show that periodically toggling the analog-simulation parameters conditioned on the state of a control qubit causes the dynamics of this control qubit to stroboscopically match the output of the one-clean-qubit (DQC1) model of computation, thereby yielding the full spectrum of the TFIM from measurements of a single spin. Classical postprocessing can then be used to isolate the N single-particle energies of the Kitaev chain from the 2^N eigenenergies of the TFIM. By varying the strength of the Rabi drive used to engineer the synthetic transverse field, the spectral signature of the crossover from the trivial to the topological regime of the Kitaev chain could then be mapped out with measurements of just one spin.

items.title: Programmable CMOS DAC Operating in Cryogenic Environments for Controlling Superconducting Qubits
items.authors: A. Pelteku, D. Reitz, M. Covington, A. Frederick, H. Adebayo, K. D. Hillaire, N. Mitran, Z. Steffen, R. Schwartz, Z. Stegen, J. X. Przybysz, J. Yager, C. Walter, T. Graves, D. Meyer, J. Clark, G. R. Boyd, A. Pesetski
items.matched: scaling up: crossbar addressing, cryo-CMOS control, qubit interconnects
items.result: Implemented cryo-CMOS current-steering DAC in planar 90 nm CMOS process providing digitally tunable pulse amplitude, rise/fall slopes, and trigger-controlled pulse width for superconducting qubit control and readout.
items.question: Can a digitally tunable CMOS current-based DAC operate reliably at cryogenic temperatures to control flux and readout in superconducting circuits?
items.limits: Demonstrated for specific superconducting circuit driving requirements at cryogenic temperatures.
items.tools: planar 90 nm CMOS process · cryogenic measurement setup · current-steering DAC architecture
items.abstract: This paper presents the design and test results of a CMOS current-based Digital to Analog Converter (DAC) that operates at cryogenic temperatures and that can be used to precisely control the amount of flux coupled to qubits or that can be used in the readout of superconducting circuits. The current pulse output can be controlled in terms of its amplitude, rise and fall slopes, via digital controls, and pulse width, via external triggers, while driving a superconducting circuit. The design has been implemented in a planar 90 nm CMOS process and test results closely match circuit predictions. The solution's wide degree of digital tunability affords potential application of the same device to many types of quantum circuits, beyond those discussed here. Due to the wide-ranging flexibility of digital CMOS control, we envision that this DAC design will enable the next generation of high-fidelity cryo-CMOS control architectures for superconducting qubits.

items.title: Dephasing-driven suppression of superradiance and metastable dynamics in the anisotropic open Rabi model
items.authors: Jivyanshu Priya, Pragna Das, Auditya Sharma
items.matched: cavity QED, atom-photon interfaces and quantum networks
items.result: Atomic spontaneous emission at rate γ stabilizes a metastable superradiant phase via a coherent phase-space bridge, whereas pure dephasing at rate δ actively destroys this coherence and suppresses superradiant order.
items.question: How do atomic spontaneous emission and pure dephasing compete with cavity loss to modify nonequilibrium criticality and metastable dynamics in the anisotropic open Rabi model?
items.limits: Semiclassical limit η= Ω/ω→∞; numerical calculations truncated at bosonic cutoff N_cutoff ≤400.
items.tools: mean-field stability analysis · exact Liouvillian diagonalization · Lindblad master equation · Wigner quasiprobability distribution
items.caption: Wigner quasiprobability distributions W(α) of the steady-state cavity field across normal, superradiant, and bistable phases under combinations of cavity loss κ, spontaneous emission γ, and pure dephasing δ.
items.abstract: Finite-component light-matter systems realize dissipative phase transitions in a single controllable atom-cavity setup, but how atomic dephasing - ubiquitous in real cavity- and circuit-QED devices - affects this criticality remains unknown. We study the anisotropic open Rabi model under cavity decay, spontaneous emission, and atomic dephasing together. We show that when spontaneous emission stabilizes a long-lived metastable superradiant phase, atomic dephasing actively competes with it - eroding its coherence and shortening the lifetime. This direct competition reveals that a dissipation channel's microscopic character, not its strength, controls its nonequilibrium criticality - a distinction directly tunable via independent spontaneous-emission and dephasing rates in circuit-QED and trapped-ion platforms.

items.title: Error Correction in a Distributed Quantum Computer
items.authors: E. M. Ainley, A. Agrawal, T. Araki, A. R. Martínez, D. Main, E. Malinowski, J. A. Blackmore, S. Chen, P. Drmota, M. Mallweger, D. P. Nadlinger, R. Srinivas, S. C. Benjamin, G. Araneda, D. M. Lucas
items.matched: Cavity-based quantum networks with single atoms and optical photons
items.result: Real-time distributed error detection and feedforward correction demonstrated across two trapped-ion quantum processors separated by ∼2m. Stabilises logical qubit in a [[2,1,1]] repetition code and actively corrects arbitrary single-qubit Pauli errors on a distributed Bell state.
items.question: Can stabiliser measurements and quantum error detection/correction be performed across spatially separated quantum processors using photonic interconnects?
items.limits: Interleaved recooling reduces entanglement generation rate from ∼100s⁻¹ to ∼10s⁻¹. Calibration drifts and gate phase offsets not fully captured in error budget.
items.tools: trapped-ion processors (⁸⁸Sr⁺, ⁴³Ca⁺) · photonic interconnects · mixed-species geometric phase gates · real-time classical feedforward (TTL link)
items.caption: Remote stabiliser measurement scheme and network qubit parity readout. Network qubit parity plotted against analysis pulse phase demonstrates syndrome discrimination between +1 and -1 eigenspaces of data-qubit pairs.
items.abstract: Building fault-tolerant quantum computers with large numbers of logical qubits requires both scalable hardware architectures and error-correcting codes that make efficient use of physical qubits. Photonic interconnects address both of these challenges by allowing the physical qubits to be distributed across multiple processors while providing the non-local connectivity necessary to implement resource-efficient codes such as high-rate quantum low-density parity-check (qLDPC) codes. A key requirement for realising this architecture is the ability to perform stabiliser measurements between remote processors, which has not previously been demonstrated experimentally. Here we report the first experimental demonstration of distributed quantum error detection and correction. We generate entanglement between network qubits in two separate trapped-ion processors and use it to perform remote syndrome measurements on data qubits. We first realise a distributed [[2, 1, 1]] repetition code, detecting phase-flip errors on a logical qubit encoded across the two modules in real time and suppressing logical errors. We then combine these mid-circuit syndrome measurements with real-time feedforward to actively correct arbitrary single-qubit Pauli errors on a distributed Bell state. These results provide an experimental foundation for quantum error correction (QEC) across modular quantum architectures.

items.title: Optimized quantum state transfer in a quasiperiodic ultracold atomic gas
items.authors: Andreas Völkering, Arnob Kumar Ghosh, Patric Holmvall, Paolo Molignini
items.matched: Quantum information with Rydberg atoms
items.result: Adiabatic edge-to-edge quantum state transfer of localized winding states across a 1D quasiperiodic optical lattice achieves fidelities up to 99.6% under locally adiabatic protocols.
items.question: How can quantum state transfer protocols based on quasiperiodic edge winding states be efficiently implemented in realistic continuum ultracold atomic systems?
items.limits: Noninteracting bosons (g=0), single-particle regime, finite-size rational approximants (N_w = 13, 21), simulation rather than experiment.
items.tools: Aubry–André–Harper (AAH) model · locally adiabatic driving protocols · MCTDH-X simulation · two-level Landau–Zener approximation
items.caption: Transfer fidelity F plotted against dimensionless transfer duration TJ_bulk/ℏ and detuning strength ρ for the tangent protocol (N=0) and the Roland-Cerf protocol (N=1), showing coherent fidelity oscillations and improved high-ρ robustness for N=1.
items.abstract: Ultracold atomic systems offer a highly controllable platform for investigating quantum state transfer through the precise dynamical manipulation of system parameters. While quantized Thouless pumping has been extensively explored in these systems, adiabatic edge-to-edge transfer of localized quantum states remains largely unexplored. Here, we consider a one-dimensional ultracold atomic gas confined in a bichromatic optical lattice realizing a quasiperiodic Aubry--André--Harper system. We use its edge-localized winding states to implement quantum state transfer between opposite boundaries. Starting from the instantaneous spectral properties of the corresponding tight-binding model, we construct locally adiabatic protocols and extend the approach to higher protocol orders. We then simulate their dynamics under the full continuum bichromatic-lattice Hamiltonian. Our results reveal a tradeoff between edge localization and the minimum spectral gap: strongly localized states require longer transfer times, but can benefit substantially from higher protocol orders. We are also able to capture the main fidelity trends and coherent oscillations over a broad parameter regime using an effective two-level Landau--Zener description. Our results provide practical guidelines for selecting experimentally accessible parameters and tailoring quantum transfer protocols in quasiperiodic ultracold atomic systems.

items.title: Error Correction in a Distributed Quantum Computer
items.authors: E. M. Ainley, A. Agrawal, T. Araki, A. R. Martínez, D. Main, E. Malinowski, J. A. Blackmore, S. Chen, P. Drmota, M. Mallweger, D. P. Nadlinger, R. Srinivas, S. C. Benjamin, G. Araneda, D. M. Lucas
items.matched: High-threshold and low-overhead fault-tolerant quantum memory
items.result: Real-time distributed error detection and feedforward correction demonstrated across two trapped-ion quantum processors separated by ∼2m. Stabilises logical qubit in a [[2,1,1]] repetition code and actively corrects arbitrary single-qubit Pauli errors on a distributed Bell state.
items.question: Can stabiliser measurements and quantum error detection/correction be performed across spatially separated quantum processors using photonic interconnects?
items.limits: Interleaved recooling reduces entanglement generation rate from ∼100s⁻¹ to ∼10s⁻¹. Calibration drifts and gate phase offsets not fully captured in error budget.
items.tools: trapped-ion processors (⁸⁸Sr⁺, ⁴³Ca⁺) · photonic interconnects · mixed-species geometric phase gates · real-time classical feedforward (TTL link)

items.abstract: Building fault-tolerant quantum computers with large numbers of logical qubits requires both scalable hardware architectures and error-correcting codes that make efficient use of physical qubits. Photonic interconnects address both of these challenges by allowing the physical qubits to be distributed across multiple processors while providing the non-local connectivity necessary to implement resource-efficient codes such as high-rate quantum low-density parity-check (qLDPC) codes. A key requirement for realising this architecture is the ability to perform stabiliser measurements between remote processors, which has not previously been demonstrated experimentally. Here we report the first experimental demonstration of distributed quantum error detection and correction. We generate entanglement between network qubits in two separate trapped-ion processors and use it to perform remote syndrome measurements on data qubits. We first realise a distributed [[2, 1, 1]] repetition code, detecting phase-flip errors on a logical qubit encoded across the two modules in real time and suppressing logical errors. We then combine these mid-circuit syndrome measurements with real-time feedforward to actively correct arbitrary single-qubit Pauli errors on a distributed Bell state. These results provide an experimental foundation for quantum error correction (QEC) across modular quantum architectures.

items.title: Extremely Low-Cost Magic State Preparation toward Fault-Tolerant Quantum Computing
items.authors: Jianshuo Gao, Xiao Yuan, Yuan Yao
items.matched: High-threshold and low-overhead fault-tolerant quantum memory
items.result: Postselected infidelity scales as 210.2p³ + O(p⁴) under uniform circuit-level depolarizing noise, bounded at 2.2×10⁻⁷ at p=10⁻³ (99.9% joint confidence, 86.9% acceptance) using 19 qubits and 82 CNOT gates.
items.question: Can co-designing the stabilizer-generator basis with flag circuits reduce the qubit and circuit overhead of fault-tolerant magic-state preparation?
items.prior: 100 CNOTs, 31 measurements, and leading correction error 25.5p² in the two-block benchmark of Daguerre and Kim (2025).
items.limits: Applies strictly to destructive postselected error-detection diagnostic; minimum-weight error correction has leading infidelity 183.81p². Omits memory errors, routing, idle time, crosstalk, and coherent leakage.
items.tools: quantum Reed-Muller to Steane code gauge fixing · jointly flagged syndrome extraction · destructive error detection · exact low-order fault enumeration · stratified Monte Carlo sampling
items.caption: Postselected logical infidelity versus physical depolarizing error rate p, showing exact analytical O(p³) scaling and the finite-p upper-bound certificate at p=10⁻³.
items.abstract: Fault-tolerant preparation of non-Clifford resource states is a major contributor to the overhead of quantum computation, motivating protocols that achieve high output fidelity with minimal qubit and circuit costs. We introduce a low-cost magic-state preparation protocol in which the choice of stabilizer generators is co-designed with the flag gadgets, allowing the syndrome-extraction circuit itself to filter correlated faults across a non-Clifford layer. The protocol prepares a logical plus state in the 15-qubit quantum Reed-Muller code, applies a transversal T gate, and gauge-fixes the same register into the seven-qubit Steane code. By reorganizing equivalent Z-type stabilizer generators into jointly flagged measurement groups, the protocol eliminates all accepted logical-error contributions arising from one or two circuit faults under destructive error detection. Under a uniform circuit-level depolarizing noise model, the postselected infidelity is 210.2p³+O(p⁴). At p=10⁻³, exact low-order enumeration combined with stratified sampling bounds the infidelity by 2.2×10⁻⁷ at 99.9% joint confidence, while retaining an acceptance probability of 86.9%. The complete circuit requires only 19 qubits and 82 CNOT gates. These results demonstrate that stabilizer-generator design can substantially reduce the cost of postselected magic-state preparation, although corrected operation and the fidelity of an unmeasured output block require separate analysis.

items.title: Sparse-Blossom Decoding in o(1) Time
items.authors: Ryo Mikami, Hayata Yamasaki
items.matched: High-threshold and low-overhead fault-tolerant quantum memory
items.result: Parallel sparse blossom decodes an O(d)-round syndrome extraction window on a distance-d rotated surface code in average parallel runtime bounded by exp[O((loglogd)²)], yielding o(1) average parallel runtime per round.
items.question: Can minimum-weight perfect matching decoding via sparse blossom be parallelized with an exact correctness guarantee and a runtime per round that scales as o(1)?
items.prior: Decoding time per round scaled as O(d^(2.34)) in sequential sparse blossom, requiring O(d^(3.34)) total latency for a d-round window (Higgott and Gidney 2023).
items.limits: Circuit-level local stochastic error model below a finite threshold p_th, with finite-size numerical comparisons assuming negligible parallelization overhead.
items.tools: parallel sparse blossom · hierarchical error clustering · minimum-weight embedded matching · rotated surface code simulation
items.caption: Event counts per shot per syndrome extraction round plotted against code distance d∈9,13,…,49, demonstrating that parallel sparse-blossom runtime per round decreases with increasing d at low physical error rates.
items.abstract: Matching-based decoding is widely used in quantum error correction, and accelerating it is key to enabling fast and scalable fault-tolerant quantum computation. Minimum-weight perfect matching (MWPM) decoding provides rigorous guarantees for error suppression, while sparse blossom enables its practical implementation at modest problem sizes. However, the runtime of existing sparse-blossom implementations unavoidably increases with problem size, motivating a rigorous parallelization framework that guarantees correctness and a runtime shorter than the syndrome-extraction timescale. Here, we present such a framework and prove that the resulting parallel sparse-blossom algorithm produces the same correction as the original, non-parallel sparse blossom. For the rotated surface code with code distance d and physical error rates below a finite threshold, we prove that the average parallel runtime of decoding for O(d) rounds of syndrome extraction is upper bounded by a quasi-polylogarithmic function of d. For a d-round decoding window, this implies that the average parallel runtime per round is o(1). We also perform numerical simulation to identify conditions under which the parallel runtime per round decreases with increasing code distance. These results suggest that increasing code distance need not lead to longer parallel decoding times, providing a foundation for scalable parallel matching-based decoding.

items.title: Modeling Quantum Error Detection with Transition Matrices
items.authors: Rohan S. Kumar, Ben Foxman, Yongshan Ding
items.matched: High-threshold and low-overhead fault-tolerant quantum memory
items.result: Code-adapted basis-population dynamics under circuit-level stochastic Pauli noise are mapped to an exact (2ⁿ+1)-dimensional Markov kernel, reducing Steane code dynamics from 129 to 11 states via orbit lumping.
items.question: At what granularity can the multi-cycle dynamics and post-selection of quantum error detection protocols under noise be modeled exactly and tractably?
items.limits: Restricted to circuit-level stochastic Pauli noise and data-preserving Clifford syndrome-extraction circuits; transition matrix scales as 2ⁿ + 1 before symmetry lumping.
items.tools: Markov transition matrices · stabilizer code-adapted basis · absorbing Markov chain reduction · Markov orbit lumping · Stim Monte Carlo simulations
items.caption: Accepted logical population and rejection probabilities as a function of integer QED cycle count for the [[4,2,2]] and [[5,1,3]] codes at physical error rate ε=10⁻³, comparing exact transition-matrix curves with 10⁶-shot Stim Monte Carlo data.
items.abstract: We construct an explicit transition matrix that exactly describes code-adapted basis-population dynamics of stabilizer codes under circuit-level stochastic Pauli noise. The matrix is expressed in a code-adapted basis that captures probability flow between logical-basis labels and syndrome sectors. For quantum error detection (QED), we incorporate post-selection by aggregating rejected outcomes into an absorbing state, so that a single transition matrix represents a full clock cycle of gates, syndrome extraction, and post-selection. Additionally, we characterize when protocol symmetries permit exact lumping to simpler, more interpretable models. The transition matrix framework enables direct application of classical stochastic-matrix techniques to analyze multi-cycle QED protocols. First, we identify a leading-order obstruction to a stationary logical-only accepted-map description, and quantify the accepted leakage injection from QED-check imperfections that causes it. Second, we express leading-order QED efficiency as a function of check frequency in terms of physically meaningful parameters, and prove that less frequent checks improve efficiency to leading order. We evaluate the framework on the [[4,2,2]] and [[5,1,3]] codes under depolarizing gate noise and readout errors: transition-matrix predictions agree with million-shot Stim Monte Carlo at the scale of the reported confidence intervals, and matrix-computed results illustrate the first-cycle transient and interval-dependent efficiency. More broadly, the transition-matrix formalism provides both an analytical foundation for QED analysis and an interpretable tool for understanding code behavior under realistic noise.

items.title: Testing and Diagnosing Parameter Miscalibration in Probabilistic Error Cancellation via Direct Fidelity Estimation
items.authors: Francesc Sabater, Tristan Kraft, Carlos A. Riofrío, Barbara Kraus
items.matched: High-threshold and low-overhead fault-tolerant quantum memory
items.result: DFE overlap Y≡Tr(ρwidetildeρ) and purity mathscrP≡Tr(widetildeρ²) of PEC-mitigated state widetildeρ serve as hardware witnesses and directional diagnostics: consistent underestimation yields Y ≤1 and mathscrP ≤1, while consistent overestimation yields Y ≥1 and mathscrP ≥1.
items.question: How to test whether the noise parameters used in Probabilistic Error Cancellation (PEC) are accurate directly on hardware, and diagnose whether they are overestimated or underestimated?
items.limits: Requires positive Pauli fidelities (>1/2 identity coefficient) and absence of hybrid miscalibration; overestimation directionality for Y in arbitrary circuits holds perturbatively under a nondegeneracy condition, while purity condition mathscrP holds non-perturbatively.
items.tools: Direct Fidelity Estimation (DFE) · Probabilistic Error Cancellation (PEC) · Two-copy purity estimator · Classically simulable surrogate circuits
items.caption: DFE overlap Tr(widetildeρρ) plotted against assumed depolarizing parameter widetildep_e for N=50 qubits and s=50, 100, 150 gates. The curve crosses 1 exactly at the true parameter p_e=0.02, being <1 for underestimated widetildep_e and >1 for overestimated widetildep_e.
items.abstract: Probabilistic Error Cancellation (PEC) is a standard technique for mitigating noise in quantum computations, but its unbiasedness relies on accurate knowledge of the underlying noise parameters. In practice, these parameters are inferred from experimental data and may be inaccurate. We introduce a protocol that tests PEC parameter consistency on hardware by applying Direct Fidelity Estimation (DFE) to the effective mitigated state. The resulting DFE overlap serves not only as a witness of parameter miscalibration but, under appropriate conditions, also reveals whether the PEC parameters have been overestimated or underestimated. We establish this behavior for arbitrary circuits under global depolarizing noise and for Clifford circuits under general Pauli-stochastic noise. For arbitrary circuits subject to Pauli-stochastic noise, the underestimation result holds generally, while the corresponding overestimation result is established perturbatively for sufficiently small consistent miscalibrations under an additional nondegeneracy condition. We further show that the purity of the effective mitigated operator provides a more general diagnostic, allowing the miscalibration direction to be identified for arbitrary circuits and arbitrary parameter deviations. Finally, we describe a two-copy PEC procedure for measuring this quantity and show that, together with the DFE overlap, it determines the Hilbert-Schmidt distance from the ideal state. The sampling overhead incurred by our protocol is the same as that of PEC, and we discuss strategies to improve it.

items.question: How can quantum computational power be directly benchmarked and compared across disparate physical and logical architectures relative to utility-scale challenge problems?
items.prior: Quantum volume and physical gate error rates; quantum volume scaling requires exponential classical verification and does not map directly to fault-tolerant utility resource requirements.

items.abstract: Quantum computing hardware is advancing rapidly toward utility-scale machines that will enable scientific breakthroughs. Many teams are pursuing distinct and difficult-to-compare routes to this goal, using different qubit technologies and logical architectures. Tracking progress toward quantum utility therefore requires rigorous benchmarks that measure computational capability relative to utility-scale challenge problems and enable fair comparison across disparate platforms. Here we demonstrate direct, cross-platform measurement of quantum computational capability using a new benchmark that quantifies the size of the largest computationally relevant quantum circuits that a machine can execute successfully and the speed at which it can execute them. We apply this quantum universal operation performance system (QUOPS) experimentally to leading processors from Quantinuum, Google, and IBM, computing directly on physical qubits. Translating state-of-the-art resource requirements for recognized challenge problems that represent useful quantum computation into effective QUOPS circuit sizes shows that computational capability must grow by 5 orders of magnitude, motivating fault-tolerant approaches. We use the same benchmark to assess the performance of a simple fault-tolerant logical-qubit processor implemented on up to eight [[7,1,3]]-encoded logical qubits using Quantinuum Helios-1, and project the growth of capability across successive generations of fault-tolerant quantum computers to show how QUOPS can track progress toward quantum scientific utility.

items.title: Reinforcement Learning for Syndrome Extraction
items.authors: John Zhuoyang Ye, Aarav Pabla, Jens Palsberg
items.matched: quantum LDPC codes and low-overhead fault tolerance
items.result: FastSched uses reinforcement learning and importance sampling to synthesize syndrome extraction schedules, reducing logical error rate by 25.9% versus AlphaSyndrome and 71.7% versus PropHunt on average, reaching a 97.8% reduction for distance-15 surface codes.
items.question: How can automatic schedule synthesis find quantum error correction syndrome extraction schedules with low logical error rates without sacrificing scalability to large code distances?
items.prior: AlphaSyndrome (MCTS) and PropHunt (MaxSAT) synthesized schedules matching or improving hand-designed baselines, but suffered from poor scaling at large distance or degraded logical error rates.
items.limits: Evaluated under simulated noise models (e.g. Brisbane noise), one noisy extraction round, ideal boundaries, and specific decoders (PyMatching, BP-OSD). Search ceilings capped at 10 to 30 minutes.
items.tools: Reinforcement learning · Importance sampling · Proximal policy optimization (PPO) · Rare-event estimation
items.caption: Logical error rate on a logarithmic vertical axis versus rotated surface-code distance from 3 to 15 on the horizontal axis. FastSched maintains lower logical error rates than AlphaSyndrome and PropHunt across all evaluated code distances.
items.abstract: A key subtask of quantum error correction is to extract a syndrome that, if nontrivial, signals an error. The number of possible ways to extract a syndrome grows exponentially with the syndrome size, and these implementations vary greatly in fault tolerance, as measured by their logical error rates. This creates a natural search problem: find an implementation with a low logical error rate. Previous work solves this problem but sacrifices either solution quality or scalability. In this paper, we use reinforcement learning and importance sampling to outperform previous work at all scales. Compared with the state of the art automatic scheduling tools AlphaSyndrome and PropHunt, our tool reduces the logical error rate by 25.9% and 71.7% on average, respectively, culminating with a reduction of 97.8% for a surface code with distance 15.

items.authors: Vadym Kliuchnikov, Justin Lietz, Fernando Pastawski
items.matched: High-threshold and low-overhead fault-tolerant quantum memory

items.question: How can detector error models be constructed incrementally and modularly from reusable logical gadgets without reanalyzing the full physical circuit?

items.limits: Stabilizer circuits with stochastic Pauli noise. Connected ports must share matching stabilizer codes and code presentations.

items.abstract: Fault-tolerant quantum programs thread together reusable logical operations, yet correcting errors requires comparing measurements across operation boundaries. Correlations tie each operation's error analysis to the computation around it. Adaptive computation makes this a runtime challenge: measurement results determine which operation comes next, so the error analysis must keep pace with execution. We introduce extended detector error models (EDEMs), which compose in sequence and in parallel, mirroring the composition of physical realizations and their detector contracts. We prove how detectors, the measurement parities used to diagnose errors, can be split across circuit boundaries, and establish conditions under which composition recovers the assembled circuit's detector error model. This structure supports symbolic precompilation and analysis of entire families of circuits. It also defines error models for decoding windows and the boundary information through which committed corrections affect subsequent windows. The same interface thus connects the design of individual logical operations to the decoding of an unfolding quantum program.

items.title: Sparse-Blossom Decoding in o(1) Time
items.authors: Ryo Mikami, Hayata Yamasaki
items.matched: Toward the first quantum simulation with quantum speedup
items.result: Parallel sparse blossom decodes an O(d)-round syndrome extraction window on a distance-d rotated surface code in average parallel runtime bounded by exp[O((loglogd)²)], yielding o(1) average parallel runtime per round.
items.question: Can minimum-weight perfect matching decoding via sparse blossom be parallelized with an exact correctness guarantee and a runtime per round that scales as o(1)?
items.prior: Decoding time per round scaled as O(d^(2.34)) in sequential sparse blossom, requiring O(d^(3.34)) total latency for a d-round window (Higgott and Gidney 2023).
items.limits: Circuit-level local stochastic error model below a finite threshold p_th, with finite-size numerical comparisons assuming negligible parallelization overhead.
items.tools: parallel sparse blossom · hierarchical error clustering · minimum-weight embedded matching · rotated surface code simulation
items.caption: Event counts per shot per syndrome extraction round plotted against code distance d∈9,13,…,49, demonstrating that parallel sparse-blossom runtime per round decreases with increasing d at low physical error rates.
items.abstract: Matching-based decoding is widely used in quantum error correction, and accelerating it is key to enabling fast and scalable fault-tolerant quantum computation. Minimum-weight perfect matching (MWPM) decoding provides rigorous guarantees for error suppression, while sparse blossom enables its practical implementation at modest problem sizes. However, the runtime of existing sparse-blossom implementations unavoidably increases with problem size, motivating a rigorous parallelization framework that guarantees correctness and a runtime shorter than the syndrome-extraction timescale. Here, we present such a framework and prove that the resulting parallel sparse-blossom algorithm produces the same correction as the original, non-parallel sparse blossom. For the rotated surface code with code distance d and physical error rates below a finite threshold, we prove that the average parallel runtime of decoding for O(d) rounds of syndrome extraction is upper bounded by a quasi-polylogarithmic function of d. For a d-round decoding window, this implies that the average parallel runtime per round is o(1). We also perform numerical simulation to identify conditions under which the parallel runtime per round decreases with increasing code distance. These results suggest that increasing code distance need not lead to longer parallel decoding times, providing a foundation for scalable parallel matching-based decoding.

items.title: A Simple Quantum Linear-System Solver via Dissipation
items.authors: Zhong-Xia Shang
items.matched: Quantum Algorithm for Linear Systems of Equations
items.result: Purely dissipative Lindbladian solves Ax=b via residual-reset jumps with trace-distance mixing time Θ(κ² log(1/ε)) and digital quantum query complexity O (κ² log(1/ε) (log(κ/ε))/(loglog(κ/ε))).
items.question: Is it possible to solve linear systems from dissipation?
items.prior: was O(κlog(1/ε)) query complexity in coherent algorithms (Costa et al. 2022, Chakraborty et al. 2023)
items.limits: Requires 0 < ε< 1/4, κ≥1, and unitary access to block encoding U_A and state preparation U_b.
items.tools: residual kernel encoding · purely dissipative Lindbladian · collective block encoding · Lindbladian simulation
items.caption: Schematic of population flow in the dissipative solver showing jump-induced reset to state |r⟩ and decay towards the target stationary state.
items.abstract: Dissipation has been recently demonstrated as a powerful primitive for designing quantum algorithms. We apply this viewpoint directly to linear-system solving, Ax=b. We construct a simple purely dissipative Lindbladian whose unique fixed point encodes the linear-system solution. We prove dimension-independent trace-distance mixing in Θ(κ²log(1/eps)) time. We then show how to run this Lindbladian on digital quantum computers via collective block encoding and Lindbladian simulation, resulting in an O (κ²log(1/eps) (log(κ/eps))/(loglog(κ/eps))) query complexity for both U_A, the block encoding of A, and U_b, the |b⟩ state preparation unitary.

items.title: Parallel Circuit Execution for Scalable Quantum Computation
items.authors: Avimita Chatterjee, W. Michael Brown, Siyuan Niu, Wibe Albert de Jong, Thomas Lubinski
items.matched: Evidence for the utility of quantum computing before fault tolerance
items.result: Parallel circuit execution on 156-qubit ibm_boston processor reduces billed QPU execution time by 3.5×--5.5× while retaining 83--92% of sequential fidelity.
items.question: How can idle qubits on large quantum processors be utilized to execute multiple independent circuits simultaneously and reduce execution time?
items.prior: Qiskit ParallelExperiment provided multi-circuit execution mechanics but required manual partition selection without error awareness.
items.limits: Dependent on availability of low-error disjoint device partitions and prone to transpiler escape constraints; multi-GPU classical scaling evaluated up to 28 qubits and 16 GPUs.
items.tools: IBM 156-qubit ibm_boston processor · CUDA-Q and MPI on NERSC Perlmutter · QED-C application-oriented benchmarks · Topology-aware greedy partition mapping algorithm
items.caption: Hellinger fidelity and billed QPU execution time on ibm_boston plotted against circuit qubit width. Parallel execution achieves 3.5×--5.5× runtime reductions while closely matching sequential fidelity across benchmarks.
items.abstract: Today's quantum processors have tens to hundreds of physical qubits, but reliable execution of arbitrary circuits remains limited to fewer than 30 entangled qubits across hardware modalities. Building upon prior work, we introduce an error- and topology-aware method for mapping multiple independent circuits onto disjoint regions of a single large-scale QPU for parallel circuit execution. For applications with many similarly sized circuits, such as observable estimation for Hamiltonian simulation, this approach can reduce billed QPU execution time, with ideal speedup proportional to the number of usable partitions. We demonstrate the approach on IBM's 156-qubit ibm_boston processor using standard QED-C benchmark and Hamiltonian-based observable-estimation workloads. Compared with standard sequential execution, parallel execution reduces billed execution time by 3.5-5.5x while retaining 83-92% of the sequential fidelity. We further evaluate the scaling of parallel circuit execution using GPU-accelerated classical simulation, distributing measurement circuits across GPUs via MPI. Using CUDA-Q on the NERSC Perlmutter system, we achieve up to 13.8x speedup on 16 GPUs (86% parallel efficiency) for an H2 electronic-structure simulation, with scaling evaluated across multiple Hamiltonians and circuit counts. These results provide an indication of the performance ceiling that parallel execution on future quantum hardware may eventually approach. Both execution modes are implemented as a runtime option within the QED-C Application-Oriented Benchmark suite. Together, the results show that circuit-level parallelism can reduce execution cost on current quantum hardware and simulation time on GPU clusters, with the potential for greater benefits as device quality and qubit counts increase.
