We use the same benchmark to assess the performance of a simple fault-tolerant logical-qubit processor implemented on up to eight [[7,1,3]]-encoded logical qubits using Quantinuum Helios-1, and project the growth of capability across successive generations of fault-tolerant quantum computers to show how QUOPS can track progress toward quantum scientific utility.

items.title: State-adapted generalized mean-field projections for Pauli propagation of Heisenberg dynamics
items.authors: Federico Tomás B. Pérez, Gabriela Wójtowicz, Martin B. Plenio

items.result: Covariance-orthogonal projection π_m^(σ₀) compresses Heisenberg observables onto at-most-m-body subspaces while preserving expectation values ⟨O⟩_(σ₀) and spatial support for product states σ₀.
items.question: How can Heisenberg-picture Pauli propagation be truncated reliably and stably during coherent many-body dynamics?
items.prior: Conventional Hilbert--Schmidt weight-based truncation and state-informed methods like xSPD discard components above weight m, losing target expectation value preservation and suffering from instability.
items.limits: Product reference states σ₀; requires exponential tail concentration Θ_r^((g))(s) ≤C_ge^(2calM₁(s))e^(-2κ_gr) for certified sufficiency; rank-deficient states can suffer compatibility failures in covariance quotient geometry.

items.abstract: The Heisenberg picture can make quantum many-body simulation efficient when evolved observables admit compact operator representation within low-dimensional structures. Conventional Pauli-string propagation and truncation techniques exploit this structure, but in coherent Hamiltonian dynamics their error control is often heuristic and their stability can be poor. We introduce a state-adapted Krylov framework based on geometric generalized mean-field projections of many-body observables onto low-body operator subspaces. The resulting dynamics approximate expectation values, do not extend spatial support beyond that prescribed by Lieb-Robinson bounds, and compress high-body correlations onto their state-relevant low-body representatives rather than simply discarding them. We derive necessary operator-entanglement obstructions to low-body representation and conditional sufficient bounds on representation and dynamical errors involving nonstabilizerness and controlled high-body tails. Numerical benchmarks show improved, stable finite-m hierarchies and simulations on large three-dimensional lattices, establishing a scalable state-adapted alternative to conventional Heisenberg-picture weight-truncation of Pauli strings.

items.authors: Ryo Mikami, Hayata Yamasaki
items.matched: Theory of Trotter Error with Commutator Scaling
items.result: Parallel sparse blossom decodes an O(d)-round syndrome extraction window on a distance-d rotated surface code in average parallel runtime bounded by exp[O((loglogd)²)], yielding o(1) average parallel runtime per round.
items.question: Can minimum-weight perfect matching decoding via sparse blossom be parallelized with an exact correctness guarantee and a runtime per round that scales as o(1)?
items.prior: Decoding time per round scaled as O(d^(2.34)) in sequential sparse blossom, requiring O(d^(3.34)) total latency for a d-round window (Higgott and Gidney 2023).
items.limits: Circuit-level local stochastic error model below a finite threshold p_th, with finite-size numerical comparisons assuming negligible parallelization overhead.
items.tools: parallel sparse blossom · hierarchical error clustering · minimum-weight embedded matching · rotated surface code simulation
items.caption: Event counts per shot per syndrome extraction round plotted against code distance d∈9,13,…,49, demonstrating that parallel sparse-blossom runtime per round decreases with increasing d at low physical error rates.
items.abstract: Matching-based decoding is widely used in quantum error correction, and accelerating it is key to enabling fast and scalable fault-tolerant quantum computation. Minimum-weight perfect matching (MWPM) decoding provides rigorous guarantees for error suppression, while sparse blossom enables its practical implementation at modest problem sizes. However, the runtime of existing sparse-blossom implementations unavoidably increases with problem size, motivating a rigorous parallelization framework that guarantees correctness and a runtime shorter than the syndrome-extraction timescale. Here, we present such a framework and prove that the resulting parallel sparse-blossom algorithm produces the same correction as the original, non-parallel sparse blossom. For the rotated surface code with code distance d and physical error rates below a finite threshold, we prove that the average parallel runtime of decoding for O(d) rounds of syndrome extraction is upper bounded by a quasi-polylogarithmic function of d. For a d-round decoding window, this implies that the average parallel runtime per round is o(1). We also perform numerical simulation to identify conditions under which the parallel runtime per round decreases with increasing code distance. These results suggest that increasing code distance need not lead to longer parallel decoding times, providing a foundation for scalable parallel matching-based decoding.

items.authors: Francesc Sabater, Tristan Kraft, Carlos A. Riofrío, Barbara Kraus

items.abstract: Probabilistic Error Cancellation (PEC) is a standard technique for mitigating noise in quantum computations, but its unbiasedness relies on accurate knowledge of the underlying noise parameters. In practice, these parameters are inferred from experimental data and may be inaccurate. We introduce a protocol that tests PEC parameter consistency on hardware by applying Direct Fidelity Estimation (DFE) to the effective mitigated state. The resulting DFE overlap serves not only as a witness of parameter miscalibration but, under appropriate conditions, also reveals whether the PEC parameters have been overestimated or underestimated. We establish this behavior for arbitrary circuits under global depolarizing noise and for Clifford circuits under general Pauli-stochastic noise. For arbitrary circuits subject to Pauli-stochastic noise, the underestimation result holds generally, while the corresponding overestimation result is established perturbatively for sufficiently small consistent miscalibrations under an additional nondegeneracy condition. We further show that the purity of the effective mitigated operator provides a more general diagnostic, allowing the miscalibration direction to be identified for arbitrary circuits and arbitrary parameter deviations. Finally, we describe a two-copy PEC procedure for measuring this quantity and show that, together with the DFE overlap, it determines the Hilbert-Schmidt distance from the ideal state. The sampling overhead incurred by our protocol is the same as that of PEC, and we discuss strategies to improve it.

items.question: Can stabiliser measurements and quantum error detection/correction be performed across spatially separated quantum processors using photonic interconnects?

items.abstract: Building fault-tolerant quantum computers with large numbers of logical qubits requires both scalable hardware architectures and error-correcting codes that make efficient use of physical qubits. Photonic interconnects address both of these challenges by allowing the physical qubits to be distributed across multiple processors while providing the non-local connectivity necessary to implement resource-efficient codes such as high-rate quantum low-density parity-check (qLDPC) codes. A key requirement for realising this architecture is the ability to perform stabiliser measurements between remote processors, which has not previously been demonstrated experimentally. Here we report the first experimental demonstration of distributed quantum error detection and correction. We generate entanglement between network qubits in two separate trapped-ion processors and use it to perform remote syndrome measurements on data qubits. We first realise a distributed [[2, 1, 1]] repetition code, detecting phase-flip errors on a logical qubit encoded across the two modules in real time and suppressing logical errors. We then combine these mid-circuit syndrome measurements with real-time feedforward to actively correct arbitrary single-qubit Pauli errors on a distributed Bell state. These results provide an experimental foundation for quantum error correction (QEC) across modular quantum architectures.

items.authors: Jacob Repicky, Girish Kumbhar, Mingkang Xia, Roman Baskov, Param Patel, Maria Nowicki, Luigi Frunzio, Steven M. Girvin, Michael Hatridge
items.matched: Cavity quantum electrodynamics for superconducting electrical circuits: An arch…
items.result: The maximum effective sub-resonant drive amplitude before the onset of chaos scales as η_max ∝γ^(0.61), where γ= ω_q / α. For four-wave iSWAP/beamsplitter gates, the interaction rate figure of merit scales weakly as αη_max² ∝α^(-0.22) ω_q^(1.22), establishing an upper limit of approximately ω_q / 20.
items.question: How does the sub-resonant drive strength threshold for chaos in transmon qubits depend on transmon parameters and drive frequency?
items.limits: Isolated transmons driven sub-resonantly; assumes transmon single-mode approximation.
items.tools: 14 transmon devices (E_J/E_C varying over two orders of magnitude) · Floquet branch analysis · semiclassical Poincaré maps
items.caption: Chaos threshold drive strength η_max plotted against the ratio γ= ω_q / α, showing the universal η_max ∝γ^(0.61) scaling across experiment and simulation.
items.abstract: Achieving fast gates and high-fidelity readout in superconducting quantum circuits often benefits from the use of large amplitude microwave drives. As the strength increases, unwanted effects such as excitation out of the logical states also become more prevalent. In transmon qubits, coherent controls relying on sub-resonant drives are fundamentally limited by the eventual appearance of strong hybridization in the spectrum. Understanding how this threshold depends on intrinsic device parameters is vital for the design and operation of circuits utilizing the transmon as a source of nonlinearity. In this work, we present an experimental study of 14 transmons with a wide range of anharmonicities, and use comparison with Floquet branch analysis and semiclassical simulations to establish a straightforward relationship between the critical value of the effective drive amplitude η_max and the ratio γ=ω_q/α, where ω_q is the transmon frequency and -α is the anharmonicity. For the case where the transmon is used as a parametrically driven coupler, these results further allow us to estimate maximum parametric interaction rates, which informs the circuit design process for optimizing gate rates and fidelities.

items.title: Universal transverse diode effects in superconducting unconventional magnet hybrids
items.authors: Pei-Hao Fu, Luca Chirolli, Jorge Cayao
items.matched: exchange gates and two-qubit operations in semiconductor double quantum dots
items.result: Superconducting unconventional magnet junctions realize transverse spin and charge diode effects with perfect rectification efficiencies (ho_y = ±1 and η_y = ±1) at zero net magnetization.
items.question: Can transverse superconducting diode effects emerge in unconventional magnet hybrids without net magnetization?
items.limits: Zero temperature calculations, tight-binding discretization with proximity-induced s-wave superconductivity.
items.tools: Bogoliubov-de Gennes tight-binding model · lattice Green's functions · Blonder-Tinkham-Klapwijk formalisms

items.abstract: We demonstrate that superconducting unconventional magnet junctions harbor transverse spin and charge diode effects with perfect rectification efficiencies. This nonreciprocal transverse transport is governed by the interplay of mirror reflections and spin rotation with respect to the Néel vector, a mechanism that is universally applicable to all unconventional magnets. Interestingly, the transverse spin diode features pure spin currents, while the charge diode yields spin-polarized charge currents, both exhibiting highly controllable rectification functionalities at vanishing net magnetization. Our results position superconducting unconventional magnets at the forefront of orthogonal engineering in next-generation transverse superconducting spintronics.

items.title: Error Correction in a Distributed Quantum Computer
items.authors: E. M. Ainley, A. Agrawal, T. Araki, A. R. Martínez, D. Main, E. Malinowski, J. A. Blackmore, S. Chen, P. Drmota, M. Mallweger, D. P. Nadlinger, R. Srinivas, S. C. Benjamin, G. Araneda, D. M. Lucas

items.question: Can stabiliser measurements and quantum error detection/correction be performed across spatially separated quantum processors using photonic interconnects?

items.abstract: Building fault-tolerant quantum computers with large numbers of logical qubits requires both scalable hardware architectures and error-correcting codes that make efficient use of physical qubits. Photonic interconnects address both of these challenges by allowing the physical qubits to be distributed across multiple processors while providing the non-local connectivity necessary to implement resource-efficient codes such as high-rate quantum low-density parity-check (qLDPC) codes. A key requirement for realising this architecture is the ability to perform stabiliser measurements between remote processors, which has not previously been demonstrated experimentally. Here we report the first experimental demonstration of distributed quantum error detection and correction. We generate entanglement between network qubits in two separate trapped-ion processors and use it to perform remote syndrome measurements on data qubits. We first realise a distributed [[2, 1, 1]] repetition code, detecting phase-flip errors on a logical qubit encoded across the two modules in real time and suppressing logical errors. We then combine these mid-circuit syndrome measurements with real-time feedforward to actively correct arbitrary single-qubit Pauli errors on a distributed Bell state. These results provide an experimental foundation for quantum error correction (QEC) across modular quantum architectures.

items.title: Strong-coupling quantum optics in free space with holes in a Fermi sea
items.authors: Hao Wang, Hayden C. Orth, Duo Xu, Emily J. Davis
items.matched: cavity QED, atom-photon interfaces and quantum networks
items.result: Pauli blocking of inelastic recoil channels by identical fermions in a trap enables directed spontaneous emission and strong light-matter coupling with single-atom cooperativity C ≥1 in free space.
items.question: Can an antenna formed by the center-of-mass wavefunction of a single atom exhibit large cooperativity C ≥1 in free space?
items.prior: A single point atom driven by a focused Gaussian mode with waist w₀ = λ had cooperativity bounded by C_point ≤3/2π².
items.limits: Single-excitation subspace; requires tight fermionic trap loading, Ω^R₂ ≫Ω^R₁, Γ_(s₁ e), and Γ_(s₂ g) gtrsim|Ω_(s₂)|, |Ω_e|, ℏk₁₂²/2m.
items.tools: Pauli blocking in a Fermi sea · Adiabatic elimination · Center-of-mass wavefunction engineering · Dressed multi-level atomic schemes
items.caption: Unidirectional emission patterns in real space and momentum space showing asymmetric spontaneous scattering induced by momentum kick k₁₂ from coherent drive fields.
items.abstract: Coherent and efficient light-matter interfaces between an atom and a single mode of the electromagnetic field are essential for quantum technologies. Traditionally, these systems employ optical cavities or waveguides to isolate a specific mode of light, but a more recent approach is to engineer antennas from ordered configurations of trapped ultracold atoms that exhibit controllable and directed scattering. In this work, we propose a method to engineer an antenna from the center-of-mass wavefunction of a single atom, which can produce directed emission and thereby exhibit strong coupling to a target mode of light in free space. We predict that the resulting single-atom cooperativity can be comparable to the current state of the art in optical cavity and waveguide QED experiments. Building on this approach, we show that a wavepacket antenna becomes a single-atom mirror in the linear response regime. We study the modified dipole-dipole interactions and band structure of chains of such emitters, which can exhibit sub- and superradiance at spacings much larger than the wavelength of the light. Extending our approach to multi-level atoms, we propose a method to achieve arbitrary spatial scattering from a single atom, including uni-directional spontaneous emission. Finally, we elucidate how our approach can enhance cooperative scattering in conventional arrays of tightly trapped atoms.

items.title: Engineering dissipation and control pulses for high-fidelity fault-tolerance quantum computing
items.authors: Shao-Wei Xu, Zhe-Yuan Zhang, Yi-Tong Shi, Ye-Hong Chen, Yan Xia
items.matched: Quantum information with Rydberg atoms
items.result: Two-photon dissipative confinement autonomously restores dephasing-induced leakage back to the logical cat-state subspace with restoration rate Γ_(R,1)≈4κ₂|α|², yielding final population P₋(t_f)≈99.64% at t_f=0.5/κ_a under pure dephasing κ_a^φ=κ_a.
items.question: How to design fast, high-fidelity state transfer protocols for dissipative cat-state qubits that are robust against systematic drive errors and suppress dephasing-induced leakage?
items.limits: Numerical simulation only. Requires drive amplitude ε_d(t)≪2κ₂|α|² and operation within the bounded time window 1/(2κ₂|α|³)≪t_f≪1/(κ_a|α|²).
items.tools: shortcut-to-adiabaticity (STA) via inverse engineering · two-photon dissipative confinement · Lindblad master equation simulations · effective two-level subspace mapping
items.caption: Final target population P₋(t_f) (red curve) and time-averaged subspace leakage P_Leak^((Avg)) (light-blue curve) plotted against total evolution time t_f∈(0,1/κ_a] in the presence of pure dephasing.
items.abstract: Cat-state qubits, a prominent class of bosonic encodings, offer a promising pathway toward hardware-efficient fault-tolerant quantum computing. In this manuscript, we propose an optimally robust control protocol for the cat-state qubits which are stabilized by engineering two-photon dissipation. By deriving an effective two-level description in the cat-state subspace and applying shortcut-to-adiabaticity via inverse engineering, we design a robust protocol to achieve fast and high-fidelity state transfer in the cat-state qubit. We analyze the sensitivity to systematic control errors and identify an optimal robustness condition that strongly suppresses errors induced by imperfections in the driving fields. Furthermore, we show that dissipative confinement efficiently suppresses leakage out of the cat-state subspace caused by the pure dephasing, highlighting an intrinsic advantage of dissipative-cat qubits. This work establishes a robust and leakage-suppressing framework for high-fidelity bosonic qubit control, offering a promising route toward scalable fault-tolerant quantum computing.

items.title: Distribution of light-matter quantum correlations with a temporally multiplexed solid-state quantum memory array
items.authors: Aya Mneimneh, Susana Plascencia, Manuel Gundin, Jonathan Hänni, Samuele Grandi, Markus Teller, Hugues de Riedmatten
items.matched: quantum memories and repeaters for long-distance links
items.result: Telecom-heralded single photons stored across 10 spatial cells and 6 temporal modes (60 spatio-temporal modes total) in a Pr³⁺:Y₂SiO₅ array yield a 60-fold enhancement in detected correlated photon rate over a 39.1 km metropolitan fiber link.
items.question: Can spatial and temporal multiplexing be combined in a solid-state quantum memory array to distribute light-matter quantum correlations over deployed metropolitan fiber?
items.limits: Round-trip communication time is 393 μs; communication trials fill up to 15% of this window. Cross-correlations limited by control-pulse fluorescence noise and neighbor crosstalk between cells separated by 200 μm.
items.tools: Pr³⁺:Y₂SiO₅ atomic frequency comb spin-wave memory · cavity-enhanced SPDC source · acousto-optic deflectors · superconducting nanowire single-photon detectors · 39.1 km deployed metropolitan fiber
items.caption: Heralding and coincidence rates as functions of the filled round-trip communication time and number of spatio-temporal modes, showing linear rate scaling up to 60 modes.
items.abstract: Multiplexed quantum memories increase the entanglement distribution rate in long-distance quantum repeater architectures by harnessing storage in several degrees of freedom. Here, we report on the distribution of light-matter quantum correlations using an array of time-multiplexed solid-state quantum memories. We store telecom-heralded single photons sequentially in up to ten memory cells using the full atomic frequency comb protocol with on-demand read-out in a Pr³⁺:Y₂SiO₅ crystal. Leveraging both spatial and temporal multiplexing, we demonstrate quantum correlations between the telecom photon and up to 60 spatio-temporal modes of the quantum memory array. We then transmit the heralding telecom photon over 39.1 km of deployed optical fiber in the Metropolitan Area of Barcelona. In a realistic scenario where the generation rate is limited by the two-way communication time, we show that up to 15 % of the $393 μs$ round-trip communication time is filled with communication trials, leading to a 60-fold enhancement in the rate of detected telecom photons correlated with the quantum memory array, compared to a single-mode memory. With increased storage times and efficiencies, our multiplexed quantum memory array will constitute the backbone of a long-distance quantum network, establishing remote entanglement at high rates.

items.authors: Onyango Stephen Okeyo

items.result: At the working point f_⋆=√barn+1 with zero detuning and zero Kerr, the collapsed mean-rung excited population of the anti-Jaynes--Cummings (AJC) vertex is exactly 1/4 (compared to 1/2 for the Jaynes--Cummings vertex), and the continuum revival-time ratio t_R^AJC/t_R^JC equals √2.

items.abstract: At atomic resonance the Jaynes--Cummings (JC) vertex of a single bosonic mode coupled to a two-level emitter is blind to f=ω/λ at zero detuning and Kerr; the anti-Jaynes--Cummings (AJC) vertex is not. We show that the mean-rung excited population of the AJC block equals exactly 1/4 at f_⋆=√barn+1, while the JC population at the same point is 1/2. The Poisson-averaged packet value at barn=16 is 0.24650, within 3.5×10⁻³ of the exact value, with the deviation reproduced by -barn/[16(barn+1)²]. At f_⋆ the modulation depth of the AJC inversion is 1/2 and the relative sensitivity of the continuum revival-time ratio r=t_R^AJC/t_R^JC is maximal with value 1/(2√barn+1). Full diagonalization on 2(n_max+1) states confirms the analytic values. The 1/4 value can be generated by Floquet-engineered counter-rotating coupling provided that the static transverse rate satisfies g₀≪g₁. Parameter translations for an ideal trapped-ion blue sideband and a flux-tunable circuit-QED coupler are reported.

items.title: Reducing Decoding Latency in Quantum Error Correction by Early Starting Clustering
items.authors: Tommaso Peduzzi, Lukas Bödeker, Markus Müller, Luis Colmenarez
items.matched: Quantum error correction below the surface code threshold
items.result: Cluster-As-You-Go (CAYG) grows and resolves syndrome clusters incrementally during stabilizer measurements, cutting post-measurement growth steps and outperforming batch Union-Find logical error rates when idling noise during decoding exceeds physical noise.
items.question: Can quantum error correction decoding begin during syndrome extraction to reduce post-measurement latency and overall logical error rates under idling decoherence?
items.prior: Standard Union-Find waits for all d syndrome extraction rounds, yielding higher accuracy but larger post-measurement latency and faster threshold degradation under idling noise.
items.limits: Phenomenological noise model with equal-strength idling decoherence, rotated surface codes only; hardware-level timing and circuit-level noise not evaluated.
items.tools: Cluster-As-You-Go (CAYG) decoding · Union-Find decoder · rotated surface codes · phenomenological noise model · Monte Carlo simulations
items.caption: Logical error probability p_L plotted against physical error rate p across code distances d=7,9,11 for four increasing idling-noise strengths 1/N, showing CAYG maintaining a higher effective threshold than standard Union-Find as idling noise increases.
items.abstract: In quantum error correction, fast low-latency decoding is essential for fault-tolerant quantum computation, as delays in processing syndrome data can lead to the backlog problem. Existing decoders, including parallelizable approaches such as Union-Find, begin decoding only after all stabilizer measurement outcomes from an error-correction cycle have been received, inherently introducing a delay before decoding begins. We introduce Cluster-As-You-Go (CAYG), a modification of the Union-Find decoder that processes syndrome information during stabilizer measurements by clustering and correcting errors as they appear. This approach reduces the size of the remaining decoding problem at the end of the quantum error correction cycle and, consequently, the time required to complete the decoding process. While this early start of clustering incurs a modest reduction in decoding accuracy, it preserves the decoder's scalability. Surface-code simulations show that the resulting reduction in post-measurement idling can outweigh the accuracy loss, yielding an improved speed-accuracy trade-off. These results demonstrate that real-time, early-starting decoding during QEC cycles is both feasible and can be advantageous for quantum error correction. Demonstrated here for the surface code, CAYG is broadly applicable to other quantum error-correcting codes, which allow for clustering-based decoding approaches, and is extensible to dedicated real-time decoding hardware.

items.title: Quantum Codes for Generalized Amplitude-damping Noise
items.authors: Sourav Dutta, Anubhab Rudra, Manav Seksaria, Anil Prabhakar, Prabha Mandayam
items.matched: High-threshold and low-overhead fault-tolerant quantum memory
items.result: Probabilistic approximate quantum error correction (PAQEC) on a five-qubit permutation-invariant code achieves fidelity loss that scales quadratically with generalized amplitude-damping strength γ, O(γ²), under post-selected recovery.
items.question: Can probabilistic and approximate quantum error correction frameworks be combined to suppress first-order generalized amplitude-damping errors in short codes?
items.prior: Deterministic quantum codes (such as the [5,1,3] stabilizer code) cannot eliminate first-order generalized amplitude-damping errors and incur fidelity loss scaling linearly with γ.
items.limits: Requires post-selection over successful recovery outcomes, reducing total success probability below 1.
items.tools: five-qubit permutation-invariant code · probabilistic approximate quantum error correction (PAQEC) · semidefinite programming · Charnes-Cooper transformation
items.caption: Entanglement fidelity and recovery probability as functions of damping strength γ at excitation parameter p=0.05. The numerically optimized code achieves higher entanglement fidelity than the [5,1] permutation-invariant code at the cost of lower success probability.
items.abstract: Quantum error correcting (QEC) plays a crucial role in protecting quantum information against decoherence and enabling scalable, reliable quantum computing. One of the most realistic and ubiquitous sources of noise affecting quantum hardware today is generalized amplitude-damping (GAD) noise. Conventional, deterministic QEC codes struggle to correct for GAD noise because of their inherent structure, leading to fidelity losses that scale linearly with the damping strength. In this work, we introduce the framework of probabilistic approximate quantum error correction (PAQEC), that combines the flexibility of approximate QEC with the potential of post-selected recovery, enabling high-fidelity, resource-efficient error correction. We construct a five-qubit permutation-invariant code that, under probabilistic recovery, achieves a fidelity loss quadratic in the damping strength, thus outperforming existing QEC codes. Formulating PAQEC as an optimization problem, we present a numerical technique based on Charnes-Cooper and semidefinite programming to identify the optimal recovery map for any PAQEC code. Our results establish PAQEC as a powerful tool for developing resource-efficient, high-fidelity quantum codes tailored to realistic noise, with promising implications for near-term quantum devices and future fault-tolerant architectures.

items.title: Fermionic quantum error correction is never free
items.authors: Yifan Tang, Ingo Roth, Philippe Faist, Zi-Wen Liu, Jens Eisert, Zhenhuan Liu
items.matched: Surface codes: Towards practical large-scale quantum computation
items.result: Code space of any non-trivial [[n, k, d_F]] fermionic code with d_F ≥3 contains zero pure fermionic Gaussian states. Exact unitary codeword preparation via q-mode non-Gaussian gates requires at least g ≥lfloor(d_F-3)/(q-2) rfloor+ lceilk/q rceil non-Gaussian gates.
items.question: Can fermionic quantum error correction and error detection be implemented using only free-fermion (Gaussian) operations?
items.limits: Pure fermionic Gaussian states; bounded-weight non-Gaussian unitary circuits acting on n modes; exact and fidelity-bounded codeword preparation.
items.tools: Wick's theorem · Knill-Laflamme conditions · fermionic covariance matrices · Schur complement conditioning
items.abstract: Fermionic platforms offer compelling architectures for quantum computing, ranging from topologically protected Majorana-based qubits to fermionic cold atoms. To achieve scalability, however, they require quantum error correction. In this work, we prove that any exact and sufficiently accurate approximate fermionic quantum error correction necessarily requires non-Gaussian operations, beyond the free-fermion regime of quadratic dynamics. This is in sharp contrast to the qubit setting, where the efficiently classically simulable stabilizer operations form the standard framework for quantum error correction. Specifically, we show that the logical space of any non-trivial fermionic error-correcting code contains no pure fermionic Gaussian state, utilizing a fundamental incompatibility between fermionic error correction and Wick's theorem. We further show that the required number of bounded-weight non-Gaussian gates for unitary codeword preparation grows at least linearly with both the code distance and the number of encoded modes, revealing an intrinsic resource overhead that increases simultaneously with error-protection strength and logical capacity. Furthermore, we analyze the performance of fermionic Gaussian operations in entanglement distillation, revealing a distinction from their bosonic counterparts. Our results reveal fundamental difficulties for fermionic error correction from the perspectives of both physical implementation and classical simulation, suggesting connections to fermionic phases of matter and state preparation complexity.

items.title: Noise-resilient sequential circuits for generating quantum order
items.authors: Konstantin Gattinger, Julian Boesl, Max McGinley, Michael Knap, Frank Pollmann
items.matched: Surface code quantum computing by lattice surgery
items.result: Unitary sequential circuits with non-Clifford gates prepare 3D symmetry-broken order and 4D (3,1) toric code topological order stably against Pauli noise, with the 4D toric code syndrome cluster size vanishing asymptotically below critical single-qubit error probability p^c_hatX ≈0.013.
items.question: Can unitary sequential quantum circuits prepare long-range ordered states stably against circuit-level Pauli noise without propagating local errors into nonlocal order-destroying defects?
items.prior: Standard sequential circuits for 1D GHZ states and 2D toric code wavefunctions are unstable to Pauli noise at any non-zero error rate due to gate-propagated errors.
items.limits: Requires spatial dimension D ≥3 for purely unitary stabilization (or D ≥2 with active measurement and classical feedback); stabilizer syndromes must form closed manifolds of dimension d ≥2.
items.tools: sequential unitary circuits · majority-vote and Toom's rule gate updates · cellular automaton simulations · higher-dimensional stabilizer syndrome analysis
items.caption: Normalized average maximum syndrome cluster diameter plotted against Pauli error probability p_hatX across multiple linear system sizes L. Below p^c_hatX ≈0.013, relative cluster size scales to zero as L increases, confirming error confinement.
items.abstract: Sequential circuits provide an optimal linear-depth route to unitarily preparing long-range ordered quantum states, but circuit-level noise can be far more damaging than noise applied after preparation: local errors may be propagated by subsequent gates into nonlocal defects that destroy the target order. In this work, we present classes of unitary sequential circuits that prepare certain non-trivial orders in the presence of Pauli noise. Our constructions exploit the spatial structure of the syndromes of the target state, which in certain cases allows us to systematically suppress the propagation of errors using strictly local gates. The strategy can be applied both to symmetry-breaking order, for which we present a 3D example, and to topological order, which we showcase on a 4D version of the toric code. We also highlight how this stability against errors necessitates non-Clifford gates, and how measurement-feedback loops can be used to stabilize lower-dimensional states as well.

items.title: WISER: Systematic Design-Space Exploration of Fault-Tolerant Global Control Trapped-Ions
items.authors: Scott Jones, Song-qing-hao Yang, Prakash Murali
items.matched: resource estimation: physical qubit and runtime budgets for useful algorithms
items.result: Optimal SAT compilation improves globally controlled WISE logical clock speed from 1.94 Hz to 4.28 Hz for a distance-7 surface code, but remains roughly 3× slower than local QCCD control at 12.8 Hz.
items.question: Is the performance gap between globally multiplexed trapped-ion control and standard QCCD an intrinsic architectural bottleneck or an artifact of suboptimal compilation and hardware choices?
items.prior: Heuristic compilation on WISE achieved 1.94 Hz clock speed and 3.3×10⁻⁶ logical error rate (Jones and Murali 2026), compared to 12.8 Hz on QCCD.

Only bivariate-bicycle distance-4 under the optimistic tier achieves <10⁻⁸ error while staying below the 1 W per logical qubit power limit.
items.abstract: Trapped-ion quantum computers are a leading candidate for scalable fault-tolerant quantum computing, but conventional Quantum Charge-Coupled Device (QCCD) architectures face severe wiring and power constraints as systems scale. The recently proposed WISE promise orders-of-magnitude reductions in wiring complexity but fundamentally alter the hardware--software interface, making it unclear whether such restrictive architectures can feasibly execute quantum error correction (QEC) and eventually support fault-tolerant workloads. We present WISER, a cross-layer architectural design-space exploration framework for globally controlled trapped-ion systems, to determine whether WISE can support early FTQC, and what hardware/compiler/QEC choices are needed. WISER combines novel WISE-specific compilation, noise modelling, and simulation and integrated them into a unified framework. WISER provides comparative lower-bound estimates of logical clock speed and logical error rate, rather than absolute hardware prediction, enabling us to identify viable operating regions while ruling out infeasible ones. To our knowledge, it is the first systematic design space exploration study targeted at WISE and scalable architectures beyond QCCD. Using WISER, we identify a narrow feasible design space requiring two-ion traps, moderate control multiplexing, aggressive recooling, and high-rate bivariate-bicycle codes. Even under ∼10× improvements in physical errors, the lower-bound cycle time to achieve < 10⁻⁸ logical error is ≈100 ms, which is 3× slower than local control. These results expose a fundamental trade-off between wiring scalability and logical throughput, suggesting that practical early fault-tolerant operation requires complementary > 10× physical error rate reductions along with substantial > 100× reduction in fault-tolerant circuit-depth.

items.matched: Fault-tolerant quantum computation by anyons

items.question: How can full-stack co-optimization across compiler, control hardware, and qubit plane reduce logical operation latency in transversal neutral-atom FTQC architectures?

items.abstract: Technological advances in neutral-atom platforms have opened a new path toward designing efficient protocols for fault-tolerant quantum computing (FTQC). However, each physical operation is still orders of magnitude slower than on other platforms, such as superconducting qubits. Therefore, architects must identify fast and efficient FTQC architectures, which require reliable modeling tools to explore various design choices across the software, classical hardware, and quantum device stacks of neutral-atom platforms. In this paper, we propose NAQsim, an open-source simulation framework for neutral-atom FTQC architectures based on transversal gates. As its key feature, NAQsim enables detailed full-stack architecture evaluation that opens opportunities to explore previously overlooked performance bottlenecks. As a first use case for NAQsim, we identify one such bottleneck, patch rotations, perform full-stack co-optimization, and finally derive a near-rotation-free architecture (D3-ROT). For practical FTQC benchmark workloads, D3-ROT achieves a 2.27x speedup from this single bottleneck alone, with minimal footprint overhead. These results point to a much broader space of full-stack optimizations that NAQsim makes accessible for transversal surface-code architectures and beyond.

html.result: Patch rotations cause 55.3% to 77.6% of execution time in transversal neutral-atom FTQC. The D3-ROT architecture eliminates this bottleneck, yielding an average <math xmlns="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML"><mrow><mn>2.27</mn><mo>×</mo></mrow></math> speedup (up to <math xmlns="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML"><mrow><mn>2.57</mn><mo>×</mo></mrow></math>) at 22.4% average footprint overhead.

items.title: CUDA-Q Logical: Retargetable Compilation for Fault-Tolerant Quantum Computing
items.authors: Alexander McCaskey, Justin Lietz, Adam Holmes, Kohei Nakaji, Vadym Kliuchnikov, Yifan Hong, Amalee Wilson, Andres Paz, Bettina Heim, Bruno Schmitt, Krysta M. Svore
items.matched: resource estimation: physical qubit and runtime budgets for useful algorithms
items.result: CUDA-Q Logical provides an MLIR-based, retargetable compiler pipeline that lowers logical quantum programs through five explicit semantic profiles (P0 to P4), directly deriving resource estimates, detector error models, and physical execution schedules from compiler artifacts while preserving provenance.
items.question: How can fault-tolerant quantum compilation unify target-independent logical intent, heterogeneous QEC encodings, physical scheduling, and real-time control to provide verifiable, reproducible resource estimates and cross-architecture comparisons?
items.limits: Deterministic and single-shot behavior only; rejects retry averaging, stochastic queues, dynamic routing, packetization, and runtime boundary-changing surgery in compact models.
items.tools: MLIR progressive lowering pipeline · CUDA-Q platform · Spacetime plan and transport modeling · Extended detector error models (EDEM) · qLDPC code surgery templates
items.caption: Progression of compiler lowering across five semantic profiles from P0 logical intent down to P4 real-time control, illustrating typed boundaries for research components and analysis passes.
items.abstract: Realizing fault-tolerant quantum computing requires mapping logical programs to heterogeneous quantum error correction (QEC) codes and diverse fault-tolerant execution models, scheduling physical resources, and coupling to real-time classical control and feedback. Specialized tools exist for each step but rely on manual composition and translation that discard assumptions and provenance, separating resource estimates from the compiler artifacts they describe, and making it difficult to validate correctness, compare architectures, or attribute costs to specific design choices. We present CUDA-Q Logical, an extensible compiler infrastructure for retargetable fault-tolerant compilation, analysis, and execution. Interoperable with CUDA-Q and other mainstream front-ends, CUDA-Q Logical progressively lowers target-independent logical programs through a constrained logical virtual machine, QEC microcode, physical gate schedules, and real-time control plans, with each layer preserving semantics and provenance, while verifying composition and resource constraints. By deriving every resource estimate directly from compiler artifacts, the framework unifies compilation and resource analysis, enabling successively refined estimates and principled cross-architecture comparison while permitting QEC codes, execution models, decoders, and hardware architectures to be introduced as modular extensions. Across workloads ranging from application-architecture studies to qLDPC surgery and detector-error-model composition, we show that schedule-derived estimates reconcile with established independent models. Crucially, this compiler-visible structure exposes cost drivers hidden by aggregate analytical formulas, carries QEC artifacts intact into simulation, and demonstrates a complete compilation pipeline for fault-tolerant quantum computing.

items.title: A Modular, Topology-Aware Software Stack for Entanglement-Based Distributed Quantum Computing
items.authors: Luke Andreesen, Shobhit Gupta, Sean Sullivan, Manish Kumar Singh

items.result: For an 18-qubit QFT circuit on a 2-QPU network, replacing all-to-all with nearest-neighbor intra-QPU connectivity increases EPR-pair consumption by more than an order of magnitude. Under stochastic link generation, shortest-duration and critical-path arbitration policies reduce completion time by 17.7±1.3% and 17.9±1.5% relative to FIFO.
items.question: How can hardware network topology and link contention be incorporated into an open-source software stack for partitioning, compiling, and scheduling distributed quantum circuits?
items.prior: Prior distributed compilers (such as Pytket-DQC) lack timestamped operation scheduling and rely on idealized, optimistic all-to-all connectivity assumptions.
items.limits: NISQ-era compilation only; does not model decoherence, noise, link fidelity degradation, entanglement distillation, or quantum error correction.
items.tools: OpenQASM compiler toolchain · Discrete-event stochastic scheduler · Quantum Network Constructor (QNC) · Hypergraph and Dynamic Interaction circuit partitioners · Cat-Entangler and Cat-Disentangler teleportation protocols

items.abstract: Distributed quantum computing (DQC) seeks to scale beyond the limits of monolithic processors by interconnecting multiple quantum processing units (QPUs) through entanglement-based links. Realizing this vision requires the co-design of hardware and software across the domains of quantum networking, compilation, and scheduling, yet existing tools remain fragmented between monolithic circuit compilers and long-distance quantum network simulators. We present an open-source, topology-informed framework for the compilation and scheduling of distributed quantum programs. Given an input circuit and a description of the target network, the framework partitions and reconstructs the circuit into a distributed program that respects the specified inter- and intra-QPU topology, covers cross-QPU operations through gate and state teleportation, and schedules the result under either deterministic or stochastic entanglement-generation models. By accepting and emitting standard OpenQASM, the framework interoperates with existing monolithic toolchains, and its standardized module interfaces allow partitioning and scheduling strategies to be interchanged and benchmarked. Using this framework, we show that the best-performing compilation strategy varies across the tested circuits and network configurations, and that both network topology and intra-QPU connectivity substantially affect the entanglement cost of execution. These findings underscore the need for a co-design approach to distributed quantum computing, which our framework is designed to support.

items.title: Practical Considerations for Processing Massive Classical Data via Quantum Oracle Sketching
items.authors: Stefano Markidis
items.matched: Toward the first quantum simulation with quantum speedup
items.result: DNA retrieval accuracy reaches >0.98 with M₀=2048 samples per oracle across Q=8 applications out of 16 288 corpus windows, scaling in relative error as E_F^((Q))∝Q²/M. Transpiled circuits remain deep, exceeding 4.17×10⁵ depth even after phase fusion.
items.question: What are the practical system and compilation requirements for implementing Quantum Oracle Sketching (QOS) on current batched quantum hardware?
items.limits: Offline simulation only; transpiled circuits require hundreds of thousands of CX gates, exceeding current NISQ coherence times.
items.tools: Quantum Oracle Sketching (QOS) · Offline phase fusion compilation · Qiskit transpiler (GenericBackendV2) · DNA sequence fingerprinting
items.caption: Fingerprint matrix relative error E_F^((Q)) and mean top-one DNA family-retrieval accuracy as functions of total sample count M across different oracle repetition counts Q.
items.abstract: Classical-to-quantum I/O is a critical bottleneck for data-intensive quantum workloads. Quantum Oracle Sketching (QOS) has been proposed to address this problem. We identify its practical requirements, including the representation of data as a probability distribution over oracle addresses, the relation between sample count, approximation error, and update cost, and the coherence and runtime support required for online execution. To study QOS on current quantum computing devices, we develop an offline realization that compiles sample blocks into empirical phase oracles and evaluate it using DNA fingerprinting. The application converges with relatively few samples, while exact phase fusion combines repeated updates to the same address. However, the compiled circuits remain too deep for current quantum computing devices. Practical QOS therefore requires lower depth oracle synthesis and interactive quantum runtimes.

items.title: OpenQARP: a modular framework for quantum application research
items.authors: Stefano Scali, Vicente P. Soloviev, Antonio Márquez Romero, Brian Coyle, Giuseppe Buonaiuto, Annie Paine, Jonathan H. Fetherolf, Marcos Diez García, Michal Krompiec, Josh Kirsopp
items.matched: Toward the first quantum simulation with quantum speedup
items.result: OpenQARP executes operator algebra one to two orders of magnitude faster than OpenFermion and matches mature compilers on two-qubit gate count while keeping strict unified conventions.
items.question: How to build an open-source quantum computing framework that eliminates silent convention errors across the research workflow while maintaining high simulator and operator performance?
items.prior: OpenFermion, Qiskit/Aer, PennyLane/Lightning, Qulacs, qsim, and pytket required cross-framework plumbing with differing qubit orderings and phase conventions.
items.limits: Benchmarks measured on a single Apple-silicon host using scalar C++ block kernels without SIMD or AVX vectorization; no pulse-level control, autodiff, or direct hardware execution engine.
items.tools: C++20 compiled core with Python interface · block-based circuit abstraction · gate fusion and flip-mask Pauli contraction · independent NumPy/SciPy testing oracles
items.caption: Run-phase simulation time on a logarithmic vertical axis plotted against register size for brickwork circuits, comparing constant-factor scaling across different quantum simulation frameworks.
items.abstract: We introduce OpenQARP, the Open Quantum Application Research Package: an open-source Python framework for quantum application research, built on a compiled C++ core. In OpenQARP, an application is assembled from an algorithm library that orchestrates three interchangeable layers: blocks describe circuits, primitives describe what to extract from them, and engines describe how they run. The release spans near-term through fault-tolerant methods, targeting problems from electronic structure to combinatorial optimization, with device-aware compilation, circuit cutting, and resource estimation over a single set of numerical conventions that the code must follow. Every numerical feature is checked against an independent oracle, and every published timing carries a correctness check. Against OpenFermion, Qiskit/Aer, PennyLane/Lightning, Qulacs, qsim, and pytket, OpenQARP is one to two orders of magnitude faster on operator algebra and among the fastest on simulation. It matches mature compilers on two-qubit gate count, and expresses a complete algorithm in the lines a framework needs rather than the plumbing a primitive stack demands.

items.title: Efficient expectation value estimation for quantum circuits via extended stabilizer frameworks and adaptive variance estimation
items.authors: Yunseo Hwang, Giwon Song, Kyoung Keun Park, Hyukjoon Kwon, Taehyun Kim
items.matched: Toward the first quantum simulation with quantum speedup
items.result: Expectation value estimation achieves linear dependence on gate-wise stabilizer extent in low-variance regime (was quadratic via Hoeffding bounds) without increasing space complexity.
items.question: How to reduce classical sample complexity and runtime overhead for estimating quantum circuit expectation values using stabilizer decompositions?
items.prior: Standard quasiprobability stabilizer simulation sample bounds depend quadratically on stabilizer extent via Hoeffding's inequality.
items.limits: Sample complexity reduction to linear scaling in stabilizer extent holds specifically in low-variance regimes; evaluated numerically on QAOA and quantum kernel circuits.
items.tools: sum-over-Clifford method · quasiprobability-based stabilizer simulation · adaptive empirical variance estimation (Bennett / Bernstein-type stopping rules) · extended stabilizer framework
items.abstract: Classical simulability of quantum circuits plays a central role in characterizing and quantifying quantum computational advantage. Typically, the presence of non-Clifford gates introduces an exponential runtime overhead for classically estimating expectation values of observables. In this work, we introduce an efficient simulation framework that integrates the sum-over-Clifford method with quasi-probability-based stabilizer simulation to directly estimate expectation values. To optimize efficiency, we incorporate a circuit-adaptive reduction via variance estimation protocol, which terminates simulations once an empirical confidence bound is sufficient to guarantee the prescribed error tolerance. Our method circumvents overly conservative Hoeffding's inequality, thereby reducing the dependence on the gate-wise stabilizer extent from quadratic to linear in the low-variance regime, while maintaining the same space complexity as previous approaches. We explicitly prove the sample-complexity reduction for random quantum circuits and T-doped Clifford circuits and also empirically validate these advantages in the quantum approximate optimization algorithm and quantum kernel method.

items.title: Derivatives of Quantum Randomness: Separating Pseudorandom Unitaries from Pseudorandom (Function-like) States
items.authors: Minki Hhan
items.matched: sampling-based quantum advantage and its classical spoofing
items.result: Unitary oracle separates pseudorandom function-like state generators (PRFSGs) from pseudorandom unitaries (PRUs). Adaptively secure, quantum-accessible PRFSGs do not imply non-adaptively secure, forward-only PRUs, even for non-unitary implementations with polynomial ancilla space.
items.question: Can pseudorandom function-like state generators be used to construct pseudorandom unitaries when unrestricted ancillary qubits are permitted?
items.prior: Partial oracle separations existed only for candidate PRU constructions with severely bounded ancilla space.
items.limits: Black-box separation relative to a unitary oracle combined with QPSPACE.
items.tools: common-Haar function-like state (CHFS) oracle · Poincaré inequalities on sphere products · low-rank gradient analysis · quantum OR test · quantum process tomography
items.abstract: Quantum computation gives rise to new pseudorandom primitives for states and unitaries, including pseudorandom state generators (PRSGs), pseudorandom function-like state generators (PRFSGs), and pseudorandom unitaries (PRUs). In this paper, we show a full unitary oracle separation between PRFSGs and PRUs. The separation holds between the strongest state notion and the weakest unitary notion: even adaptively secure, quantum-accessible PRFSGs do not imply non-adaptively secure, forward-only PRUs, even when their implementations are allowed to be non-unitary and use an arbitrary number of ancillary qubits. This reveals a fundamental distinction between pseudorandomness for quantum states and for quantum unitaries. Our main technical idea is to view a candidate PRU construction with access to state generation oracles as a map from the underlying oracle states to implemented unitaries, and to study the derivatives of this map. These derivatives are inherently low rank, and we exploit this low-rank structure to distinguish the resulting unitaries from truly random ones. We believe this differential perspective may be useful for studying other structural questions about quantum states and unitaries.

items.title: Variational Real-Time Dynamics on Reduced Operator Manifolds
items.authors: Aeishah Ameera Anuar, PV Sriluckshmy, Riccardo Rossi, Fedor Simkovic
items.matched: Toward the first quantum simulation with quantum speedup
items.result: Operator-projected variational quantum real-time evolution (OVQRTE) updates parameterized circuits by matching Ehrenfest equations on polynomial-sized operator sets without quantum geometric tensor calculation. Reaches ground-state energy error ∼3×10⁻³ when generating QSCI subspaces on a 20-qubit simulator and executes on up to 24 superconducting qubits.
items.question: How can variational real-time dynamics be formulated to avoid measuring the quantum geometric tensor while reducing quantum circuit and measurement costs?
items.limits: Demonstrated for systems up to 24 qubits, tested with N_s=22 SPSA samples per gradient step, requires selected reduced operator manifolds.
items.tools: Operator-projected variational quantum real-time evolution (OVQRTE) · Simultaneous perturbation stochastic approximation (SPSA) · Quantum-selected configuration interaction (QSCI) · Low-depth unitary coupled cluster Jastrow (LUCJ) ansatz · IQM Emerald superconducting processor

items.abstract: Accurate real-time simulation of correlated quantum systems remains challenging for both classical methods and near-term quantum hardware. We introduce operator-projected variational quantum real-time evolution (OVQRTE), which updates a parameterized circuit by enforcing the Ehrenfest equations for a selected set of observables. OVQRTE requires only expectation-value measurements, while the choice of operator set enables a systematic trade-off between accuracy and measurement cost, substantially reducing quantum-resource requirements relative to existing variational real-time-evolution algorithms. After implementing OVQRTE dynamics of Heisenberg model on a simulator, we benchmark the algorithm for the Anderson impurity models on the IQM Emerald superconducting processor using up to 24 qubits. We further use OVQRTE to sample computational-basis states for quantum-selected configuration interaction (QSCI), enabling the calculation of the ground-state energy and density of states within a self-consistent ghost-Gutzwiller Ansatz (gGut) embedding loop. Our results establish OVQRTE as a promising approach for investigating correlated condensed-matter systems on near-term quantum hardware.

items.title: Quantum Codes for Generalized Amplitude-damping Noise
items.authors: Sourav Dutta, Anubhab Rudra, Manav Seksaria, Anil Prabhakar, Prabha Mandayam
items.matched: Toward the first quantum simulation with quantum speedup
items.result: Probabilistic approximate quantum error correction (PAQEC) on a five-qubit permutation-invariant code achieves fidelity loss that scales quadratically with generalized amplitude-damping strength γ, O(γ²), under post-selected recovery.
items.question: Can probabilistic and approximate quantum error correction frameworks be combined to suppress first-order generalized amplitude-damping errors in short codes?
items.prior: Deterministic quantum codes (such as the [5,1,3] stabilizer code) cannot eliminate first-order generalized amplitude-damping errors and incur fidelity loss scaling linearly with γ.
items.limits: Requires post-selection over successful recovery outcomes, reducing total success probability below 1.
items.tools: five-qubit permutation-invariant code · probabilistic approximate quantum error correction (PAQEC) · semidefinite programming · Charnes-Cooper transformation
items.caption: Entanglement fidelity and recovery probability as functions of damping strength γ at excitation parameter p=0.05. The numerically optimized code achieves higher entanglement fidelity than the [5,1] permutation-invariant code at the cost of lower success probability.
items.abstract: Quantum error correcting (QEC) plays a crucial role in protecting quantum information against decoherence and enabling scalable, reliable quantum computing. One of the most realistic and ubiquitous sources of noise affecting quantum hardware today is generalized amplitude-damping (GAD) noise. Conventional, deterministic QEC codes struggle to correct for GAD noise because of their inherent structure, leading to fidelity losses that scale linearly with the damping strength. In this work, we introduce the framework of probabilistic approximate quantum error correction (PAQEC), that combines the flexibility of approximate QEC with the potential of post-selected recovery, enabling high-fidelity, resource-efficient error correction. We construct a five-qubit permutation-invariant code that, under probabilistic recovery, achieves a fidelity loss quadratic in the damping strength, thus outperforming existing QEC codes. Formulating PAQEC as an optimization problem, we present a numerical technique based on Charnes-Cooper and semidefinite programming to identify the optimal recovery map for any PAQEC code. Our results establish PAQEC as a powerful tool for developing resource-efficient, high-fidelity quantum codes tailored to realistic noise, with promising implications for near-term quantum devices and future fault-tolerant architectures.

items.abstract: The role of entanglement in quantum optimization remains actively debated. To address this question, we focus on the fixed-parameter expanding-depth regime of the quantum approximate optimization algorithm (QAOA), where a compact two-parameter schedule is trained once on small instances and then applied as the problem size and circuit depth increase. To probe this regime beyond full state-vector simulation, we perform approximate matrix product state simulations for up to 50 qubits and 100 layers and quantify entanglement by the bond dimension. We observe an entangle--disentangle profile, with the peak bond dimension decreasing with depth and eventually saturating. This observation motivates an extreme approximation: projecting the state onto the product-state manifold (bond dimension one) after every two-qubit interaction. Based on this approximation, we introduce BOND-1, a quantum-inspired classical solver. Despite the drastic simplification, BOND-1 achieves cut ratios above 0.95 relative to the best known values on standard GSet MaxCut benchmarks with up to 20000 variables, and in some cases it matches those values. It achieves these results without per-instance optimization and has linear memory cost, while per-instance tuning can provide further improvement. These results show that, in this regime, a substantial fraction of the optimization power of QAOA survives even in the complete absence of entanglement. Our conclusions, however, are specific to this setting and do not imply that entanglement is unnecessary for quantum optimization in general.

items.title: Variational Real-Time Dynamics on Reduced Operator Manifolds
items.authors: Aeishah Ameera Anuar, PV Sriluckshmy, Riccardo Rossi, Fedor Simkovic
items.matched: Probing many-body dynamics on a 51-atom quantum simulator
items.result: Operator-projected variational quantum real-time evolution (OVQRTE) updates parameterized circuits by matching Ehrenfest equations on polynomial-sized operator sets without quantum geometric tensor calculation. Reaches ground-state energy error ∼3×10⁻³ when generating QSCI subspaces on a 20-qubit simulator and executes on up to 24 superconducting qubits.
items.question: How can variational real-time dynamics be formulated to avoid measuring the quantum geometric tensor while reducing quantum circuit and measurement costs?
items.limits: Demonstrated for systems up to 24 qubits, tested with N_s=22 SPSA samples per gradient step, requires selected reduced operator manifolds.
items.tools: Operator-projected variational quantum real-time evolution (OVQRTE) · Simultaneous perturbation stochastic approximation (SPSA) · Quantum-selected configuration interaction (QSCI) · Low-depth unitary coupled cluster Jastrow (LUCJ) ansatz · IQM Emerald superconducting processor
items.caption: Energy error |E-E_FCI| as a function of the cutoff fraction of the configuration interaction subspace size R, comparing exact time evolution to OVQRTE with SPSA gradient estimation across various evolution iterations for a 20-qubit system.
items.abstract: Accurate real-time simulation of correlated quantum systems remains challenging for both classical methods and near-term quantum hardware. We introduce operator-projected variational quantum real-time evolution (OVQRTE), which updates a parameterized circuit by enforcing the Ehrenfest equations for a selected set of observables. OVQRTE requires only expectation-value measurements, while the choice of operator set enables a systematic trade-off between accuracy and measurement cost, substantially reducing quantum-resource requirements relative to existing variational real-time-evolution algorithms. After implementing OVQRTE dynamics of Heisenberg model on a simulator, we benchmark the algorithm for the Anderson impurity models on the IQM Emerald superconducting processor using up to 24 qubits. We further use OVQRTE to sample computational-basis states for quantum-selected configuration interaction (QSCI), enabling the calculation of the ground-state energy and density of states within a self-consistent ghost-Gutzwiller Ansatz (gGut) embedding loop. Our results establish OVQRTE as a promising approach for investigating correlated condensed-matter systems on near-term quantum hardware.

items.title: NAQsim: Full-Stack Architecture Simulation Framework for Fast and Space-Efficient Neutral Atom Quantum Computing
items.authors: Yosuke Ueno, Shinichi Sunami, Toshihide Hinokuma, Yasunari Suzuki, Akihisa Goban, Hayata Yamasaki, Teruo Tanimoto, Ilkwon Byun
items.matched: Probing many-body dynamics on a 51-atom quantum simulator
items.result: Patch rotations cause 55.3% to 77.6% of execution time in transversal neutral-atom FTQC. The D3-ROT architecture eliminates this bottleneck, yielding an average 2.27× speedup (up to 2.57×) at 22.4% average footprint overhead.
items.question: How can full-stack co-optimization across compiler, control hardware, and qubit plane reduce logical operation latency in transversal neutral-atom FTQC architectures?
items.prior: Patch rotations executed via space-efficient reflection on baseline transversal surface-code architectures.
items.limits: Evaluated via classical CPU simulation across 8 FTQC benchmark circuits (QPE and FTCircuitBench) using rotated transversal surface codes.
items.tools: NAQsim architecture simulation framework · SLM laser toggling with AOD atom holding · heterogeneous qubit-plane rotation patches · rotation distribution compiler pass
items.caption: Per-layer latency breakdown (bars, left axis) and logical error rate (line, right axis) across six routing and patch-rotation architectures, showing D3-ROT minimizing latency without sacrificing error rates.
items.abstract: Technological advances in neutral-atom platforms have opened a new path toward designing efficient protocols for fault-tolerant quantum computing (FTQC). However, each physical operation is still orders of magnitude slower than on other platforms, such as superconducting qubits. Therefore, architects must identify fast and efficient FTQC architectures, which require reliable modeling tools to explore various design choices across the software, classical hardware, and quantum device stacks of neutral-atom platforms. In this paper, we propose NAQsim, an open-source simulation framework for neutral-atom FTQC architectures based on transversal gates. As its key feature, NAQsim enables detailed full-stack architecture evaluation that opens opportunities to explore previously overlooked performance bottlenecks. As a first use case for NAQsim, we identify one such bottleneck, patch rotations, perform full-stack co-optimization, and finally derive a near-rotation-free architecture (D3-ROT). For practical FTQC benchmark workloads, D3-ROT achieves a 2.27x speedup from this single bottleneck alone, with minimal footprint overhead. These results point to a much broader space of full-stack optimizations that NAQsim makes accessible for transversal surface-code architectures and beyond.

html.result: Patch rotations cause 55.3% to 77.6% of execution time in transversal neutral-atom FTQC. The D3-ROT architecture eliminates this bottleneck, yielding an average <math xmlns="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML"><mrow><mn>2.27</mn><mo>×</mo></mrow></math> speedup (up to <math xmlns="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML"><mrow><mn>2.57</mn><mo>×</mo></mrow></math>) at 22.4% average footprint overhead.

items.title: OpenQARP: a modular framework for quantum application research
items.authors: Stefano Scali, Vicente P. Soloviev, Antonio Márquez Romero, Brian Coyle, Giuseppe Buonaiuto, Annie Paine, Jonathan H. Fetherolf, Marcos Diez García, Michal Krompiec, Josh Kirsopp
items.matched: Theory of Trotter Error with Commutator Scaling
items.result: OpenQARP executes operator algebra one to two orders of magnitude faster than OpenFermion and matches mature compilers on two-qubit gate count while keeping strict unified conventions.
items.question: How to build an open-source quantum computing framework that eliminates silent convention errors across the research workflow while maintaining high simulator and operator performance?
items.prior: OpenFermion, Qiskit/Aer, PennyLane/Lightning, Qulacs, qsim, and pytket required cross-framework plumbing with differing qubit orderings and phase conventions.
items.limits: Benchmarks measured on a single Apple-silicon host using scalar C++ block kernels without SIMD or AVX vectorization; no pulse-level control, autodiff, or direct hardware execution engine.
items.tools: C++20 compiled core with Python interface · block-based circuit abstraction · gate fusion and flip-mask Pauli contraction · independent NumPy/SciPy testing oracles
items.caption: Run-phase simulation time on a logarithmic vertical axis plotted against register size for brickwork circuits, comparing constant-factor scaling across different quantum simulation frameworks.
items.abstract: We introduce OpenQARP, the Open Quantum Application Research Package: an open-source Python framework for quantum application research, built on a compiled C++ core. In OpenQARP, an application is assembled from an algorithm library that orchestrates three interchangeable layers: blocks describe circuits, primitives describe what to extract from them, and engines describe how they run. The release spans near-term through fault-tolerant methods, targeting problems from electronic structure to combinatorial optimization, with device-aware compilation, circuit cutting, and resource estimation over a single set of numerical conventions that the code must follow. Every numerical feature is checked against an independent oracle, and every published timing carries a correctness check. Against OpenFermion, Qiskit/Aer, PennyLane/Lightning, Qulacs, qsim, and pytket, OpenQARP is one to two orders of magnitude faster on operator algebra and among the fastest on simulation. It matches mature compilers on two-qubit gate count, and expresses a complete algorithm in the lines a framework needs rather than the plumbing a primitive stack demands.

items.title: Open Quantum Systems
items.authors: Erik Torrontegui, Ricardo Puebla
items.matched: thermalization, many-body localization and quantum scars in driven systems
items.result: Pedagogical review and lecture notes covering open quantum systems, microscopic derivations of GKSL master equations, Liouvillian spectral properties, and foundational quantum thermodynamics.
items.question: How do environmental interactions generate decoherence, dissipation, and thermodynamic behavior in reduced quantum systems?
items.limits: Primarily treats weak-coupling Markovian regimes via Born-Markov and secular approximations; omits non-Markovian dynamics, strong-coupling thermodynamics, and collision models.
items.tools: density matrix formalism · GKSL master equation · Liouvillian superoperators · Born-Markov approximation · quantum data processing inequality

items.abstract: Open quantum systems describe quantum systems that interact unavoidably with their environments. These notes introduce the physical origins of decoherence and dissipation in realistic settings, developing the theoretical framework of reduced dynamics and quantum master equations within the connection to thermodynamics in the quantum regime. Additionally, a set of relevant exercises are proposed to reinforce the acquisition of knowledge. The text equips readers with the tools to model and analyze open quantum dynamics.

items.title: A Modular, Topology-Aware Software Stack for Entanglement-Based Distributed Quantum Computing
items.authors: Luke Andreesen, Shobhit Gupta, Sean Sullivan, Manish Kumar Singh
items.matched: Evidence for the utility of quantum computing before fault tolerance
items.result: For an 18-qubit QFT circuit on a 2-QPU network, replacing all-to-all with nearest-neighbor intra-QPU connectivity increases EPR-pair consumption by more than an order of magnitude. Under stochastic link generation, shortest-duration and critical-path arbitration policies reduce completion time by 17.7±1.3% and 17.9±1.5% relative to FIFO.
items.question: How can hardware network topology and link contention be incorporated into an open-source software stack for partitioning, compiling, and scheduling distributed quantum circuits?
items.prior: Prior distributed compilers (such as Pytket-DQC) lack timestamped operation scheduling and rely on idealized, optimistic all-to-all connectivity assumptions.
items.limits: NISQ-era compilation only; does not model decoherence, noise, link fidelity degradation, entanglement distillation, or quantum error correction.
items.tools: OpenQASM compiler toolchain · Discrete-event stochastic scheduler · Quantum Network Constructor (QNC) · Hypergraph and Dynamic Interaction circuit partitioners · Cat-Entangler and Cat-Disentangler teleportation protocols
items.caption: EPR-pair consumption (y-axis) for 18-qubit QFT and 64-qubit Adder circuits on a 2-QPU network under all-to-all versus nearest-neighbor intra-QPU connectivity (x-axis) across three partitioning strategies.
items.abstract: Distributed quantum computing (DQC) seeks to scale beyond the limits of monolithic processors by interconnecting multiple quantum processing units (QPUs) through entanglement-based links. Realizing this vision requires the co-design of hardware and software across the domains of quantum networking, compilation, and scheduling, yet existing tools remain fragmented between monolithic circuit compilers and long-distance quantum network simulators. We present an open-source, topology-informed framework for the compilation and scheduling of distributed quantum programs. Given an input circuit and a description of the target network, the framework partitions and reconstructs the circuit into a distributed program that respects the specified inter- and intra-QPU topology, covers cross-QPU operations through gate and state teleportation, and schedules the result under either deterministic or stochastic entanglement-generation models. By accepting and emitting standard OpenQASM, the framework interoperates with existing monolithic toolchains, and its standardized module interfaces allow partitioning and scheduling strategies to be interchanged and benchmarked. Using this framework, we show that the best-performing compilation strategy varies across the tested circuits and network configurations, and that both network topology and intra-QPU connectivity substantially affect the entanglement cost of execution. These findings underscore the need for a co-design approach to distributed quantum computing, which our framework is designed to support.

Under stochastic link generation, shortest-duration and critical-path arbitration policies reduce completion time by <math xmlns="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML"><mrow><mn>17.7</mn><mo>±</mo><mn>1.3</mn><mi>%</mi></mrow></math> and <math xmlns="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML"><mrow><mn>17.9</mn><mo>±</mo><mn>1.5</mn><mi>%</mi></mrow></math> relative to FIFO.

items.title: Exact quantum circuits for a Heisenberg triangle with Dzyaloshinskii-Moriya interaction
items.authors: Andrey Zhukov
items.matched: Probing many-body dynamics on a 51-atom quantum simulator
items.result: Exact quantum circuits for three-spin Heisenberg-DM triangles require at most 8 CNOT gates for pure DM interactions, 10 CNOT gates for uniform exchange and DM couplings, and 14 CNOT gates for unequal couplings satisfying J² = D₁₂D₂₃ + D₂₃D₃₁ + D₃₁D₁₂.
items.question: How can coupled time evolution on a three-spin Heisenberg triangle with Dzyaloshinskii–Moriya interactions be compiled into exact, time-independent-depth quantum circuits across the full Hilbert space?
items.limits: Unequal DM with exchange requires J² = D₁₂D₂₃ + D₂₃D₃₁ + D₃₁D₁₂. Valid on spin-1/2 systems without noise or decoherence.
items.tools: unitary basis transformation · quaternion parameter matching · local z-rotations · symmetric Strang step analytical retuning
items.caption: Exact circuit implementations of three-spin triangle evolution. Panel (a) uses 8 CNOT gates for pure DM interactions with arbitrary couplings, and panel (b) uses 10 CNOT gates for equal Heisenberg and DM couplings.
items.abstract: We construct exact quantum circuits for a three-spin Heisenberg triangle with Dzyaloshinskii-Moriya (DM) interaction. A change of basis reduces pure DM evolution with arbitrary couplings to two single-qubit rotations, giving a circuit with at most 8 CNOT gates. When J and D are each the same on all bonds, one fixed basis gives a circuit with at most 10 CNOT gates for any real J,D,t. Local spin rotations extend the construction to a family with unequal DM couplings and nonzero exchange, requiring at most 14 CNOT gates. All circuits act on the full Hilbert space. An alternative pure DM implementation uses five two-qubit DM gates: analytically retuning the angles of one symmetric Strang step makes it exact. A 12-spin kagome example illustrates the use of these exact local blocks in lattice simulation.
