items.title: Quantum Compiler Design for Fault-Tolerant Quantum Computing
items.authors: Chenghong Zhu, Jiahan Chen, Keming He, Hongshun Yao, Zhaohui Yang, Jin-Guo Liu, Anbang Wu, Xiaotong Ni, Xingsheng Luan, Zhuo Fu, Shenggen Zheng, Xin Wang
items.matched: Evidence for the utility of quantum computing before fault tolerance
items.result: Presents a full-stack taxonomy organizing fault-tolerant quantum computing compilation into three interacting layers: logical-level QEC optimization, physical-level hardware realization across superconducting, trapped-ion, and neutral-atom platforms, and classical real-time decoder runtime integration.
items.question: How should quantum compilers be architected across the entire hardware and software stack to bridge logical fault-tolerant operations, physical syndrome extraction, and real-time classical decoding?
items.limits: Literature survey covering peer-reviewed papers and substantive preprints available through June 2026.
items.tools: Lattice surgery and code surgery · Detector error models · Magic-state distillation scheduling · Real-time decoding and frame tracking
items.caption: Full-stack abstraction of QEC-protected quantum computation, illustrating the compilation flow from logical circuit synthesis to physical hardware mapping and the classical decoding feedback loop.
items.abstract: Scalable quantum computation is expected to rely on fault-tolerant quantum computation (FTQC), in which quantum error correction (QEC) suppresses physical errors sufficiently to support reliable logical operations. This requires quantum compilation to move beyond general-purpose circuit optimization toward encoding-aware and protocol-structured compilation across the full stack of fault-tolerant quantum computers. Beyond circuit synthesis and hardware mapping, an FTQC compiler must lower algorithm-level operations into the logical gate set supported by the chosen code, coordinate encoded data and ancilla resources, realize logical operations together with repeated syndrome extraction under hardware constraints, and provide the resulting measurement stream to real-time decoding. This survey presents a full-stack view of compiler design for QEC-protected quantum computation. We organize existing work into three interacting layers: logical-level QEC compilation, physical-level QEC realization, and decoder runtime integration. At the logical level, we review surface-code lattice-surgery compilers, beyond-surface-code code-surgery frameworks including emerging qLDPC approaches, and compilation support for non-Clifford operations such as magic-state distillation and code switching. At the physical level, we survey hardware-aware QEC realization on superconducting, trapped-ion, and neutral-atom platforms. We further examine decoder models, real-time decoding systems, and frame-management mechanisms that close the feedback loop during fault-tolerant execution. Finally, we identify open challenges in cross-layer optimization, qLDPC compilation, compiler-decoder co-design, runtime adaptivity, and the development of integrated and benchmarkable FTQC compilation stacks. An actively maintained paper list is available at: github.com/chenghongz/QEC-compiler-design.

items.title: Real-Space Renormalization of Stabilizer Rényi Entropies in Spin Chains
items.authors: Sonja Gombar, Petar Mali, Slobodan Radovsević, Milica Rutonjski, Milan Pantić, Milica Pavkov-Hrvojević
items.matched: Theory of Trotter Error with Commutator Scaling
items.result: Real-space renormalization yields a closed-form analytical expression for stabilizer Rényi entropies (quantum magic) in the low-energy, large-distance regime of a class of spin Hamiltonians.
items.question: How do stabilizer Rényi entropies evolve under coarse-graining across different quantum phases in spin chains?
items.limits: Valid specifically in the low-energy, large-distance regime.
items.tools: real-space renormalization group · stabilizer Rényi entropy · spin chain Hamiltonians
items.abstract: Stabilizer states constitute an important class of quantum states that can be generated from computational-basis states using Pauli operators and Clifford gates. Although they may exhibit substantial multipartite entanglement, quantum circuits restricted to stabilizer operations can be efficiently simulated classically and therefore cannot, by themselves, provide a quantum computational advantage. Such an advantage requires non-stabilizer resources, commonly referred to as quantum magic. In this paper, we investigate the non-stabilizerness of quantum states arising in a class of spin Hamiltonians by computing their stabilizer Rényi entropies. Using real-space renormalization-group techniques, we obtain a closed-form expression valid in the low-energy, large-distance regime. We analyze how quantum magic evolves under coarse-graining and explore its behavior across different parameter regimes and quantum phases.

items.title: Large-scale NMR simulation on a trapped-ion quantum computer
items.authors: Pascal Stadler, Alec Owens, Etienne Granet, David Muñoz Ramo, Michael Marthaler
items.matched: Probing many-body dynamics on a 51-atom quantum simulator
items.result: Simulated liquid-state proton NMR spectrum of 1,2-di-tert-butyl-diphosphane on trapped-ion hardware across 70 Trotter steps and circuit depth 1442, reproducing methyl peak at 1.35 ppm and the weak double peak at 4.1 ppm.
items.question: Can digital quantum hardware accurately reproduce the nontrivial NMR spectral features of classically challenging multi-spin molecules?
items.prior: Failed to reproduce the distinctive 3.9–4.3 ppm double-peak structure on 22-qubit IBM superconducting and IonQ trapped-ion hardware (prior hardware demonstration).
items.limits: Simulated effective 21-spin model rather than full 22-spin Hamiltonian, removing two outer proton peaks. Maximum evolution time limited to 29.4 ms (spectral resolution ~0.07 ppm), preventing resolution of ~0.01 ppm fine splittings.
items.tools: Quantinuum System Model H2-1 trapped-ion quantum computer · Trotterized real-time evolution · Singlet-triplet subspace projection · Leakage detection and post-selection · Pauli twirling and dynamical decoupling
items.caption: Simulated proton NMR spectrum (intensity versus chemical shift in ppm) comparing Quantinuum H2-1 hardware execution against full classical reference and time-truncated classical reference spectra.
items.abstract: Simulating nuclear magnetic resonance (NMR) spectra is a promising application of quantum simulation. Using Quantinuum's System Model H2, a trapped-ion quantum computer, we demonstrate an end-to-end, large-scale digital NMR simulation of a classically challenging benchmark molecule, 1,2-di-tert-butyl-diphosphane. We implement a hardware-efficient reduction of the nuclear-spin Hamiltonian, enabling Trotterized real-time evolution of an effective 21-spin model with tailored error suppression to reduce the effects of device noise. The reconstructed liquid-state proton NMR spectrum agrees with classical reference calculations and reproduces key spectroscopic features that previous quantum hardware demonstrations did not capture. Given the widespread use of NMR in chemical analysis and industrial research, these results advance digital quantum simulation of NMR spectra towards practical quantum utility.

items.title: Exact efficient simulation of noisy logical magic states using Clifford stabilizers
items.authors: Yugo Takada, Stephen D. Bartlett, Dominic J. Williamson
items.matched: Evidence for the utility of quantum computing before fault tolerance
items.result: Simulates noisy preparation of logical magic states via an equivalent Clifford circuit in polynomial time and space, with no dependence on stabilizer or Pauli rank. Validated on magic state cultivation up to fault distance f=7.
items.question: Can noisy preparation circuits for third-level Clifford-hierarchy logical magic states under circuit-level Pauli errors be simulated exactly in classical polynomial time?
items.prior: Existing rank-decomposition algorithms scale exponentially with target-state stabilizer or Pauli rank, and Clifford proxies (such as S|+⟩ instead of T|+⟩) yield unverified approximations.
items.limits: Restricted to circuit-level Pauli noise models and states satisfying the algebraic Clifford-stabilizer commutation criteria. Statistical uncertainty remains for extremely low logical error rates (f=7) due to Monte Carlo sampling costs.
items.tools: Clifford-stabilizer group formalism · Pauli proxy algorithm · stim TableauSimulator · PyMatching decoder
items.caption: Logical error rate and acceptance rate versus physical error rate p for f=3 magic state cultivation. Clifford-stabilizer simulation matches exact state-vector simulation across all values of p.
items.abstract: The preparation of high-fidelity logical magic states is a crucial subroutine for universal fault-tolerant quantum computation (FTQC). Predicting the performance of FTQC and developing improved protocols rely on numerical methods to classically simulate logical magic state preparation in the presence of noise. Clifford logic on Pauli-stabilizer codes with circuit-level Pauli errors can be efficiently simulated using Pauli-stabilizer formalism, but the non-Clifford operations required to prepare logical magic states render generic simulation inefficient. We introduce Clifford-stabilizer simulation, an exact and efficient algorithm based on updating a Clifford-stabilizer group to simulate noisy preparation protocols for a broad class of logical magic states used to implement non-Clifford gates in the third level of the Clifford hierarchy under circuit-level Pauli errors. Clifford-stabilizer simulation applies to a range of operations that commonly appear in preparation protocols for such logical magic states, including Pauli-stabilizer measurements, logical Clifford measurements, and transversal non-Clifford gates. Our algorithm for Clifford-stabilizer simulation maps a non-Clifford circuit with sampled circuit-level Pauli errors to a Clifford circuit that exactly reproduces its measurement outcome distribution, achieving time and space complexities polynomial in relevant protocol parameters. We perform exact simulation of magic state cultivation up to fault distance 7 by Clifford-stabilizer simulation. Our method provides a route to perform exact benchmarking of large-scale logical magic state preparation protocols required for useful FTQC.

items.title: Two-Dimensional Materials toward CMOS-Compatible Scalable Quantum Hardware
items.authors: Mara Lieberegts, Ye Wang
items.matched: Semiconductor spin qubits
items.result: Evaluates 2D materials and van der Waals interfaces to mitigate fabrication-induced chemical residues, structural disorder, and interface non-uniformity in scalable solid-state quantum chips using CMOS-compatible processes.
items.question: Whether CMOS channel fabrication processes for 2D materials can be transferred to solid-state quantum hardware to improve coherence and scalability.
items.limits: Perspective and literature assessment; focus on solid-state qubit platforms compatible with standard semiconductor fabrication.
items.tools: 2D materials · van der Waals interfaces · CMOS manufacturing processes
items.abstract: Manufacturability is one of several constraints on developing solid-state quantum processors, along with qubit performance, control, connectivity, cryogenic operation, and fault tolerance. Chemical residues, structural disorder, and non-uniform interfaces introduced during fabrication can compromise qubit coherence. Two-dimensional (2D) materials, with their atomically thin crystals and van der Waals interfaces, offer routes to address some of these challenges. Their concurrent development as next-generation CMOS channel materials motivates an examination of whether relevant processes can be transferred to quantum chips. This Perspective evaluates the opportunities and limitations of 2D materials for CMOS-compatible quantum hardware.

items.title: Phase-stable voltage bias for Josephson photonics devices
items.authors: Amir Hosein Esmaeili, Naveen Nehra, Alexandre Paquette, Mona Arabmohammadi, Baptiste Monge, Alexandre Rogalle, Francois Cyrenne-Bergeron, Yannick Lapointe, Nicolas Lavoie, Nicolas Bourlet, Max Hofheinz
items.matched: Charge-insensitive qubit design derived from the Cooper pair box
items.result: Coherent phase reference transferred from a Josephson voltage standard via superconducting order parameter increases ICTA averaged gain by 14 dB to ~27 dB and achieves degenerate phase-sensitive amplification.
items.question: How can a stable phase reference be provided to dc-biased Josephson photonics devices to suppress voltage-noise-induced linewidth broadening and enable phase-coherent parametric operation?
items.prior: Unstabilized ICTA had maximum gain of 13 dB, ~1.5 photon input-referred noise, and lacked degenerate phase-sensitive features due to phase diffusion across >2π within ~30 ns.
items.limits: Millikelvin operation with low RF power (-65 dBm to -40 dBm). Resonator linewidth Γ/2π ≈ 1.2 GHz. Squeezing deforms into an S-shape at 31 dB gain due to amplifier saturation.
items.tools: Josephson voltage standard (JVS) · Inelastic Cooper-pair tunneling amplifier (ICTA) · Superconducting on-chip low-pass filter · SQUID
items.caption: Gain and noise versus frequency for unstabilized and JVS-stabilized ICTA. Activating the JVS at 12 GHz locks the Josephson frequency over a ±50 MHz bias range, boosts peak gain from 13 dB to 27 dB, and reaches input noise of 0.5 photons at degeneracy.
items.abstract: Parametric interactions are foundational to superconducting quantum technologies, yet conventional microwave-driven pumping introduces parasitic Kerr nonlinearities and higher-order harmonics that limit device performance. Josephson Photonics (JP) avoids these parasitics by utilizing dc-biased junctions but has remained constrained by high phase noise and the absence of a stable phase reference. Here, we overcome this limitation by integrating a Josephson voltage standard (JVS) to establish a noise-tolerant phase reference, and demonstrate that this reference is coherently transferred to an inelastic Cooper-pair tunneling amplifier (ICTA) via the superconducting order parameter.The resulting low-phase-noise architecture yields a 14-dB enhancement in averaged gain and better quantum-limited noise performance. Critically, the phase reference enables the first observation of phase-sensitive gain and sqeezing in a dc-biased amplifier. By reconciling clean, Kerr-free nonlinearities with phase-coherent drive, our architecture establishes a robust platform for high-purity parametric processes in superconducting circuits.

items.title: Two-qubit gates for the soft 0-π qubit
items.authors: Zhenxing Liu, Eli Weissler, Joshua Combes
items.matched: transmon and fluxonium coherence, single- and two-qubit gate fidelity
items.result: Unprotected CZ gate for capacitively coupled soft 0-π qubits achieves simulated fidelity of approximately 99.9% at gate time of approximately 160ns.
items.question: Can an unprotected two-qubit gate with high fidelity and short duration be designed for experimentally realizable soft 0-π superconducting qubits?
items.limits: Simulated in zero-disorder limit with identical circuit components; uses phenomenological noise model with reduced 60-level Hilbert subspace.

items.caption: Gate error (1-F) versus gate time t_g for the CZ gate under closed-system unitary evolution and open-system noise models with coherence times T₁=T_φ=T∈3, 30, 170 μs.
items.abstract: The 0-π qubit promises longer lifetimes than the transmon, making it a strong candidate for a next-generation, lower-error qubit. Gyenis et al. experimentally demonstrated an unprotected single-qubit gate in the soft 0-π regime [1], but no corresponding two-qubit gate has yet been proposed. We propose an unprotected CZ gate for capacitively coupled soft 0-π qubits. The gate uses a direct transition between a computational state and a higher non-computational state. Assuming negligible device disorder and a phenomenological noise model, the simulated CZ gate achieves a fidelity of approximately 99.9% at a gate time of approximately 160 ns.

items.title: Quantum Simulation of Two-Dimensional Free Dirac Hamiltonian in Multimode Circuit QED
items.authors: Jiwon Kang, Jiuk Lee, Eliya Blumenthal, Shay Hacohen-Gourgy, Eunseong Kim
items.matched: Semiconductor spin qubits
items.result: Implemented a programmable 2+1D free massive Dirac Hamiltonian in multimode circuit QED. Observed rotational Zitterbewegung whose oscillation frequency increases while amplitude decreases with higher effective mass ΔΩ.
items.question: Can a fully programmable two-dimensional massive Dirac Hamiltonian, with dynamical quantum operators for both momentum components, be simulated in circuit QED?
items.prior: 1D Dirac dynamics and 2D massless Weyl dynamics were demonstrated in trapped ions, while photonic lattices and fixed-coupling superconducting circuits lacked independent dynamical quantum momentum degrees of freedom.
items.limits: Fidelity bounded by transmon charging energy E_c/h = 230MHz limiting drive power, spin-locking decoherence (T_(2ρ) = 17 μs), non-RWA terms, and ±5kHz Rabi calibration uncertainty.
items.tools: transmon qubit · multimode 3D flute cavity (TE101 and TE102 modes) · double-sideband microwave driving · characteristic function measurement

items.abstract: Two-dimensional massive Dirac systems feature a gapped Dirac-cone dispersion central to a broad range of phenomena in condensed-matter and topological physics. While quantum simulations have demonstrated one-dimensional Dirac dynamics and two-dimensional massless Weyl dynamics, programmable simulation of massive two-dimensional Dirac dynamics remains experimentally unexplored. Here, we realize a programmable two-dimensional free Dirac Hamiltonian in circuit QED, with independently tunable spin-momentum couplings and mass, using a single Rabi-driven qubit coupled to two modes of a multimode cavity. Using this Hamiltonian, we observe rotational Zitterbewegung of a two-dimensional massive Dirac particle and its dependence on the effective mass. Time-dependent master-equation simulations incorporating measured decoherence, corrections beyond the rotating-wave approximation (RWA), and anharmonicity of the transmon reproduce the observed dynamics. Our results establish multimode circuit QED as a compact, programmable platform for higher-dimensional relativistic quantum dynamics and provide a foundation for exploring dynamical and topological phenomena in gapped Dirac systems.

items.title: Probing proximity-induced superconductivity in bilayer graphene using gate-defined quantum dots
items.authors: Philipp Schmidt, Mathies Funke, Till Tenger, Katarina Stanojević, Hubert Dulisch, Kenji Watanabe, Takashi Taniguchi, Fabian Hassler, Christian Volk, Szabolcs Csonka, Christoph Stampfer
items.matched: Semiconductor spin qubits
items.result: Proximity-induced superconducting gap reaches up to 80 μeV in bilayer graphene contacted by NbSe₂ and follows a dwell-time-limited ballistic decay Δ^*(x) = πℏv / (4x) with v ≈5.2 ×10⁴ m/s, remaining detectable over distances exceeding 1 μm.
items.question: How does the proximity-induced superconducting gap decay spatially in a gate-defined bilayer graphene channel coupled to a layered superconductor?
items.limits: Base temperature ≈80 mK; out-of-plane critical magnetic field B_c ≈8 mT; effective velocity v extracted near the flattened band edge with order-unity uncertainty.
items.tools: bilayer graphene encapsulated in hexagonal boron nitride · few-layer superconducting NbSe₂ · electrostatic split- and finger-gate quantum dot definition · Coulomb blockade and finite-bias tunneling spectroscopy
items.caption: Measured proximity-induced gap Δ^* as a function of distance x from the NbSe₂ edge, showing ballistic 1/x decay across quantum dots defined at four gate locations.
items.abstract: Van der Waals heterostructures offer a direct way of combining two-dimensional (2D) materials with different electronic properties, such as 2D semiconductors, metals, and superconductors, in a single device. Bilayer graphene (BLG) is particularly attractive in this context, as its electrically tunable band gap enables local control of tunnel barriers and quantum dots. Here, we realize an all-2D hybrid platform based on BLG proximitized by superconducting NbSe₂. Using local electrostatic gates, we define tunnel barriers and quantum dots at different distances from the lateral superconductor-semiconductor interface. The quantum dots serve as local spectroscopic probes of the proximitized BLG channel segment, forming tunable superconductor-quantum dot-normal conductor junction devices. Coulomb blockade and finite-bias spectroscopy reveal a proximity-induced superconducting gap of up to 80 μeV and allow to track its evolution with increasing distance from the NbSe₂ contact. We find that the local density of states remains suppressed over distances exceeding 1 μm, consistent with superconducting proximity through a highly ballistic BLG channel. Our results show that BLG-superconductor hybrids offer a controllable platform where quantum dots and quantum point contacts can be well combined with superconductivity.

items.title: Pump-Free Microwave-Optical Bell Pair Generation for Teleportation-Based Quantum Transduction
items.authors: Fangxin Li, Jaesung Heo, Zhaoyou Wang, Benjamin Pingault, Xingyu Gao, Tengyang Ruan, Anjun Chu, David D. Awschalom, Andrew N. Cleland, Andrew P. Higginbotham, Alexander A. High, Liang Jiang

items.result: Protocol generates microwave-optical heralded Bell pairs without an optical pump, reaching heralding rates up to 3.71 kHz with 0.97 fidelity in a ⁸⁷Rb ensemble.
items.question: Can microwave-optical Bell pairs be generated for teleportation-based transduction without relying on an optical pump?
items.limits: Theoretical and numerical simulation; assumes zero optical pump during generation, trapping fields switched off in ensembles, and transmon relaxation time T_(1,t)=300 µs.
items.tools: MO-NODE protocol · cavity QED · three-level transmon · Purcell-enhanced emission · single spins, atomic ensembles, and spin-phonon systems
items.caption: Heralding rate and Bell-state fidelity plotted against transmon relaxation time T_(1,t) across color centers, atomic ensembles, and phonon-mediated platforms.
items.abstract: The coherent conversion between microwave and optical photons, known as quantum transduction, is critical for connecting superconducting processors to optical networks. Existing methods are limited by complications associated with optical pumping. We propose a pump-free microwave-optical Bell-pair source for teleportation-based transduction. Using a spin or atomic system resonantly coupled to optical and microwave cavities, the scheme generates loss-robust heralded Bell pairs. Across color centers, atomic ensembles, and phonon-mediated systems, this assembly achieves kilohertz-range heralding rates with high fidelity.

items.title: Optical Quantum Computing
items.authors: Hamza Hasnaoui, Leonardo Limongi, Taira Giordani, Beatrice Polacchi, Alberto Quaranta, Martino Bernard, Fabio Sciarrino, Mirko Lobino
items.matched: photonic qubits, linear-optical computing and boson sampling
items.result: Surveys discrete- and continuous-variable optical quantum computing architectures, measurement-based cluster-state models, and non-universal algorithms (boson sampling, VQEs, QML).
items.question: How do optical encoding schemes and computing architectures compare across universal and non-universal quantum platforms?
items.limits: Photonic scaling is constrained by weak single-photon nonlinearities, probabilistic gate generation, and optical propagation losses.
items.tools: integrated photonics · continuous-variable squeeze states · discrete-variable cluster states · linear optical interferometry
items.caption: Taxonomy mapping discrete-variable and continuous-variable universal optical quantum computing models alongside non-universal photonic applications.
items.abstract: Under the label of optical quantum computing, there are a variety of protocols and experiments that use the quantum properties of light to achieve a computational advantage over classical computing machines. In this review, we describe some of the main implementations, which differ in the type of encoding and in how the computation is performed, whether using gates or cluster states. For each protocol, we describe advantages and challenges with an overview of the experimental results obtained, summarized in tables. Because of the great relevance achieved in this field, there is a section dedicated to non-universal quantum computation with photons, where boson sampling, variational quantum eigensolvers, and quantum machine learning applications are described. The aim is to give the reader the broadest overview of the applications where photons and their quantum properties play a key role in computation.

items.title: Giant-atom-mediated photon blockade
items.authors: C. Cui, W. Y. Hu, Y. Q. Ji, H. T. Cui, Yan-Hui Zhou, H. Z. Shen
items.matched: cavity QED, atom-photon interfaces and quantum networks
items.result: Multipoint coupling of giant atom provides additional destructive interference paths, enabling simultaneous unconventional photon blockade in two and three coupled cavities with driven first cavity. Point-atom configuration cannot produce simultaneous unconventional photon blockade.
items.question: Can multipoint coupling of a giant atom enable simultaneous unconventional photon blockade across multiple coupled cavities?
items.limits: Weak driving regime (F ≪κ), equal cavity and atomic dissipations κ₁=κ₂=κ₃=γ≡κ, theoretical model without experimental verification.
items.tools: Lindblad master equation · effective non-Hermitian Hamiltonian · few-photon state truncation
items.caption: log₁₀g⁽²⁾_o(0) in a three-cavity system driven at cavity a₁ versus coupling phase θ. Shows simultaneous dips to minimum values in all three cavities at θ_opt=1.2732π and θ_opt=0.4456π.
items.abstract: Photon blockade is a phenomenon where the presence of system nonlinearity causes the output to consist of single photons, which has been extensively studied in point atom systems, but it is barely explored in giant atom ones. In this paper, we propose giant atom-mediated photon blockade scheme based on two cavities and three cavities systems with driving field applied to the first cavity. We show that simultaneous unconventional photon blockades (UPBs) can not occur in the point atom system (the atom coupling only to the leftmost cavity) due to there always existing a cavity to have a single path. In contrast, the spatially extended nature of giant atom enables coupling to multiple cavities and allows for the introduction of a phase and coupling strength. Consequently, simultaneous UPBs in multiple cavities can be obtained due to the multipath destructive interference. Moreover, by manipulating the detuning, we observe simultaneous conventional photon blockades (CPBs) in multiple cavities. Finally, we study simultaneous two-photon blockades (2PBs) in point atom multiple cavities system.

items.title: A Programmable Rydberg Quantum Bus for Nonlocal Connectivity
items.authors: X. Jin, F. Yang, Weibin Li, X. Q. Shao
items.matched: Quantum information with Rydberg atoms
items.result: Dispersive Rydberg atom chains act as coherent quantum buses to mediate effective quasi-all-to-all interactions between data units via virtual excitations, analytically derived using Green's-function continued fractions.
items.question: Can a Rydberg atom array provide a stationary quantum bus to mediate coherent nonlocal connectivity between distant data units?
items.limits: Off-resonant dispersive regime with J_μ ≪min_k |E_k|; validated with Gaussian positional uncertainty σ= 0.02~μm and Rydberg lifetimes up to T = 77~K.
items.tools: Green's function continued-fraction method · Feshbach partitioning · Monte Carlo wavefunction trajectories · Floquet engineering
items.caption: Population dynamics of data units coupled to a nine-atom Rydberg chain across single, double, and triple excitation manifolds, plotted against dimensionless time for V/J=40 and Δ/J=80.
items.abstract: Scalable quantum networks require processing nodes with flexible internal connectivity, yet neutral-atom architectures remain constrained by the strong spatial dependence of native Rydberg interactions. Here we show that a Rydberg atom chain can act as a coherent quantum bus, converting a locally connected one-dimensional architecture into an effectively nonlocal interaction network. Virtual excitations in the dispersive regime mediate controllable interactions between spatially separated data units, which we derive analytically using a Green's-function continued-fraction method. The resulting mechanism is not restricted to single-excitation dynamics and supports several distinct functionalities, including Floquet-engineered chiral transport, remote entanglement of mechanical oscillators, and destructive interference for selectively suppressing unwanted dipole exchange. Simulations incorporating full long-range Rydberg interactions, atomic position fluctuations, and finite Rydberg-state lifetimes show that the mediated dynamics remain robust under experimentally relevant conditions. These results establish Rydberg chains as programmable coherent mediators for extending the internal connectivity of neutral-atom quantum nodes toward quasi-all-to-all coupling, providing a hardware-level route toward scalable and reconfigurable quantum-network architectures.

items.title: Programmable Hong--Ou--Mandel interference in a giant-atom beam splitter
items.authors: Ruolin Chai, Lei Du, Guoqing Cai, Alejandro Vivas-Viaña, Anton Frisk Kockum, Yong Li
items.matched: Quantum information with Rydberg atoms
items.result: Two-level giant atom coupled to two waveguides via two points with tunable phase differences θ_a,θ_b acts as a programmable 50:50 beam splitter, yielding a Hong–Ou–Mandel dip and continuous tuning between two-photon bunching and antibunching.
items.question: Can a giant atom with tunable coupling phases serve as a programmable Hong–Ou–Mandel interferometer and enable coupling-phase quantum parameter estimation?
items.limits: Theoretical model assuming identical coupled cavities, two-level approximation for the giant atom, rotating-wave approximation, and lossless wave-packet propagation.
items.tools: waveguide quantum electrodynamics · coupled-cavity arrays · two-photon wave-packet scattering simulation · classical and quantum Fisher information
items.caption: Coincidence and bunching probabilities versus initial wave-packet displacement δx₀ (showing the HOM dip) and versus coupling phases θ_a,θ_b, demonstrating continuous control over two-photon output correlations.
items.abstract: The Hong--Ou--Mandel (HOM) effect is a hallmark of two-photon quantum interference, in which two indistinguishable photons impinging on a balanced beam splitter bunch into the same output port. Here, we show that a giant atom (GA), coupled to two waveguides through two coupling points each, can function as a programmable HOM interferometer, enabling continuous control over single-photon beam splitting and two-photon interference. This programmability arises from coupling-phase differences in the GA, which tune its self-interference and directionality, and thereby its scattering response. To characterize the two-photon interference, we analyze the scattering of two Gaussian single-photon wave packets injected through different waveguides and evaluate the bunching and antibunching (coincidence) probabilities of the resulting four output ports. At the operating point where the GA acts as an effective 50:50 beam splitter for single photons, we observe a pronounced HOM dip as the relative input delay between the two wave packets is varied. Away from this point, adjusting the coupling phases continuously tunes the two-photon output statistics between bunching into the same output port and antibunching across distinct output ports. In addition, we explore an application to quantum parameter estimation, showing that small deviations of coupling phases can be estimated from the two-photon output statistics, with the achievable sensitivity quantified by the classical Fisher information associated with a binary coincidence measurement. Our giant-atom beam splitter thus provides a programmable platform for two-photon interference in waveguide quantum electrodynamics, with potential applications in quantum information processing, quantum communication, and quantum sensing.

items.title: Ancilla-assisted dark-state quantum gates in ultracold polar molecules
items.authors: Yan Lu, Xiao-Feng Shi
items.matched: Quantum information with Rydberg atoms
items.result: Two-qubit and multi-qubit controlled-phase gates C(φ) can be implemented in optically trapped polar molecules via an ancilla-assisted dark-state mechanism driven solely by two smooth adiabatic microwave π pulses on the ancilla.
items.question: How can high-fidelity entangling quantum gates be realized in optically trapped polar molecules without suffering from motional decoherence or Rydberg-state decay?
items.limits: Theoretical and numerical simulation; assumes zero rotational Zeeman effect or weak rotational Zeeman effect relative to nuclear spin Zeeman effect (evaluated for ²³Na¹³³Cs at B=2G); requires specific tweezer alignment to suppress inter-data molecule DDI.
items.tools: dipole-dipole interaction (DDI) · adiabatic dark-state evolution · microwave driving · optical tweezer geometry optimization · quantized motional coupling analysis
items.caption: Gate infidelity log₁₀(1-F) of the ancilla-assisted CZ gate as a function of the microwave field polarization impurity parameters ς₀ and ς.
items.abstract: High-fidelity entangling gates are useful for circuit-based quantum computing, yet their realization in a scalable platform is challenging. Optically trapped ultracold polar molecules offer a potentially scalable platform. Here, we introduce a two-qubit molecular entangling gate via a novel ancilla-assisted dark-state mechanism, where high fidelity is achievable. In particular, we find that by using appropriate qubit states for the ancilla and the data qubits, dark states can appear, and entanglement can emerge by driving the ancilla only. It is also feasible to extend the two-qubit gate to a multi-qubit gate via the same dark-state mechanism.

items.title: Cavity-induced intertwining of density and pairing order in a degenerate Fermi gas
items.authors: Sankalp Sharma, Farokh Mivehvar, Helmut Ritsch, Tomasz Wasak
items.matched: cavity QED, atom-photon interfaces and quantum networks
items.result: In transversely driven Fermi gas inside an optical cavity, bare attraction triggers direct transition into an intertwined charge-density-wave plus pair-density-wave superradiant phase, whereas repulsive interaction separates density-wave ordering from finite-momentum pairing until higher pump power.
items.question: How preexisting superfluidity and photon-pair coupling govern the sequence and nature of self-organized spatial and pairing orders in a degenerate Fermi gas?
items.limits: Zero temperature (T=0), effective 1D geometry along cavity axis, dispersive regime (large single-atom and molecular detunings Δ_e, Δ_B), mean-field cavity treatment.
items.tools: Hartree-Fock-Bogoliubov (HFB) mean-field theory · Linear response susceptibility analysis · Adiabatic elimination of molecular/excited transitions · Dispersive two-channel light-matter Hamiltonian
items.caption: Mean-field zero-temperature phase diagram versus pump strength β and bare contact interaction g₀/(E_Rλ_c), distinguishing normal, superfluid, CDW superradiant, and intertwined CDW+PDW phases.
items.abstract: Recent quantum gas cavity-QED experiments demonstrated simultaneous coupling of photons to single atom transitions as well as correlated pairs of ultracold fermions trapped inside optical cavities. This enables simultaneous control over density ordering and pairing. Using extensive numerical simulations, we show that in a transversely driven, two-component degenerate Fermi gas, the interplay of cavity-induced and bare atom--atom interactions controls not only the power threshold for self-organization, but also the type of spatial ordering in the Z₂-symmetry-broken superradiant state. In the repulsive interaction regime, unpaired or weakly paired fermions first self-organize through a charge-density-wave instability, and finite-momentum pairing only occurs at much stronger pump strengths. In contrast, an attractive superfluid undergoes a joint density--pairing instability, directly entering into intertwined phase with charge-density-wave and pair-density-wave orders. At strong pumping the photon-enhanced pair interaction generates localized density and pairing order even when the bare contact interaction is repulsive. In this cavity-dominated regime strong spatial localization suppresses the long range superfluid coherence. Our results identify the role of cavity-induced atomic interactions in supporting intertwined fermionic orders and pave the way for exploring exotic states with multiple orders in highly controlled hybrid light-matter systems.

items.title: Comparing magic state cultivation methods using matrix product states
items.authors: Tom Hartweg, Asier Piñeiro Orioli
items.matched: Surface code quantum computing by lattice surgery
items.result: For d=5 regular surface-code fold-transversal cultivation, $|Tangle$ logical error rates match $|Sangle$ Clifford proxy error rates across the tested noise range. A rotated surface-code scheme achieves ∼1.3× lower expected space-time cost while reaching 10⁻⁹ logical error rate.
items.question: What is the exact non-Clifford performance and logical error rate of fold-transversal magic state cultivation schemes on surface codes?
items.prior: Color-code cultivation (Gidney et al.) showed a 7× to 30× higher logical error rate for |T⟩ state cultivation compared to the |S⟩ Clifford proxy.
items.limits: Depolarising SD6 circuit noise model, post-selection on all syndrome detectors and final noiseless decoding, classical simulation on commodity CPU.
items.tools: matrix-product states (MPS) · Clifford-augmented MPS (CAMPS) · Pauli pre-screening · subset sampling · Stim
items.caption: Logical error rate versus physical depolarising error rate p for d=3 and d=5 magic state cultivation schemes comparing |S⟩ (Stim Clifford proxy) and |T⟩ (exact CAMPS simulation) outputs.
items.abstract: Magic state cultivation prepares high-fidelity magic states at low expected space-time costs; however, the exact performance of some schemes is unsettled due to the difficulty in simulating non-Clifford circuits. Here, we use matrix-product states (MPS) based methods to compute the exact performance of two types of fold-transversal cultivation schemes: (i) the Sahay et al method based on the regular surface code S gate, and (ii) a method we propose based on a partially fault-tolerant fold-transversal S gate. We show that for the former protocol at d=5, the |T⟩ output reaches similar logical error rates to the |S⟩ output, traditionally used as a cheap full Clifford proxy. This contrasts with the ∼10× discrepancy reported for the d=5 colour-code scheme of Gidney et al. We also find that our new d=5 scheme has ∼1.3× lower expected space-time cost while still reaching 10⁻⁹ logical error rate. We show that MPS and Clifford-augmented MPS (CAMPS) perform on par with or even better than the recently introduced near-Clifford simulator Clifft on the hardest d=5 regular surface code scheme. Additionally, to speed up simulation, we propose a new pre-screening method based on simple Pauli propagation, lowering by up to three orders of magnitude the required number of exact simulations, and use several simulator-agnostic sampling methods such as subset sampling.

items.title: Exact logical error rates for magic state cultivation
items.authors: Kwok Ho Wan, Ainhoa Zapirain
items.matched: High-threshold and low-overhead fault-tolerant quantum memory
items.result: Exact logical error rates for magic state cultivation computed without Monte Carlo sampling; P_L⁽⁵⁾(p=10⁻³) = 3.32842537…×10⁻⁹ with series expansion P_L⁽⁵⁾(x) = 574/375x³ + 972959741/810000x⁴ + O(x⁵) for x=p/(1-p).
items.question: What are the exact post-selected logical error rates and acceptance probabilities of magic state cultivation circuits across all fault orders using actual T gates instead of sampling with S-gate proxies?
items.limits: Standard uniform circuit-level depolarising noise at parameter p. Excludes escape, grafting, and decoding stages; logical readout is assumed noiseless.
items.tools: Pauli propagation · binary tensor network contraction · Chinese remainder theorem over modular primes · exact polynomial series expansion in x=p/(1-p)
items.caption: Logical error rate (left), acceptance probability (middle), and truncated series relative error (right) for d=5 cultivation as functions of noise strength p. The analytical curves agree with published Monte Carlo sampling intervals from Clifft and SOFT.
items.abstract: We compute exactly the acceptance and logical error rates for the distance d=3 and d=5 magic state cultivation circuits from Clifft [arXiv:2604.27058] and SOFT [arXiv:2512.23037] using Pauli propagation and binary tensor contraction. Actual T gates are studied, not the S-gate proxy used for sampling. The calculation includes every fault order at several circuit-level noise strengths (p). We provide a series expansion form to the logical error rates, through order (p/(1-p))¹⁰. The analytical results recover the numerical values from Clifft and SOFT at both d=3 and d=5 to within their sampling uncertainty. Then, we show that the d=3 and d=5 circuits actually have fault distances of d_fault=2 and d_fault=3 respectively, explaining the similar distance degrading effects from the companion code of [Quantum 10, 2134 (2026)].

items.title: Diagnosing and Restoring the Degraded Fault Distance of Magic State Cultivation
items.authors: Tim Chan, Armands Strikis, Zhu Sun, Zhenyu Cai
items.matched: High-threshold and low-overhead fault-tolerant quantum memory
items.result: Flagged double-check circuits eliminate malignant hook errors in magic state cultivation, suppressing pre-escape logical error rate from O(p³) to O(p⁵) and achieving a 4.9× error rate improvement at p = 10⁻³ for a 1.36× attempt overhead.
items.question: Why does T-state cultivation suffer higher logical error rates and lower fault distances than S-state cultivation under circuit-level noise, and how can the full fault distance be restored?
items.prior: Unflagged distance-3 (distance-5) T-state cultivation degraded to fault distance 2 (fault distance 3), while S-state cultivation retained full fault distance 3 (fault distance 5).
items.limits: Evaluated under standard circuit-level depolarising noise at error rate p = 10⁻³; applies to fixed logical-qubit count with physical qubit count n.
items.tools: circuit-level depolarising noise simulations · analytic propagation of Pauli hook errors into coherent Clifford errors · O(n³)-time Clifford acceptance probability algorithm · flagged verification circuits
items.abstract: T-state cultivation is a resource-efficient protocol producing logical T states but recent benchmarks show that its logical error rate is considerably higher than intended i.e. than S-state cultivation, which is the analogous protocol for producing logical S states. In this paper, we explain this T-S discrepancy by analytically showing, under circuit-level depolarising noise, that distance-3 (-5) T-state cultivation has fault distance 2 (3) due to Pauli hook errors that propagate to coherent Clifford errors after its final double-check circuit; such errors remain Pauli in S-state cultivation, which consequently retains fault distance 3 (5). As part of our analysis we derive a general formula, and an O(n³)-time algorithm for fixed logical-qubit count, for the acceptance probability of a logical mixed state afflicted with a Clifford error, where n is the physical qubit count. We then design flags that detect the malignant hook errors in cultivation, improving the pre-escape logical error rate from O(p³) to O(p⁵). At noise level p =10⁻³, this is a 4.9× improvement, costing a 1.36× increase in attempts per accepted shot.

items.title: Algorithmic Design of Heralded Linear Optical Circuits for Multipartite Entanglement
items.authors: Jaehee Kim, Hon Wai Lau, William J. Munro, Joonsuk Huh, Seungbeom Chin
items.matched: High-threshold and low-overhead fault-tolerant quantum memory
items.result: Linear quantum graph framework automates design of heralded linear optical circuits for multipartite entangled states, producing an N=4 cluster state circuit with 26 beam splitters (10 initial photons).
items.question: How can heralded linear optical circuits for arbitrary multipartite entangled quantum states be designed systematically rather than via state-specific manual trial and error?
items.prior: Generating an N=4 cluster state required 45 beam splitters with 9 photons at a success probability of 2.05×10⁻³ (Banchi et al. 2024 / Ref. [16]).
items.limits: Unweighted initial graph search; ideal photon-number-resolving detectors; computational scaling grows exponentially with ancilla mode count M.
items.tools: effective perfect matching (EPM) bipartite graphs · linear quantum graph (LQG) translation rules · graph canonization · reduced density matrix spectral signature matching
items.caption: Heralded linear optical circuit schematic for generating the 4-qubit cluster state using two ancilla panels, four system panels, and six photon-subtraction detection panels.
items.abstract: Heralded multipartite entanglement is a key resource for various quantum information tasks. However, designing linear optical circuits that generate specific target states is generally challenging due to the complexity of the required optical structures. Here we formulate the design of heralded photonic circuits as an algorithmic graph-search problem. Our framework enables the automated construction and optimization of heralded photonic circuits by substantially reducing the search space using the linear quantum graph (LQG) picture. Our strategy reconstructs circuit structures as graphs in the picture and identifies suitable graphs automatically. As a result, we design efficient schemes for a broad range of useful multipartite resource states, including hypergraph magic states, quantum error correcting codes, general three-qubit states and length-1 caterpillar graph states. Our work establishes an algorithmic framework for the systematic discovery of heralded resource states, laying the foundation for the automated design of increasingly complex multipartite entangled resources.

items.title: Quantum Encodings, Private Messages, and Communication Complexity
items.authors: Tom Gur, Miryam Mi-Ying Huang, Er-Cheng Tang
items.matched: Asymptotically good Quantum and locally testable classical LDPC codes
items.result: Proves equivalence between quantum decomposable randomized encodings (QDRE) and quantum private simultaneous message protocols (QPSM). Every n-to-m-qubit channel has an m-qubit quantum communication QPSM with exponential entanglement, while with ≤c n pre-shared entanglement, communication is bounded by Ω(n).
items.question: Is the linear dependence of quantum randomized encoding size on circuit size inherent, or can it be characterized more tightly via pre-shared entanglement and communication complexity?
items.prior: Prior QDRE constructions scaled encoding size linearly with circuit size |Q|.
items.limits: Small quantum communication protocols for general channels require pre-shared entanglement exponential in n. Bounded linear entanglement yields an unavoidable worst-case Ω(n) communication/encoding lower bound.
items.tools: quantum private simultaneous message protocols (QPSM) · Pauli mixing · port-teleportation · distributed inner product estimation (DIPE) reductions
items.caption: Schematic of the Pauli-Port Complementarity protocol showing non-interactive local teleportation using pre-shared entanglement before quantum and classical messages are forwarded to the referee.
items.abstract: We study the complexity of quantum decomposable randomized encodings (QDRE). We establish a bi-directional connection between the QDRE model and the communication complexity model of quantum private simultaneous message protocols (QPSM), where classical communication is free, and quantum communication is the primary complexity measure. We show the following upper and lower bounds. (1) For every quantum channel mapping n to m qubits, we give a QPSM protocol with quantum communication m, using exponential pre-shared entanglement. In particular, constant-output channels have O(1) quantum communication, and classical-output channels require no quantum communication. (2) With O(n) pre-shared entanglement, every one-qubit-output channel has an O(n)-quantum-communication QPSM protocol. Conversely, there exists a channel and a constant c>0 for which any protocol with at most cn pre-shared entanglement requires Ω(n) quantum communication. (3) In contrast, we identify a structured class of quantum channels, Clifford-induced channels, for which there exist QPSM protocols with O(n) pre-shared entangled qubits and only O(1) quantum communication complexity. Through our connection, we obtain analogous upper and lower bounds on the quantum encoding size of QDRE. Our results show that the amount of pre-shared entanglement plays a central role in quantum encoding size and quantum communication complexity.

items.title: Optical Quantum Computing
items.authors: Hamza Hasnaoui, Leonardo Limongi, Taira Giordani, Beatrice Polacchi, Alberto Quaranta, Martino Bernard, Fabio Sciarrino, Mirko Lobino
items.matched: Fault-tolerant quantum computation by anyons
items.result: Surveys discrete- and continuous-variable optical quantum computing architectures, measurement-based cluster-state models, and non-universal algorithms (boson sampling, VQEs, QML).
items.question: How do optical encoding schemes and computing architectures compare across universal and non-universal quantum platforms?
items.limits: Photonic scaling is constrained by weak single-photon nonlinearities, probabilistic gate generation, and optical propagation losses.
items.tools: integrated photonics · continuous-variable squeeze states · discrete-variable cluster states · linear optical interferometry
items.caption: Taxonomy mapping discrete-variable and continuous-variable universal optical quantum computing models alongside non-universal photonic applications.
items.abstract: Under the label of optical quantum computing, there are a variety of protocols and experiments that use the quantum properties of light to achieve a computational advantage over classical computing machines. In this review, we describe some of the main implementations, which differ in the type of encoding and in how the computation is performed, whether using gates or cluster states. For each protocol, we describe advantages and challenges with an overview of the experimental results obtained, summarized in tables. Because of the great relevance achieved in this field, there is a section dedicated to non-universal quantum computation with photons, where boson sampling, variational quantum eigensolvers, and quantum machine learning applications are described. The aim is to give the reader the broadest overview of the applications where photons and their quantum properties play a key role in computation.

items.title: Query-Optimal and Gate-Efficient Lindbladian Simulation
items.authors: Boyang Chen, Minbo Gao, Xinzhao Wang, Shuo Zhou
items.matched: Surface codes: Towards practical large-scale quantum computation
items.result: Approximates Lindbladian evolution to diamond-norm error ε using O (τ+(log(1/ε))/(log(e+log(1/ε)/τ))) oracle queries for τ=(α_H+α_B²)t, matching the Hamiltonian simulation lower bound.
items.question: What is the optimal query complexity of simulating Lindbladian dynamics as a function of evolution time and target precision?

items.limits: Requires block encoding of Hamiltonian and projected unitary encoding of stacked jump operators. Time-dependent case requires Lipschitz continuity and coherent time-indexed oracle access.

Blue connections show M⊗I_S acting as in ( 51 ); the other connections implement the projections, swaps, and phases in the explicit action of G in ( 53 ).
items.abstract: We give a quantum algorithm for Lindbladian simulation given a block encoding of the Hamiltonian H and a projected unitary encoding of the stacked jump operator B=∑_(k=1)^m |k⟩⊗L_k, with normalization factors α_H and α_B, respectively. For evolution time t, set τ=(α_H+α_B²)t. The algorithm approximates the evolution channel to diamond-norm error ε using O (τ+(log(1/ε))/(log(e+log(1/ε)/τ))) oracle queries, matching the query lower bound for Hamiltonian simulation. The number of additional one- and two-qubit gates is linear in the query complexity up to polylogarithmic factors. The query- and gate-complexity bounds extend to Lipschitz-continuous time-dependent Lindbladians under coherent time-indexed oracle access. Our construction uses a one-query transducer that implements a product of rational approximations to short-time evolution when supplied with a catalyst. We bound the error from omitting the catalyst by exploiting orthogonality between different sequences of Kraus labels. The gate implementation combines a compressed Kraus-label representation, which stores only the positions and values of the nonzero labels, with the rotation factorization of Chen et al.

items.abstract: Can an attacker turn influence over an artificial intelligence (AI) adviser into a harmful quantum error-correction update? We identify an ambiguity in passive syndrome records that obstructs recovery selection, then show how additional calibration measurements support certified recovery updates under uncertainty and drift. In an odd-distance square toric code with error-free preparation, syndrome measurements, and recovery operations, opposite coherent X rotations produce identical passive syndrome-history distributions. Yet a fixed phase correction can help at one sign and harm at the other. A terminal logical measurement on known encoded calibration states supplies the missing sign information. A separate evaluator accepts an update only when calibration uncertainty and a justified drift bound certify improvement over the current recovery, without assuming that the adviser recommends correctly. In simulated advice attacks, calibration-confidence checks reject harmful proposals while retaining beneficial updates under honest advice. We derive sufficient limits on calibration age that require improvement through deployment. In matched simulations, a validated channel-specific bound retains more beneficial updates than the general bound after accounting for evaluation time, while preventing the tested harmful activations under the stated drift assumption. A separate surface-code experiment includes stochastic circuit faults and noise changing during acquisition. Deterministic controllers achieve at least as many beneficial updates with the same observations. Violating the drift assumption permits harmful acceptance in the toric experiment. The results identify information required for recovery selection, establish conditional guarantees against harmful updates, and quantify the recovery improvements forgone through conservative acceptance.

items.abstract: We study the complexity of quantum decomposable randomized encodings (QDRE). We establish a bi-directional connection between the QDRE model and the communication complexity model of quantum private simultaneous message protocols (QPSM), where classical communication is free, and quantum communication is the primary complexity measure. We show the following upper and lower bounds. (1) For every quantum channel mapping n to m qubits, we give a QPSM protocol with quantum communication m, using exponential pre-shared entanglement. In particular, constant-output channels have O(1) quantum communication, and classical-output channels require no quantum communication. (2) With O(n) pre-shared entanglement, every one-qubit-output channel has an O(n)-quantum-communication QPSM protocol. Conversely, there exists a channel and a constant c>0 for which any protocol with at most cn pre-shared entanglement requires Ω(n) quantum communication. (3) In contrast, we identify a structured class of quantum channels, Clifford-induced channels, for which there exist QPSM protocols with O(n) pre-shared entangled qubits and only O(1) quantum communication complexity. Through our connection, we obtain analogous upper and lower bounds on the quantum encoding size of QDRE. Our results show that the amount of pre-shared entanglement plays a central role in quantum encoding size and quantum communication complexity.

items.abstract: We give a quantum algorithm for Lindbladian simulation given a block encoding of the Hamiltonian H and a projected unitary encoding of the stacked jump operator B=∑_(k=1)^m |k⟩⊗L_k, with normalization factors α_H and α_B, respectively. For evolution time t, set τ=(α_H+α_B²)t. The algorithm approximates the evolution channel to diamond-norm error ε using O (τ+(log(1/ε))/(log(e+log(1/ε)/τ))) oracle queries, matching the query lower bound for Hamiltonian simulation. The number of additional one- and two-qubit gates is linear in the query complexity up to polylogarithmic factors. The query- and gate-complexity bounds extend to Lipschitz-continuous time-dependent Lindbladians under coherent time-indexed oracle access. Our construction uses a one-query transducer that implements a product of rational approximations to short-time evolution when supplied with a catalyst. We bound the error from omitting the catalyst by exploiting orthogonality between different sequences of Kraus labels. The gate implementation combines a compressed Kraus-label representation, which stores only the positions and values of the nonzero labels, with the rotation factorization of Chen et al.

items.abstract: Estimating quantum state properties is essential across a wide range of applications, from studying quantum many-body physics to benchmarking quantum hardware. We present Qurrium, a Python package built on Qiskit that implements randomized measurement protocols for estimating purity, second-order Rényi entropy, expectation values of Pauli observables, and state overlap. In this paper, we focus on the classical shadow protocol and demonstrate two workflows in Qurrium. One is the end-to-end workflow that integrates quantum circuit preparation, simulation, measurement, and analysis. The other is the standalone estimation workflow that accepts pre-collected measurement data from any hardware platform in Qurrium's data format. We demonstrate both workflows through examples of a cluster state and an Ising time-evolved state. Furthermore, we report results obtained from a superconducting quantum processor developed by Academia Sinica and analyzed using the standalone estimation workflow. Qurrium is built on Qiskit, the dominant framework in quantum computing software, making it directly accessible to the large community of researchers already working with Qiskit. The source code is openly available at https://github.com/qurrium/qurrium and the example code is provided at https://github.com/qurrium/classical-shadow-examples.

items.title: QiT: Quantum-Inspired Transformer for Visual Recognition Task
items.authors: Badri N. Patro, Vijay Agneeswaran
items.matched: Quantum singular value transformation and beyond: exponential improvements for…

On a 1-epoch benchmark, QiT runs 882–997× faster than a 4-qubit PennyLane simulator while running 1.58–1.76× slower than standard classical ViT.
items.question: Can quantum-motivated structural motifs like periodic angle encodings and multiplicative interactions be realized as scalable, fully classical Transformer operations for visual recognition without quantum hardware?
items.prior: 4-qubit simulated quantum Transformer in PennyLane, which is 882–997× slower on wall-clock time in 1-epoch testing.
items.limits: All point estimates without repeated seeds or uncertainty intervals. No controlled component ablations against parameter-matched classical ViTs. Emulates functional motifs without physical entanglement or quantum speedup.
items.tools: trigonometric angle-inspired token encoding · periodic-feature self-attention (cosine kernel) · gated multiplicative channel mixer · PennyLane circuit simulator baseline
items.caption: Schematic of the QiT encoder block showing token angle encoding into sine/cosine features, followed by kernel attention and a gated surrogate mixer replacing quantum circuits with classical tensor operations.
items.abstract: Quantum machine learning offers a compelling representational perspective: angle-encoded states inhabit Hilbert spaces in which periodic similarities and interactions can be expressed naturally. Realizing this perspective for visual recognition remains difficult, however, because present quantum neural networks are constrained by limited qubit counts, costly circuit simulation and measurement, noise, and unstable optimization on noisy intermediate-scale quantum devices. We investigate whether useful structural ideas from quantum models can instead be realized as scalable classical Transformer operations. We introduce QiT, a Quantum-inspired Transformer for vision tasks with three components: (i) angle-inspired encoding that maps image tokens to learned trigonometric Hilbert-space features analogous to quantum rotation-based state encoding; (ii) self-attention over these periodic features, inducing a classical cosine kernel approximated to quantum fidelity kernels; and (iii) gated multiplicative emulation, a trainable classical surrogate for interaction terms found in variational circuits. All components are differentiable tensor operations, so QiT claims neither quantum computation nor quantum speedup and retains the O(N²D) attention complexity of a standard Vision Transformer. Across image-classification benchmarks, QiT is competitive with a matched classical Transformer while avoiding the severe runtime cost observed for a small simulated quantum Transformer. QiT-B reaches 78.3% ImageNet-1K top-1 accuracy with 45.7M parameters and 11.5 GFLOPs. These results position QiT as a scalable baseline for isolating and evaluating quantum-motivated inductive biases in visual recognition.

items.abstract: In this introductory review, we present and compare four algorithms for the numerical integration of the Lindblad equation for one-dimensional quantum lattice systems. All four methods are based on Matrix Product State representations and can be viewed as extensions of the Time-Evolving Block Decimation (TEBD) algorithm to open quantum systems. Two approaches directly integrate the vectorized Lindblad equation, one of them explicitly enforcing the positivity of the density matrix. The other two rely on stochastic unravelings of the Lindblad equation, namely the quantum trajectory and quantum state diffusion approaches. We discuss the principles, numerical implementation, accuracy, and computational efficiency of the different methods, and benchmark them against an exactly solvable free fermion model.

items.title: Fast Evaluation of the Sixth-Order Time-Convolutionless Master-Equation Generator and Beyond
items.authors: Jiahao Chen, Sirui Chen, Dragomir Davidovic
items.matched: Probing many-body dynamics on a 51-atom quantum simulator
items.result: Evaluates the complete Hadamard-reduced sixth-order time-convolutionless master-equation generator time series in O(N_tlog² N_t) operations and O(N_t) storage at fixed system dimension.
items.question: How can the two remaining ordered integrals in the sixth-order time-convolutionless master-equation generator be evaluated faster than direct quadrature?
items.prior: Direct quadrature of the Hadamard-reduced TCL6 generator requires O(N_t³) operations at fixed system dimension.
items.limits: Stationary centered Gaussian bath, finite-dimensional system, single Hermitian coupling operator, and dynamics within the perturbative TCL validity regime.
items.tools: Hadamard reduction · exact dyadic recursion · 1D causal convolutions (FFT) · ordered time-gap coordinates
items.caption: Runtime scaling versus grid size N_t up to 2²⁵ points on one CPU core, showing the O(N_tlog² N_t) scaling of the full TCL6 generator and isolated history kernels compared to direct integration.
items.abstract: Direct quadrature of the Hadamard-reduced sixth-order time-convolutionless (TCL6) generator at all N_t sampled times requires O(N_t³) operations at fixed system dimension. We derive an exact reduction for a finite-dimensional system coupled through one Hermitian operator to a stationary centered Gaussian bath. By separating fixed operator coefficients from scalar bath kernels, the complete TCL6 time series is reduced to cumulative sums and first-order recurrences, one-dimensional causal convolutions, and an exact dyadic recursion for interlocked histories. With the algorithm, evaluating the complete TCL6 time series requires O(N_tlog² N_t) operations at fixed system dimension. In addition, we show that TCL2n can be evaluated with O(N_tlogⁿ⁻¹ N_t) complexity. A fixed finite Matsubara expansion of the bath correlation function permits O(N_tlogN_t) evaluation at any fixed TCL order. These reductions enable fast long-time simulations of non-Markovian open quantum systems within the regime of validity of the TCL expansion.

items.authors: João Barata, Ying-Ying Li, Bo Wang, Hua Xing Zhu
items.matched: analog quantum simulation of lattice models on cold atoms or superconducting ar…
items.result: Formulation of lattice detector operators via continuity current j_j^E reproduces continuum energy-flow observables E(hatn) and matches 2d Ising CFT predictions at criticality.
items.question: Can asymptotic energy-flow detector observables be formulated and computed quantitatively on finite lattice spin systems?
items.limits: Exploratory calculations on 1D spin chains (N=24, 48 sites); results retain finite-bandwidth and packet-preparation systematic dependence.
items.tools: DMRG · Time-Evolving Block Decimation (TEBD) · Matrix Product States (MPS) · Krylov subspace / Ritz states

items.abstract: Detector observables pose a fundamental challenge for nonperturbative lattice methods due to their intrinsically real-time and asymptotic nature. We propose quantum simulation platforms as an ideal setting for studying these observables. Using quantum spin systems as a demonstration, we construct lattice detector operators and establish their connection to continuum energy-flow observables. We demonstrate this framework in the 1+1-dimensional quantum Ising model, where finite lattice calculations show quantitative agreement with conformal field theory expectations at criticality. These results support the interpretation of the lattice flow operators as regulated counterparts of continuum detectors in the scaling and asymptotic limits, providing a concrete route toward realizing high-energy collider physics on table-top quantum platforms.

items.title: Graph lattice sums and graph zeta functions for long-range interacting quantum lattice models
items.authors: Andreas Alexander Buchheit, Andreas Rupp
items.matched: analog quantum simulation of lattice models on cold atoms or superconducting ar…
items.result: Evaluates high-order graph lattice sums for long-range interacting quantum models deterministically, reducing compute times from tens of thousands of core-hours down to 10 minutes on a single core for a 10th-order series (7,136 graphs, up to 30-dimensional sums) on a 4,096-point 3D momentum grid.
items.question: How can the high-dimensional oscillatory graph lattice sums in linked-cluster perturbation theory of long-range interacting quantum lattice models be computed without stochastic Monte Carlo methods?
items.prior: Monte Carlo graph lattice sums required cluster-scale runtimes (typically a full day on a cluster per momentum evaluation) and suffered from stochastic error.
items.limits: Monoatomic Bravais lattices; gapped quantum lattice models within the perturbative convergence radius.
items.tools: Epstein zeta functions · graph block factorization and caching · series-parallel convolution algebra · tensor-network bucket elimination · fast Fourier transforms
items.caption: Three-dimensional dispersion relation ω(k,λ) across the Brillouin zone of a 3D long-range transverse-field Ising model on a cubic lattice at λ=-0.03 and power-law exponent ν=4, showing non-analytic behaviour at the Γ point.
items.abstract: Taming the exponential increase of the Hilbert space dimension with system size in the simulation of gapped quantum lattice models is of the highest relevance for understanding and designing exotic quantum materials, where nonlocal interactions are of particular interest. High-order linked-cluster expansions provide access the solution of the eigenvalue problem for the infinite system, yet rely on the computation of high-dimensional oscillatory lattice sums with a graph structure, only approachable with Monte Carlo methods so far. This work resolves this issue, rendering all required graph lattice sums, referred to as graph zeta functions for kernels involving power-laws, computable. The resulting method reduces the evaluation time for state-of-the art series expansions from tenthousands of core-hours to minutes. After factorizing the lattice sum over blocks, each block is evaluated by the cheapest available strategy depending on its treewidth tw. Basic blocks admit analytic forms in terms of generalized zeta functions. Series-parallel blocks with tw≤2 can be computed at linear cost in the number of graph nodes and in the size of the momentum grid using a semi-analytical algebra based on Epstein zeta functions and rapidly decaying Fourier series. Finally, for tw>2, the method is combined with tensor-network bucket elimination yielding polynomial scaling of numerical work and memory in momentum grid size with exponents only growing with tw rather than with the number of vertices. Through use of FFT, the full momentum grid is recovered at the cost of a single momentum evaluation. We provide a detailed analysis of the precision and runtime of our method against analytic and numerical benchmarks. We further reproduce published Monte Carlo data for the transverse-field Ising model on different 1D, 2D, and 3D lattices, obtaining full agreement.

items.title: A Programmable Rydberg Quantum Bus for Nonlocal Connectivity
items.authors: X. Jin, F. Yang, Weibin Li, X. Q. Shao
items.matched: Probing many-body dynamics on a 51-atom quantum simulator
items.result: Dispersive Rydberg atom chains act as coherent quantum buses to mediate effective quasi-all-to-all interactions between data units via virtual excitations, analytically derived using Green's-function continued fractions.
items.question: Can a Rydberg atom array provide a stationary quantum bus to mediate coherent nonlocal connectivity between distant data units?
items.limits: Off-resonant dispersive regime with J_μ ≪min_k |E_k|; validated with Gaussian positional uncertainty σ= 0.02~μm and Rydberg lifetimes up to T = 77~K.
items.tools: Green's function continued-fraction method · Feshbach partitioning · Monte Carlo wavefunction trajectories · Floquet engineering
items.caption: Population dynamics of data units coupled to a nine-atom Rydberg chain across single, double, and triple excitation manifolds, plotted against dimensionless time for V/J=40 and Δ/J=80.
items.abstract: Scalable quantum networks require processing nodes with flexible internal connectivity, yet neutral-atom architectures remain constrained by the strong spatial dependence of native Rydberg interactions. Here we show that a Rydberg atom chain can act as a coherent quantum bus, converting a locally connected one-dimensional architecture into an effectively nonlocal interaction network. Virtual excitations in the dispersive regime mediate controllable interactions between spatially separated data units, which we derive analytically using a Green's-function continued-fraction method. The resulting mechanism is not restricted to single-excitation dynamics and supports several distinct functionalities, including Floquet-engineered chiral transport, remote entanglement of mechanical oscillators, and destructive interference for selectively suppressing unwanted dipole exchange. Simulations incorporating full long-range Rydberg interactions, atomic position fluctuations, and finite Rydberg-state lifetimes show that the mediated dynamics remain robust under experimentally relevant conditions. These results establish Rydberg chains as programmable coherent mediators for extending the internal connectivity of neutral-atom quantum nodes toward quasi-all-to-all coupling, providing a hardware-level route toward scalable and reconfigurable quantum-network architectures.

items.title: Quantum electrodynamics of equilibrium systems: A rigorous Maxwell-regularized functional-theoretic formulation
items.authors: Markus Penz, Christian Jöns, Michael Ruggenthaler, Angel Rubio
items.matched: thermalization, many-body localization and quantum scars in driven systems
items.result: Reformulates non-relativistic quantum electrodynamics as a density-functional theory over combined internal and external Maxwell sources, yielding a Moreau--Yosida regularized universal functional that removes the ultraviolet cutoff non-perturbatively via a Kohn--Sham construction.
items.question: How can equilibrium non-relativistic quantum electrodynamics be formulated non-perturbatively as an exact, mathematically regularized density-functional theory without unphysical representability issues and with the ultraviolet cutoff removed?
items.limits: Equilibrium ground states in Coulomb gauge. Requires confining potentials (e.g. harmonic) or periodic boundaries to break translational invariance.
items.tools: Maxwell duality · Moreau--Yosida regularization · Kohn--Sham auxiliary construction · Pauli--Fierz Hamiltonian · Vainberg--Bregman distance
items.caption: Comparison between standard density-functional schemes (which treat external sources as fixed Hamiltonian parameters) and Maxwell-regularized functional theories (which incorporate field energy to combine internal observables with external sources into regularized mixed quantities).
items.abstract: A framework for quantum electrodynamics of equilibrium systems is proposed that takes the Maxwell equations as foundational and links them to the structure of density-functional theory for the quantum system. By switching from purely internal observables like the one-particle density to combined internal and external quantities, the external sources and their energy are taken into account. A fully regularized functional theory emerges that avoids the usual representability problems. With the Kohn-Sham construction that links to an auxiliary uncoupled system, the ultra-violet cutoff can be removed and one arrives at a fully renormalized and non-perturbative light-matter description. Regularized forms of density-functional theory with and without magnetic fields appear as boundary cases, while the emergent physical picture reproduces the macroscopic Maxwell equations.

items.title: Remote Adiabatic Controlled-Z Gate between Distant Superconducting Qubits
items.authors: Si-Yu Xu, Yi-Rong Jin, Wen-Gang Zhang, Hai-Feng Yu
items.matched: Superconducting Qubits: Current State of Play
items.result: Coaxial cable mediating multi-mode ZZ interaction achieves remote adiabatic controlled-Z gate with optimized infidelity of 4.71×10⁻⁷ and 376.7 ns duration for 30-cm cable length without tunable couplers.
items.question: Can an adiabatic CZ gate be realized across a remote multi-mode coaxial cable coupling architecture with low leakage and high-fidelity conditional phase accumulation?
items.limits: Numerical simulation assuming zero decoherence. Ten standing-wave cable modes included.
items.tools: time-dependent Hamiltonian evolution · multi-mode standing-wave coaxial cable model · virtual-Z phase correction · transmon frequency tuning
items.caption: Infidelity mapped against both qubit working frequencies, showing a minimum of 4.71×10⁻⁷ at $(4.6390, 4.5112)$ GHz. Panels also display infidelity under ±0.5 MHz frequency drift and performance across cable lengths within 30.00 ±0.10 cm.
items.abstract: Direct entangling gates between spatially separated qubits are a key capability for modular quantum computing. They enable nonlocal quantum circuits to be executed across different processor modules, thereby alleviating single-chip scaling constraints and expanding the effective connectivity of the system. Here, we propose and numerically investigate a remote adiabatic controlled-Z gate between two frequency-tunable superconducting qubits connected by a multi-mode coaxial cable. The cable-mediated interaction enables the gate to be implemented without additional tunable couplers, preserving a simple circuit architecture. For a 30-cm cable, simulations incorporating ten standing-wave modes yield an optimized gate infidelity of 4.71×10⁻⁷ with a duration of 376.7 ns in the absence of decoherence. The gate maintains high fidelity under qubit-frequency fluctuations and millimeter-scale cable-length variations. Calculations for 50- and 100-cm cable situations demonstrate its potential for even larger cryogenic systems. These results provide a promising approach to extending high-fidelity quantum operations beyond individual chips and toward scalable, interconnected superconducting quantum processors.
