items.title: Optical Quantum Computing
items.authors: Hamza Hasnaoui, Leonardo Limongi, Taira Giordani, Beatrice Polacchi, Alberto Quaranta, Martino Bernard, Fabio Sciarrino, Mirko Lobino
items.matched: Circuit quantum electrodynamics
items.result: Surveys discrete- and continuous-variable optical quantum computing architectures, measurement-based cluster-state models, and non-universal algorithms (boson sampling, VQEs, QML).
items.question: How do optical encoding schemes and computing architectures compare across universal and non-universal quantum platforms?
items.limits: Photonic scaling is constrained by weak single-photon nonlinearities, probabilistic gate generation, and optical propagation losses.
items.tools: integrated photonics · continuous-variable squeeze states · discrete-variable cluster states · linear optical interferometry
items.caption: Taxonomy mapping discrete-variable and continuous-variable universal optical quantum computing models alongside non-universal photonic applications.
items.abstract: Under the label of optical quantum computing, there are a variety of protocols and experiments that use the quantum properties of light to achieve a computational advantage over classical computing machines. In this review, we describe some of the main implementations, which differ in the type of encoding and in how the computation is performed, whether using gates or cluster states. For each protocol, we describe advantages and challenges with an overview of the experimental results obtained, summarized in tables. Because of the great relevance achieved in this field, there is a section dedicated to non-universal quantum computation with photons, where boson sampling, variational quantum eigensolvers, and quantum machine learning applications are described. The aim is to give the reader the broadest overview of the applications where photons and their quantum properties play a key role in computation.

items.title: Entropy spectroscopy of a tunable two-site Hubbard molecule
items.authors: Uhjin Kim, Seokyeong Lee, Gibum Yun, Dongsung T. Park, Soobeom Choi, Sangwoo Jeong, Donghoon Kim, V. Umansky, Yunchul Chung, Hyoungsoon Choi, H. -S. Sim, Hyung Kook Choi
items.matched: Semiconductor spin qubits
items.result: Measured total thermodynamic entropy of a tunable two-site Hubbard molecule across the transition from isolated dots to a merged single dot via single-charge-sensor spectroscopy, resolving thermal suppression of antibonding and triplet states as interdot tunneling increases.
items.question: Which microscopic orbital and spin states remain thermally active in a two-site Hubbard system as tunneling competes with interactions?
items.prior: Charge-based entropy readout was established only for single quantum dots.
items.limits: Requires shifting both dot levels simultaneously at fixed detuning.
items.tools: GaAs/AlGaAs double quantum dot · single-charge-sensor entropy spectroscopy · two-site Hubbard model
items.abstract: Determining which microscopic states remain thermally active when tunneling and interactions compete is a central question in Hubbard physics. Here we develop an entropy measurement protocol for a double quantum dot, extending the charge-based approach established for a single dot, and measure the total entropy of a tunable two-site Hubbard molecule realized in a GaAs double dot. By shifting both dot levels together at fixed detuning, the entropy is correctly probed with only a single charge sensor. As interdot tunneling increases, the system evolves from two atomic-like dots through hybridized molecular states to a merged single dot. Across this evolution, the entropy decreases as tunnel-induced energy splitting exceeds the thermal energy and suppresses the occupation of higher-energy states. The measurements resolve the diminishing contribution of antibonding states and the changing thermal contributions of hybridized singlet and triplet states, in quantitative agreement with a two-site Hubbard model. By distinguishing states with the same charge configuration but different orbital and spin content, entropy reveals how tunneling and interactions determine the thermally active states of the minimal Hubbard system.

items.result: Perpendicular electric field E_⊥ tunes exciton-dispersion anisotropy to produce linear transverse exciton transport in monolayer and twisted bilayer TiSiCO, with bilayer transverse conductivities reaching several 1/h at 100 K.
items.question: Can perpendicular electric fields in valley-layer-coupled 2D materials control exciton dispersion anisotropy to generate and tune linear transverse exciton transport?
items.limits: Zero-Berry-curvature limit; neglects side-jump and skew-scattering high-temperature disorder processes.
items.tools: Effective exciton Hamiltonian · Semiclassical Boltzmann transport theory · Relaxation-time approximation · First-principles tight-binding parameters
items.caption: Twist angle θ versus layer-resolved transverse exciton conductivities σ_H^sys, σ_tra^(sys,AS), and σ_tra^(sys,S) at E_⊥=-2 eV/nm and E_⊥=0 eV/nm (T=100 K). Shows competition between the layer counterflow Hall response and dispersion-anisotropy-induced components.
items.abstract: Valley-layer coupling (VLC) two-dimensional (2D) materials define a distinct class of quantum systems in which valleys are related by crystal, rather than time-reversal (T) symmetry, enabling gate-controlled valley-contrasted layer polarization. Here we extend this concept to excitons. Using TiSiCo as a prototype VLC material, we show that a perpendicular electric field E_⊥ controls exciton- dispersion anisotropy and thereby generates unconventional linear transverse exciton transport in both monolayer and twisted bilayer structures. In the monolayer, this response is characterized by anisotropy-induced transverse conductivities, arising from the antisymmetric combination of diagonal elements in the conductivity tensor and strongly tunable by E_⊥. In the twisted bilayer, symmetry additionally permits transverse responses from the symmetric part of the conductivity tensor. Since intralayer excitons in different layers are connected by the Förster coupling, these symmetric and antisymmetric responses coexist and compete with the recently proposed T-even layer Hall and Nernst exciton counterflow. This interplay is highly tunable by twisted angle, temperature, and the direction of the in-plane driving force, providing a route to disentangle distinct transverse exciton transport signals experimentally. Our results establish E_⊥ as a powerful knob for controlling exciton transport via VLC and identify VLC 2D materials as a promising platform for engineered excitonic phenomena.

items.title: Giant-atom-mediated photon blockade
items.authors: C. Cui, W. Y. Hu, Y. Q. Ji, H. T. Cui, Yan-Hui Zhou, H. Z. Shen
items.matched: Circuit quantum electrodynamics
items.result: Multipoint coupling of giant atom provides additional destructive interference paths, enabling simultaneous unconventional photon blockade in two and three coupled cavities with driven first cavity. Point-atom configuration cannot produce simultaneous unconventional photon blockade.
items.question: Can multipoint coupling of a giant atom enable simultaneous unconventional photon blockade across multiple coupled cavities?
items.limits: Weak driving regime (F ≪κ), equal cavity and atomic dissipations κ₁=κ₂=κ₃=γ≡κ, theoretical model without experimental verification.
items.tools: Lindblad master equation · effective non-Hermitian Hamiltonian · few-photon state truncation
items.caption: log₁₀g⁽²⁾_o(0) in a three-cavity system driven at cavity a₁ versus coupling phase θ. Shows simultaneous dips to minimum values in all three cavities at θ_opt=1.2732π and θ_opt=0.4456π.
items.abstract: Photon blockade is a phenomenon where the presence of system nonlinearity causes the output to consist of single photons, which has been extensively studied in point atom systems, but it is barely explored in giant atom ones. In this paper, we propose giant atom-mediated photon blockade scheme based on two cavities and three cavities systems with driving field applied to the first cavity. We show that simultaneous unconventional photon blockades (UPBs) can not occur in the point atom system (the atom coupling only to the leftmost cavity) due to there always existing a cavity to have a single path. In contrast, the spatially extended nature of giant atom enables coupling to multiple cavities and allows for the introduction of a phase and coupling strength. Consequently, simultaneous UPBs in multiple cavities can be obtained due to the multipath destructive interference. Moreover, by manipulating the detuning, we observe simultaneous conventional photon blockades (CPBs) in multiple cavities. Finally, we study simultaneous two-photon blockades (2PBs) in point atom multiple cavities system.

items.title: Ancilla-assisted dark-state quantum gates in ultracold polar molecules
items.authors: Yan Lu, Xiao-Feng Shi
items.matched: transmon and fluxonium coherence, single- and two-qubit gate fidelity
items.result: Two-qubit and multi-qubit controlled-phase gates C(φ) can be implemented in optically trapped polar molecules via an ancilla-assisted dark-state mechanism driven solely by two smooth adiabatic microwave π pulses on the ancilla.
items.question: How can high-fidelity entangling quantum gates be realized in optically trapped polar molecules without suffering from motional decoherence or Rydberg-state decay?
items.limits: Theoretical and numerical simulation; assumes zero rotational Zeeman effect or weak rotational Zeeman effect relative to nuclear spin Zeeman effect (evaluated for ²³Na¹³³Cs at B=2G); requires specific tweezer alignment to suppress inter-data molecule DDI.
items.tools: dipole-dipole interaction (DDI) · adiabatic dark-state evolution · microwave driving · optical tweezer geometry optimization · quantized motional coupling analysis
items.caption: Gate infidelity log₁₀(1-F) of the ancilla-assisted CZ gate as a function of the microwave field polarization impurity parameters ς₀ and ς.
items.abstract: High-fidelity entangling gates are useful for circuit-based quantum computing, yet their realization in a scalable platform is challenging. Optically trapped ultracold polar molecules offer a potentially scalable platform. Here, we introduce a two-qubit molecular entangling gate via a novel ancilla-assisted dark-state mechanism, where high fidelity is achievable. In particular, we find that by using appropriate qubit states for the ancilla and the data qubits, dark states can appear, and entanglement can emerge by driving the ancilla only. It is also feasible to extend the two-qubit gate to a multi-qubit gate via the same dark-state mechanism.

items.title: Chiral classical and quantum acoustics with hole-spin qubits
items.authors: Zhanning Wang, Yongtao Li, Nelson E. Rivas, Gonzalo García, Irene Castro, Rubén Seoane Souto, Daniel Ramos, José C. Abadillo-Uriel
items.matched: Semiconductor spin qubits
items.result: Counterpropagating surface acoustic waves show gate-tunable spin-acoustic chirality up to χ=0.996, yielding a 470-fold transition-strength contrast that enables bichromatic coherence protection with T_(2,2)^*=167~μs (up from T₂^*=7.19~μs).
items.question: How do counterpropagating Rayleigh surface acoustic waves couple to gate-defined hole-spin qubits, and can their directional response be controlled electrostatically?
items.limits: Simulations assume planar Ge quantum well, weak-coupling regime with local defect-mode coupling g₀/2π∼1~kHz, ideal unit phonon-detection efficiency, zero dark counts, and zero reset time.
items.tools: Six-band Luttinger-Kohn Hamiltonian · Bir-Pikus strain theory · 3D piezoelectric finite-element method (FEM) · Master equation simulation
items.caption: Timestamp-corrected conditional Bell-state fidelity F_Bell^cond plotted against magnetic-field orientation θ_B and relative qubit displacement s=2Δx/λ_PnC. High-fidelity entanglement ridges broaden when acoustic chirality suppresses spatial standing-wave interference nodes.
items.abstract: Gate-defined hole spins combine strong spin-orbit coupling with exceptional strain sensitivity, making surface acoustic waves a natural route to remote, phase-coherent control. We show that counterpropagating surface acoustic waves can differ in coupling strength and in whether they predominantly drive spin rotations or modulate the qubit frequency. We call the transverse transition-strength imbalance spin-acoustic chirality and show that it is tunable through gate-controlled reshaping of the dot confinement. Combining a multiband Luttinger-Kohn Hamiltonian with the Bir-Pikus description of strain and 3D piezoelectric finite-element simulations, we obtain the acoustic g-matrix modulation governing coherent SAW driving. Quantizing the same strain-mediated interaction yields the corresponding single-phonon coupling, and a generalized anisotropic Rabi interaction with co-rotating, counter-rotating, and longitudinal components, linking classical chirality to quantum anisotropy and directional one-phonon emission. Magnetic field orientation and dot shape tune the acoustic chirality and operator selectivity. We illustrate this framework through bichromatic coherence protection and phonon-mediated heralded Bell-state initialization.

items.title: Quantum computers will not be that different: A blueprint for quantum computer architecture at scale
items.authors: Torsten Hoefler, Matthias Troyer
items.matched: Demonstration of a small programmable quantum computer with atomic qubits
items.result: Proposes architecture blueprint treating scalable quantum computers as classical heterogeneous accelerators with clean ISA abstraction, specialized recurring hardware, and QEC/control pipelines organized like high-performance network stacks.
items.question: How should utility-scale, fault-tolerant quantum computing systems be architected from a system-level cost-performance perspective?
items.limits: Architectural and design-level blueprint; does not present physical hardware implementation.
items.tools: system architecture analysis · ISA abstraction layering · network stack analogies for QEC · heterogeneous accelerator design principles
items.abstract: Quantum computers are technologically novel and unusual, but at system scale they should be engineered using many of the same principles that govern classical heterogeneous accelerators. This paper argues that utility-scale quantum architecture is primarily a cost-performance problem across a coupled quantum-classical system, leading to a blueprint for scalable quantum processing unit (QPU) design. Our architecture blueprint is organized around clean logical abstractions, hiding details and complexity of physical qubit modalities below the instruction set architecture (ISA) boundary, and specializes recurring functions aggressively to minimize the cost for utility scale quantum computations. Its low-level implementation through specialized local hardware for control, readout, and quantum error correction (QEC) closely resembles the architecture of high-performance network stacks. One of our main insights is that the design principles and the resulting architecture closely follow established practice from classical computing and networking.

items.title: Rydberg quantum antennas for chip-interfaced single-photon source array
items.authors: Yan-Lei Zhang, Dong-Qi Ma, Guang-Jie Chen, Qing-Xuan Jie, Liang Chen, Ya-Dong Hu, Zhu-Bo Wang, Guang-Can Guo, Chang-Ling Zou
items.matched: neutral atom tweezer arrays and Rydberg blockade entangling gates
items.result: Standing-wave optical tweezer atomic chain emits directional single photons with collection efficiency η> 70% into waveguide mode and second-order correlation g⁽²⁾ < 0.01 (with g⁽²⁾ < 10⁻³ during radiation for N=10).
items.question: How can neutral-atom arrays be efficiently and directionally coupled to on-chip waveguide networks as scalable, indistinguishable single-photon sources?
items.limits: Numerical simulation assuming C₆ = 8GHz/μm⁶, sub-wavelength spacing a < 0.5λ₀, instantaneous lossless mapping from Rydberg state |r⟩ to |s⟩, and neglecting thermal motion or laser field distortion.
items.tools: Standing-wave optical tweezer (SWAT) · Rydberg blockade · Master equation solver · Phased-array collective emission modeling
items.caption: Solid lines show collection efficiency η and dotted lines show g⁽²⁾ as functions of collection half-angle θ and atom number N, demonstrating η= 90% at θ= 0.6 for N=10 with g⁽²⁾ < 10⁻⁴.
items.abstract: We propose a Rydberg quantum antenna, consisting of a one-dimensional chain of neutral atoms trapped in a standing-wave optical tweezer, as a chip-interfaced single-photon source. Rydberg blockade induces a single collective excitation in the atomic chain, while its ordered geometry shapes the photon emission into a directional beam, thereby realizing a quantum antenna that emits strictly one photon at a time. Through numerical simulations, we demonstrate single-photon collection efficiencies into a waveguide exceeding 70% through a high-NA lens with a negligible multiple excitation probability. These performance are robust against probabilistic atom loading in the standing-wave dipole traps, requiring only ten atoms, indicating experimental feasibility. The Rydberg quantum antenna thus offers a unique route toward scalable arrays of high-efficiency, high-purity, and identical single-photon sources interfaced with a photonic chip, addressing key challenges in photonic quantum information technology.

items.title: Fast Unitary Preparation of Surface-Code Logical States on Neutral-Atom Hardware
items.authors: Ludwig Schmid, Robert Wille
items.matched: Quantum information with Rydberg atoms
items.result: Bidirectional middle-out CNOT cascade prepares surface-code logical states in depth (d+3)/2 with fault distance d in the protected error direction, requiring ≈3/4(d+3) collective AOD shuttles and ≈1/4(d+3) row pickups.
items.question: How can unitary stabilizer-expanding surface-code state preparation be adapted to minimize depth and shuttling constraints on neutral-atom processors?
items.prior: Unitary single-pivot preparation was 3(d-1) CZ layers and 4(d-1) shuttles; unidirectional cascade was d CZ layers and ≈3/2d shuttles.
items.limits: Fault-tolerant only in protected direction (conjugate direction allows weight-2 errors requiring an intermediate QEC round). Circuit-level numerical simulation up to 10⁷ shots under calibrated device noise, not physical hardware measurement.
items.tools: Acousto-optic-deflector (AOD) shuttling · Global Rydberg CZ gates · Bloqade toolchain · Stim · PyMatching
items.caption: Logical error rate versus noise scaling factor across code distances 3, 7, and 11. Bidirectional cascade remains sub-threshold at scaling factor 1 for both logical states, outperforming unidirectional and single-pivot methods.
items.abstract: Preparing logical states is a constantly recurring primitive at the start of any surface-code-based quantum computation. The standard measurement-based protocol is expensive on neutral atoms, since measurements are orders of magnitude slower than gates and, on single-zone architectures, additionally require shuttling the atoms to a readout zone. In this work, we present a measurement-free, unitary preparation of surface-code Pauli eigenstates tailored to neutral atoms. A bidirectional stabilizer-expanding CNOT cascade grows the patch from its middle line outward in depth (d+3)/2, while retaining fault distance d in the protected error direction. Each layer maps to one collective atom move followed by a single global Rydberg pulse, with about one row pickup per two layers. We compile and simulate the resulting schedules with the open-source bloqade toolchain under a hardware-calibrated, circuit-level neutral-atom noise model. The bidirectional cascade achieves the lowest logical error rate at every distance, and is the only construction tested that operates below threshold for both logical states at the considered device-level noise.

items.title: Neutral atom quantum computing for materials science and quantum chemistry
items.authors: J. D. Pritchard
items.matched: Quantum information with Rydberg atoms
items.result: Neutral atom arrays scale past 10³ physical qubits and provide >99.5% two-qubit gate fidelities, enabling continuous-time Hamiltonian simulation, QUBO/MWIS graph optimisation, and transversal logical operations for quantum chemistry and materials science.
items.question: How do neutral atom quantum computing platforms address simulation and optimisation challenges in materials science and quantum chemistry across analogue and digital paradigms?

items.abstract: Neutral atom arrays have emerged as versatile platforms for performing both digital and analogue quantum computing and simulation, with demonstrations ranging from large-scale programmable Hamiltonians realising topological phases or weighted graph optimisation to error-corrected logical qubits with transverse gate operations. This paper provides a broad overview to the neutral atom platform, and the potential applications relevant to materials science and quantum chemistry.

items.title: Achieving the limits of automorphism gates
items.authors: Jin Ming Koh, Shayan Majidy, Aranya Chakraborty, Anqi Gong, Shi Jie Samuel Tan, Norman Y. Yao
items.matched: Surface codes: Towards practical large-scale quantum computation
items.result: For stabilizer codes encoding k≥3 logical qubits, largest logical group achievable via automorphisms is generated by all addressable S and CX gates, requiring n=Θ(2^k) physical qubits (n=2^k-1 exactly). By contrast, all addressable diagonal Clifford gates require only n=k(k+1)/2 = Θ(k²) physical qubits via physical single-qubit Cliffords alone.
items.question: What is the maximum logical gate group achievable by automorphism gates on stabilizer codes, and what is the minimum physical-qubit cost needed to realize it?
items.limits: Restricted to stabilizer codes (with refinements for CSS and self-dual CSS codes); physical operations limited to single-qubit Clifford gates and qubit permutations (extended to single-qubit diagonal gates for higher hierarchy levels).
items.tools: stabilizer code theory · symplectic group and Clifford group classification · complete-hypergraph codes · concatenated non-CSS codes
items.caption: Gate group size as a function of the number of logical qubits k across different gate implementations. Solid curves show automorphism, transversal, and permutation gate limits, while dotted lines show diagonal gate groups up to level t of the Clifford hierarchy.
items.abstract: Universal fault-tolerant quantum computing combines versatile but expensive operations with specialized but cheap ones. Its efficiency depends on how much computation can be pushed onto the cheap operations and on the size of the code needed to do so. Automorphism gates provide such cheap operations using only physical single-qubit Clifford gates and qubit permutations. Yet no general theory characterizes their maximum logical power or the minimum code size needed to attain it. We develop such a theory. For stabilizer codes encoding k≥3 logical qubits, we show that the largest logical group attainable by automorphisms is generated by all addressable S and CX gates, and we construct codes attaining it. While this group contains exponentially fewer gates than the full Clifford group, adding one suitable non-Clifford gate yields universality. We further classify the largest logical groups attainable using qubit permutations, physical single-qubit Cliffords, or both across general stabilizer and CSS codes, and derive refined bounds for self-dual CSS subclasses. Achieving the maximum-size logical group through automorphisms requires n=Θ(2^k) physical qubits. By contrast, all addressable diagonal Clifford gates, generated by S and CZ, require only n=Θ(k²) physical qubits when implemented using physical single-qubit Cliffords alone. Both bounds are tight. This polynomial qubit cost extends beyond Cliffords to all addressable diagonal gates at any fixed level of the Clifford hierarchy, using physical single-qubit diagonal gates. Thus, for full addressability, the sharpest physical-qubit cost divide lies between diagonal and CX-type gates, not between Clifford and non-Clifford gates.

items.title: QECirc: A Community-Driven, FAIR Library of Quantum Error Correction Circuits
items.authors: Ludwig Schmid, Tom Peham, Robert Wille
items.matched: High-threshold and low-overhead fault-tolerant quantum memory
items.result: Created QECirc (qecirc.com), an open, verified library providing standardized Stim and OpenQASM implementations for quantum error correction circuits spanning encoders, state preparation, and logical gates.
items.question: How can quantum error correction circuits scattered across papers and ad-hoc repositories be standardized, verified, and made interoperable?
items.prior: Error Correction Zoo catalogs QEC code properties, but lacks concrete, format-agnostic implementation circuits.
items.limits: Syndrome-extraction schedules and larger qLDPC code families such as bivariate-bicycle codes remain planned work.
items.tools: QECirc · Stim · OpenQASM · Crumble · Quirk
items.abstract: Quantum error correction (QEC) underpins fault-tolerant quantum computing, but the circuits that realize QEC codes (encoders, logical state-preparation and gate routines, and syndrome-extraction schedules) are scattered across papers and one-off repositories in incompatible formats, often documented too sparsely to reconstruct or reuse. We present QECirc (https://qecirc.com/), a community-driven, open library that makes QEC circuits Findable, Accessible, Interoperable, and Reusable (FAIR). Each entry links to its underlying code, ships in Stim and OpenQASM with interactive visualizations, and is checked for correctness before publication. In short, where a catalog such as the Error Correction Zoo describes the codes, QECirc provides the concrete circuits that realize them.

items.title: Scalable logical qubits
items.authors: Matthias Troyer, Chetan Nayak, John Martinis
items.matched: High-threshold and low-overhead fault-tolerant quantum memory
items.result: Defines scalable logical qubits and establishes a unified framework evaluating them across four coupled dimensions: reliability, scale, capability, and performance.
items.question: How to define, benchmark, and compare progress in fault-tolerant logical qubits for utility-scale quantum computing.
items.limits: Conceptual/benchmarking framework; assumes fault-tolerant operations, real-time decoding, and scaling to hundreds or thousands of logical qubits.
items.tools: quantum error correction (QEC) · fault-tolerant universal operations · real-time decoding and feedback
items.abstract: Utility-scale quantum computing will require executing long, complex algorithms with end-to-end error rates far below what physical qubits can support directly. Error-corrected logical qubits are needed to achieve this goal. To make the progress on logical qubits measurable and comparable we introduce the definition of scalable logical qubits: logical qubits preserved for long computations by repeated quantum error correction, capable of fault-tolerant universal operations with low-latency real-time decoding and feedback, and replicable to the hundreds or thousands, as required by applications. We characterize these scalable logical qubits along four coupled dimensions: reliability, scale, capability, and performance, and discuss trade-offs among these dimensions.

items.title: Coherent error threshold for quantum LDPC codes
items.authors: Zhengyi Han, Yuanchen Zhao, Yijia Xu, Yixu Wang, Zi-Wen Liu
items.matched: Quantum Low-Density Parity-Check Codes
items.result: Proves general stabilizer qLDPC codes with distance d_n = Ω(logn) have nonzero code capacity thresholds under local coherent noise, with logical diamond-distance error decaying as sup_U ε_n^⋆(U,η) ≤C√ne^(-cd_n) for optimal recovery and sup_U ε_n^MW(U,η) ≤2n/(χ_MW(1-ρ_MW))ρ_MW^d_n under minimum-weight decoding.
items.question: Do general quantum LDPC codes admit rigorous nonzero error correction thresholds under coherent and general local noise?
items.prior: Rigorous fault tolerance under coherent noise had been established for constant-rate qLDPC codes with linear distance d = Θ(n) (Fawzi et al. 2024), but not for sublinear distance codes such as topological or quantum expander codes.
items.limits: Applies to code capacity model: noiseless syndrome measurements and recovery circuits following depth-D, bounded-support (r) local coherent or local CPTP noise.
items.tools: cluster resummation · approximate quantum error correction (AQEC) · diamond norm bounds on complementary channels · minimum-weight decoding analysis
items.caption: Schematic of the cluster resummation technique, showing how differentiating with respect to the interpolation parameter t marks a single connected large component while resumming all disconnected error configurations.
items.abstract: A key appeal of quantum low-density parity check (qLDPC) codes is their ability to suppress stochastic Pauli noise below nonzero thresholds. Coherent errors are fundamentally different: they produce superpositions of error patterns whose amplitudes can interfere even after syndrome measurement. Rigorous understanding of coherent errors remains limited. Here we show that general qLDPC codes admit a nonzero code capacity threshold against local coherent noise and more generally local channel noise. For any family of qLDPC codes with distance d=Ω(logn), we show that there is a constant noise strength below which the logical recovery error in diamond distance decays exponentially with the code distance. The result is established for optimal recovery as well as the minimum-weight decoder. The key technical ingredient is what we call a emphcluster resummation: rather than bounding superposed error configurations one by one, we isolate a large connected error cluster in the channel expansion and exactly resum all errors disconnected from it before taking norms. Standard cluster counting then yields exponential suppression. This work resolves a longstanding challenge in fault tolerance theory, providing general robustness guarantees for qLDPC codes against coherent noise and laying a rigorous foundation for future studies of fault-tolerant quantum technologies.

items.title: Fast Unitary Preparation of Surface-Code Logical States on Neutral-Atom Hardware
items.authors: Ludwig Schmid, Robert Wille
items.matched: High-threshold and low-overhead fault-tolerant quantum memory
items.result: Bidirectional middle-out CNOT cascade prepares surface-code logical states in depth (d+3)/2 with fault distance d in the protected error direction, requiring ≈3/4(d+3) collective AOD shuttles and ≈1/4(d+3) row pickups.
items.question: How can unitary stabilizer-expanding surface-code state preparation be adapted to minimize depth and shuttling constraints on neutral-atom processors?
items.prior: Unitary single-pivot preparation was 3(d-1) CZ layers and 4(d-1) shuttles; unidirectional cascade was d CZ layers and ≈3/2d shuttles.
items.limits: Fault-tolerant only in protected direction (conjugate direction allows weight-2 errors requiring an intermediate QEC round). Circuit-level numerical simulation up to 10⁷ shots under calibrated device noise, not physical hardware measurement.
items.tools: Acousto-optic-deflector (AOD) shuttling · Global Rydberg CZ gates · Bloqade toolchain · Stim · PyMatching
items.caption: Logical error rate versus noise scaling factor across code distances 3, 7, and 11. Bidirectional cascade remains sub-threshold at scaling factor 1 for both logical states, outperforming unidirectional and single-pivot methods.
items.abstract: Preparing logical states is a constantly recurring primitive at the start of any surface-code-based quantum computation. The standard measurement-based protocol is expensive on neutral atoms, since measurements are orders of magnitude slower than gates and, on single-zone architectures, additionally require shuttling the atoms to a readout zone. In this work, we present a measurement-free, unitary preparation of surface-code Pauli eigenstates tailored to neutral atoms. A bidirectional stabilizer-expanding CNOT cascade grows the patch from its middle line outward in depth (d+3)/2, while retaining fault distance d in the protected error direction. Each layer maps to one collective atom move followed by a single global Rydberg pulse, with about one row pickup per two layers. We compile and simulate the resulting schedules with the open-source bloqade toolchain under a hardware-calibrated, circuit-level neutral-atom noise model. The bidirectional cascade achieves the lowest logical error rate at every distance, and is the only construction tested that operates below threshold for both logical states at the considered device-level noise.

items.title: Scalable entanglement distribution using encoded hybrid repeater chains
items.authors: Stav Haldar, Saikat Guha, Don Towsley, Filip Rozpkedek
items.matched: High-threshold and low-overhead fault-tolerant quantum memory
items.result: Hybrid quantum repeater chains combining fast, multiplexable type-1 memories with long-coherence type-2 memories achieve higher end-to-end entanglement distribution rates than pure architectures of either platform alone, even when inter-platform gate errors are non-zero.
items.question: How should heterogeneous quantum memory platforms and quantum error-correction capabilities be allocated along a repeater chain to maximize entanglement distribution rates under realistic hardware constraints?
items.limits: Circuit-level noise model simulations; fixed inter-node spacing of l₀=20km; independent logical error channels after physical combinatorial counting.
items.tools: Monte Carlo circuit-level noise simulations · Fault-tolerant stabilizer measurement via GHZ ancillae · Modified swap-as-soon-as-possible (swap-ASAP) policy · Three-qubit repetition, Steane [[7,1,3]], and Shor [[9,1,3]] codes
items.caption: Entanglement distribution rate and end-to-end fidelity plotted against total chain distance L at l₀=20km spacing. Encoded hybrid architectures maintain non-zero distribution rates out to thousands of kilometers, outperforming pure type-1 and type-2 setups.
items.abstract: Long-distance entanglement distribution requires error correction protocols to compensate for qubit decoherence in quantum memories and noise introduced during entanglement swapping. We argue that repeater chains with error-correction capabilities should exploit more than one physical platform, combining the complementary strengths of different quantum memory technologies into a single hybrid repeater architecture. An important constituent of such an architecture is a hybrid repeater which combines type-1 memories, characterized by fast entanglement generation rates and suitability for multiplexing, and type-2 memories that offer long coherence times and low two-qubit gate error rates. Taking the resource-intensive nature of hybrid nodes into account, we propose and analyze repeater chains in which only a subset of nodes need to be hybrid, while the remaining nodes are simpler first-generation repeaters with no error-correction capability. Through detailed Monte Carlo simulations of fault-tolerant encoded repeater chain protocols based on the three-qubit phase-flip repetition code, the [[7,1,3]] Steane code, and the [[9,1,3]] Shor code, we demonstrate that these hybrid architectures outperform pure architectures based on a single memory platform in terms of end-to-end entanglement distribution rate. In our study we develop a full circuit-level noise model of our architectures and examine the impact of an imperfect interface between the two platforms on our hybrid architecture. We also develop a modified version of the swap-as-soon-as-possible policy with multiplexing, more suited to our architecture where some nodes perform error-correction while others do not. This modified policy significantly reduces the information storage time in memory qubits relative to the previously considered swap policies in encoded repeater chains.

items.result: Utility-scale quantum processing units (QPUs) should follow classical heterogeneous accelerator and network stack architectures, hiding physical qubit modalities below the ISA boundary via specialized local control, readout, and QEC hardware.
items.question: How should utility-scale quantum computer architectures be designed to optimize cost-performance across coupled quantum-classical systems?
items.limits: Architectural and systems-level conceptual framework; details depend on physical qubit modality implementation below ISA.
items.tools: ISA abstraction layers · specialized local QEC hardware · high-performance network stack design principles · classical accelerator architecture models
items.abstract: Quantum computers are technologically novel and unusual, but at system scale they should be engineered using many of the same principles that govern classical heterogeneous accelerators. This paper argues that utility-scale quantum architecture is primarily a cost-performance problem across a coupled quantum-classical system, leading to a blueprint for scalable quantum processing unit (QPU) design. Our architecture blueprint is organized around clean logical abstractions, hiding details and complexity of physical qubit modalities below the instruction set architecture (ISA) boundary, and specializes recurring functions aggressively to minimize the cost for utility scale quantum computations. Its low-level implementation through specialized local hardware for control, readout, and quantum error correction (QEC) closely resembles the architecture of high-performance network stacks. One of our main insights is that the design principles and the resulting architecture closely follow established practice from classical computing and networking.

items.title: Blind Quantum Computation with a Small Quantum Server
items.authors: Daniel Lovsted, Filipa C. R. Peres, Joshua Nevin, Selman Ipek, Anne Broadbent
items.matched: High-threshold and low-overhead fault-tolerant quantum memory
items.result: Constructed blind quantum computation (Blind PBC) requiring a quantum server of only t qubits for an n-qubit circuit with t non-Clifford T gates, achieving perfect information-theoretic input secrecy with four-way random state preparation and a single t-qubit quantum communication step.
items.question: How can blind quantum computation be performed while minimizing the required quantum processor size on the server?
items.prior: Server size was n+t qubits for single-instance communication or n+1 qubits with t sequential communication rounds in quantum computing on encrypted data (QCED).
items.limits: Hides computational basis input x (or orthonormal stabilizer bases) but reveals circuit structure C. Qubit virtualization incurs classical sampling cost exponential in simulated virtual qubit count k.
items.tools: Pauli-based computation (PBC) · Magic state teleportation gadgets · One-way four-phase quantum state encryption · Tailored resource computation (TRC)
items.caption: Comparison of standard Pauli-based computation (a) with Blind PBC (b), illustrating state preparation with client random phase rotations S^c_iZ^d_i, adaptive Pauli observable measurement via client-side circuit modification PBC.Sel(C^*_x), and output sample decoding.
items.abstract: Blind quantum computation (BQC) allows low-resource clients to securely delegate computations to a quantum server, but server resource costs scale with the computation size, posing a bottleneck for implementations. By leveraging Pauli-based computation (PBC), we achieve BQC with a server whose size depends only on the non-Clifford gate count. Our protocol inherits fault tolerance and qubit virtualization from PBC and reveals that classical-client BQC is possible even in the absence of classical simulability. Finally, we present an entanglement-based dual protocol that performs a resource state computation with a dramatically reduced execution cost.

items.title: State-Space-Based FIR Filtering on a Quantum Computer
items.authors: Roope Salmi, Davide Rocchesso, Vesa Välimäki
items.matched: Toward the first quantum simulation with quantum speedup
items.result: Realizes bounded finite impulse response (FIR) filtering on a quantum computer via a unitary state-space lattice decomposition without mid-circuit measurements or gain loss, demonstrated on N=32 samples with filter order M=12.
items.question: How can discrete-time sample-based linear signal processing and FIR filters be implemented in a composable unitary quantum circuit without losing signal gain?
items.prior: In prior quantum FIR filters (Majumdar et al. 2021), input samples were consumed without reuse, preventing composability without intermediate classical conversion.
items.limits: Simulated on ideal quantum simulator with 1024-shot sampling; requires known power complementary transfer function and large circuit depths (59,292 elementary gates for N=32, M=12) requiring fault-tolerant hardware.
items.tools: Vaidyanathan unitary lattice filterbank decomposition · quantum delay and transposition gates · Hadamard test · Qiskit simulator
items.caption: Sample index n versus normalized amplitude for two parallel input signals (impulse x₀(n) and fractal sequence x₁(n), red) and their resulting lowpass filtered outputs (y₀(n) and y₁(n), blue), comparing exact statevector amplitudes with 1024-shot Hadamard test estimates.
items.abstract: Many signal processing tasks require intensive computations. Quantum computing promises to accelerate certain tasks, but algorithms must be designed around the limitations of quantum mechanics. This paper provides a quantum implementation of finite impulse response (FIR) filters, which are a widely used tool in classical signal processing. The filter can be parallelized and composed as part of larger quantum algorithms, with potential for speedups using quantum amplitude estimation and future fault-tolerant quantum hardware. To accomplish these properties, we introduce a state-space framework wherein sample-based signal processing is performed with unitary quantum circuits. We present the quantum delay gate as the quantum analog of the delay line in discrete-time signal processing. Unitary circuits intrinsically describe lossless systems, but we also implement lowpass and other bounded filters by emulating a projection operator. The FIR filter implementation is tested and demonstrated with a quantum circuit simulator.

items.title: Quantum WalkScore: Benchmarking Quantum Computers on the Graph Nodefinding Problem
items.authors: Noé Olivier, Michel Nowak
items.matched: Toward the first quantum simulation with quantum speedup
items.result: Defines Quantum WalkScore (QWS), an application-oriented benchmark quantifying the largest problem size (n,d) on cycle and 2D-torus graphs where discrete-time quantum walks with amplitude amplification find a target node with measured success probability p_exp(n,d) ≥p^*(n,d) before first failure.
items.question: How can discrete-time quantum walks combined with amplitude amplification benchmark quantum computers on graph search problems?
items.limits: Applies to gate-based quantum computers on cycle and 2D-torus graphs; walk step counts require textsfnum-w≥d and textsfnum-w≡dpmod2.
items.tools: Discrete-time quantum walks (DTQW) · Quantum amplitude amplification (AA) · IBM Heron r2, Heron r3, and Nighthawk r1 QPUs · Noiseless quantum circuit simulation

items.abstract: Recent advances in quantum computing hardware toward fault-tolerance have increased interest in evaluating near-term quantum platforms on application-relevant quantum algorithms. In this work, we introduce Quantum WalkScore (QWS), a scalable application-oriented benchmark designed to assess the performance of NISQ and future fault-tolerant quantum computers in executing essential quantum routines --discrete-time quantum walks and quantum amplitude amplification-- to solve the graph nodefinding problem (marked-vertex search). QWS quantifies performance by scoring the largest problem size for which a designated target node can be found with success probability above a defined threshold. In addition to the complete protocol description, we provide example parameter-selection scenarios designed from noiseless simulation results and demonstrate QWS evaluation through experimental runs on multiple generations of IBM real quantum processors.

items.title: The effects of shot noise on the quantum computation of NMR spectra
items.authors: Sebastian Walch, Keith R. Fratus, Jan-Michael Reiner, Igor Lesanovsky
items.matched: Toward the first quantum simulation with quantum speedup
items.result: The number of quantum measurement shots required to reconstruct NMR spectra at fixed accuracy scales sub-exponentially with spin-chain length L, showing a pronounced flattening for 1D and 2D molecular geometries with distance-decaying couplings up to L=50.
items.question: How does the number of projective measurement shots required to compute NMR spectra to a given accuracy scale with the number of nuclear spins?
items.limits: Low-field NMR setting only. All gate noise, decoherence, and Trotterization errors neglected (pure shot-noise limit). Full Heisenberg dynamics verified only up to L=12 and on four real molecules.
items.tools: Exact diagonalization · Ising NMR toy Hamiltonian benchmark · Repeated-measurement shot-noise simulation · Fast Fourier transform (FFT)
items.caption: Spectral infidelity versus system size L (at R=1024 shots) for 1D chains and four real molecules under full Heisenberg interactions, demonstrating weak growth with L.
items.abstract: Recent advances in the field of quantum computing hardware motivate the search for applications which demonstrate so-called quantum advantage. One promising use case that has been identified is the simulation of quantum many-body systems. The computational resources required for performing such a simulation on a classical computer generally grow exponentially with the size of the system being modeled, which is ultimately due to the exponential growth of the Hilbert space in which the dynamics of such a system take place. While digital quantum computers natively evolve quantum states directly in such a Hilbert space, thus naively avoiding this problem, the result of such a computation is typically not obtained as a deterministic output. Rather, it requires projective measurements which are fundamentally affected by shot noise. Any desired expectation values must therefore be reconstructed from repeated measurements, making the number of those measurements a relevant computational resource, and thus an important consideration for any potential claims of quantum advantage. In this work, we study how this resource scales with system size (a scaling which itself depends on the desired accuracy of the final result), using the simulation of nuclear magnetic resonance (NMR) spectra as a test case. We study this scaling for both real-world molecules, as well as a class of model NMR Hamiltonians which allow for efficient large-scale simulations with one-dimensional, two-dimensional, and all-to-all interactions. We find that the required resources increase only weakly with molecular size, far below the exponential growth of the underlying Hilbert space. This result suggests that shot noise should not pose a fundamental barrier to achieving quantum advantage in the simulation of NMR systems, and perhaps for many-body systems more broadly.

items.authors: Yin Yang, Yue Yu, Long Zhang
items.matched: Quantum Algorithm for Linear Systems of Equations

items.abstract: Quantum linear systems algorithms (QLSAs) aim to solve linear systems Abbx=bbb exponentially faster than classical methods under certain conditions. In this work, we develop quantum algorithms for solving linear algebraic equations from an ODE-based perspective. Inspired by the linear combination of Hamiltonian simulation (LCHS) representation in the Fourier approach citeChilds2017QLSA, we express the solution bbx as a linear combination of solutions to a system of linear convection equations, which become Schrödinger-type equations with unitary evolutions in the Fourier domain. We refer to this representation as LC-Schrödingerization. Based on this result, we construct an LCHS-based quantum algorithm with two LCHS instances: one for time-marching and one for numerical integration. The key construction uses the derivative of a Gaussian-smoothed hat function and recovers the solution over a fixed auxiliary interval. This permits a truncation time independent of the target accuracy and avoids the loss in success probability from selecting a single grid point. Periodization and explicit Fourier coefficients provide the corresponding projection error bounds. Under the stated oracle assumptions and given a constant-factor estimate of the solution norm, direct simulation of the select operators and block preconditioning achieve the optimal matrix-query complexity O(κ_Alogfrac1ε) without using variable-time amplitude amplification (VTAA). The same upper bound holds for queries to the right-hand-side preparation oracle.

items.question: Does there exist an efficient quantum algorithm that outputs a path between the entrance and exit vertices of a welded tree?
items.prior: Childs, Coudron, and Gilani (CCG23) proved pathfinding hardness restricted to rooted and genuine quantum algorithms, but general quantum algorithms remained open.
items.limits: Welded tree graphs of height n (N = 2ⁿ leaves) with q ≤√N/100 queries and a single-cycle weld distribution with fixed edge colorings.
items.tools: compressed permutation oracles · fresh compressed oracle framework · quantum discrete walk column-direction states
items.caption: Schematic of the fresh compressed oracle rule restricting weld query assignments. Gray nodes mark visited database records, green nodes are valid fresh connections, and red nodes are forbidden to prevent cycles or premature component joining.
items.abstract: Starting from the entrance of a welded tree, a quantum walk algorithm can find its exit vertex exponentially faster than any classical algorithm. However, it has been an open question whether any quantum algorithm is able to efficiently find a path from the entrance to the exit. We answer this by proving an exponential quantum query lower bound for finding such path. Specifically, for trees of height n, any quantum query algorithm requires at least Ω(2^(n/24)) queries in order to succeed with constant probability. Our proof uses the compressed permutation oracle technique in order to construct databases which track the graph information an algorithm has learned and forgotten, and show that no efficient quantum algorithm can build an entrance-to-exit path in these records.

items.title: QECirc: A Community-Driven, FAIR Library of Quantum Error Correction Circuits
items.authors: Ludwig Schmid, Tom Peham, Robert Wille
items.matched: Toward the first quantum simulation with quantum speedup
items.result: Created QECirc (qecirc.com), an open, verified library providing standardized Stim and OpenQASM implementations for quantum error correction circuits spanning encoders, state preparation, and logical gates.
items.question: How can quantum error correction circuits scattered across papers and ad-hoc repositories be standardized, verified, and made interoperable?
items.prior: Error Correction Zoo catalogs QEC code properties, but lacks concrete, format-agnostic implementation circuits.
items.limits: Syndrome-extraction schedules and larger qLDPC code families such as bivariate-bicycle codes remain planned work.
items.tools: QECirc · Stim · OpenQASM · Crumble · Quirk
items.abstract: Quantum error correction (QEC) underpins fault-tolerant quantum computing, but the circuits that realize QEC codes (encoders, logical state-preparation and gate routines, and syndrome-extraction schedules) are scattered across papers and one-off repositories in incompatible formats, often documented too sparsely to reconstruct or reuse. We present QECirc (https://qecirc.com/), a community-driven, open library that makes QEC circuits Findable, Accessible, Interoperable, and Reusable (FAIR). Each entry links to its underlying code, ships in Stim and OpenQASM with interactive visualizations, and is checked for correctness before publication. In short, where a catalog such as the Error Correction Zoo describes the codes, QECirc provides the concrete circuits that realize them.

items.title: Scalable Simulation of Quantum Dynamics on Topological Quantum Hardware
items.authors: Kritanjan Polley, Mark E. Tuckerman
items.matched: quantum chemistry and electronic structure on quantum computers
items.result: Unitary propagators for real-time molecular and condensed-phase dynamics are synthesized via Solovay-Kitaev braiding of Fibonacci and Ising anyons, achieving an accuracy target of 10⁻⁸ across two-level, spin-boson, and molecular reaction systems.
items.question: Can real-time quantum dynamics in molecular and condensed-phase systems be represented and executed using non-Abelian anyon braiding on topological quantum hardware?
items.limits: Classical digital simulation of anyon braiding circuits rather than execution on topological quantum hardware; requires probabilistic imaginary time evolution for thermal states.
items.tools: Fibonacci and Ising anyon braiding · Solovay-Kitaev algorithm · Givens rotations · Tensor network path integrals · Probabilistic imaginary time evolution (PITE)
items.caption: Population dynamics versus time for a two-level system under exact unitary evolution compared to Fibonacci and Ising anyon braiding sequences generated by the Solovay-Kitaev algorithm with 10⁻⁷ infidelity.
items.abstract: Quantum computers offer a significant advantage in simulating quantum systems compared to classical computers for certain problems, although most current applications are limited to calculating static molecular properties using hybrid quantum-classical hardware. In this work, we establish a framework for the representation of quantum dynamics in molecular and condensed matter systems, designed for execution on topological quantum hardware. By leveraging the non-Abelian braiding statistics of Fibonacci and Ising anyons, we utilize the Solovay-Kitaev algorithm to approximate unitary propagators for a range of systems. We demonstrate the efficacy of these algorithms across a hierarchy of complexity, from two-level systems and one dimensional double-well potentials to condensed phase spin-boson models, simple molecules, and molecular reaction kinetics. These algorithms provide a scalable and robust pathway for simulating many-body condensed phase chemical physics on fault-tolerant quantum devices.

items.title: Quantum computers will not be that different: A blueprint for quantum computer architecture at scale
items.authors: Torsten Hoefler, Matthias Troyer
items.matched: Practical quantum advantage in quantum simulation
items.result: Proposes architecture blueprint treating utility-scale quantum systems as classical heterogeneous accelerators with clean instruction set architecture (ISA) boundaries and specialized hardware for control, readout, and error correction.
items.question: How should utility-scale quantum computing systems be architected to optimize cost-performance across coupled quantum-classical infrastructure?
items.limits: Architectural proposal without physical hardware implementation or empirical benchmarking.
items.tools: heterogeneous accelerator design principles · layered instruction set architecture (ISA) · high-performance network stack analogies · classical-quantum co-design
items.abstract: Quantum computers are technologically novel and unusual, but at system scale they should be engineered using many of the same principles that govern classical heterogeneous accelerators. This paper argues that utility-scale quantum architecture is primarily a cost-performance problem across a coupled quantum-classical system, leading to a blueprint for scalable quantum processing unit (QPU) design. Our architecture blueprint is organized around clean logical abstractions, hiding details and complexity of physical qubit modalities below the instruction set architecture (ISA) boundary, and specializes recurring functions aggressively to minimize the cost for utility scale quantum computations. Its low-level implementation through specialized local hardware for control, readout, and quantum error correction (QEC) closely resembles the architecture of high-performance network stacks. One of our main insights is that the design principles and the resulting architecture closely follow established practice from classical computing and networking.

items.title: The effects of shot noise on the quantum computation of NMR spectra
items.authors: Sebastian Walch, Keith R. Fratus, Jan-Michael Reiner, Igor Lesanovsky
items.matched: Probing many-body dynamics on a 51-atom quantum simulator
items.result: The number of quantum measurement shots required to reconstruct NMR spectra at fixed accuracy scales sub-exponentially with spin-chain length L, showing a pronounced flattening for 1D and 2D molecular geometries with distance-decaying couplings up to L=50.
items.question: How does the number of projective measurement shots required to compute NMR spectra to a given accuracy scale with the number of nuclear spins?
items.limits: Low-field NMR setting only. All gate noise, decoherence, and Trotterization errors neglected (pure shot-noise limit). Full Heisenberg dynamics verified only up to L=12 and on four real molecules.
items.tools: Exact diagonalization · Ising NMR toy Hamiltonian benchmark · Repeated-measurement shot-noise simulation · Fast Fourier transform (FFT)
items.caption: Spectral infidelity versus system size L (at R=1024 shots) for 1D chains and four real molecules under full Heisenberg interactions, demonstrating weak growth with L.
items.abstract: Recent advances in the field of quantum computing hardware motivate the search for applications which demonstrate so-called quantum advantage. One promising use case that has been identified is the simulation of quantum many-body systems. The computational resources required for performing such a simulation on a classical computer generally grow exponentially with the size of the system being modeled, which is ultimately due to the exponential growth of the Hilbert space in which the dynamics of such a system take place. While digital quantum computers natively evolve quantum states directly in such a Hilbert space, thus naively avoiding this problem, the result of such a computation is typically not obtained as a deterministic output. Rather, it requires projective measurements which are fundamentally affected by shot noise. Any desired expectation values must therefore be reconstructed from repeated measurements, making the number of those measurements a relevant computational resource, and thus an important consideration for any potential claims of quantum advantage. In this work, we study how this resource scales with system size (a scaling which itself depends on the desired accuracy of the final result), using the simulation of nuclear magnetic resonance (NMR) spectra as a test case. We study this scaling for both real-world molecules, as well as a class of model NMR Hamiltonians which allow for efficient large-scale simulations with one-dimensional, two-dimensional, and all-to-all interactions. We find that the required resources increase only weakly with molecular size, far below the exponential growth of the underlying Hilbert space. This result suggests that shot noise should not pose a fundamental barrier to achieving quantum advantage in the simulation of NMR systems, and perhaps for many-body systems more broadly.

items.title: Suzuki-Trotter Decompositions and other Methods for Quantum Time Evolution
items.authors: Johann Ostmeyer
items.matched: Theory of Trotter Error with Commutator Scaling
items.result: Reviews recent advances in Suzuki-Trotter decompositions, improved error bounds, and alternative quantum time-evolution methods for classical and noisy quantum computing platforms.
items.question: How do modern Suzuki-Trotter splitting methods and alternative algorithms perform in practical quantum time evolution?
items.limits: Mathematical proofs and technical implementation details omitted.
items.tools: Suzuki-Trotter decompositions · Multi-product formulae · Quantum signal processing · Time-dependent variational principle (TDVP) · Processed methods and symplectic integrators
items.abstract: (Suzuki-)Trotter decompositions, splitting methods, (Lie) product formulae... The most common numerical methods for the time evolution of quantum systems come with many names. And they are used practically everywhere with applications ranging from the solution of classical equations of motion and various Monte Carlo simulations to the real and imaginary time evolution on classical as well as quantum computers. Here we review the state of the art of said methods, focussing especially on the progress made over the last few years. We highlight recently discovered efficient time evolution algorithms and explain how best to use them in practice. A central part of this work is the estimation of error bounds that has improved greatly within the past decade. The relevance of time evolution methods for quantum computing is discussed with a focus on noisy hardware. Finally, a comprehensive overview of generalisations, related methods and alternatives to Trotterization is provided. This includes time-dependent Hamiltonian dynamics, processed methods, multi-product formulae, symplectic integrators, TDVP for tensor networks, quantum signal processing, Crouch-Grossman methods and more. The overall perspective in this work is that of a theoretical physicist. All mathematical proofs as well as some technical details are omitted for easier readability. Instead, this review serves as a hands-on guide and, of course, as a starting point for references that provide further details.

items.title: Quantum WalkScore: Benchmarking Quantum Computers on the Graph Nodefinding Problem
items.authors: Noé Olivier, Michel Nowak
items.matched: Probing many-body dynamics on a 51-atom quantum simulator
items.result: Defines Quantum WalkScore (QWS), an application-oriented benchmark quantifying the largest problem size (n,d) on cycle and 2D-torus graphs where discrete-time quantum walks with amplitude amplification find a target node with measured success probability p_exp(n,d) ≥p^*(n,d) before first failure.
items.question: How can discrete-time quantum walks combined with amplitude amplification benchmark quantum computers on graph search problems?
items.limits: Applies to gate-based quantum computers on cycle and 2D-torus graphs; walk step counts require textsfnum-w≥d and textsfnum-w≡dpmod2.
items.tools: Discrete-time quantum walks (DTQW) · Quantum amplitude amplification (AA) · IBM Heron r2, Heron r3, and Nighthawk r1 QPUs · Noiseless quantum circuit simulation
items.caption: Cycle and 2D-torus graph structures for nodefinding instances of sizes n=4 and n=3 with target nodes located at varied distances d from the source.
items.abstract: Recent advances in quantum computing hardware toward fault-tolerance have increased interest in evaluating near-term quantum platforms on application-relevant quantum algorithms. In this work, we introduce Quantum WalkScore (QWS), a scalable application-oriented benchmark designed to assess the performance of NISQ and future fault-tolerant quantum computers in executing essential quantum routines --discrete-time quantum walks and quantum amplitude amplification-- to solve the graph nodefinding problem (marked-vertex search). QWS quantifies performance by scoring the largest problem size for which a designated target node can be found with success probability above a defined threshold. In addition to the complete protocol description, we provide example parameter-selection scenarios designed from noiseless simulation results and demonstrate QWS evaluation through experimental runs on multiple generations of IBM real quantum processors.

items.abstract: This work describes a variational technique to solve non-Hermitian quantum systems, in particular those with negative coupling quartic self-interaction. Differences of applying variational methods from standard quantum mechanics to non-Hermitian quantum mechanics -- including potential pitfalls -- are highlighted. A successful implementation of the variational approach for the non-Hermitian case is presented. The technique is used to analyze scalar quantum field theory in d=2 with negative quartic self-interaction in the Hamiltonian formulation in lattice discretization.

items.title: Particle Physics Driven by Quantum Technology - Quantum Simulations and Quantum Sensing
items.authors: Itay M. Bloch, Marcela Carena, Yifan Chen, Xinran Li, Ying-Ying Li, Jing Shu
items.matched: Probing many-body dynamics on a 51-atom quantum simulator
items.result: Review synthesizes quantum algorithms for nonperturbative quantum field theory dynamics alongside quantum sensing platforms (cavities, circuits, magnetometry, and pair-breaking superconducting detectors with thresholds around 0.1 meV) for dark matter and gravitational wave searches.
items.question: How can quantum simulation and quantum sensing technologies be applied to resolve nonperturbative dynamics and detect subtle beyond-the-Standard-Model physics?
items.limits: Digital quantum field theory algorithms are limited by digitization of higher-dimensional non-Abelian gauge theories, state preparation, and continuum extrapolation; sensor sensitivity is limited by low-energy excess events, excess quasiparticles, and two-level system noise.
items.tools: digital quantum simulation · superconducting cavities and LC circuits · quantum magnetometry · pair-breaking superconducting sensors (TES, KID, SNSPD)
items.caption: Schematic overview connecting superconducting platforms to particle physics applications: cavity and pair-breaking quantum sensors for dark matter and gravitational waves (left) and transmon-based processors for non-perturbative quantum field simulations (right).
items.abstract: We review recent advances in particle physics enabled and motivated by the rapid progress of quantum technologies. The continued development of quantum computing toward large-scale, fault-tolerant systems has the potential to address dynamical problems that remain extremely challenging for classical computational approaches, opening new avenues for studying nonperturbative dynamical processes. Tabletop detectors and quantum-enhanced technologies have reached unprecedented sensitivities, enabling novel searches for ultralight particles, gravitational waves, and other physics beyond the Standard Model in parameter regimes previously inaccessible to conventional instrumentation. Taken together, these developments highlight a rapidly evolving landscape in which quantum technologies are beginning to reshape fundamental physics. We aim to synthesize recent progress and illuminate the opportunities they present for advancing particle physics in the coming years.

items.title: State-Space-Based FIR Filtering on a Quantum Computer
items.authors: Roope Salmi, Davide Rocchesso, Vesa Välimäki
items.matched: Practical quantum advantage in quantum simulation
items.result: Realizes bounded finite impulse response (FIR) filtering on a quantum computer via a unitary state-space lattice decomposition without mid-circuit measurements or gain loss, demonstrated on N=32 samples with filter order M=12.
items.question: How can discrete-time sample-based linear signal processing and FIR filters be implemented in a composable unitary quantum circuit without losing signal gain?
items.prior: In prior quantum FIR filters (Majumdar et al. 2021), input samples were consumed without reuse, preventing composability without intermediate classical conversion.
items.limits: Simulated on ideal quantum simulator with 1024-shot sampling; requires known power complementary transfer function and large circuit depths (59,292 elementary gates for N=32, M=12) requiring fault-tolerant hardware.
items.tools: Vaidyanathan unitary lattice filterbank decomposition · quantum delay and transposition gates · Hadamard test · Qiskit simulator
items.caption: Sample index n versus normalized amplitude for two parallel input signals (impulse x₀(n) and fractal sequence x₁(n), red) and their resulting lowpass filtered outputs (y₀(n) and y₁(n), blue), comparing exact statevector amplitudes with 1024-shot Hadamard test estimates.
items.abstract: Many signal processing tasks require intensive computations. Quantum computing promises to accelerate certain tasks, but algorithms must be designed around the limitations of quantum mechanics. This paper provides a quantum implementation of finite impulse response (FIR) filters, which are a widely used tool in classical signal processing. The filter can be parallelized and composed as part of larger quantum algorithms, with potential for speedups using quantum amplitude estimation and future fault-tolerant quantum hardware. To accomplish these properties, we introduce a state-space framework wherein sample-based signal processing is performed with unitary quantum circuits. We present the quantum delay gate as the quantum analog of the delay line in discrete-time signal processing. Unitary circuits intrinsically describe lossless systems, but we also implement lowpass and other bounded filters by emulating a projection operator. The FIR filter implementation is tested and demonstrated with a quantum circuit simulator.

items.question: Can flopping-mode hole spin qubits simultaneously achieve strong transverse spin-electric coupling, suppressed charge-noise sensitivity, and long relaxation times at low magnetic fields?
items.prior: EDSR on planar Ge single-QD qubits required drive powers around -27dBm (10mV gate voltage) at low magnetic fields.
items.limits: Measured at |	B| = 5mT nearly in-plane magnetic field and dilution refrigerator temperatures (20mK base); coherent control operates at Zeeman-degeneracy sweet-spots.
items.tools: planar strained Ge/SiGe heterostructure · flopping-mode double quantum dot hole qubit · single-hole transistor charge sensor · electric dipole spin resonance (EDSR) · Pauli spin blockade (PSB) readout

items.abstract: Hole spin qubits in semiconductor quantum dots (QDs) enable high-fidelity all-electric control, but conventional electric dipole spin resonance (EDSR) can require substantial rf drive power at the low magnetic fields that are favorable for qubit coherence and readout. In planar Ge hole spin qubits, this can reach -27 dBm at the device, posing challenges for scalable architectures due to heating and crosstalk. Here, we demonstrate a flopping-mode (FM) qubit in Ge, where a single spin is delocalized in a double QD, combining first-order protection against charge noise with exceptionally efficient electric driving. By mapping out coherence sweet-spots as a function of magnetic field orientation we achieve T₂^*= 1.4μs, T₂^Hahn= 11.5 μs, T^(φ, CPMG32)₂= 130 μs, and T₁= 226 μs, and a single-qubit gate fidelity of up to 99.76% for a gate time t_(Xπ) = 88 ns. Importantly, these results are obtained at a nearly in-plane magnetic field of 5 mT using only -52 dBm drive power at the device. We further find that qubit relaxation in this regime is consistent with a two-photon Orbach process, providing a route for further optimization. Our results demonstrate that FM-EDSR supports ultra-low-power, high-fidelity single-qubit operations, improvements that could benefit scalable hole-spin-based architectures and hybrid spin-photon interfaces.

items.title: Highly uniform first-electron position in qubit arrays fabricated on dedicated QSOI(R) 300mm commercial platform
items.authors: Johan Pelloux-Prayer, Elise Prin, Giselle A. Elbaz, Pierre-Louis Julliard, Amaryllis Comiti, Clément Nguyen, Sylvain Martin, Patrick Torresani, Renan Lethiecq, Carlos Augusto Suarez Segovia, Franck Arnaud, Etienne Nowak, Tristan Meunier, Bruna Cardoso Paz

items.result: 300mm wafer-scale QSOI platform achieves 69% yield for first-electron charge detection across 546 plunger-gate stability diagrams, with first-electron position dispersion of 21mV ±35mV over 377 quantum dots.
items.question: Can an adapted commercial 28nm FD-SOI CMOS platform achieve wafer-scale electrostatic uniformity and reproducible few-electron quantum dot operation?
items.prior: Standard 28nm FD-SOI had room-temperature threshold-voltage dispersion σ_V_TH = 385mV (reduced to 41.1mV here); matched-pair ΔV_TH/√2 standard deviation was 59 mV in prior 300mm Si qubit arrays.
items.limits: Tested on a single best-performing wafer split at ∼2K wafer temperature under DC probing; automated charge detection routine did not dynamically optimize detector sensitivity.
items.tools: 300mm QSOI quantum platform · cryogenic semi-automatic wafer prober (sub-2K) · charge sensing with single-electron transistors (SET) · TCAD electrostatics simulation
items.caption: Left: wafer map showing charge-stability diagrams across 91 dies. Right: histogram of the gate voltage corresponding to the first detected electron across 377 quantum dots, centered at 21mV with a ±35mV spread.
items.abstract: We report progress toward the development of a quantum silicon-on-insulator (QSOI(R)) technology compatible with 300mm CMOS fabrication and adapted from the 28nm Fully-Depleted SOI (28nm FD-SOI) platform for scalable quantum computing. We compare quantum devices fabricated with standard 28nm FD-SOI and QSOI(R) technologies, and show striking improvements of room temperature electrostatic properties of the individual device. Moreover, the QSOI(R) technology has significantly reduced the device variability and the dispersion of device properties at the wafer level. Transistor metrics are reproduced by TCAD simulations showing that the electrostatics of the devices behave as expected for QSOI(R) technology. Wafer-scale measurements at sub-2K show reproducible quantum dots down to the few-electron regime with 69% yield for successful charge detection of the first electron and a dispersion of the first electron position of ±35 mV over 377 quantum dots. These results establish QSOI(R) as a promising platform for CMOS-compatible quantum device co-integration.

items.title: Neutral atom quantum computing for materials science and quantum chemistry
items.authors: J. D. Pritchard
items.matched: Semiconductor spin qubits

items.question: How do neutral atom quantum computing platforms address simulation and optimisation challenges in materials science and quantum chemistry across analogue and digital paradigms?
items.limits: Materials and chemistry applications require utility-scale hardware (10⁵ physical qubits, >10⁶ T-gates), far exceeding current device sizes. Single-species mid-circuit readout causes light scattering and crosstalk.

items.abstract: Neutral atom arrays have emerged as versatile platforms for performing both digital and analogue quantum computing and simulation, with demonstrations ranging from large-scale programmable Hamiltonians realising topological phases or weighted graph optimisation to error-corrected logical qubits with transverse gate operations. This paper provides a broad overview to the neutral atom platform, and the potential applications relevant to materials science and quantum chemistry.

items.title: Single-atom-based asynchronous photonic interconnect for scalable modular quantum computing
items.authors: Jérémy Raskop, Nadav Kandel, Yaniv Amichy, Yaron Jarach, Tal Kanonich, Andrei Militaru, Johannes Fink, Barak Dayan
items.matched: photonic qubits, linear-optical computing and boson sampling
items.result: Memory-assisted single-atom interconnect achieves linear scaling with photon delivery probability tildep , reducing the attempt rate required for a 10⁴ s⁻¹ entanglement rate from 190 MHz (type-II fusion) to 3.2 MHz at tildep=1% .
items.question: How to scale entanglement rates between modular quantum processing units linearly with low single-photon delivery probabilities without requiring two-photon interference or simultaneous photon arrival?
items.prior: Linear-optics type-II fusion BSM gates scale quadratically as 0.5p² and require simultaneous arrival of indistinguishable photons, needing an attempt rate R_bs ≃190 MHz at tildep=1% for 10⁴ s⁻¹ entanglement rate.
items.limits: Infidelity budgets δ=1%--5% limit waiting window length due to unheralded photon-atom scattering and atom dephasing barT₂^*; excludes input state preparation errors, motional ground-state cooling downtime, and atom reloading.
items.tools: trapped single ⁸⁷Rb atom in fiber Fabry–Perot microcavity · symmetric Duan–Kimble cavity reflection photon–atom CZ gate · dual-rail path encoding · Monte Carlo simulations
items.caption: Entanglement rate and performance metrics plotted against attempt rate and delivery probability, showing a nearly 60-fold reduction in required repetition rate to reach 10⁴ s⁻¹ compared to type-II fusion.
items.abstract: Scaling quantum computation beyond the capacity of a single quantum processing unit requires quantum interconnects between modular processors. Optical photons are natural carriers for distributing entanglement between these processors. Most loss-resilient protocols use photonic Bell-state measurements based on the linear-optics type-II fusion gate. The resulting entanglement rate scales quadratically with each processor's typically low photon-delivery probability. Here we analyze a memory-assisted quantum interconnect using a near-deterministic, robust photon--atom controlled-Z gate via a single atom trapped in a high-finesse cavity. Detecting and measuring a photon from one processor heralds entanglement between that processor and the atom. This entanglement is preserved while the process repeats with the second processor until the second photon is detected and measured. Reading out the atomic qubit finalizes the entanglement between the processors. As the entanglement is mediated by the atom, the photons from both processors do not need to be indistinguishable, removing a major source of infidelity. Furthermore, by removing the simultaneous photon-arrival requirement, the protocol allows the entanglement rate to scale linearly rather than quadratically with photon-arrival probability over a wide parameter range. We derive entanglement rates under realistic parameters, accounting for decay of the atom's entanglement with the first processor and for decoherence caused by unheralded photon interactions. The nanosecond-scale of the gate and read-out operations leads to orders-of-magnitude entanglement-rate gain over linear optics, removing a key bottleneck in modular quantum computing.
