items.title: Polariton Bell Node for Quantum Repeaters
items.authors: Junhui Cao, Alexey Kavokin
items.matched: quantum memories and repeaters for long-distance links
items.result: Polariton spin-dependent scattering enables a deterministic controlled-Z gate with a minimum interaction threshold c_min = √2-1, achieving complete Bell-state discrimination with identification error scaling as O(s⁴) for pulse bandwidth s.
items.question: Can spin-dependent exciton-polariton interactions and cavity mode splittings implement a deterministic Bell-state measurement for quantum repeaters?
items.prior: was c=1 for a one-sided scalar Kerr gate reference
items.limits: Theoretical calculation assuming strong-coupling regime, single-mode one-sided port, coherent control loading/readout, and negligible control transverse precession.
items.tools: planar semiconductor microcavity · exciton-polaritons · TE-TM splitting · one-sided input-output scattering theory · POVM formalism
items.caption: Analytic interaction threshold c_min(u) and detuning branches x_± plotted against normalized TE-TM splitting u = Ω_LT/κ, showing the transition from zero detuning to non-zero detuning at u = 1/√2.
items.abstract: We propose a Bell-measurement node for quantum repeaters based on a planar semiconductor microcavity operating in the strong-coupling regime. Cavity photons hybridize with quantum-well excitons to form polaritons combining properties of photons and matter quasiparticles. A control photon loaded into one polariton mode changes the polarization response seen by a subsequently incident target photon. This conditional rotation is governed by the interplay of self-induced Larmor precession triggered by spin-dependent exciton-exciton interactions and the polarization beats caused by the splitting of transverse-electric and transverse-magnetic cavity modes. We identify conditions of the experiment that enable implementation of a controlled-Z gate and allow to distinguish all four Bell states in the ideal limit. The one-sided scattering scheme provides a lower interaction threshold than a scalar Kerr reference under the same assumptions. At a selected operating point, the bandwidth-induced identification error scales as the fourth power of the pulse bandwidth in the narrow-band limit. An additional fixed input rotation reduces this error even further. We describe the entanglement swapping between remote memories and determine the minimum quality of the elementary links needed to obtain an entangled output.

items.title: Autonomous stabilization of many-body entanglement with Floquet Hamiltonians and weak measurement
items.authors: Charlotte Franke, Dorian A. Gangloff
items.matched: Quantum information with Rydberg atoms
items.result: Interleaving Floquet engineering with weak measurement autonomously stabilizes nuclear spin squeezing down to -12.8 dB below the standard quantum limit (R=0.9) and collective Schrödinger-cat states with fidelity >0.9.
items.question: How can Floquet Hamiltonian engineering be combined with engineered dissipation without continuous reservoir noise disrupting the coherent drive?
items.limits: Simulated in central-spin systems with weak non-collinear coupling A_nc/ω_n ≪1, per-cycle measurement strength ε≤0.1, and nuclear ensemble dephasing T₂ ≈1 ms to 100 ms.
items.tools: Floquet Hamiltonian engineering · stroboscopic weak measurement · central-spin quantum dot model · Lindblad master equation · adiabatic elimination
items.caption: Squeezing parameter ξ_R² and cat infidelity 1 - F versus evolution time and stroboscopic cycle number M, showing autonomous relaxation to steady-state floors below the standard quantum limit.
items.abstract: Reaching a technological advantage with large quantum systems requires safeguarding their many-body entanglement. Dissipation typically acts to decohere a quantum system via random projective noise but, when judiciously engineered together with coherent interactions, it can funnel the system towards a target entangled state. The native interactions and dissipative channels available to most systems are, however, difficult to combine effectively. Here we propose interleaving Floquet Hamiltonian engineering, which allows the construction of non-native coherent interactions, with weak measurement, which enables a tuneable dissipative channel, to enable programmable and autonomous stabilization of many-body entanglement. We show this analytically and numerically for the central-spin system of a semiconductor quantum dot, for which we construct spin-squeezed and Schrödinger-cat states that are stabilized against realistic levels of dephasing. Our approach is applicable to any system compatible with periodic drives and tuneable measurement strength and could enable novel approaches to practical error correction.

items.title: Giant-Atom-Induced High-Order Output Zeros in a Coupled-Cavity Array
items.authors: Mengxue Li, Bo Liu, H. Z. Shen, H. D. Liu, Gangcheng Wang
items.matched: cavity QED, atom-photon interfaces and quantum networks
items.result: Nonlocal interference from a two-site giant atom in a 1D cavity array achieves second-order coherent perfect absorption and third-order zero transmission without exceptional points or momentum-dependent input phases, suppressing finite-bandwidth wave-packet residuals as R⁽ⁿ⁾ ∝σ⁻²ⁿ.
items.question: Can giant-atom nonlocal interference produce high-order scattering zeros and broaden absorption and zero-transmission bandwidths without relying on exceptional points or momentum-dependent input phases?
items.limits: Single-excitation regime, nearest-neighbor cavity hopping only, effective loss modeled solely on giant atom, symmetric coupling magnitudes g₁=g₂=g.
items.tools: tight-binding coupled-cavity array model · wave-function matching method · S-matrix formalism · wave-packet time-evolution simulations
items.caption: Plots show the output residual intensity log₁₀R_CPA for Gaussian wave packets against inverse width σ⁻¹ and detuning δk_c/π. At zero detuning, the residual scales as σ⁻² for first-order coherent perfect absorption and as σ⁻⁴ for second-order coherent perfect absorption.
items.abstract: Coherent perfect absorption, zero transmission and zero reflection are several scattering phenomena governed by interference engineering in Hermitian and non-Hermitian systems. Higher-order coherent perfect absorption can significantly broaden the absorption bandwidth, while existing implementations rely on scattering zero degeneracy induced by exceptional points or additional momentum-dependent phase delays introduced in incident waves. We propose a scheme where a giant atom couples to a one-dimensional coupled-cavity array at two spatially separated sites. The spatially separated coupling configuration of the giant atom generates tunable nonlocal interference phases that dominate the scattering interference process. We further investigate the zero-reflection and zero-transmission behaviors under single-sided incidence. Remarkably, we find that for certain parameter choices, zero transmission can persist over the entire propagating band, rather than being restricted to a single momentum. Our results reveal that the giant-atom interference mechanism enables bandwidth-enhanced coherent perfect absorption and bandwidth-enhanced zero transmission in the absence of exceptional points and incident momentum-dependent phase delays. Our work provides a physical route for coherent wave manipulation in coupled-cavity quantum networks.

items.title: Experimental Measurement and Theoretical Analysis of Energy Relaxation Rates of an Interacting Two-Qubit System on a D-Wave Quantum Annealer
items.authors: Yusei Amano, Sorato Suzuki, Hiroki Kuji, Tetsuro Nikuni, Takashi Imoto, Yuichiro Matsuzaki
items.matched: Quantum information with Rydberg atoms
items.result: Energy relaxation rates of first excited states in interacting two-qubit systems on a D-Wave annealer are predicted within a factor of ≈4 using local relaxation parameters calibrated from uncoupled single-qubit reference measurements.
items.question: Can relaxation measurements of constituent physical qubits performed with interaction turned off predict the energy relaxation rate of the interacting multiqubit system?
items.limits: Low-temperature limit retaining only downward transitions; transitions near 1.5 GHz; neglects inter-qubit noise correlations; model systematically underestimates relaxation rates in the small-transition-matrix-element regime.
items.tools: D-Wave Advantage 4.1 quantum annealer · Reverse-annealing protocol · GKSL master equation with independent local σ^z-noise · Exact diagonalization
items.caption: Predicted versus experimentally measured energy relaxation rates for interacting two-qubit systems, showing predictions calibrated from uncoupled single-qubit data track measurements within a factor of approximately four.
items.abstract: In D-Wave quantum annealers, various properties of the ground state have been clarified, whereas the correspondence between theory and experiment for energy relaxation rates in multiqubit excited states remains insufficiently understood. Here, we measured the energy relaxation rates of the first excited states in single-qubit systems and interacting two-qubit systems using a D-Wave quantum annealer. We analyzed the measured relaxation rates using a Gorini-Kossakowski-Sudarshan-Lindblad master equation with independent local σ^z-type noise channels. The calculated relaxation rates reproduced the overall trends observed experimentally, supporting the model at a qualitative level. We then used the relaxation rates measured for the uncoupled single-qubit systems to calibrate the local relaxation parameters and predict the relaxation rates of the interacting two-qubit systems. The predicted rates remained within a factor of approximately four of the measured rates. These results show that the relaxation measurements on individual qubits can provide a practical estimate of relaxation in small interacting quantum systems and may help clarify relaxation mechanisms in programmable quantum annealers.

items.title: Persistent Quantum-Enhanced Frequency Sensing with T^{-3/2} Scaling
items.authors: Clayton Z. C. Ho, Hao Wu, Grant D. Mitts, Joshua A. Rabinowitz, Eric R. Hudson
items.matched: Quantum information with Rydberg atoms
items.result: Fock-state-enhanced quantum heterodyne protocol decouples sensitivity from dephasing-limited interrogation time τ, sustaining T^(-3/2) scaling across seven orders of magnitude in measurement time. The |n=3⟩ Fock state achieves 7.1(1.0) dB gain over n=0, reaching 0.5μHz frequency precision on an 86 MHz carrier (6×10⁻¹⁵ fractional precision).
items.question: Can quantum metrological advantage in frequency sensing persist to long measurement times without being eliminated by accelerated decoherence of nonclassical states?
items.prior: Pulsed dynamical-decoupling Qdyne implementations in solid-state spin defects were restricted to tens of MHz.
items.limits: Operating bandwidth limited by Nyquist rate 1/(2 T_s); single trapped ion mode in cryogenic environment; ultimate precision bounded by reference clock stability.
items.tools: trapped ⁴⁰Ca⁺ ion in cryogenic linear Paul trap · motional Raman transitions for Hamiltonian frequency mixing · Fock state overlap readout · quantum heterodyne (Qdyne) protocol
items.caption: Frequency precision σ_δ versus total measurement time T for Fock states n=0,1,2,3. Precision follows T^(-3/2) scaling up to long measurement times, showing persistent quantum metrological gain for higher n states over n=0.
items.abstract: Quantum sensing uses nonclassical states to improve measurement sensitivity, but the same states that provide metrological gain also decohere more rapidly. This limits the usable interrogation time and, in practice, often precludes improvement in ultimate sensitivity - realized useful quantum advantage has consequently remained rare. Here, we restore persistent quantum advantage by embedding Fock-state enhancement within a quantum heterodyne (Qdyne) protocol, decoupling sensitivity from the decoherence-limited interrogation time τ. Measurements are acquired at short τ where the quantum-enhanced gain is optimal, while precision accumulates with the total measurement time. Demonstrated on the motional mode of a trapped 40Ca+ ion, we observe quantum-enhanced precision that persists to measurement times seven orders of magnitude beyond the dephasing limit, scaling as T^{-3/2} with no indication of saturation. Using the n=3 Fock state, we reach a frequency precision of 0.5uHz relative to an 86MHz carrier, achieving a fractional precision ~6x10^{-15}. This represents a quantum-enhanced gain of 7.1(10) dB over the n=0 state, in agreement with Fisher information predictions. This is the first demonstration of Qdyne beyond solid-state spin-defects. Further, by using the quantum harmonic oscillator to perform frequency mixing, we extend operation beyond 1GHz, two orders of magnitude above the ceiling of pulsed dynamical-decoupling implementations. These results recover quantum advantage at the long timescales required to improve ultimate sensitivity, with direct implications for nanoscale NMR and quantum logic spectroscopy.

items.title: Denser Planar Color Codes
items.authors: Noah Shutty
items.matched: Surface code quantum computing by lattice surgery
items.result: Superdense 4.8.8 color code memory achieves distance d using q=(2d²+5d-5)/2 total physical qubits with a twelve-layer CNOT cycle. Requires asymptotically 2/3 as many qubits as triangular 6.6.6 color codes and 1/2 as many as rotated surface codes.
items.question: Can 4.8.8 color codes achieve lower total physical qubit overhead than 6.6.6 color codes and surface codes under circuit-level noise and ancilla costs?
items.prior: Data qubit overhead ratio n/(kd²) was 1 for rotated surface codes and 3/4 for 6.6.6 color codes (Bombin 2006, Landahl 2014), while 4.8.8 reached 1/2 without ancilla or circuit noise optimizations.
items.limits: Circuit-level SI1000 noise model with native CZ gates at p=10⁻³ and p=5×10⁻⁴; planar triangular and torus codes with nearest-neighbor 2D square lattice connectivity.
items.tools: Brickwork lattice embedding · Superdense syndrome extraction · Pauli frame tracking · Tesseract decoder · Stim circuit simulation

items.abstract: We consider the 4.8.8 color code in a brickwork layout on the square lattice with nearest-neighbor gates. We identify periodic superdense circuits with twelve CNOT layers that appear to preserve the full distance of these codes. Including ancillas, the family uses q=(2d²+5d-5)/2 physical qubits for distance d: asymptotically 2/3 as many as the triangular 6.6.6 color code and 1/2 as many as the rotated surface code at the same code distance. Circuit-level simulations targeting superconducting architectures demonstrate favorable scaling of 4.8.8 color codes at plausible physical noise rates, including both for planar codes and their toroidal cousins under periodic boundary conditions.

items.authors: Paul Webster, Tom Peham, Lawrence Z. Cohen

items.abstract: We show how the Pinnacle architecture can be adapted to be compatible with superconducting qubits, where the connectivity between qubits must be fixed at fabrication. Specifically, we present a modified instantiation of the architecture that has fixed connectivity degree of eight. With this instantiation, we show that a 2048-bit RSA integer can be factored in one month with approximately 120 000 physical qubits, given a physical error rate of 10⁻³, code cycle time of 1 microsecond and reaction time of 10 microseconds.

items.title: Single-atom-based asynchronous photonic interconnect for scalable modular quantum computing
items.authors: Jérémy Raskop, Nadav Kandel, Yaniv Amichy, Yaron Jarach, Tal Kanonich, Andrei Militaru, Johannes Fink, Barak Dayan
items.matched: High-threshold and low-overhead fault-tolerant quantum memory
items.result: Memory-assisted single-atom interconnect achieves linear scaling with photon delivery probability tildep , reducing the attempt rate required for a 10⁴ s⁻¹ entanglement rate from 190 MHz (type-II fusion) to 3.2 MHz at tildep=1% .
items.question: How to scale entanglement rates between modular quantum processing units linearly with low single-photon delivery probabilities without requiring two-photon interference or simultaneous photon arrival?
items.prior: Linear-optics type-II fusion BSM gates scale quadratically as 0.5p² and require simultaneous arrival of indistinguishable photons, needing an attempt rate R_bs ≃190 MHz at tildep=1% for 10⁴ s⁻¹ entanglement rate.
items.limits: Infidelity budgets δ=1%--5% limit waiting window length due to unheralded photon-atom scattering and atom dephasing barT₂^*; excludes input state preparation errors, motional ground-state cooling downtime, and atom reloading.
items.tools: trapped single ⁸⁷Rb atom in fiber Fabry–Perot microcavity · symmetric Duan–Kimble cavity reflection photon–atom CZ gate · dual-rail path encoding · Monte Carlo simulations
items.caption: Entanglement rate and performance metrics plotted against attempt rate and delivery probability, showing a nearly 60-fold reduction in required repetition rate to reach 10⁴ s⁻¹ compared to type-II fusion.
items.abstract: Scaling quantum computation beyond the capacity of a single quantum processing unit requires quantum interconnects between modular processors. Optical photons are natural carriers for distributing entanglement between these processors. Most loss-resilient protocols use photonic Bell-state measurements based on the linear-optics type-II fusion gate. The resulting entanglement rate scales quadratically with each processor's typically low photon-delivery probability. Here we analyze a memory-assisted quantum interconnect using a near-deterministic, robust photon--atom controlled-Z gate via a single atom trapped in a high-finesse cavity. Detecting and measuring a photon from one processor heralds entanglement between that processor and the atom. This entanglement is preserved while the process repeats with the second processor until the second photon is detected and measured. Reading out the atomic qubit finalizes the entanglement between the processors. As the entanglement is mediated by the atom, the photons from both processors do not need to be indistinguishable, removing a major source of infidelity. Furthermore, by removing the simultaneous photon-arrival requirement, the protocol allows the entanglement rate to scale linearly rather than quadratically with photon-arrival probability over a wide parameter range. We derive entanglement rates under realistic parameters, accounting for decay of the atom's entanglement with the first processor and for decoherence caused by unheralded photon interactions. The nanosecond-scale of the gate and read-out operations leads to orders-of-magnitude entanglement-rate gain over linear optics, removing a key bottleneck in modular quantum computing.

items.abstract: Quantum oracles act as reversible black-box operators that encode classical Boolean functions into quantum states, enabling efficient function evaluation in quantum superposition. The resource efficiency of oracle implementation is critical to the performance of numerous quantum algorithms. Most state-of-the-art oracle synthesis approaches rely on compact Boolean function representations such as exclusive-sum-of-products (ESOP), yet still suffer from excessive T-count and CX-count for large-scale functions. In this paper, we propose a novel compact representation named X-Map decision diagram (XMDD) for Boolean functions, which integrates local invertible maps and complement edges to achieve higher compression efficiency. Based on XMDD, we further develop an optimized quantum oracle synthesis algorithm. Extensive experimental results demonstrate that, for Boolean functions with more than seven input variables, our method outperforms the state-of-the-art ESOP-based approach and Qiskit in nearly all test cases, achieving simultaneous reduction in both T-count and CX-count without an obvious trade-off. Moreover, we show that the performance can be further boosted by employing more optimal variable orderings. The proposed XMDD-based framework provides a scalable and resource-efficient solution for practical oracle synthesis in near-term and fault-tolerant quantum computing.

items.authors: Raul Martinez, Miguel Sanchez-Beato, Mario Calonge

items.abstract: The Variational Quantum Eigensolver (VQE) requires a large number of measurements to evaluate molecular Hamiltonians. Expressing a molecular Hamiltonian as a linear combination of Pauli strings creates a measurement bottleneck: non-commuting Pauli strings cannot be measured simultaneously. Consequently, mutually commuting Pauli strings must be grouped and measured together to minimise the number of quantum-state preparations. This task maps to the minimum clique cover problem on a commutativity graph, an NP-hard problem typically addressed using classical heuristics. Although an Ising-model formulation has recently been explored on fully connected CMOS Ising machines and demonstrated on physical quantum annealers only at small scale, the embedding cost that governs its behaviour on hardware with sparse connectivity, where each logical variable must be represented by a chain of physical qubits, has not been characterised. In this work, we formulate the Pauli-grouping problem as a standard QUBO colouring model and study its scalability on a D-Wave quantum annealer. Across a series of molecular systems and for both qubit-wise and full commutativity, we quantify the growth in the number of logical variables and the QUBO interaction density, characterise the physical-qubit and chain-length overhead required for embedding on the Zephyr topology, and compare the annealer's time-to-solution and solution quality with those of heuristic classical baselines. This analysis identifies the threshold of molecular complexity beyond which hardware connectivity prevents viable embedding, and shows that a second, practical limit is reached earlier. The threshold therefore measures how far current annealers are from the regime in which pre-optimising a VQE measurement scheme on hardware would be worth considering.

items.title: Weighted Quantum Signal Processing: Low-Depth Polynomial Approximation with Applications to Kolmogorov-Arnold Networks
items.authors: Rohit Sarma Sarkar, Rupayan Bhattacharjee, Elias F. Combarro, Michele Grossi, Lirandë Pira, Carmen G. Almudéver, Sergi Abadal, Eduard Alarcon
items.matched: Quantum singular value transformation and beyond: exponential improvements for…
items.result: Assigns weight functions to the central rotation operator in Quantum Signal Processing (WQSP), achieving linear-to-exponential parameter and circuit-depth reductions for realizing arbitrary bounded univariate polynomials.
items.question: How can the circuit depth, parameter count, and parity constraints of Quantum Signal Processing be reduced for polynomial and continuous function approximation?
items.limits: Theoretical bounds and variational quantum circuit simulations.
items.tools: Weighted Quantum Signal Processing (WQSP) · Kolmogorov-Arnold Networks (KANs) · Single-qubit rotation parameterization
items.abstract: Quantum Signal Processing is a powerful quantum framework for generating and approximating univariate polynomials. However, QSP is often limited by circuit-depth bottlenecks and parity constraints on the class of realizable polynomials. In this work, we introduce Weighted Quantum Signal Processing, an extension of QSP in which a weight function is assigned to the central rotation operator. This formulation provides a deeper understanding of QSP, which emerges as the special case of WQSP with unit weights. The choice of weights determines the structure and expressive capabilities of WQSP circuits. When the weights are natural numbers greater than one, WQSP reduces to a pruned version of QSP, revealing parameter redundancies in the standard framework. Through appropriate selection of integer weights, WQSP achieves linear-to-exponential reductions in the number of parameters required to realize arbitrary bounded univariate polynomials while preserving approximation quality. For generic weights, we establish corresponding approximation error bounds and show that, in many cases, the approximation is exact. We analyze WQSP from both a deterministic perspective, where polynomial generation is formulated as the solution of a linear system, and a quantum machine learning perspective, where WQSP serves as a structured and expressive quantum learning model. We further employ this learning framework to parameterize learnable activation functions in Kolmogorov--Arnold Networks for multivariate function approximation. Our results show that WQSP provides a compact, flexible, and theoretically grounded framework for realizing arbitrary univariate polynomials while requiring significantly fewer trainable parameters than conventional QSP. This yields expressive and parameter-efficient neural architectures, highlighting the potential of WQSP as a scalable primitive for quantum-enhanced machine learning.

items.abstract: Feedback-based quantum algorithms recently gained attention by demonstrating how quantum computers can be used to solve optimization problems without resorting to hybrid quantum-classical architectures. Recent progress made with Feedback-based Algorithm for Quantum Optimization (FALQON) variants significantly reduced the depth of the required circuits. In this work, we merge the time-rescaled and second-order FALQON variants into a unified framework. The results show an important improvement over past modifications, reducing circuit depth and allowing a more flexible choice of time-steps, while maintaining stable solutions. This FALQON variant makes it suitable for the NISQ era.

items.title: Single-atom-based asynchronous photonic interconnect for scalable modular quantum computing
items.authors: Jérémy Raskop, Nadav Kandel, Yaniv Amichy, Yaron Jarach, Tal Kanonich, Andrei Militaru, Johannes Fink, Barak Dayan
items.matched: Quantum Computing in the NISQ era and beyond
items.result: Memory-assisted single-atom interconnect achieves linear scaling with photon delivery probability tildep , reducing the attempt rate required for a 10⁴ s⁻¹ entanglement rate from 190 MHz (type-II fusion) to 3.2 MHz at tildep=1% .
items.question: How to scale entanglement rates between modular quantum processing units linearly with low single-photon delivery probabilities without requiring two-photon interference or simultaneous photon arrival?
items.prior: Linear-optics type-II fusion BSM gates scale quadratically as 0.5p² and require simultaneous arrival of indistinguishable photons, needing an attempt rate R_bs ≃190 MHz at tildep=1% for 10⁴ s⁻¹ entanglement rate.

items.tools: trapped single ⁸⁷Rb atom in fiber Fabry–Perot microcavity · symmetric Duan–Kimble cavity reflection photon–atom CZ gate · dual-rail path encoding · Monte Carlo simulations

items.abstract: Scaling quantum computation beyond the capacity of a single quantum processing unit requires quantum interconnects between modular processors. Optical photons are natural carriers for distributing entanglement between these processors. Most loss-resilient protocols use photonic Bell-state measurements based on the linear-optics type-II fusion gate. The resulting entanglement rate scales quadratically with each processor's typically low photon-delivery probability. Here we analyze a memory-assisted quantum interconnect using a near-deterministic, robust photon--atom controlled-Z gate via a single atom trapped in a high-finesse cavity. Detecting and measuring a photon from one processor heralds entanglement between that processor and the atom. This entanglement is preserved while the process repeats with the second processor until the second photon is detected and measured. Reading out the atomic qubit finalizes the entanglement between the processors. As the entanglement is mediated by the atom, the photons from both processors do not need to be indistinguishable, removing a major source of infidelity. Furthermore, by removing the simultaneous photon-arrival requirement, the protocol allows the entanglement rate to scale linearly rather than quadratically with photon-arrival probability over a wide parameter range. We derive entanglement rates under realistic parameters, accounting for decay of the atom's entanglement with the first processor and for decoherence caused by unheralded photon interactions. The nanosecond-scale of the gate and read-out operations leads to orders-of-magnitude entanglement-rate gain over linear optics, removing a key bottleneck in modular quantum computing.

items.result: Introduced Unified Cluster Quality Metric (UCQM) combining 6 covariance- and graph-derived descriptors; 2D square topology achieved the highest UCQM across squeezing range r ∈[0.2, 1.8] and scaled to N=100 modes with O(N³) computational cost.
items.question: How can continuous-variable cluster states with different topologies, squeezing parameters, and connectivity patterns be quantitatively compared across multiple structural resource dimensions?
items.limits: Restricted to Gaussian states, uniform squeezing parameter r, and ideal CZ interactions; excludes non-Gaussian resources, mode-dependent squeezing, and correlated experimental loss.
items.tools: Unified Cluster Quality Metric (UCQM) · Gaussian covariance matrix formalism · continuous-variable cluster state graph theory · homodyne tomography descriptors
items.caption: UCQM score plotted against squeezing parameter r ∈[0.2, 1.8] for path, star, and square topologies. The square lattice maintains the highest overall quality score across all evaluated squeezing levels.
items.abstract: Continuous-variable (CV) cluster states constitute one of the central resources for measurement-based quantum computation (MBQC). Despite substantial progress in their theoretical development and experimental realization, comparing the quality of different cluster-state topologies remains challenging, as existing approaches typically rely either on qualitative inspection of covariance matrices or on individual metrics that characterize only a single aspect of the underlying correlation structure. In this work, we propose a quantitative evaluation framework that integrates six complementary descriptors of CV cluster states: total correlation strength (SSC), correlation uniformity (CAV), error resilience (EVC), communication overhead (COM), path redundancy (RED), and bottleneck vulnerability (BOT). These quantities are combined into a single Unified Cluster Quality Metric (UCQM), providing a consistent basis for evaluating and comparing different cluster-state architectures. The proposed framework is applied to four-mode path, square, and star cluster topologies over the squeezing range r ∈[0.2,1.8]. Across the investigated parameter regime, the square topology consistently achieves the highest UCQM score, indicating the most balanced structural characteristics among the topologies considered and supporting its suitability for measurement-based quantum computation. Because all six metrics are derived directly from covariance-matrix elements together with graph connectivity, the framework naturally extends to arbitrary N-mode cluster states, higher-dimensional lattice geometries, and experimentally reconstructed covariance matrices. Beyond providing a single numerical score, UCQM offers a unified perspective for analyzing the structural quality of CV cluster states and establishes a practical framework for their systematic comparison, optimization, and future design.

items.title: Efficient MPO Construction for Long-Range Hamiltonians with Periodic Boundary Conditions: Application to Many-Body Dynamics
items.authors: Xin Wang, Bo Xiong
items.matched: tensor network and matrix product state methods, and classical simulability of…
items.result: MPO bond dimension scales as D_r^chain=r+2 under OBC and D_r^ring=(r²+3r+4)/2 under PBC by embedding finite-range periodic channels directly into an open-boundary MPO, yielding average TDVP relative error of 0.58% for occupation and under 1.5% for correlations against RK4.
items.question: How can compact MPOs incorporating both periodic boundary conditions and finite-range interactions be constructed for stable TDVP time evolution without breaking canonical gauge?
items.prior: was maximum bond dimension scaling as 2^r for interaction range r in TEBD-based MPOs constructed from nonlocal exponentials
items.limits: Spin-1/2 chain quench dynamics simulation over 0.7~μs, benchmarked up to third-nearest neighbors (r=3) and system sizes up to N=24.
items.tools: matrix product operators · time-dependent variational principle · fourth-order Runge-Kutta benchmark
items.caption: Time evolution and relative errors of average occupation n and spatial correlations C_r (r=1,2,3) comparing TDVP to RK4 under a quench protocol up to 0.7~μs. Relative error stays below 1% for occupation and below 5% for correlations across all interaction ranges.
items.abstract: Matrix product operator (MPO) serves as a fundamental component in tensor network simulations of quantum many-body dynamics. We employ an MPO construction that introduces additional propagation channels to embed both periodic boundary conditions and finite-range couplings directly into an open boundary MPO. We apply this construction within the time-dependent variational principle (TDVP) framework to simulate quench dynamics in a spin-1/2 chain with finite-range interactions, and benchmark the results numerically against the fourth-order Runge-Kutta method, finding excellent agreement for both single-body and two-body observables. The approach offers a practical route for tensor network simulations of many-body dynamics in periodic finite-range systems.

items.title: Pauli-string grouping for VQE measurement reduction on a sparse-connectivity quantum annealer
items.authors: Raul Martinez, Miguel Sanchez-Beato, Mario Calonge
items.matched: quantum chemistry and electronic structure on quantum computers
items.result: Only H₂ embeds onto current quantum annealing hardware for VQE Pauli-string grouping; all other molecular instances exceed the 4 800-qubit Zephyr Z₁₂ graph by factors between 23 and 2.0×10⁵, with BeH₂ under full commutativity requiring at least a Z₅₉ topology (>10⁵ physical qubits).
items.question: What is the physical-qubit embedding overhead, scalability limit, and practical performance of the Pauli-grouping colouring QUBO on a sparse-connectivity quantum annealer compared to classical heuristics?
items.prior: Small-scale colouring QUBO implementations on D-Wave processors exhibited rapid decay of valid samples with variable count (Jattana et al., 2023), but without characterizing the minor-embedding overhead or hardware graph capacity limits.
items.limits: Evaluated on six molecular Hamiltonians in the STO-3G basis using Bravyi-Kitaev mapping and standard one-hot QUBO formulation. Compared against classical greedy heuristics rather than exact solvers.
items.tools: D-Wave Advantage2_system1 (Zephyr topology) · D-Wave Leap Hybrid BQM solver · One-hot Minimum Vertex Colouring QUBO · Degree-counting minor-embedding lower bounds · Classical graph colouring heuristics (LF, RLF, Degree-Based)
items.caption: Compares grouping quality (number of Pauli groups) and computational cost (wall-clock time) for molecular Hamiltonians under full commutativity across classical heuristics and D-Wave solvers.
items.abstract: The Variational Quantum Eigensolver (VQE) requires a large number of measurements to evaluate molecular Hamiltonians. Expressing a molecular Hamiltonian as a linear combination of Pauli strings creates a measurement bottleneck: non-commuting Pauli strings cannot be measured simultaneously. Consequently, mutually commuting Pauli strings must be grouped and measured together to minimise the number of quantum-state preparations. This task maps to the minimum clique cover problem on a commutativity graph, an NP-hard problem typically addressed using classical heuristics. Although an Ising-model formulation has recently been explored on fully connected CMOS Ising machines and demonstrated on physical quantum annealers only at small scale, the embedding cost that governs its behaviour on hardware with sparse connectivity, where each logical variable must be represented by a chain of physical qubits, has not been characterised. In this work, we formulate the Pauli-grouping problem as a standard QUBO colouring model and study its scalability on a D-Wave quantum annealer. Across a series of molecular systems and for both qubit-wise and full commutativity, we quantify the growth in the number of logical variables and the QUBO interaction density, characterise the physical-qubit and chain-length overhead required for embedding on the Zephyr topology, and compare the annealer's time-to-solution and solution quality with those of heuristic classical baselines. This analysis identifies the threshold of molecular complexity beyond which hardware connectivity prevents viable embedding, and shows that a second, practical limit is reached earlier. The threshold therefore measures how far current annealers are from the regime in which pre-optimising a VQE measurement scheme on hardware would be worth considering.

items.title: Time rescaling for second-order feedback-based quantum optimization
items.authors: Leticia Bertuzzi, João P. Engster, Evandro C. R. da Rosa, Eduardo I. Duzzioni
items.matched: quantum chemistry and electronic structure on quantum computers
items.result: Unifying time-rescaling with second-order feedback in FALQON (TR-Hy-FALQON) reaches the Goemans-Williamson approximation ratio threshold r_GW in 19 layers for 12-vertex 3-regular graphs and 13 layers for 14-vertex Erdős–Rényi graphs (p=0.3), yielding 40-layer approximation ratios of 0.968 and 0.966.
items.question: Can time-rescaled dynamics and second-order feedback laws be merged into a unified FALQON framework to reduce circuit depth without classical optimization?
items.prior: SO-FALQON required 32 layers for 3-regular graphs and 19 layers for Erdős–Rényi graphs to reach r_GW, while TR-FALQON failed to reach r_GW within 40 layers on 3-regular graphs and took 24 layers on Erdős–Rényi graphs.
items.limits: Numerical simulations; tested on 12-vertex 3-regular graphs and 14-vertex Erdős–Rényi graphs (p=0.3) for the MaxCut problem; capped hybrid switching between second- and first-order update rules.
items.tools: Feedback-based Algorithm for Quantum Optimization (FALQON) · Quantum Lyapunov control · Time-rescaling dynamics · Second-order energy expansion
items.caption: Approximation ratio as a function of quantum circuit layers across FALQON variants and QAOA on 12-vertex 3-regular graphs and 14-vertex Erdős–Rényi graphs, comparing 30-instance averages against single-instance runs.
items.abstract: Feedback-based quantum algorithms recently gained attention by demonstrating how quantum computers can be used to solve optimization problems without resorting to hybrid quantum-classical architectures. Recent progress made with Feedback-based Algorithm for Quantum Optimization (FALQON) variants significantly reduced the depth of the required circuits. In this work, we merge the time-rescaled and second-order FALQON variants into a unified framework. The results show an important improvement over past modifications, reducing circuit depth and allowing a more flexible choice of time-steps, while maintaining stable solutions. This FALQON variant makes it suitable for the NISQ era.

items.title: Autonomous stabilization of many-body entanglement with Floquet Hamiltonians and weak measurement
items.authors: Charlotte Franke, Dorian A. Gangloff
items.matched: Semiconductor spin qubits
items.result: Interleaving Floquet engineering with weak measurement autonomously stabilizes nuclear spin squeezing down to -12.8 dB below the standard quantum limit (R=0.9) and collective Schrödinger-cat states with fidelity >0.9.
items.question: How can Floquet Hamiltonian engineering be combined with engineered dissipation without continuous reservoir noise disrupting the coherent drive?
items.limits: Simulated in central-spin systems with weak non-collinear coupling A_nc/ω_n ≪1, per-cycle measurement strength ε≤0.1, and nuclear ensemble dephasing T₂ ≈1 ms to 100 ms.
items.tools: Floquet Hamiltonian engineering · stroboscopic weak measurement · central-spin quantum dot model · Lindblad master equation · adiabatic elimination
items.caption: Squeezing parameter ξ_R² and cat infidelity 1 - F versus evolution time and stroboscopic cycle number M, showing autonomous relaxation to steady-state floors below the standard quantum limit.
items.abstract: Reaching a technological advantage with large quantum systems requires safeguarding their many-body entanglement. Dissipation typically acts to decohere a quantum system via random projective noise but, when judiciously engineered together with coherent interactions, it can funnel the system towards a target entangled state. The native interactions and dissipative channels available to most systems are, however, difficult to combine effectively. Here we propose interleaving Floquet Hamiltonian engineering, which allows the construction of non-native coherent interactions, with weak measurement, which enables a tuneable dissipative channel, to enable programmable and autonomous stabilization of many-body entanglement. We show this analytically and numerically for the central-spin system of a semiconductor quantum dot, for which we construct spin-squeezed and Schrödinger-cat states that are stabilized against realistic levels of dephasing. Our approach is applicable to any system compatible with periodic drives and tuneable measurement strength and could enable novel approaches to practical error correction.

items.title: Experimental Measurement and Theoretical Analysis of Energy Relaxation Rates of an Interacting Two-Qubit System on a D-Wave Quantum Annealer
items.authors: Yusei Amano, Sorato Suzuki, Hiroki Kuji, Tetsuro Nikuni, Takashi Imoto, Yuichiro Matsuzaki
items.matched: Semiconductor spin qubits
items.result: Energy relaxation rates of first excited states in interacting two-qubit systems on a D-Wave annealer are predicted within a factor of ≈4 using local relaxation parameters calibrated from uncoupled single-qubit reference measurements.
items.question: Can relaxation measurements of constituent physical qubits performed with interaction turned off predict the energy relaxation rate of the interacting multiqubit system?
items.limits: Low-temperature limit retaining only downward transitions; transitions near 1.5 GHz; neglects inter-qubit noise correlations; model systematically underestimates relaxation rates in the small-transition-matrix-element regime.
items.tools: D-Wave Advantage 4.1 quantum annealer · Reverse-annealing protocol · GKSL master equation with independent local σ^z-noise · Exact diagonalization
items.caption: Predicted versus experimentally measured energy relaxation rates for interacting two-qubit systems, showing predictions calibrated from uncoupled single-qubit data track measurements within a factor of approximately four.
items.abstract: In D-Wave quantum annealers, various properties of the ground state have been clarified, whereas the correspondence between theory and experiment for energy relaxation rates in multiqubit excited states remains insufficiently understood. Here, we measured the energy relaxation rates of the first excited states in single-qubit systems and interacting two-qubit systems using a D-Wave quantum annealer. We analyzed the measured relaxation rates using a Gorini-Kossakowski-Sudarshan-Lindblad master equation with independent local σ^z-type noise channels. The calculated relaxation rates reproduced the overall trends observed experimentally, supporting the model at a qualitative level. We then used the relaxation rates measured for the uncoupled single-qubit systems to calibrate the local relaxation parameters and predict the relaxation rates of the interacting two-qubit systems. The predicted rates remained within a factor of approximately four of the measured rates. These results show that the relaxation measurements on individual qubits can provide a practical estimate of relaxation in small interacting quantum systems and may help clarify relaxation mechanisms in programmable quantum annealers.

items.title: Transport statistics and thermoelectric performance of Hofstadters butterfly
items.authors: Friedemann Queißer, Gernot Schaller
items.matched: transmon and fluxonium coherence, single- and two-qubit gate fidelity
items.result: Optimal lead-system coupling τ_L=τ_R=4τ in a finite Hofstadter lattice yields near-unit transmission plateaus T(ω)≈1 via topologically protected boundary modes, violating standard thermodynamic uncertainty relation bounds and enhancing thermoelectric power and cooling currents.
items.question: How do non-equilibrium transport statistics and thermoelectric performance behave across finite-size Hofstadter lattices coupled to reservoirs?
items.limits: Non-interacting single-particle transport, single-site lead-to-system contacts, stationary regime.
items.tools: Non-equilibrium Green's functions (NEGF) · Levitov-Lesovik counting statistics · Hofstadter lattice Hamiltonian · Tight-binding semi-infinite chain leads
items.caption: Dimensionless output power P and cooling current I_Q (top), along with efficiency η and coefficient of performance κ (bottom), plotted against dimensionless bias voltage across a finite Hofstadter system.
items.abstract: We investigate electrons subject to a magnetic field that may tunnel along a square lattice and additionally to two electronic leads. Using non-equilibrium Greens functions we evaluate the transmission and from that particle and energy currents and zero-frequency noise of the setup. We identify sweet spots for which the transmission reaches unity over broad frequency windows -- carried by topologically protected boundary modes that are quite robust against local fluctuations of on-site energies. These transmission plateaus can be exploited for the implementation robust current standards, clocks and thermoelectric devices.

items.title: A thermal microwave bus for neutral atom quantum computing
items.authors: Matthew J. H. Kendall, Christopher J. Watson, Michael Ben Shem, Jonathan D. Breeze
items.matched: neutral atom tweezer arrays and Rydberg blockade entangling gates
items.result: Bichromatic Raman gate mediating interaction via a 3D microwave cavity virtually populates Rydberg states and cancels dispersive shifts, reaching gate fidelity F = 0.997.
items.question: Can microwave cavity-mediated entangling gates overcome the shuttling-time bottleneck and thermal sensitivity in neutral-atom arrays at finite cryogenic temperatures?
items.prior: was 0.76 for optical cavity deterministic CZ gates (Steiner 2023)
items.limits: Numerical open-system simulations of up to 4 atoms, analytical Magnus-expansion bounds, requires cryogenic temperatures (T lesssim1K) and high-Q cavity (Q > 10⁹).
items.tools: 3D re-entrant microwave cavity · Open quantum system Lindblad simulations · Schrieffer-Wolff perturbation theory · Optical tweezer array
items.caption: Error-correction round time plotted against code distance d for the toric code and gross code, comparing purely shuttling-based qubit movement with the hybrid cavity-bus scheme.
items.abstract: High-fidelity two-qubit gates in neutral-atom arrays rely on the Rydberg blockade, which is intrinsically short ranged and requires long range connectivity to be achieved through atom shuttling. We propose a four level architecture, where the typical ground state qubit can be leveraged for its long lifetime and the Rydberg states couple to a microwave cavity, allowing for long range cavity mediated gates. We first find the thermal dependence of two established protocols, the dispersive iSWAP native to the Tavis-Cummings model and the Controlled phase gate generated from driving the cavity. We simulate them under the presence of Rydberg decay, thermal photons, finite cavity linewidth and find fidelities which accompany closed form bounds. We then introduce the bichromatic Raman gate, which only virtually populates the Rydberg states and cancels dispersive shifts to mitigate both atomic and cavity decay, achieving a fidelity of F = 0.997. Finally, we consider a full optical tweezer array in a microwave cavity, and show that using a cavity mediated gate to close the periodic boundaries of the toric code shortens an error correction round by a factor of 2.3 for realistic array sizes. This was then applied to the wider family of Bivariate bicycle codes, and we find that it shortens a round of the gross code by a factor of 4.8.

items.title: Deterministic synthesis and processing of frequency-bin qubits in a macroscopically coherent quantum memory
items.authors: S. A. Moiseev
items.matched: photonic qubits, linear-optical computing and boson sampling
items.result: Cavity-assisted quantum memory using pre-created long-lived macroscopic spin coherence synthesizes and stores arbitrary frequency-bin photonic qubits using only RF rotations via spectrally nonlocal impedance matching.
items.question: Can pre-created long-lived macroscopic spin coherence in a cavity-assisted quantum memory be used to deterministically synthesize, store, and process arbitrary frequency-bin photonic states without optical pulse shaping?
items.prior: Extends the single-spin-coherence PLMC protocol (Moiseev 2024), which required optical controls and stored only single-frequency photonic states.
items.limits: Spectral width of input pulse must be much smaller than inhomogeneous absorption linewidth and cavity linewidth (δω_s ≪Δ_in, κ_(2,3)); requires strongly correlated inhomogeneous optical broadening and negligible ground-state spin dephasing during the protocol.
items.tools: Pre-created Long-lived Macroscopic (PLM) spin coherence · Dual-mode optical cavity · Rare-earth-ion-doped crystals · Spectrally nonlocal impedance matching · Heisenberg-Langevin input-output formalism
items.caption: Panel (a) shows the 5-level rare-earth ion level scheme and the optical/RF pulse timing sequence. Panel (b) shows the crystal inside a dual-mode optical resonator controlled by an RF coil.
items.abstract: Quantum information processing requires efficient storage and manipulation of photonic states.Here, we advance a cavity-assisted quantum memory protocol based on Pre-created Long-lived Macroscopic (PLM) coherence, thereby transforming quantum memory from a passive storage device into a platform for deterministic in-memory photonic processing. It is demonstrated that spin PLM coherence enables all-optical control of quantum memory using robust radio-frequency rotations alone. Here, the spin coherence serves as a distributed coherent quantum bus, which mediates the deterministic synthesis and storage of frequency-bin states through spectrally nonlocal impedance matching. We identify an inherent time-reversal symmetry in the underlying dynamical equations, ensuring unitary evolution of the quantum memory operations. The presented results demonstrate a unified platform for quantum storage and optical signal processing, enabling controlled manipulation of frequency-bin photonic qubits and paving the way for scalable multimode quantum networks based on spectral-encoding architectures.

items.title: Anomalously enhanced lifetimes of low angular momentum Rydberg states in singly charged alkaline-earth metal ions
items.authors: Simon Euchner, Weibin Li, Igor Lesanovsky
items.matched: Quantum information with Rydberg atoms
items.result: Lifetimes of low angular momentum Rydberg P states in singly charged alkaline-earth metal ions are enhanced by factors > 8 relative to Hydrogenic scaling predictions, approaching neutral alkali-metal atom lifetimes. In ⁴⁰Ca⁺, P-state lifetimes are up to ∼20 times higher than S states with the same principal quantum number.
items.question: Do Rydberg states in singly charged alkaline-earth metal ions strictly follow the Hydrogenic scaling law that predicts a 16-fold lifetime reduction compared to neutral alkali-metal atoms?
items.prior: Hydrogenic scaling τ(Z_eff) ∝Z_eff⁻⁴ predicted ionic Rydberg state lifetimes are reduced by a factor of 16 relative to neutral atoms.
items.limits: Calculations assume single active valence electron in parametric model potentials within the dipole approximation, tested for n = 20 to 80 at T = 0 K and T = 300 K.
items.tools: Parametric model potentials · AlkCalc single-electron Hamiltonian diagonalisation · Einstein-A radiative rate calculations · Black-body radiation transition model
items.caption: Computed Rydberg S and P state lifetimes of ⁸⁵Rb and ⁸⁸Sr⁺ alongside their ratio versus principal quantum number n at T=0 K and T=300 K, showing deviation of P states from the predicted Hydrogenic scaling ratio of 16.
items.abstract: Trapped ions excited to high-lying electronic states, so-called Rydberg states, open new opportunities for quantum simulation and quantum computing. Generally, the fidelity of quantum coherent operations critically depends on the longevity of Rydberg states. However, scaling laws predict that the lifetimes of Rydberg states in singly charged alkaline-earth metal ions are 16 times shorter, compared to their neutral atom counterparts. Here, we show that this is not generally the case. We report an anomalous lifetime enhancement of certain low angular momentum ionic Rydberg series by factors larger than eight. The anomaly is present at both zero and finite temperature, although it is caused by different mechanisms. At zero temperature, the anomalously enhanced lifetimes are caused by accidental cancellations of the relevant dipole transition matrix elements, while at room temperature the anomaly originates from the enlarged energetic separation of ionic Rydberg levels with respect to neutral-atom levels.

items.title: Quantum Mpemba effect from Stark localization
items.authors: Nico Albert, Masudul Haque, Shovan Dutta
items.matched: Quantum information with Rydberg atoms
items.result: Combining Wannier-Stark localization with local dissipative hopping induces a quantum Mpemba effect where localized single-particle lifetimes scale super-exponentially as τ_j≈1/(γ)[(j-2)!]²(Δ/J)^(2(j-2)) for γ≪Δ.
items.question: How can an energy landscape with local dissipation be designed in a quantum system to produce an anomalous relaxation hierarchy analogous to the classical Mpemba effect?
items.limits: Strong-localization regime J/Δlesssim1, local Markovian jump dissipation restricted to an isolated boundary site.
items.tools: Wannier-Stark localization · Lindblad master equation · Quantum trajectory unraveling · Padé interpolation perturbation theory
items.caption: Energy versus time for states initialized at different lattice sites j, showing faster relaxation for higher-energy states near the dissipative site, alongside quantum jump trajectories and perturbation-theory timescale predictions.
items.abstract: In classical systems, rugged potential energy landscapes provide a transparent mechanism for the celebrated Mpemba effect, in which hotter initial states cool down faster. This picture generally does not survive in quantum systems. Here we show how to design a quantum energy landscape with local dissipation leading to an Mpemba effect with parametrically separated timescales. Our approach uses Stark localization to design an energy landscape and localized incoherent hopping as cooling mechanism. The hops are triggered by rare "detection" events whose rate grows with energy, allowing hotter states to cool faster and producing super-exponentially separated cooling rates for localized initial states. We further show that the effect is dramatically enhanced by collective hopping of bound pairs in the presence of attractive on-site interactions. These findings have clear experimental signatures accessible in present-day setups.

items.authors: Karen Mamian, Georgy A. Kazakov, Thorsten Schumm, Charles Roques-Carmes

Instability is minimized when collective cooperativity C_N = 1 in the low-saturation limit and C_(N,opt) = 1 + 4Ω²/(6γγ_⊥) under saturation.
items.question: How can collective cavity quantum electrodynamics overcome the mismatch between short nuclear coherence time and long radiative lifetime in solid-state ²²⁹Th clocks?

items.abstract: Solid-state frequency standards are generally limited by strong decoherence, rendering conventional interrogation schemes inefficient. The ²²⁹Th nuclear clock provides a unique and timely platform for solid-state optical metrology and nuclear cavity quantum electrodynamics (QED), featuring a coherence time many orders of magnitude shorter than the radiative lifetime in current experiments. Here, we propose and analyze three cavity QED-enhanced clock interrogation schemes that turn this timescale mismatch into an advantage, leveraging collective coupling of thorium nuclei to nanophotonic modes to enable fast interrogation and detection despite the long population lifetime. We reveal the central role of collective cooperativity in determining the clock frequency instability, and derive the optimal conditions (power, working-point detuning, thorium density) for clock operation.

items.title: Nonequilibrium energy transport and fluctuations in two-photon-driven nonlinear quantum optical systems
items.authors: Y. T. Chen, Y. W. Lu, J. C. Lu, C. Wang
items.matched: Quantum information with Rydberg atoms
items.result: Two-photon driving strongly enhances the drive input energy current and signal-to-noise ratio via multiphoton resonances ω_d^((m)) ≃ω₀ + (2m-1)U, substantially modifying non-Gaussian higher-order current cumulants compared to single-photon driving.
items.question: How two-photon driving reorganizes nonlinear dressed-state transitions to control nonequilibrium average energy current and higher-order current fluctuations in open quantum optical systems.
items.limits: Weak-driving regime, low-energy three-state approximation, Ohmic spectral density.
items.tools: rotating-frame driven quantum master equation · full counting statistics · dressed-state eigenbasis expansion
items.caption: Drive input energy current log₁₀(J_P), second-order fluctuations log₁₀(J⁽²⁾_l), and signal-to-noise ratio S_l versus drive frequency ω_d, showing enhancement when two-photon loss is added to single-photon dissipation.
items.abstract: Understanding nonequilibrium transport and fluctuations driven by nonclassical light in nonlinear quantum optical systems is challenging. Here, we formulate a driven quantum master equation in the rotating frame combined with full counting statistics, retaining the drive-induced frequency shifts in the system-reservoir interactions and providing a unified description of drive-assisted incoherent transitions based on the rotated system dressed-basis. Applied to a Kerr resonator and a nonlinear Jaynes-Cummings model, the approach reveals pronounced multiphoton-resonant enhancement of the drive input energy current, with significant high peaks under two-photon driving compared to the single-photon case. The two-photon resonance relations are analytically obtained. Resonance structure in the nonlinear Jaynes-Cummings model nonlinearly relies on qubit-photon couplings, with additional dressed-state branches. A low-energy-state approximation attributes the resonant current enhancement to dressed-state hybridization and efficient activation of incoherent energy exchange processes. Beyond the average current, two-photon-driving induced energy exchange picture near resonance also substantially modifies the second-order current fluctuation and higher-order current cumulant, while increasing the time-normalized signal-to-noise ratio. Adding two-photon loss introduces extra incoherent photon-pair exchange pathways and further reshapes the current and its fluctuations. We hope these results may deepen interpretation of photon driving and quantum dissipation cooperatively governing nonequilibrium energy transport and fluctuations.

items.title: Gaussian quantum reservoir computing with a hybrid cavity magnomechanical system
items.authors: Hajar Assil, Khadija El Anouz, Abderrahim El Allati, Gian Luca Giorgi
items.matched: photonic qubits, linear-optical computing and boson sampling
items.result: A 4-mode hybrid cavity magnomechanical system operated in the linearized Gaussian regime enables quantum reservoir computing and delayed signal reconstruction using quadrature fluctuation covariance features. For finite measurement budgets (N_m = 10¹⁰ shots), intermediate encoding strength ε_Δ minimizes reconstruction error.
items.question: Can a hybrid cavity magnomechanical platform act as a continuous-variable Gaussian quantum reservoir computer when driven through an auxiliary-cavity detuning port?
items.limits: Linearized Gaussian regime at T = 50mK; offline state tomography without continuous-measurement back-action; numerical simulation.
items.tools: quantum Langevin equations · covariance matrix feature extraction · ridge regression linear readout · Wishart finite-sampling statistics
items.caption: Delayed signal reconstruction NMSE plotted against delay τ and encoding strength ε_Δ / 2π across finite measurement counts N_m = 10⁴ to 10¹⁰ versus ideal limit N_m →∞, revealing a statistical trade-off minimum in reconstruction error.
items.abstract: We propose a quantum reservoir computing framework based on a hybrid cavity magnomechanical system in the linearized Gaussian regime. The reservoir combines microwave-cavity, magnon, and mechanical degrees of freedom, and is extended by an auxiliary cavity acting as an input port, with time-dependent signals encoded in its detuning. The covariance matrix of the quadrature fluctuations provides the features for a trained linear readout. Using linear-memory, nonlinearmemory, and parity-check benchmarks, we find strong temporal memory together with more limited nonlinear processing, whose balance is controlled by the reservoir evolution time, and we show that intermode correlations substantially enhance the information accessible to the readout. The same architecture reconstructs a time-dependent signal encoded in the auxiliary-cavity detuning, with an accuracy governed by the interplay between the internal couplings and the encoding strength, and robust against Gaussian detuning noise. Accounting for finite measurement statistics reveals a trade-off between encoding strength and the precision of the covariance estimation, so that the optimal encoding depends on the available measurement budget. These results establish hybrid cavity magnomechanical systems as a promising platform for continuous-variable quantum reservoir computing with potential applications in signal probing.

items.authors: Stefano Carsi
items.matched: cavity QED, atom-photon interfaces and quantum networks
items.result: Twin-beam communication alphabet extended from 2 to 4 states (2 bits per use) using superimposed thermal noise, with record-and-resend attacks detected at 90% probability for attacked fractions f ≈0.10 to 0.40 across block sizes N = 8×10⁴ down to 5×10³.
items.question: Can a twin-beam quantum communication protocol be extended from binary to four-state encoding while retaining eavesdropping detection via the noise reduction factor?
items.prior: Binary hybrid encoding scheme by Razzoli et al. [4] delivering 1 bit per symbol using mean photon number with noise reduction factor R as a security witness.
items.limits: Channel detection efficiency η= 9.0 ±3%; state discrimination on R limited by calibration mismatch and test statistics fluctuations; communication evaluated on bootstrapped blocks from stored datasets rather than live independent transmissions.
items.tools: mesoscopic twin-beam parametric down-conversion source · silicon photomultipliers (SiPMs) · rotating ground-glass diffuser for thermal noise generation · single-arm Fano factor (⟨m⟩, F) threshold decoding and ML classifiers · noise reduction factor eavesdropping monitoring
items.caption: Detection probability of record-and-resend attack versus attacked fraction f across block sizes N = 5×10³, 2×10⁴, and 8×10⁴, compared to a 5% false-alarm baseline.
items.abstract: Twin-beam (TWB) states generated by parametric down-conversion exhibit strong photon-number correlations that can be exploited for quantum communication. In the mesoscopic regime, these correlations can be directly investigated using photon-number-resolving detectors, such as silicon photomultipliers (SiPMs). Their nonclassical nature is quantified by the noise reduction factor (NRF), which provides a witness of quantum correlations and a means of monitoring channel security. In this work, a quantum communication protocol based on TWB states, originally proposed for binary encoding, is extended to a four-state scheme capable of transmitting two bits per use. Information is encoded by combining two mean photon-number values and two mode numbers of thermal noise superimposed on one arm of the twin beam, defining four distinguishable states in the (m,R) plane. While the mean detected photon number enables the retrieval of one bit, the NRF provides discrimination of the second bit and a security check against intercept-and-resend attacks, which introduce additional noise and degrade the quantum correlations. The protocol is investigated through two experimental measurement campaigns. First, the twin-beam source is characterized in terms of photon-number statistics, NRF, and detection efficiency to establish the operating conditions of the communication channel. Subsequently, the four-state protocol is implemented and evaluated through the analysis of state distributions and their 95% confidence regions, error probability as a function of sample size, and a comparative assessment of machine learning classifiers for state discrimination. Finally, the response of the NRF to an intercept-and-resend attack is investigated to assess the protocol's ability to detect eavesdropping.

items.title: Modular fault-tolerant quantum computing on a non-CSS code
items.authors: Robert Freund, Friederike Butt, César Benito, Ivan Pogorelov, Marcel Meyer, Alex Steiner, Alejandro Bermudez, Markus Müller, Thomas Monz
items.matched: High-threshold and low-overhead fault-tolerant quantum memory
items.result: Realized complete set of modular fault-tolerant logical operations for the non-CSS [[5,1,3]] code on a 16-qubit trapped-ion processor, including state teleportation, QEC with real-time feedback, and magic-state injection yielding 85±8 % average gate fidelity for a logical T gate.
items.question: Can universal modular fault-tolerant quantum operations, including inter-register state teleportation and non-Clifford gate injection, be realized experimentally on a compact non-CSS quantum error-correcting code?
items.prior: Logical teleportation and lattice-surgery primitives had previously been demonstrated only on topological Calderbank–Shor–Steane (CSS) codes (such as surface and color codes).
items.limits: State preparation uses postselection on syndrome verification flags; SPAM-error removal method requires trace-preserving noise channels and is restricted to operations without error-detection postselection.
items.tools: 16-qubit linear Paul trap (⁴⁰Ca⁺ ions) · non-CSS $[[5, 1, 3]]$ code · real-time mid-circuit measurement and feedback · logical Pauli process tomography
items.caption: Magic-state preparation circuit and quantum process tomography of the non-Clifford logical T gate injection, showing reconstructed logical Pauli transfer matrix elements and process fidelity.
items.abstract: Modularization promises to break down the design and implementation complexity of large scale quantum processors into smaller manageable subtasks. In this approach, quantum channels, realized for instance through physical rerouting of qubits or quantum teleportation, connect multiple modules. Each of those modules hosts a subset of qubits, e.g. multiple logical qubits, and provides quantum operations on them. In this work, we implement for the first time all logical operations required for modular fault-tolerant universal quantum computing with a non-Calderbank-Shor-Steane (CSS) code, the perfect $[[5, 1, 3]]$ code, on a trapped-ion quantum computer. This code is the smallest quantum error-correcting (QEC) code capable of correcting any single-qubit error, making it a compact alternative to larger CSS codes. We demonstrate logical state teleportation and a full suite of fault-tolerant operations required for universal logical control, including logical state preparation, QEC with real-time feedback, logical measurements, magic-state preparation, logical entangling operations, and magic-state injection. Moreover, we characterize the logical spectator error picked up by idling logical qubits during quantum operations on distinct qubit registers and demonstrate a logical Pauli quantum process tomography that minimizes required sampling resources for logical tomography.

items.title: Flow-Based Lattice Surgery Optimization with Runtime T Gate Scheduling
items.authors: Raymond Iacobacci, Tianyi Hao, Neer Patel, Siyuan Niu
items.matched: lattice surgery, logical qubit layout and compilation to a fault-tolerant instr…
items.result: Jointly compiles Clifford routing via maximum-flow and runtime magic state cultivation in a 3D topological pipe diagram, cutting spacetime volume by 2.3× (geometric mean) and running 10.8× faster than TopoLS under free magic states, and cutting volume by 2.3× at code distance d=13 relative to PureMagic.
items.question: How can topological lattice surgery compilation simultaneously embed full circuit layers of Clifford operations and account for stochastic, in-place magic state cultivation in a single 3D representation?
items.prior: TopoLS routes Clifford gates sequentially or via MCTS order search while omitting magic state preparation footprints; PureMagic schedules cultivation on a 2D layout with per-instruction path search.
items.limits: Evaluated on rotated surface codes with distances d=11, 13, 15; volume advantage drops to 1.6× at d=15 where expected cultivation time rises to 5.5 logical cycles.
items.tools: ZX-calculus · 3D topological pipe diagrams · Maximum-flow formulation · Magic state cultivation (MSC) · Runtime delay mechanisms
items.caption: Execution latency per logical cycle compared between PureMagic and FlowRouter across circuit benchmarks, showing runtime dispatch speed relative to surface code cycle times.
items.abstract: Lattice surgery on the surface code is a leading route to fault-tolerant quantum computation. Compiling logical circuits into lattice surgery operations is a pivotal step that determines the resource cost of a computation. Prior compilers build on idealized assumptions, and one that works in practical settings remains to be developed. Existing works are either unscalable or route one gate at a time within a layer, so the embedding depends on the order of gates and opportunities to route many gates at once are lost. In addition, they assume magic states are always available and cost-free, even though preparing one costs more than a Clifford operation. We present FlowRouter, the first topological lattice surgery compiler that places Clifford routing and stochastic magic state cultivation inside a single 3D embedding. At compile time, FlowRouter formulates the routing of an entire circuit layer as a maximum-flow problem, embedding many gates simultaneously. At runtime, it allows magic states to be cultivated at every idling patch, works with the realistic cultivation process with multiplexing and multi-stage post-selections, and absorbs the stochasticity by introducing delay mechanisms that add as little spacetime volume as possible. With magic states assumed free, FlowRouter reduces spacetime volume by 2.3x and compiles 10.8x faster than the state-of-the-art static topological lattice surgery compiler. With the cultivation-aware setting that includes both Clifford and magic state cost, FlowRouter reduces spacetime volume by 2.3x on a distance-13 surface code when compared with the state-of-the-art runtime compiler.

items.abstract: For a general entanglement-assisted or unassisted quantum error-correcting code, a set of erasures, and an associated repair group, we propose a linear algebraic procedure to compute a reduced set of observables and a reduced repair group of codeword qudits for correcting the given erasures. The procedure has cubic complexity in the repair group size and the computed set of observables has the smallest possible size for correcting the given erasures. We specialize the general procedure to quantum codes constructed from Euclidean and Hermitian orthogonality, and provide closed-form upper bounds on the size of reduced repair groups for those special cases. Based on these closed-form bounds, we propose quantum counterparts of the information locality of classical local recovery.

items.title: A thermal microwave bus for neutral atom quantum computing
items.authors: Matthew J. H. Kendall, Christopher J. Watson, Michael Ben Shem, Jonathan D. Breeze

items.question: Can microwave cavity-mediated entangling gates overcome the shuttling-time bottleneck and thermal sensitivity in neutral-atom arrays at finite cryogenic temperatures?
items.prior: was 0.76 for optical cavity deterministic CZ gates (Steiner 2023)
items.limits: Numerical open-system simulations of up to 4 atoms, analytical Magnus-expansion bounds, requires cryogenic temperatures (T lesssim1K) and high-Q cavity (Q > 10⁹).
items.tools: 3D re-entrant microwave cavity · Open quantum system Lindblad simulations · Schrieffer-Wolff perturbation theory · Optical tweezer array

items.abstract: High-fidelity two-qubit gates in neutral-atom arrays rely on the Rydberg blockade, which is intrinsically short ranged and requires long range connectivity to be achieved through atom shuttling. We propose a four level architecture, where the typical ground state qubit can be leveraged for its long lifetime and the Rydberg states couple to a microwave cavity, allowing for long range cavity mediated gates. We first find the thermal dependence of two established protocols, the dispersive iSWAP native to the Tavis-Cummings model and the Controlled phase gate generated from driving the cavity. We simulate them under the presence of Rydberg decay, thermal photons, finite cavity linewidth and find fidelities which accompany closed form bounds. We then introduce the bichromatic Raman gate, which only virtually populates the Rydberg states and cancels dispersive shifts to mitigate both atomic and cavity decay, achieving a fidelity of F = 0.997. Finally, we consider a full optical tweezer array in a microwave cavity, and show that using a cavity mediated gate to close the periodic boundaries of the toric code shortens an error correction round by a factor of 2.3 for realistic array sizes. This was then applied to the wider family of Bivariate bicycle codes, and we find that it shortens a round of the gross code by a factor of 4.8.

items.title: Metric Self-Dual Completion and Optimal Additive Hardness for Quantum and Graph-State Distance
items.authors: Rafail Ostrovsky
items.matched: How to factor 2048 bit RSA integers in 8 hours using 20 million noisy qubits
items.result: NP-hard to approximate quantum code distance and graph-state distance within additive error $c N$ for constant c>0, via deterministic reductions.
items.question: Does quantum-code distance or graph-state distance admit a linear additive hardness gap under deterministic reductions?
items.prior: Additive hardness gap was N^(1/2) for quantum code distance (Kapshikar and Kundu 2023; Grigorescu et al. 2024) and N^(1/3) for graph-state distance (Grigorescu et al. 2024).
items.limits: CSS codes with identical X- and Z-check spaces, constant rate, and constant relative distance. Does not establish hardness for quantum LDPC codes.
items.tools: Metric self-dual completion · Prefix-sum construction · Deterministic Karp reductions · Dual-good to self-dual conversion
items.abstract: We prove that the quantum code distance is NP-hard to approximate within an additive error of $c N$, for some constant c >0, where N is the number of qubits. Our reductions are deterministic. This improves the previous square-root additive gap to Ω(N) and resolves the explicitly stated linear-gap question of Kapshikar and Kundu. Our result holds for CSS codes with identical X- and Z-check spaces, and with a constant rate and constant relative distance. For every fixed λ>1, there is a constant c>0 such that hardness still holds even when every nonidentity stabilizer has weight greater than λ times the quantum distance. We also improve the hardness gap of graph state distance on N vertices of Grigorescu, Jha, and Samperton from cube-root to Ω(N), resolving their explicitly stated open question. Both hardness results are asymptotically optimal since both distances are at most N. Our graph state distance hardness result holds for balanced bipartite graphs with a binary adjacency matrix that is its own inverse (mod 2). Our main technique for both hardness bounds above is classical: we show how to convert any code C of length m into a self-dual code A(C) of length N=Θ(m) while exactly doubling the original coset metric. The conversion is deterministic and efficient. We call it the metric self-dual completion of C. It comes with a linear embedding τ: F₂^m hookrightarrowF₂^N. The embedding doubles all Hamming distances between vectors in F₂^m and all pairwise distances between corresponding cosets. The embedding also guarantees that all codewords of A(C) of weight at most 2m are exactly τ(C).

items.abstract: Recently, a hybrid qudit-qubit algorithm [1] was presented for solving the integer programming problem with a polynomial quantum advantage. In this work, we investigate the algorithm [1] to understand the role of qudits (d-dimensional quantum system) by conducting a comparative resource analysis with its qubit-only implementation and the classical simulability of the algorithm by exploring the entanglement structure. The resource analysis part is performed in terms of logical gate counts, and fault-tolerant physical resources, including non-Clifford gates. The hybrid qudit-qubit implementation has a more compact structure of the unitary operators as opposed to its qubit-only simulation which reduces the logical and fault-tolerant resource requirements. Two example problems, one with qutrits (d=3) and the other with ququint (d=5), when contrasted with their qubit-only implementation, within a simplified fault-tolerant resource model, showed ∼180 × and ∼2220× fewer total resource count, respectively. For the entanglement study, volume-law-like entropy growth and signatures of multi-partite entanglement is observed leading to increasing difficulty in the classical simulation of the algorithm. The algorithm generates synergistic tri-partite entanglement even for a quadratic problem, revealing that the algorithmic structure itself can generate higher-order entanglement in the system independent of the problem.

items.question: How can universal quantum computation and the Gottesman-Knill theorem be formulated for Bose-Einstein condensate (BEC) qubit systems spanning (N+1)-dimensional SU(2) representations?
