items.abstract: Quantum computing promises to outperform classical computing for certain computational tasks. One of the key concepts underlying this potential is universality. Universality has been extensively studied not only for qubits but also for higher-dimensional quantum systems, such as qutrits and qudits, which span Hilbert spaces of dimension greater than two. However, the concept of universality in Bose-Einstein condensates (BECs) qubit systems, which have been proposed relatively recently, remains insufficiently understood. In this work, we analyzed universality in BECs qubit systems. Our results clarify the theoretical aspects of universality in quantum computation within the class of ((N+1))-dimensional representations of SU(2), taking into account two distinct representations of the quantum states.

items.title: A Near-Optimal Joint Lower Bound for Sparse Quantum Linear System Solvers
items.authors: Dhrumil Patel
items.matched: Quantum Algorithm for Linear Systems of Equations
items.result: Proves the query complexity lower bound Ω(κ√slog(1/ε)) for quantum linear system solvers in the sparse-access model, capturing condition number κ, sparsity s, and precision ε simultaneously.
items.question: What is the joint query complexity lower bound for quantum linear system solvers as a function of condition number, sparsity, and precision in the sparse-access model?
items.prior: Was Ω(κlog(1/ε)) across κ,ε (Harrow & Kothari / somma et al.) and Ω(κ√s) for constant ε (Mori et al. 2026).
items.limits: Holds in the standard sparse-matrix oracle access model for real, symmetric, but indefinite input matrices; requires κ≥31 and s≥5.
items.tools: Position-Parity Boolean problem · negative-weight adversary method · Lee-Roland XOR lemma · linear system state reduction
items.abstract: Quantum linear system solvers form one of the central algorithmic primitives in quantum computing, with applications ranging from differential equations and optimization to machine learning. Their cost is commonly measured through query complexity, which counts the number of oracle calls needed to access the input matrix. In the sparse-access model, this complexity is governed by three parameters: the condition number κ, the sparsity s of the input matrix, and the target precision ε. The dependence on κ and ε is already well understood through the lower bound Ω(κlog(1/ε)), which matches the best known scaling in these parameters. Once the sparsity s is included, however, the expected lower bound has long been conjectured to be Ω(κ√slog(1/ε)). Recent work by Mori et al. [Quantum Sci. Tech. 11 035063 (2026)] made an important step towards this goal by establishing the lower bound Ω(κ√s) for constant error ε. In this work, we complete the picture and prove the full joint lower bound Ω(κ√slog(1/ε)) in the sparse-access model, thereby establishing the anticipated dependence on all three parameters simultaneously.

items.title: Quantum Computing Solution of the Bethe-Salpeter Equation for Relativistic Scalar Bound States via Tensor-Network VQE
items.authors: Gerhard Hellstern
items.matched: Toward the first quantum simulation with quantum speedup
items.result: Discretized Euclidean O(4) ladder Bethe-Salpeter equation mapped to n qubits yields maximum von Neumann entanglement entropy S_vN^max ∈[0.544, 0.568] bits across N=16 to 128 (n=4 to 7), proving the system is classically tractable with bond dimension χ=2 achieving ≥99% MPS fidelity.
items.question: Can the homogeneous Bethe-Salpeter equation for relativistic two-body bound states be formulated and solved efficiently using gate-based VQE with tensor-network ansätze?
items.limits: Scalar ladder approximation in Euclidean space with O(4) single S-wave channel; numerical simulations up to n=7 qubits (N=128) without physical quantum processor noise.
items.tools: Wick rotation to Euclidean space · O(4) S-wave partial-wave projection · Gauss-Legendre discretization · Pauli decomposition · Matrix Product State (MPS) VQE
items.caption: Plots maximum von Neumann entanglement entropy S_vN^max against N, Schmidt weight decay, and cumulative fidelity vs bond dimension χ, demonstrating that χ=2 provides ≥99% state fidelity across all tested discretization sizes.
items.abstract: We present a gate-based quantum computing solution of the homogeneous Bethe-Salpeter equation (hBSE) for the bound state of two massive relativistic scalar particles interacting via ladder-approximation scalar exchange. After Wick rotation to Euclidean space and O(4) S-wave partial-wave projection, the hBSE is reduced to a symmetric matrix eigenvalue problem of dimension N = 2^n. We decompose the resulting Hamiltonian into a sum of n-qubit Pauli operators and solve it with the Variational Quantum Eigensolver (VQE) using a Matrix Product State (MPS) tensor-network ansatz. For N=16 (n=4 qubits), the VQE recovers the maximum eigenvalue - which encodes the minimum coupling constant for binding - to better than 1 % mean relative error compared to classical diagonalization. Entanglement analysis of the BSE amplitude shows low, area-law-like entanglement over the tested sizes, which motivates the MPS ansatz. A critical analysis of three independent barriers - exponential Pauli overhead, approximately size-independent low entanglement, and decreasing VQE gradient scales for the tested ansatz, consistent with generic barren-plateau concerns at larger n - reveals that the specific problem studied here lies in a classically tractable regime: over the tested range it is well described by low-bond-dimension tensor networks and efficiently handled by MPS/Lanczos methods. This negative result provides, to our knowledge, the first entanglement quantification of the BSE amplitude in qubit encoding, establishes the Pauli Hamiltonian framework for future BSE variants, and identifies 2D Minkowski-space BSE, N-body bound states, and non-ladder kernels as physically motivated extensions where genuine quantum advantage may become plausible.

items.title: Zero-Knowledge Proofs of Quantumness
items.authors: Duong Hieu Phan, Weiqiang Wen, Xingyu Yan, Jinwei Zheng
items.matched: dequantization and classical algorithms that match quantum claims
items.result: Zero-knowledge proofs of quantumness prevent classical verifiers from extracting computational advantage or problem solutions from quantum provers by adding an extractable non-interactive zero-knowledge argument to the verifier's challenge.
items.question: How can a quantum prover demonstrate quantum capability to a classical verifier without allowing a malicious verifier to solve hard problem instances?
items.limits: Relies on the post-quantum hardness of the learning with errors problem and standard common reference string setup for NIZK.
items.tools: extractable non-interactive zero-knowledge (NIZK) · learning with errors (LWE) · trapdoor claw-free (TCF) functions · Shor factoring
items.caption: Schematic comparing real interaction between a quantum prover and classical verifier with a probabilistic polynomial-time classical simulator interacting with the same verifier.
items.abstract: With the rapid development of quantum computers, proofs of quantumness have recently become an interesting research direction. However, in current schemes for proofs of quantumness, quantum provers face the risk of being maliciously exploited by classical verifiers. Through malicious strategies in interaction with quantum provers, classical verifiers could solve some instances of hard problems that arise from the specific scheme in use. This is due to the lack of formalization that prevents malicious verifiers from extracting useful information in proofs of quantumness. To address this issue, we formalize zero-knowledge proofs of quantumness. Intuitively, the zero-knowledge property necessitates that the information gained by the classical verifier from interactions with the quantum prover should not surpass what can be simulated using a simulated classical prover interacting with the same verifier. As a result, the new zero-knowledge notion can prevent a malicious verifier from exploiting quantum advantage. We find that the classical zero-knowledge proof is sufficient to compile some existing proofs of quantumness schemes into zero-knowledge proofs of quantumness schemes. It appears to be more general to require zero-knowledge proof on the verifier side instead of the prover side. This helps to regulate the verifier's behavior from malicious to be honest-but-curious. As a result, both parties will play not only one role in the proofs of quantumness but also the dual role in the classical zero-knowledge proof. Specifically, Shor's factoring-based scheme and the learning with errors-based scheme in [Brakerski et al., FOCS, 2018] can be transformed into zero-knowledge proofs of quantumness by requiring an extractable non-interactive zero-knowledge argument on the verifier side. Zero-knowledge proofs of quantumness can thus be viewed as an enhanced security notion for proofs of quantumness.

items.title: Modular fault-tolerant quantum computing on a non-CSS code
items.authors: Robert Freund, Friederike Butt, César Benito, Ivan Pogorelov, Marcel Meyer, Alex Steiner, Alejandro Bermudez, Markus Müller, Thomas Monz
items.matched: Toward the first quantum simulation with quantum speedup
items.result: Realized complete set of modular fault-tolerant logical operations for the non-CSS [[5,1,3]] code on a 16-qubit trapped-ion processor, including state teleportation, QEC with real-time feedback, and magic-state injection yielding 85±8 % average gate fidelity for a logical T gate.
items.question: Can universal modular fault-tolerant quantum operations, including inter-register state teleportation and non-Clifford gate injection, be realized experimentally on a compact non-CSS quantum error-correcting code?
items.prior: Logical teleportation and lattice-surgery primitives had previously been demonstrated only on topological Calderbank–Shor–Steane (CSS) codes (such as surface and color codes).
items.limits: State preparation uses postselection on syndrome verification flags; SPAM-error removal method requires trace-preserving noise channels and is restricted to operations without error-detection postselection.
items.tools: 16-qubit linear Paul trap (⁴⁰Ca⁺ ions) · non-CSS $[[5, 1, 3]]$ code · real-time mid-circuit measurement and feedback · logical Pauli process tomography
items.caption: Magic-state preparation circuit and quantum process tomography of the non-Clifford logical T gate injection, showing reconstructed logical Pauli transfer matrix elements and process fidelity.
items.abstract: Modularization promises to break down the design and implementation complexity of large scale quantum processors into smaller manageable subtasks. In this approach, quantum channels, realized for instance through physical rerouting of qubits or quantum teleportation, connect multiple modules. Each of those modules hosts a subset of qubits, e.g. multiple logical qubits, and provides quantum operations on them. In this work, we implement for the first time all logical operations required for modular fault-tolerant universal quantum computing with a non-Calderbank-Shor-Steane (CSS) code, the perfect $[[5, 1, 3]]$ code, on a trapped-ion quantum computer. This code is the smallest quantum error-correcting (QEC) code capable of correcting any single-qubit error, making it a compact alternative to larger CSS codes. We demonstrate logical state teleportation and a full suite of fault-tolerant operations required for universal logical control, including logical state preparation, QEC with real-time feedback, logical measurements, magic-state preparation, logical entangling operations, and magic-state injection. Moreover, we characterize the logical spectator error picked up by idling logical qubits during quantum operations on distinct qubit registers and demonstrate a logical Pauli quantum process tomography that minimizes required sampling resources for logical tomography.

items.title: Near-optimal incoherent tomography of low-rank quantum channels
items.authors: Kean Chen, Aadil Oufkir
items.matched: Hamiltonian Simulation by Qubitization
items.result: Incoherent quantum channel tomography to diamond-norm error ε requires Ω(d₁ d₂ r²/ε²) queries and can be achieved with O(d₁ d₂ r² log(2d₁)/ε²) queries for general channels, or Θ(d₁ d₂ r²/ε²) when non-zero Choi eigenvalues are Ω(d₁/r).
items.question: What is the query complexity of quantum channel tomography under the diamond norm in the incoherent model?
items.prior: Known only for r=1 and r=d₁ d₂; coherent tomography takes Θ(d₁ d₂ r/ε²) for dilation rate τ= r d₂ / d₁ ≥1+Ω(1) and Θ(d₁ d₂ r/ε) for τ=1.
items.limits: Holds for incoherent protocols (no quantum memory across queries, measurements after each query); success probability at least 2/3; d₂ ≥2 and d₁ ≤r d₂.
items.tools: Matrix Multiplicative Weight Update · Haar-random basis measurements · Nyström sandwich estimator · van Trees-type Fisher information bound
items.abstract: We study tomography for quantum channels with input dimension d₁, output dimension d₂, and Kraus rank at most r, to within diamond norm error ε, using adaptive experiments that retain no quantum memory between channel queries. - For quantum channels whose non-zero Choi eigenvalues are bounded below by Ω(d₁/r), we establish optimal query upper and lower bounds Θ(d₁d₂r²/ε²). The upper bound is achieved by a nonadaptive algorithm that uses the estimator from [Surawy-Stepney et al., Quantum (2022)], together with a new diamond-norm analysis. The lower bound applies to arbitrary adaptive incoherent protocols and follows from a new local family of channels and a uniform one-query Fisher-information bound. - For general channels, we establish an upper bound O(d₁d₂r²log(2d₁)/ε²), nearly matching the above lower bound Ω(d₁d₂r²/ε²). To achieve this, we generalize the above nonadaptive algorithm by adapting the input state over O(log(2d₁)) rounds with the Matrix Multiplicative Weight Update algorithm.

items.title: Quantum Computing Solution of the Bethe-Salpeter Equation for Relativistic Scalar Bound States via Tensor-Network VQE
items.authors: Gerhard Hellstern
items.matched: Theory of Trotter Error with Commutator Scaling
items.result: Discretized Euclidean O(4) ladder Bethe-Salpeter equation mapped to n qubits yields maximum von Neumann entanglement entropy S_vN^max ∈[0.544, 0.568] bits across N=16 to 128 (n=4 to 7), proving the system is classically tractable with bond dimension χ=2 achieving ≥99% MPS fidelity.
items.question: Can the homogeneous Bethe-Salpeter equation for relativistic two-body bound states be formulated and solved efficiently using gate-based VQE with tensor-network ansätze?
items.limits: Scalar ladder approximation in Euclidean space with O(4) single S-wave channel; numerical simulations up to n=7 qubits (N=128) without physical quantum processor noise.
items.tools: Wick rotation to Euclidean space · O(4) S-wave partial-wave projection · Gauss-Legendre discretization · Pauli decomposition · Matrix Product State (MPS) VQE
items.caption: Plots maximum von Neumann entanglement entropy S_vN^max against N, Schmidt weight decay, and cumulative fidelity vs bond dimension χ, demonstrating that χ=2 provides ≥99% state fidelity across all tested discretization sizes.
items.abstract: We present a gate-based quantum computing solution of the homogeneous Bethe-Salpeter equation (hBSE) for the bound state of two massive relativistic scalar particles interacting via ladder-approximation scalar exchange. After Wick rotation to Euclidean space and O(4) S-wave partial-wave projection, the hBSE is reduced to a symmetric matrix eigenvalue problem of dimension N = 2^n. We decompose the resulting Hamiltonian into a sum of n-qubit Pauli operators and solve it with the Variational Quantum Eigensolver (VQE) using a Matrix Product State (MPS) tensor-network ansatz. For N=16 (n=4 qubits), the VQE recovers the maximum eigenvalue - which encodes the minimum coupling constant for binding - to better than 1 % mean relative error compared to classical diagonalization. Entanglement analysis of the BSE amplitude shows low, area-law-like entanglement over the tested sizes, which motivates the MPS ansatz. A critical analysis of three independent barriers - exponential Pauli overhead, approximately size-independent low entanglement, and decreasing VQE gradient scales for the tested ansatz, consistent with generic barren-plateau concerns at larger n - reveals that the specific problem studied here lies in a classically tractable regime: over the tested range it is well described by low-bond-dimension tensor networks and efficiently handled by MPS/Lanczos methods. This negative result provides, to our knowledge, the first entanglement quantification of the BSE amplitude in qubit encoding, establishes the Pauli Hamiltonian framework for future BSE variants, and identifies 2D Minkowski-space BSE, N-body bound states, and non-ladder kernels as physically motivated extensions where genuine quantum advantage may become plausible.

items.authors: Genji Fujii

Proves an analogue of Gottesman-Knill theorem for BEC circuits composed of Stokes-Hermite Clifford gates and Fock basis measurements.
items.question: How can universal quantum computation and the Gottesman-Knill theorem be formulated for Bose-Einstein condensate (BEC) qubit systems spanning (N+1)-dimensional SU(2) representations?
items.limits: Excludes distorted Bloch spheres caused by errors. Assumes Fock states can be fully manipulated as qudits without specifying experimental physical implementations.
items.tools: Stokes operators · BEC coherent states · Gottesman-Knill theorem extension · Controlled-Bloch-Sphere Universality (CBSU)
items.abstract: Quantum computing promises to outperform classical computing for certain computational tasks. One of the key concepts underlying this potential is universality. Universality has been extensively studied not only for qubits but also for higher-dimensional quantum systems, such as qutrits and qudits, which span Hilbert spaces of dimension greater than two. However, the concept of universality in Bose-Einstein condensates (BECs) qubit systems, which have been proposed relatively recently, remains insufficiently understood. In this work, we analyzed universality in BECs qubit systems. Our results clarify the theoretical aspects of universality in quantum computation within the class of ((N+1))-dimensional representations of SU(2), taking into account two distinct representations of the quantum states.

items.title: A QSVT-Based Quantum Jacobi Algorithm for Linear Systems with Application to the Poisson Equation
items.authors: Louisa M. Piskol, Thorsten Grahs, Stefan Langer, Oleksandr Kyriienko
items.matched: Probing many-body dynamics on a 51-atom quantum simulator
items.result: QSVT-based quantum Jacobi algorithm solves linear systems using polynomial transformation of a block-encoded operator with constant ancilla overhead and circuit depth scaling linearly with iteration count k.
items.question: Can the classical Jacobi iterative method be implemented on gate-based quantum computers with constant ancilla overhead instead of linear ancilla growth?

items.limits: Iteration matrix M=D⁻¹R must be Hermitian (or normal) to yield matrix polynomials via QSVT; requires efficient state preparation and block encodings.
items.tools: Quantum Singular Value Transformation (QSVT) · Block encodings · Linear combination of unitaries (LCU)
items.caption: Quantum circuit schematic combining three QSVT subroutines via LCU using signal qubit a_s, select ancillae a₁, a₂, and block-encoding ancilla a_M.
items.abstract: Many computational fluid dynamics (CFD) algorithms solve partial differential equations by discretization, resulting in large and sparse systems of linear equations. While iterative methods are widely used to solve these systems classically, most existing quantum linear system solvers target the solution through matrix inversion rather than approximating it using an iterative procedure. In this work, we develop a quantum implementation of the Jacobi method based on quantum singular value transformation (QSVT). By reformulating the Jacobi iteration as a polynomial transformation of a block-encoded operator, the algorithm requires only a constant ancilla overhead with respect to the number of iterations while maintaining a circuit depth that scales linearly with the iteration number. We demonstrate the algorithm for one- and two-dimensional Poisson problems, including the pressure Poisson equation arising in Chorin's projection method for the lid-driven cavity flow. The proposed algorithm provides a promising building block for future quantum implementations of multigrid methods and preconditioning techniques, bringing quantum algorithms closer to established CFD solution strategies.

items.tools: 16-qubit linear Paul trap (⁴⁰Ca⁺ ions) · non-CSS $[[5, 1, 3]]$ code · real-time mid-circuit measurement and feedback · logical Pauli process tomography
items.caption: Magic-state preparation circuit and quantum process tomography of the non-Clifford logical T gate injection, showing reconstructed logical Pauli transfer matrix elements and process fidelity.
items.abstract: Modularization promises to break down the design and implementation complexity of large scale quantum processors into smaller manageable subtasks. In this approach, quantum channels, realized for instance through physical rerouting of qubits or quantum teleportation, connect multiple modules. Each of those modules hosts a subset of qubits, e.g. multiple logical qubits, and provides quantum operations on them. In this work, we implement for the first time all logical operations required for modular fault-tolerant universal quantum computing with a non-Calderbank-Shor-Steane (CSS) code, the perfect $[[5, 1, 3]]$ code, on a trapped-ion quantum computer. This code is the smallest quantum error-correcting (QEC) code capable of correcting any single-qubit error, making it a compact alternative to larger CSS codes. We demonstrate logical state teleportation and a full suite of fault-tolerant operations required for universal logical control, including logical state preparation, QEC with real-time feedback, logical measurements, magic-state preparation, logical entangling operations, and magic-state injection. Moreover, we characterize the logical spectator error picked up by idling logical qubits during quantum operations on distinct qubit registers and demonstrate a logical Pauli quantum process tomography that minimizes required sampling resources for logical tomography.

items.result: Majorana BBGKY closure at the two-particle level with projective positivity purification simulates non-number-conserving and spin dynamics in O(N⁶) time, capturing strong-coupling Hubbard transport and early Kitaev flux motion missed by Hartree-Fock.
items.question: Can a two-particle reduced-density-matrix method formulated in Majorana fermions simulate non-equilibrium dynamics in systems lacking fermion-number conservation?
items.prior: Hartree-Fock (one-particle reduced density matrix) misses strong-coupling dynamics and gauge-correlated flux motion entirely.
items.limits: Scaling O(N⁶). Positivity projection introduces non-unitary effective irreversibility that causes artificial thermalization at late times; post-projection gauge reconstruction degrades when magnetic fields act on multiple sites.
items.tools: Majorana antisymmetrized reduced density matrices · BBGKY hierarchy truncation · three-particle cumulant reconstruction · projective positivity purification · exact diagonalization
items.caption: Evolution of brakethatn_(1,↑) versus time after a quench in a 4-site Hubbard model. Hartree-Fock fails to capture strong-coupling dynamics, while the two-particle method matches exact diagonalization at early times before projection damping sets in.
items.abstract: We introduce a time-dependent two-particle (TP) reduced-density-matrix algorithm for systems of interacting Majorana fermions. We close the BBGKY hierarchy at the two-particle level by reconstructing the three-particle reduced density matrix from lower-order correlations. To stabilize the evolution, we impose a positivity projection on the two-particle density matrix while preserving chosen conserved quantities such as the energy. We benchmark the approach on quenches in the one-dimensional Hubbard model and on flux dynamics in the Kitaev honeycomb model. For the Hubbard quench, TP captures strong-coupling dynamics missed by Hartree--Fock (HF). For the Kitaev quenches, TP accurately reproduces the early-time flux dynamics in several regimes and provides a substantial improvement over HF when two-particle correlations are important. We further show that gauge coherence is essential for flux dynamics. The projection procedure however introduces an effective irreversibility, which affects the long-time dynamics.

items.authors: Ginanjar Utama, Hermawan Kresno Dipojono
items.matched: Probing many-body dynamics on a 51-atom quantum simulator
items.result: Introduced clifford_qc, an open-source Python research toolkit integrating sparse Clifford/Pauli operator algebra, subspace/variational eigensolvers, and shared measurement caching with provenance-tracking and explicit device cost models.
items.question: How can quantum simulation workflows integrate operator algebra, subspace methods, and measurement resource allocation within a consistent, reproducible framework?

items.tools: clifford_qc Python package · Sparse Pauli-word Clifford algebra · Measurement outcome caching · Subspace eigensolvers (QSE, A-CASE, VQE) · Provenance and evidence-gating pipeline
items.caption: Number of compiled measurement settings (left axis, blue) and maximum logical entangling depth per setting (right axis, red) as a function of commuting block size k for two 8-qubit active-space banks. It demonstrates how larger commuting blocks reduce readout settings but increase entangling circuit overhead.
items.abstract: clifford_qc is a Python research toolkit for constructing quantum models, comparing variational and subspace eigensolvers, and estimating measurement resources. A common sparse Pauli algebra connects Hamiltonians, density operators, gates, and candidate-selection observables, while dedicated interfaces handle circuit programs, execution, and statistical estimates. We introduce the representation with a worked gradient example and trace a molecular calculation through reusable model preparation, an independent solve, and optional reference validation. Shared measurement caches reuse outcomes across observables on the same reference state; packed coefficient storage and streaming expose a memory-recomputation tradeoff. Committed small-system benchmarks show how these interfaces support comparisons with explicit accuracy and cost assumptions. Fully commuting measurement reduces the shots needed to certify a fixed first-order energy functional, but entangling-gate time and connectivity can offset the saving or make the protocol inadmissible under illustrative device models. Other studies identify a subspace bias floor that more shots cannot remove, an indeterminate comparison of fermionic encodings across instances, and an approximate-restriction screen whose required comparison fails before sampling. Generated tables, provenance records, and manuscript checks connect the reported claims to their inputs, although evidence labels are not yet validated uniformly. The package supports reproducible method development; these results establish neither hardware performance nor a general simulation speedup.

It demonstrates how larger commuting blocks reduce readout settings but increase entangling circuit overhead.

items.title: Coherence protection of a silicon hole spin qubit with phase-modulated microwave driving
items.authors: Sayyid I. Ibad, Yusuke Sato, Takuma Kuno, Itaru Yanagi, Toshiyuki Mine, Ryuta Tsuchiya, Digh Hisamoto, Hiroyuki Mizuno, Raisei Mizokuchi, Jun Yoneda, Tetsuo Kodera
items.matched: Silicon quantum electronics
items.result: Phase-modulated concatenated continuous driving (CCD) stabilizes Rabi oscillations and extends oscillation decay time for silicon hole spin qubits while maintaining coherent gate control.
items.question: Can low-frequency charge and hyperfine noise in silicon hole spin qubits be suppressed during coherent driving via microwave phase modulation?
items.limits: Subject to low-frequency noise from intrinsic spin-orbit coupling and residual nuclear spins in the silicon substrate.
items.tools: silicon quantum dot hole spin qubit · phase-modulated concatenated continuous driving (CCD) · microwave phase modulation · all-electrical spin-orbit control
items.abstract: Hole spins in silicon quantum dots are a promising platform for quantum computing due to their strong intrinsic spin-orbit coupling (SOC), which enables fast, all-electrical control. However, this coupling also increases their susceptibility to charge noise, thereby limiting coherence times. Moreover, holes in silicon are also affected by hyperfine interactions with residual nuclear spins in the silicon substrate, introducing a non-negligible source of low-frequency noise. Here, we implement a phase-modulated concatenated continuous driving (CCD) technique for hole spin qubits to suppress low-frequency noise through microwave phase modulation. This approach stabilizes Rabi oscillations and extends the oscillation decay time compared to the conventional method. Furthermore, by defining a qubit in the CCD frame, we achieve coherent control while simultaneously protecting the qubit from noise, confirming coherence protection during gate operations. These results demonstrate a viable route toward noise-robust hole spin qubits.

items.result: Superconductor-altermagnet-superconductor junctions engineered into the 2φ-junction regime provide intrinsic charge-noise protection via qubit wavefunction parity while retaining large anharmonicity from coherent double-Cooper-pair tunneling.
items.question: Can altermagnetic Josephson junctions realize programmable non-sinusoidal current-phase relations that combine high coherence with strong anharmonicity in superconducting qubits?
items.prior: Unconventional d-wave superconducting qubits such as flowermon and d-mon enhance anharmonicity via higher CPR harmonics, but operate in the φ-junction regime and suffer from quasiparticle and charge noise.
items.limits: Short-junction limit (L ≪ξ₀); symmetric junction design for the flux-tunable SQUID; single- and double-Cooper-pair harmonics retained.
items.tools: Furusaki-Tsukada formula · Andreev bound state model · superconductor-altermagnet-superconductor trilayer · SQUID-based transmon architecture
items.caption: Transition frequency, anharmonicity, transverse charge-noise coupling strength N_DC^Q, and longitudinal flux-noise coupling strength N_DP^Flux plotted versus external flux φ_ext and harmonic ratio η.
items.abstract: Altermagnets, characterized by vanishing net magnetization and momentum-dependent spin splitting, provide a promising platform for next-generation Josephson devices. Here, we exploit the Josephson effect in superconductor-altermagnet-superconductor junctions and show how to engineer prescribed current-phase relations by device design. Based on these programmable Josephson potentials utilizing altermagnetism, we propose a new class of transmon-like superconducting qubits that combine large anharmonicity with enhanced robustness against decoherence via coherent two-Cooper-pair tunneling. We show that in the 2φ-junction regime, this kind of qubit provides intrinsic protection against charge noise due to parity protection. Magnetic flux can be used to precisely control the qubit and, under appropriate bias, this architecture further suppresses charge and flux noise. Our results establish altermagnets as a versatile platform for Josephson-potential engineering and open a new route toward high-performance superconducting qubits combining high coherence, large anharmonicity, and broad tunability.

items.title: Deterministic synthesis and processing of frequency-bin qubits in a macroscopically coherent quantum memory
items.authors: S. A. Moiseev
items.matched: Circuit quantum electrodynamics
items.result: Cavity-assisted quantum memory using pre-created long-lived macroscopic spin coherence synthesizes and stores arbitrary frequency-bin photonic qubits using only RF rotations via spectrally nonlocal impedance matching.
items.question: Can pre-created long-lived macroscopic spin coherence in a cavity-assisted quantum memory be used to deterministically synthesize, store, and process arbitrary frequency-bin photonic states without optical pulse shaping?
items.prior: Extends the single-spin-coherence PLMC protocol (Moiseev 2024), which required optical controls and stored only single-frequency photonic states.
items.limits: Spectral width of input pulse must be much smaller than inhomogeneous absorption linewidth and cavity linewidth (δω_s ≪Δ_in, κ_(2,3)); requires strongly correlated inhomogeneous optical broadening and negligible ground-state spin dephasing during the protocol.
items.tools: Pre-created Long-lived Macroscopic (PLM) spin coherence · Dual-mode optical cavity · Rare-earth-ion-doped crystals · Spectrally nonlocal impedance matching · Heisenberg-Langevin input-output formalism
items.caption: Panel (a) shows the 5-level rare-earth ion level scheme and the optical/RF pulse timing sequence. Panel (b) shows the crystal inside a dual-mode optical resonator controlled by an RF coil.
items.abstract: Quantum information processing requires efficient storage and manipulation of photonic states.Here, we advance a cavity-assisted quantum memory protocol based on Pre-created Long-lived Macroscopic (PLM) coherence, thereby transforming quantum memory from a passive storage device into a platform for deterministic in-memory photonic processing. It is demonstrated that spin PLM coherence enables all-optical control of quantum memory using robust radio-frequency rotations alone. Here, the spin coherence serves as a distributed coherent quantum bus, which mediates the deterministic synthesis and storage of frequency-bin states through spectrally nonlocal impedance matching. We identify an inherent time-reversal symmetry in the underlying dynamical equations, ensuring unitary evolution of the quantum memory operations. The presented results demonstrate a unified platform for quantum storage and optical signal processing, enabling controlled manipulation of frequency-bin photonic qubits and paving the way for scalable multimode quantum networks based on spectral-encoding architectures.

items.title: Nonequilibrium energy transport and fluctuations in two-photon-driven nonlinear quantum optical systems
items.authors: Y. T. Chen, Y. W. Lu, J. C. Lu, C. Wang
items.matched: Charge-insensitive qubit design derived from the Cooper pair box
items.result: Two-photon driving strongly enhances the drive input energy current and signal-to-noise ratio via multiphoton resonances ω_d^((m)) ≃ω₀ + (2m-1)U, substantially modifying non-Gaussian higher-order current cumulants compared to single-photon driving.
items.question: How two-photon driving reorganizes nonlinear dressed-state transitions to control nonequilibrium average energy current and higher-order current fluctuations in open quantum optical systems.
items.limits: Weak-driving regime, low-energy three-state approximation, Ohmic spectral density.
items.tools: rotating-frame driven quantum master equation · full counting statistics · dressed-state eigenbasis expansion
items.caption: Drive input energy current log₁₀(J_P), second-order fluctuations log₁₀(J⁽²⁾_l), and signal-to-noise ratio S_l versus drive frequency ω_d, showing enhancement when two-photon loss is added to single-photon dissipation.
items.abstract: Understanding nonequilibrium transport and fluctuations driven by nonclassical light in nonlinear quantum optical systems is challenging. Here, we formulate a driven quantum master equation in the rotating frame combined with full counting statistics, retaining the drive-induced frequency shifts in the system-reservoir interactions and providing a unified description of drive-assisted incoherent transitions based on the rotated system dressed-basis. Applied to a Kerr resonator and a nonlinear Jaynes-Cummings model, the approach reveals pronounced multiphoton-resonant enhancement of the drive input energy current, with significant high peaks under two-photon driving compared to the single-photon case. The two-photon resonance relations are analytically obtained. Resonance structure in the nonlinear Jaynes-Cummings model nonlinearly relies on qubit-photon couplings, with additional dressed-state branches. A low-energy-state approximation attributes the resonant current enhancement to dressed-state hybridization and efficient activation of incoherent energy exchange processes. Beyond the average current, two-photon-driving induced energy exchange picture near resonance also substantially modifies the second-order current fluctuation and higher-order current cumulant, while increasing the time-normalized signal-to-noise ratio. Adding two-photon loss introduces extra incoherent photon-pair exchange pathways and further reshapes the current and its fluctuations. We hope these results may deepen interpretation of photon driving and quantum dissipation cooperatively governing nonequilibrium energy transport and fluctuations.

items.title: Extracting Electromagnetic Bare Mode Couplings in Large Superconducting Quantum Processors
items.authors: Reza Molavi, Ebrahim Forati, Yaxing Zhang, Andrey R. Klots, Juan Atalaya, Brandon W. Langley, Dogan A. Timucin, Moein Nazari, Ghazi Khan, Zlatko K. Minev, Alexander N. Korotkov, Michel H. Devoret
items.matched: Cavity quantum electrodynamics for superconducting electrical circuits: An arch…
items.result: Avoided-crossing, energy participation ratio (EPR), induced electromotive force (EMF), and impedance-matrix methods extract transmon-to-package bare mode couplings with relative deviation under 5%.
items.question: How can weak electromagnetic couplings between localized transmon qubits and distributed package modes be accurately and efficiently extracted in multi-scale superconducting processor simulations?
items.limits: Numerical full-wave simulations; transmons modeled as linear LC resonators under the rotating-wave approximation; assumes weak coupling to bare modes.
items.tools: 3D electromagnetic solvers · Energy participation ratio (EPR) · Induced EMF method · Impedance matrix synthesis · Avoided-level-crossing analysis
items.caption: Coupling strength g/2 arπ between individual transmons and the fundamental package mode across 25 array positions, comparing avoided crossing, EPR, induced EMF, and impedance matrix techniques.
items.abstract: High-fidelity control of superconducting quantum processors requires accurate characterization of electromagnetic coupling strengths among the device's constituent elements. Accurately extracting these couplings across large-scale architectures, presently featuring hundreds of qubits, poses a challenging multi-scale modeling problem. This requires resolving scales from the nanometer-scale geometry of Josephson junctions and their leads to the centimeter-scale size of the enclosing metallic packages. We present four numerical coupling extraction methods based on the avoided level crossing, the energy participation ratio, the induced electromotive force, and the impedance matrix. These methods are tailored to work with commercially available 3D electromagnetic solvers. We benchmark these techniques on a 10×10 array of transmon qubits, extracting their couplings to standing package modes. Our results show that these methods yield consistent coupling strengths with a maximum relative difference of less than 5%.

items.title: Performance optimization of cascaded traveling wave Josephson parametric amplifiers
items.authors: Ilari Lilja, Ekaterina Mukhanova, Stanislav Khaldeev, Ilya Golokolenov, Visa Vesterinen, Pertti Hakonen
items.matched: Cavity quantum electrodynamics for superconducting electrical circuits: An arch…
items.result: Cascading a 736-element SNAIL-based TWPA and a 1632-element TWPA achieves nearly 30 dB total gain over ~1 GHz bandwidth, with added noise near (1/2)ℏω and a 1 dB compression point of -101 dBm.
items.question: Can low added noise and high gain be achieved simultaneously by cascading two TWPAs, with the first optimized for minimum added noise and the second for high gain?
items.prior: was around 20 dB gain in single TWPAs with comparable noise and compression
items.limits: Requires interstage bandpass filtering to prevent wideband amplified quantum noise and idler tones from saturating the second amplifier stage; gain ripples persist from imperfect interstage impedance matching.
items.tools: SNAIL-based traveling-wave parametric amplifiers · interstage 5–6 GHz bandpass filter · Y-factor method calibration stage · dilution refrigerator
items.caption: Gain versus frequency for individual and simultaneous TWPA operation, gain saturation versus pump power, and gain compression alongside signal-to-noise ratio improvement as a function of probe power at 5.503 GHz.
items.abstract: Traveling-wave parametric amplifiers (TWPAs) based on Josephson metamaterials provide broadband gain with near-quantum-limited added noise. Whereas long nonlinear metamaterial devices can deliver high gain, short arrays suffer less from dissipation, pump depletion, and internal standing waves which can degrade noise performance. Here, we demonstrate a cascaded TWPA architecture that combines the advantages of both approaches by employing a short (736-element), low-dissipation Superconducting Nonlinear Asymmetric Inductive eLement (SNAIL)-based TWPA as the first amplification stage, followed by a conventional long (1632-element) TWPA that provides additional gain. The resulting amplifier cascade achieves nearly 30 dB of total gain over a tunable bandwidth of approximately 1 GHz while maintaining added noise close to the quantum limit. Our results establish a cascade of TWPAs as a practical approach for high-gain, broadband, quantum amplification with applications in quantum information processing, multi-mode entanglement, and quantum sensing applications at microwave frequencies.

items.title: The Superconducting Talbot Effect in Phased-Array Josephson Junctions
items.authors: Hechen Ren, Ziying Li
items.matched: Semiconductor spin qubits
items.result: Proximitized Cooper pairs from periodic superconducting leads produce a real-space Talbot carpet repeating at Z_T = λ_p / (1 - √1 - λ_p² / d²), steerable via inter-lead phase differences Δφ to extract Fermi wavelengths with sub-9% fitting error.
items.question: Can macroscopic quantum near-field diffraction occur for proximitized Cooper pairs in a ballistic 2DEG, and can active phase control map its Fermi surface?
items.limits: Ballistic 2DEG regime; requires sub-wavelength lithographic pitch (d ∼200 nm) and planar junction lengths L lesssim1 μm due to r⁻² power-law decay of induced order parameter.
items.tools: phased-array Josephson junctions · Vernier-scale collector arrays · Kwant tight-binding BdG simulations · Green's function Cooper-pair propagator model
items.caption: Real-space induced superconducting order parameter showing Talbot self-imaging at integer Z_T and inverted patterns at half-integer Z_T for helical and spin-degenerate 2DEGs, with corresponding critical-current oscillations versus pair wavelength λ_p.
items.abstract: We introduce the superconducting Talbot effect---a macroscopic quantum self-imaging phenomenon occurring when proximitized Cooper pairs propagate through a ballistic two-dimensional electron gas. By configuring periodic superconducting leads into a phased-array Josephson junction with programmable phase differences, we demonstrate active steering of the resulting superconducting Talbot carpet. To overcome transport resolution limits, we design a Vernier-scale collector array that performs sub-wavelength sampling of the fractional Talbot pattern. This approach maps real-space quantum interference with high robustness to disorder, enabling direct extraction of Fermi wavelengths across helical, spin-degenerate, and spin-orbit-split Fermi surfaces. Tight-binding numerical calculations on a square lattice validate the real-space interference patterns. Our results establish a versatile framework for coherent wavefront engineering and quantum materials diagnostics in superconducting optics.

items.title: Observation of Kondo Effect in Rhombohedral Graphene Superlattices
items.authors: Xin Liao, Qing Yin, Huiwen Wang, Jing-Wei Dong, Jun-Xi Chen, Si-Li Wu, Cai-Zhen Li, Guowei Lyu, Kenji Watanabe, Takashi Taniguchi, Wei Jiang, Yu-Gui Yao, Zhi-Min Liao
items.matched: Semiconductor spin qubits
items.result: Kondo effect observed in hexalayer rhombohedral graphene moiré superlattices. With increasing magnetic field, longitudinal magnetoresistance transitions from increasing to decreasing across critical field B_c, while Hall resistance R_xy reverses sign near B_c; longitudinal resistance R_xx increases logarithmically as temperature decreases before transitioning to a T² heavy-fermion liquid behavior.
items.question: Can the Kondo effect be realized and tuned via topological flat bands in rhombohedral graphene moiré superlattices?
items.limits: Observed in hexalayer rhombohedral graphene moiré structures under low temperatures and external magnetic and displacement fields.
items.tools: hexalayer rhombohedral graphene moiré superlattice · magneto-transport measurements · temperature-dependent transport measurements · electrostatic gating (carrier density n and displacement field D tuning)
items.abstract: Kondo effect in strongly correlated systems arises from the antiferromagnetic coupling between itinerant conduction electrons and localized magnetic moments, giving rise to a variety of exotic quantum phenomena. Two-dimensional moiré superlattice systems provide a highly tunable platform featuring topological flat bands, where Wannier orbitals are spatially confined by the periodic moiré potential and serve as localized magnetic moments, enabling the observable Kondo effect. Here we experimentally demonstrate Kondo interactions in hexalayer rhombohedral graphene moiré superlattices through magneto-transport and temperature-dependent measurements. With increasing magnetic field, the magnetoresistance exhibits an increase-decrease transition across a critical field B_c, while the Hall resistance R_xy undergoes a sign reversal near B_c. Moreover, as temperature decreases, the longitudinal resistance R_xx first increases logarithmically and then decreases following a T^2 behavior, indicating a transition to heavy fermion liquid. These behaviors can be consistently explained by the breakdown of Kondo singlets induced by either magnetic field or temperature, which liberates carriers previously bound to localized moments, thereby enhancing conductivity and altering the dominant carrier type. Furthermore, our results demonstrate that the Kondo interaction can be continuously tuned by both carrier density n and displacement electric field D, and suggest the emergence of a Kondo insulating state. Our findings provide deep insight into the Kondo effect in moiré engineered flat-band systems, paving the path for exploring exotic correlated quantum phases.

items.title: In-orbit operation of a programmable quantum photonic processor
items.authors: Simon Steiner, Peter Schiansky, Antonius Scherer, Riccardo Albiero, Mathias Dragosits, Zhenghao Yin, Martin Mauser, Patrik Zahálka, Raphael Pimenta, Cristóbal Melo, Cédric Léonard, Abhiram Rajan, Niki Di Giano, Antonino Caime, Roberto Osellame, Francesco Ceccarelli, Daniel Martínez, Tobias Guggemos, Iris Agresti, Philip Walther
items.matched: Quantum information with Rydberg atoms
items.result: Demonstrated an in-orbit programmable quantum photonic processor operating on a nanosatellite, generating and manipulating two-photon states in a six-mode universal integrated circuit and observing two-photon Hong-Ou-Mandel interference.
items.question: Can quantum interference conditions (spectral degeneracy, phase stability, and optical alignment) be established and maintained on a programmable photonic circuit in space?
items.limits: Payload constrained to 10 W average power, 9.8 kg mass, and 15 x 15 x 45.3 cm volume; low-noise coincidence measurements restricted to ~30 min per 92 min orbit during Earth shadow due to sunlight leakage and radiation-induced detector noise.
items.tools: Type-II SPDC in ppKTP crystal · 6x6 reconfigurable universal photonic integrated circuit (uPIC) · Single-photon avalanche photodiodes (SPADs) · Custom FPGA System on a Module (SoM)
items.caption: Normalized two-photon coincidence counts plotted against the ppKTP crystal temperature, showing the characteristic Hong-Ou-Mandel interference dip observed during orbital operation across multiple days.
items.abstract: Quantum technologies promise computational capabilities beyond the reach of classical systems. A forward-looking application lies in satellite missions, which increasingly depend on onboard computing under stringent constraints on size, weight and power. Quantum photonics is particularly attractive here: photon interference can enhance the machine-learning models needed to process large onboard data volumes, at fixed hardware resources. However, harnessing this interference requires more than generating single photons, as they must remain mutually indistinguishable: a fragile condition that is hard to maintain within the technically demanding framework of a space mission, which includes a rocket launch, strong thermal drifts, and radiation. This is why quantum states of light, though already generated and transmitted in orbit for secure communication and fundamental tests, have never been used as a computational resource. Here, we report a programmable quantum photonic platform operating on a nanosatellite, processing two photons in a six-mode universal integrated circuit. By programming distinct unitaries and tuning the photons into indistinguishability, we observe two-photon interference, establishing the on-board generation, manipulation and detection of non-classical light. This extends space-based technologies towards in-orbit quantum-assisted computing, for instance local encoding of Earth-observation data, or nodes in a distributed quantum network.

items.title: Strong coupling of a reconfigurable ¹⁷¹Yb atom array to a tunable telecom-band nanofiber cavity
items.authors: Hideki Ozawa, Neville Chen, Yusuke Hisai, Shunichiro Hashimoto, Kenichi N. Komagata, Remi T. Oddon, Shanjou Yang, Seitaro Horikawa, Seigo Kikura, Shigehito Miki, Takao Aoki, Tadayuki Yoshitake, Hideki Konishi, Shinichi Sunami, Akihisa Goban, Ryotaro Inoue
items.matched: Cavity-based quantum networks with single atoms and optical photons
items.result: Strong atom-cavity coupling on the telecom ³P₀↔³D₁ transition of ¹⁷¹Yb at 1389 nm reaches single-atom internal cooperativity C_in=5.6(1.0) with single-atom coupling strength g/2π=1.86(17) MHz. Collective coupling scales as √N up to N=5 atoms across a ∼200~μm length.
items.question: Can neutral atoms in a reconfigurable tweezer array achieve the single-atom strong-coupling cavity-QED regime directly on a telecom-band transition using a nanofiber cavity?
items.prior: Strong coupling in nanofiber cavities was previously demonstrated only with single trapped alkali atoms at non-telecom wavelengths (e.g. Kato 2015, Goban 2012), while prior telecom atom-cavity interfaces lacked single-atom strong coupling.
items.limits: Operated with single-sided cavity geometry at 1~μm standoff from the nanofiber axis; internal loss rate κ_in/2π=1.28(6) MHz; entanglement rate projection of 40 kHz neglects detector and transmission losses.
items.tools: 550-nm-diameter nanofiber cavity with fiber Bragg gratings · 759-nm optical tweezer array · ¹⁷¹Yb atoms on ³P₀↔³D₁ transition at 1389 nm · cavity reflection spectroscopy
items.caption: Cavity reflection as a function of detuning from the cavity resonance, showing the empty cavity dip (gray) versus vacuum Rabi splitting (purple) induced by a single trapped ¹⁷¹Yb atom positioned 1~μm from the nanofiber axis.
items.abstract: Nanophotonic cavities provide strong atom-photon coupling in a compact, directly fiber-coupled geometry, while a reconfigurable array of ¹⁷¹Yb atoms combines high-fidelity gates with a metastable qubit state coupled directly to a telecom-band transition, making the two a natural interface between neutral-atom quantum processors and telecom quantum networks. Here, we realize strong atom-cavity coupling on the ³P₀ ↔³D₁ transition of ¹⁷¹Yb, establishing, to our knowledge, the first neutral-atom cavity-QED system to reach the single-atom strong-coupling regime on a telecom-band atomic transition. Reflection spectroscopy of a single-sided cavity yields a single-atom internal cooperativity of C_in=5.6(1.0) and collective coupling following √N scaling up to N=5 atoms, with homogeneous coupling at antinodes over ∼200 μm along the nanofiber. Thermal tuning of a fiber Bragg grating provides in situ control of the cavity outcoupling rate over two orders of magnitude from the undercoupled to the overcoupled regime, relevant for various atom-cavity protocols. We confirm compatibility with reconfigurable atom arrays by demonstrating 99.95(6)% imaging fidelity and trap lifetimes comparable to free-space array, at 1 μm from the nanofiber axis. Moreover, the diameter-engineered antireflection design of the nanofiber enables tweezer-based atom transport across the nanofiber with no measurable loss or heating at 4.5 μm above the nanofiber, supporting a two-layer architecture for the nanofiber-integrated atom array. From the demonstrated atom-cavity coupling, atom capacity, and cavity mode profile, we project time-multiplexed remote atom-atom entanglement generation at 40 kHz, with prospects for further scaling through technical enhancements and channel multiplexing.

items.title: Error Suppression in Distributed Quantum Computing with Heterogeneous-Distance Lattice Surgery
items.authors: Daniel Dilley, Anastashia Jebraeilli, Rayat Roy, Shobhit Gupta, Alvin Gonzales, Zain Saleem
items.matched: Cavity-based quantum networks with single atoms and optical photons
items.result: Heterogeneous-distance lattice surgery with an enlarged ancilla (d_A=2d+1) spanning the inter-QPU boundary achieves logical readout error rates nearly independent of link noise, cutting 5-11-5 physical qubit sites by 28.4% compared to uniform distance-9 (373 vs 521 qubits).
items.question: How effectively can additional fault-tolerant error protection be concentrated at a noisy quantum processor interface while preserving the code distance of local data patches?
items.prior: Uniform distance-3 and distance-5 implementations, which exhibit steep increases in logical error rates as link noise grows; at p_link=10⁻², heterogeneous 3-7-3 reduces decoding failure by factors of ≈13 and ≈19 relative to uniform distance-3.
items.limits: Evaluated under circuit-level stochastic depolarizing noise with fixed local noise p_local=10⁻⁴; excludes idle noise, link-generation latency/failures, leakage, and correlated link faults. Requires more total inter-QPU gate applications despite fewer physical sites.
items.tools: Rotated surface codes · 8-DAM (eight-data-patch ancilla-mediated) architecture · Traveling stabilizer syndrome scheduling · Circuit-level Stim simulations
items.caption: Control-X decoding failure probability per CNOT plotted against physical link error probability p_link from 10⁻³ to 10⁻². Heterogeneous 5-11-5 stays nearly flat and matches uniform distance-9 at high link noise while outperforming uniform distance-5 and -7.
items.abstract: Distributed quantum computing requires fault-tolerant operations across inter-QPU links that can be substantially noisier than local gates. Uniformly increasing code distance provides additional protection but also enlarges data patches used for local storage and computation. Here, we introduce distributed heterogeneous-distance lattice surgery using an eight-data-patch ancilla-mediated (8-DAM) architecture, which will be useful for near-term quantum devices with less qubit overhead. In this architecture, the central ancilla spanning the inter-QPU boundary is enlarged while the data patches retain distance d. The protocol uses traveling stabilizers to suppress hook errors during merge and split operations between these unequal-distance patches. Circuit-level simulations of rotated surface codes at fixed local depolarizing noise show that logical-readout error rates depend only weakly on link noise. The resulting advantage over conventional lattice surgery grows as link errors increase. Comparisons with uniform distance implementations demonstrate comparable logical error suppression with reduced physical-qubit overhead. We also demonstrate how 8-DAM layouts support two simultaneous distributed logical CNOT operations between four logical data qubits using a single enlarged ancilla. At higher link noise, this construction yields lower logical error rates and more stability than two independent distributed logical CNOTs. These results support selective ancilla enlargement as a resource-efficient approach to fault-tolerant distributed quantum computing.

items.title: Tensor Network Simulation of Dynamic Circuits
items.authors: Innocenzo Fulginiti, Alessandro Poggiali, Christian Mendl
items.matched: Probing many-body dynamics on a 51-atom quantum simulator
items.result: DMRG-based tensor network simulation natively evaluates dynamic circuits via single-path stochastic sampling and multi-path branch ensemble tracking on MPS and TTN structures, achieving scalable branch propagation with bounded peak memory on 27-qubit random circuits.
items.question: How can tensor-network DMRG algorithms be extended to classically simulate dynamic quantum circuits with mid-circuit measurements and classical feedforward without exponential path overhead?
items.limits: Evaluated up to 27 qubits and depth 8; fixed bond dimensions χ∈8, 16, 32; multi-path branch count capped at M=8.
items.tools: DMRG quantum circuit simulation · Matrix Product States (MPS) · Tree Tensor Networks (TTN) · Single-path stochastic sampling · Multi-path branch pruning
items.caption: Runtime (left) and peak memory usage (right) versus qubit count for dynamic GHZ state preparation comparing unpruned multi-path simulation against single-path sampling with 16, 64, and 256 runs.
items.abstract: Dynamic circuits, which incorporate mid-circuit measurements and classically controlled operations, extend the expressive power of quantum programs and are central to applications such as quantum error correction, state preparation, and distributed quantum algorithms. However, their classical simulation is challenging due to the exponential growth of execution branches induced by mid-circuit measurements. In this work, we develop a tensor network approach for simulating dynamic circuits by extending a DMRG-based method for quantum circuit simulation to support dynamic circuit operations. To address the exponential proliferation of execution branches, we introduce and compare two strategies: a single-path stochastic approach that samples individual measurement outcomes, and a multi-path approach that maintains an ensemble of branches. We benchmark these methods on standard dynamic circuits, including the teleportation protocol and GHZ state preparation, as well as on random dynamic circuits. Our analysis explores the trade-offs between simulation accuracy and computational efficiency. These results provide a practical and scalable framework for the classical simulation of dynamic circuits.

items.title: A Syndrome-Extraction Framework for Distributed Lattice Surgery on Arbitrary Rotated Surface-Code Layouts
items.authors: Pritesh Thakur, Daniel Dilley, Zain Saleem
items.matched: High-threshold and low-overhead fault-tolerant quantum memory
items.result: Seam construction for distributed lattice surgery maintains minimum CNOT depth of 4, achieves fault distance d-1, and delivers lower, more stable logical error rates than alternating or interleaving schedules under link noise swept from 10p to 100p (with bulk noise p = 10⁻⁴).
items.question: How can distributed lattice surgery merge rotated surface-code patches with arbitrary boundaries across noisy inter-module links while avoiding distance-reducing hook errors and minimizing CNOT depth?
items.prior: Prior Bell-measurement lattice surgery achieved a fault distance of 3d/4 under noisy bulk conditions (and standard interleaving schedules required larger qubit overheads and higher CNOT depth).
items.limits: Evaluated via circuit-level numerical simulations under uniform depolarizing noise with fixed bulk error rate p = 10⁻⁴. Requires native three-qubit CXX gates at module seams.
items.tools: Bell-state mediated split ancilla checks · Three-qubit native CXX parity measurements · Algebraic detector annotation · Stim quantum circuit simulator
items.caption: Merged rotated surface-code layout for logical Pauli-XX measurement, showing weight-4 stabilizers at module seams split into paired weight-2 checks mediated across the boundary.
items.abstract: Modular quantum computing is a leading candidate for scalable fault tolerant quantum computation. Performing lattice surgery using surface code patches in different modules requires the use of inter-module gates that are noisier than the local gates. Furthermore, the merged layouts during lattice surgery expose multiple directions in which hook errors can propagate to reduce the fault distance. Existing hook-avoiding schedules either increase the syndrome extraction circuit depth, or let link faults propagate into the bulk. We introduce a seam construction that allows splitting arbitrary merged rotated surface code layout into smaller patches with uniform boundaries that could keep their own hook-avoiding N/Z shaped schedule. At the seam we split weight-4 stabilizers into pairs of weight-2 stabilizers that are mediated through a Bell pair and measured within a CNOT depth of 4. We also employ the use of three-qubit textttCXX gates for parity measurements at the seam to maintain the minimum CNOT depth. Through this seam construction, we confine the elevated link error at the seam, protecting the bulk from higher error rate. We also give a custom detector annotator for such seams that can find the detector space, annotate detectors in the Stim circuits, and ensure that they are suitable to use by matching decoders. We implement our construction for the logical Pauli-XX measurement lattice surgery and a cross-shaped spatial junction and sweep the link error rate from 10 times to 100 times a fixed bulk error rate, and show that our construction gives the lowest and most stable logical error rate than the other frameworks compared here.

items.title: Error Suppression in Distributed Quantum Computing with Heterogeneous-Distance Lattice Surgery
items.authors: Daniel Dilley, Anastashia Jebraeilli, Rayat Roy, Shobhit Gupta, Alvin Gonzales, Zain Saleem
items.matched: Surface code quantum computing by lattice surgery
items.result: Heterogeneous-distance lattice surgery with an enlarged ancilla (d_A=2d+1) spanning the inter-QPU boundary achieves logical readout error rates nearly independent of link noise, cutting 5-11-5 physical qubit sites by 28.4% compared to uniform distance-9 (373 vs 521 qubits).
items.question: How effectively can additional fault-tolerant error protection be concentrated at a noisy quantum processor interface while preserving the code distance of local data patches?
items.prior: Uniform distance-3 and distance-5 implementations, which exhibit steep increases in logical error rates as link noise grows; at p_link=10⁻², heterogeneous 3-7-3 reduces decoding failure by factors of ≈13 and ≈19 relative to uniform distance-3.

items.tools: Rotated surface codes · 8-DAM (eight-data-patch ancilla-mediated) architecture · Traveling stabilizer syndrome scheduling · Circuit-level Stim simulations

items.abstract: Distributed quantum computing requires fault-tolerant operations across inter-QPU links that can be substantially noisier than local gates. Uniformly increasing code distance provides additional protection but also enlarges data patches used for local storage and computation. Here, we introduce distributed heterogeneous-distance lattice surgery using an eight-data-patch ancilla-mediated (8-DAM) architecture, which will be useful for near-term quantum devices with less qubit overhead. In this architecture, the central ancilla spanning the inter-QPU boundary is enlarged while the data patches retain distance d. The protocol uses traveling stabilizers to suppress hook errors during merge and split operations between these unequal-distance patches. Circuit-level simulations of rotated surface codes at fixed local depolarizing noise show that logical-readout error rates depend only weakly on link noise. The resulting advantage over conventional lattice surgery grows as link errors increase. Comparisons with uniform distance implementations demonstrate comparable logical error suppression with reduced physical-qubit overhead. We also demonstrate how 8-DAM layouts support two simultaneous distributed logical CNOT operations between four logical data qubits using a single enlarged ancilla. At higher link noise, this construction yields lower logical error rates and more stability than two independent distributed logical CNOTs. These results support selective ancilla enlargement as a resource-efficient approach to fault-tolerant distributed quantum computing.

items.title: Error Correction Properties of Covariant Bosonic Encodings
items.authors: Frederic St-Amand, Jean-Philippe Burelle, Baptiste Royer
items.matched: Quantum Low-Density Parity-Check Codes
items.result: Quantum error correction matrices are morphisms of group representations; Schur's lemma forces error matrix blocks to vanish when the symmetric power of the error representation shares no irreducible component with the codespace representation, reducing Knill-Laflamme conditions to character decomposition checks.
items.question: How can finite-group representation theory be used to systematically construct multimode covariant bosonic codes and determine their error-correction capabilities?
items.limits: Analyzes finite subgroups of SU(2) under the amplitude damping channel; predicts error correctability in principle without specifying recovery protocols.
items.tools: Jordan-Schwinger map · Finite-group representation theory · Schur's lemma · Knill-Laflamme conditions · Near-optimal fidelity
items.caption: Plots near-optimal infidelity 1-tildeF against initial coherent state parameters under the amplitude damping channel with photon loss probability γ= 0.095 for the two-mode quaternion code.
items.abstract: Bosonic codes offer a promising approach towards hardware-efficient fault tolerance, with many leading examples such as the cat-code and the GKP code organized by an underlying symmetry. We build on a representation-theoretic framework of quantum error correction to formalize the construction and analysis of multimode symmetric bosonic codes, focusing on finite groups. Here, a physical, logical representation and an initial seed state together define the codewords via a covariant encoding. A central observation is that QEC matrices can be viewed as morphisms of group representations, so that Schur's lemma forces entire irreducible representations blocks to vanish. We recover several known single- and two-mode bosonic codes and build and analyze the error protection capabilities of three codes based on finite subgroups of SU(2). We analyze the impact of reducibility of the logical representation and optimize the seed state using the near-optimal fidelity.

items.title: Exploring Asymmetric QEC Code Concatenation
items.authors: Sayam Sethi, Maxwell Poster, Aditi Awasthi, Willers Yang, Joshua Viszlai, Jonathan Mark Baker
items.matched: Quantum Low-Density Parity-Check Codes
items.result: Alternating mixed Hadamard deformations within each concatenation level (`Alternate_Mixed_within_Level`) yields near-identical X and Z logical error rates while minimizing total logical error rate across one to four concatenation levels. Undeformed concatenation exhibits up to a 60× higher Z error rate than X error rate at concatenation level l=4.
items.question: How can Clifford deformations balance the asymmetric X and Z syndrome checks and logical error rates in concatenated [[4,1,2]] Iceberg codes?
items.prior: Undeformed concatenated [[4,1,2]] Iceberg code produced skewed X and Z error rates due to having asymmetric check counts (2×X and 1×Z).
items.limits: Code capacity phenomenological depolarizing noise (unbiased and 8× biased), single-qubit Hadamard deformations only, simulated up to four concatenation levels with 500,000 Monte Carlo shots.
items.tools: Hadamard Clifford deformations · Concatenated [[4,1,2]] Iceberg code · Level-by-level soft-information maximum-likelihood decoding · Monte-Carlo error simulations
items.caption: Logical error rate versus physical error rate under unbiased noise across concatenation levels l=1 to 4, comparing total, X, and Z LER and the Z/X error ratio across six deformation strategies.
items.abstract: Concatenated quantum error-correcting codes have recently gained popularity because they improve the effective distance of a joint code without requiring the discovery of new codes with desirable parameters. A common building block for such studies is the [[4,1,2]] Iceberg code, the smallest error-detecting code and therefore the one with the lowest resource overhead. However, it has an asymmetric number of X and Z checks, and concatenating it produces skewed logical error rates (LERs) between the X and Z observables. This asymmetry can be mitigated by Clifford-deforming the individual blocks of the concatenation, but the space of possible Hadamard deformations grows doubly exponentially with the number of concatenation levels. We formalize this deformation space and investigate it by proposing six concrete deformation strategies, which we compare under a code capacity (with and without bias) noise model using a concatenated maximum-likelihood soft-information decoder. Among the strategies we study, one one of them achieves near-identical X and Z LERs in a logical-memory experiment while simultaneously reducing the total LER (the sum of the X and Z error rates).

Undeformed concatenation exhibits up to a <math xmlns="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML"><mrow><mn>60</mn><mo>×</mo></mrow></math> higher <math xmlns="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML"><mi>Z</mi></math> error rate than <math xmlns="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML"><mi>X</mi></math> error rate at concatenation level <math xmlns="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML"><mrow><mi>l</mi><mo>=</mo><mn>4</mn></mrow></math>.

items.title: Transversal non-Clifford gates on good quantum locally testable codes
items.authors: Yiming Li, Zimu Li, Zi-Wen Liu
items.matched: Asymptotically good Quantum and locally testable classical LDPC codes
items.result: Asymptotically good [ ldN, ldΘ(N), ldΘ(N)] qLDPC and qLTC codes with soundness Θ(1) support nontrivial transversal logical C^(r-1)Z non-Clifford gates for any integer r≥2.
items.question: Can asymptotically good quantum LDPC codes and quantum locally testable codes directly support transversal non-Clifford logical gates simultaneously with linear distance and constant soundness?
items.prior: Nontrivial transversal logical multi-controlled-Z gates were achieved on almost-good qLDPC codes and qLTCs with polylogarithmic losses in distance and soundness (Li-Li-Liu 2026).
items.limits: Characteristic 2 base fields; odd-sheeted covering towers; asymptotic N→∞ regime.
items.tools: arithmetic cubical complexes · projective Reed-Solomon local codes · cup product pairing with sheaf coefficients · covering space transfer map · Moore determinants
items.abstract: We achieve nontrivial transversal logical multi-controlled-Z gates with asymptotically optimal parameters simultaneously on quantum low-density parity check codes and quantum locally testable codes, by applying the gate framework of [arXiv:2604.01874] to the recent good qLTC construction of [arXiv:2609.20780]. To this end, we use the covering space method to construct a nonzero cup product pairing on a finite arithmetic cubical complex. This differs from the previous construction of almost-good codes, whose base space is a hypergraph product. We express the pairing as a coefficient in a product of Moore determinants and prove polynomial nonvanishing by a bipartite multigraph specialization. We then construct covering spaces to obtain an asymptotic family of good qLTCs on which the pulled-back pairing induces the desired nontrivial transversal logical action.

items.title: When Quantum Meets AI: Quantum Methods for Machine Learning and Machine Learning Methods for Quantum Systems
items.authors: Tak Hur
items.matched: Surface codes: Towards practical large-scale quantum computation
items.result: Mamba-based surface code decoder matches Transformer accuracy while reducing inference cost scaling from quartic to quadratic in code distance. Multi-shift stochastic reconfiguration lowers checkpoint-local validation residuals and update variance in neural quantum state optimization.
items.question: How can learned quantum representations, margin-based bounds, state-space architectures, and regularized stochastic reconfiguration improve quantum machine learning and neural quantum error decoding?
items.prior: Transformer-based neural decoders scaled quartically with code distance in inference cost; fixed-shift stochastic reconfiguration suffered from sample-noise-induced bias-variance instability.
items.limits: Demonstrated on specific benchmark datasets, NMR hardware, and simulated surface code memory experiments under explicit decoder-induced noise models; multi-shift SR adds computational overhead per update.
items.tools: Neural Quantum Embedding (NQE) · DQC1 classification on NMR quantum processor · Mamba state-space neural decoder · Multi-shift stochastic reconfiguration (SR) · Margin-based quantum generalization bounds
items.abstract: This thesis studies the intersection of quantum computing and artificial intelligence in two directions: quantum methods for machine learning and machine learning methods for quantum systems. For quantum machine learning, Neural Quantum Embedding learns data representations that increase the trace distance between embedded class ensembles, lowering an embedding-dependent bound on empirical risk and improving classification on noisy quantum hardware. A training objective based on the Hilbert-Schmidt inner product extends this approach to deterministic quantum computation with one qubit (DQC1) and is demonstrated on an NMR quantum processor. A margin-based generalization analysis then connects quantum neural network performance to quantum state discrimination. In the studied benchmarks, margin distributions predict generalization more reliably than parameter-count metrics. For quantum systems, a Mamba-based neural decoder for surface codes matches a reproduced Transformer baseline in memory experiments while reducing inference-cost scaling from quartic to quadratic in code distance. Under an explicit decoder-induced-noise model, it achieves lower logical error rates and a higher effective threshold. For neural quantum states, stochastic reconfiguration is interpreted as tangent-space ridge regression, with its diagonal shift controlling the bias-variance trade-off under finite Monte Carlo sampling. Multi-shift stochastic reconfiguration reduces checkpoint-local validation residuals and update variance relative to fixed-shift SR, at additional computational cost. Together, these contributions show how learned representations, statistical control, and hardware constraints shape the exchange between quantum computing and machine learning.

items.title: Strong matchgate designs in nearly optimal depth
items.authors: Maxwell West, M. Cerezo, Martin Larocca
items.matched: How to factor 2048 bit RSA integers in 8 hours using 20 million noisy qubits
items.result: Strong ε-approximate relative error matchgate k-designs can be generated in depth O(k² rt(G)lognlog(n/ε)) on a graph G with routing number rt(G), and exact strong matchgate 3-designs in depth O(rt(G)logn) without ancillae.
items.question: Can non-local qubit connectivity enable the formation of matchgate designs in sublinear circuit depth, circumventing the linear-depth barrier present in one-dimensional architectures?
items.prior: 1D nearest-neighbour circuits require Ω(n) depth to form approximate 2-designs over matchgates.
items.limits: Applies to ancilla-free circuits; depth requires connectivity graphs G with low routing number (rt(G)=2 for all-to-all connectivity).
items.tools: random walks on the matchgate group · fermionic routing algorithm · representation theory of SO(2n) · circuit layer compression
items.caption: Schematic of the design construction showing generation via random 2-Majorana rotations, compression into parallel non-overlapping commuting layers, and compilation through a fermionic routing permutation.
items.abstract: Understanding the resources required to generate approximately random unitaries over various groups is a natural goal of quantum information theory. With respect to one notion of approximation, that of a design, it is known that the full unitary group can be approximated in logarithmic depth by one-dimensional circuits of nearest-neighbour 2-local gates. On the other hand, remarkably, circuits with this connectivity cannot form designs over the matchgate group in sublinear depth. Here we show that this dramatic slowdown can disappear when using a general qubit connectivity graph G of routing number rt(G). Indeed, in this setting one can obtain (strong) ε-approximate relative error matchgate k-designs in depth O(k²rt(G)lognlog(n/ε)). For all-to-all connectivity, rt(G)=2. Our construction is conceptually simple, involving a random walk on the matchgate group, and no ancillae. As a technical byproduct, we improve upon the state of the art for fermionic routing, obtaining an O(rt(G)logn) depth router. Additionally, for k=3, we obtain an exact strong matchgate design in O(rt(G)logn) depth, again without ancillae. Under all-to-all connectivity, our fermionic router and 3-designs are optimal. Notably, our results imply that quantum algorithms for fermionic tomography which require drawing from a matchgate 3-design may be exponentially sped up on quantum computers with all-to-all connectivity, relative to their strictly one-dimensional counterparts.
