items.abstract: We construct quantum locally testable codes (LTCs) with constant rate, distance, soundness and locality under a variant of a product expansion conjecture of Bafna and Vyas about Reed-Solomon codes. In particular, we use the high-dimensional expansion framework of Dinur, Lin and Vidick for constructing quantum LTCs, instantiated with the non-Abelian cubical complexes of Rungtanapirom, Stix and Vdovina. Our code is obtained by equipping the complex with carefully chosen Reed-Solomon local codes whose symmetries are compatible with those of the complex.

items.title: Thermodynamic Proof of Quantumness without Structure
items.authors: Florian Meier, Hayata Yamasaki
items.matched: quantum algorithms with provable speedup, query and gate complexity bounds
items.result: Any classical machine solving the structureless Yamakawa–Zhandry search problem with constant success probability must generate entropy S[ρ] ≥Θ(λ2^(λ^c)), requiring exponential Landauer heat dissipation and energy consumption W ≥k_B T S[ρ], whereas the quantum solver needs only polynomial energy.
items.question: Does the exponential quantum advantage for unstructured search persist for macroscopic physical resources like energy consumption?
items.prior: Exponential quantum energy advantage was proven only for Simon's problem with a highly structured oracle (Meier & Yamasaki 2024), leaving unstructured search open.
items.limits: Asymptotic security parameter λ, random oracle model, constant success probability Δ> 0, cyclic computation reset to standard initial state.
items.tools: Yamakawa–Zhandry search problem · Landauer's principle · random oracle model · stopping-time entropy minimization
items.caption: Classical energy-consumption lower bound k_B T S at T = 300K versus security parameter λ, compared against macroscopic benchmarks like CERN annual energy consumption.
items.abstract: Demonstrating that a machine performs genuinely quantum operations is a central challenge in quantum information processing. Existing proofs of quantumness typically rely on computational tasks that are infeasible for classical machines under assumptions such as computational hardness, or explicit bounds on classical runtime, memory, or oracle queries. Here we introduce an alternative paradigm: a thermodynamic proof of quantumness based on energy consumption. Using the search problem of Yamakawa and Zhandry with a structureless uniformly random oracle, we show that any classical machine solving the task with constant success probability must generate entropy that grows exponentially with the security parameter. By Landauer's principle, this implies an exponential lower bound on heat dissipation and hence on the energy consumption of any cyclic classical implementation. In contrast, the corresponding quantum prover solves the task with polynomial query and gate complexity, giving polynomial energy consumption under standard assumptions for quantum implementations. Thus, in the random-oracle setting, sufficiently low energy consumption in a successful implementation certifies quantumness through a macroscopic thermodynamic observation of energy consumption.

items.title: When Quantum Meets AI: Quantum Methods for Machine Learning and Machine Learning Methods for Quantum Systems
items.authors: Tak Hur
items.matched: Quantum singular value transformation and beyond: exponential improvements for…
items.result: Mamba-based neural decoder matches Transformer accuracy on surface codes while dropping inference-cost scaling from quartic to quadratic in code distance. Multi-shift stochastic reconfiguration reduces validation residuals and update variance in neural quantum states.
items.question: How do learned representations, statistical regularization, and hardware constraints optimize quantum machine learning and classical neural methods for quantum error correction and simulation?
items.prior: Transformer neural decoders scaled quartically with surface code distance; fixed-shift stochastic reconfiguration suffered from sample-noise trade-offs.
items.limits: NMR demonstrations limited to small-scale DQC1; multi-shift SR adds computational cost; Mamba decoder evaluated under specific decoder-induced noise models.
items.tools: Neural Quantum Embedding · DQC1 on NMR processor · Mamba state-space decoder · multi-shift stochastic reconfiguration
items.abstract: This thesis studies the intersection of quantum computing and artificial intelligence in two directions: quantum methods for machine learning and machine learning methods for quantum systems. For quantum machine learning, Neural Quantum Embedding learns data representations that increase the trace distance between embedded class ensembles, lowering an embedding-dependent bound on empirical risk and improving classification on noisy quantum hardware. A training objective based on the Hilbert-Schmidt inner product extends this approach to deterministic quantum computation with one qubit (DQC1) and is demonstrated on an NMR quantum processor. A margin-based generalization analysis then connects quantum neural network performance to quantum state discrimination. In the studied benchmarks, margin distributions predict generalization more reliably than parameter-count metrics. For quantum systems, a Mamba-based neural decoder for surface codes matches a reproduced Transformer baseline in memory experiments while reducing inference-cost scaling from quartic to quadratic in code distance. Under an explicit decoder-induced-noise model, it achieves lower logical error rates and a higher effective threshold. For neural quantum states, stochastic reconfiguration is interpreted as tangent-space ridge regression, with its diagonal shift controlling the bias-variance trade-off under finite Monte Carlo sampling. Multi-shift stochastic reconfiguration reduces checkpoint-local validation residuals and update variance relative to fixed-shift SR, at additional computational cost. Together, these contributions show how learned representations, statistical control, and hardware constraints shape the exchange between quantum computing and machine learning.

items.title: Tensor Network Simulation of Dynamic Circuits
items.authors: Innocenzo Fulginiti, Alessandro Poggiali, Christian Mendl
items.matched: Toward the first quantum simulation with quantum speedup
items.result: DMRG-based tensor network simulation natively evaluates dynamic circuits via single-path stochastic sampling and multi-path branch ensemble tracking on MPS and TTN structures, achieving scalable branch propagation with bounded peak memory on 27-qubit random circuits.
items.question: How can tensor-network DMRG algorithms be extended to classically simulate dynamic quantum circuits with mid-circuit measurements and classical feedforward without exponential path overhead?
items.limits: Evaluated up to 27 qubits and depth 8; fixed bond dimensions χ∈8, 16, 32; multi-path branch count capped at M=8.
items.tools: DMRG quantum circuit simulation · Matrix Product States (MPS) · Tree Tensor Networks (TTN) · Single-path stochastic sampling · Multi-path branch pruning
items.caption: Runtime (left) and peak memory usage (right) versus qubit count for dynamic GHZ state preparation comparing unpruned multi-path simulation against single-path sampling with 16, 64, and 256 runs.
items.abstract: Dynamic circuits, which incorporate mid-circuit measurements and classically controlled operations, extend the expressive power of quantum programs and are central to applications such as quantum error correction, state preparation, and distributed quantum algorithms. However, their classical simulation is challenging due to the exponential growth of execution branches induced by mid-circuit measurements. In this work, we develop a tensor network approach for simulating dynamic circuits by extending a DMRG-based method for quantum circuit simulation to support dynamic circuit operations. To address the exponential proliferation of execution branches, we introduce and compare two strategies: a single-path stochastic approach that samples individual measurement outcomes, and a multi-path approach that maintains an ensemble of branches. We benchmark these methods on standard dynamic circuits, including the teleportation protocol and GHZ state preparation, as well as on random dynamic circuits. Our analysis explores the trade-offs between simulation accuracy and computational efficiency. These results provide a practical and scalable framework for the classical simulation of dynamic circuits.

items.title: Lattice Lindbladian simulation by patching and merging
items.authors: Kaoru Mizuta
items.matched: Probing many-body dynamics on a 51-atom quantum simulator
items.result: Simulates generic lattice Lindbladian observables with gate count O((Nt)^(3/2 - 1/(4d+2)) polylog(Nt/ε)) per sample (in 1D, O((Nt)^(4/3) polylog(Nt/ε))) at sampling complexity Θ(ε⁻²). Achieves O(Nt polylog(Nt/ε)) for sparsely dissipative lattice dynamics.
items.question: Can quantum simulation algorithms for generic lattice Lindbladians achieve gate counts approaching the fundamental lower bound Ω(Nt) while retaining polylogarithmic error scaling?
items.prior: Best previous gate count for generic lattice Lindbladian observables with polylogarithmic error scaling was O((Nt)^(3/2) polylog(Nt/ε)) via extrapolation of second-order product formulas.
items.limits: Finite-range interactions and dissipation on d-dimensional lattices with d ∈O(1). Generic algorithm estimates observables via sampling rather than outputting coherent quantum states.
items.tools: dissipative patching lemma · reversed dynamics merging · quasi-probabilistic sampling · linear combination of unitaries
items.caption: Schematic of patching and merging strategies for generic local Lindbladians: decomposition into blocks of size R_p with boundary regions of size R, followed by merging to absorb backward time evolution.
items.abstract: Simulating the dynamics of dissipative quantum many-body systems governed by local Lindbladians is a fundamental task in quantum computation. While the near-optimal gate count has been achieved for Hamiltonian simulation, comparable results for Lindbladian simulation remain elusive. In this work, we develop quantum algorithms for lattice Lindbladians by exploiting their locality. First, we consider sparsely dissipative systems, in which the dissipation is sparsely located, including boundary-driven systems. We establish a near-optimal quantum algorithm for their dynamics with gate count O(Nt polylog(Nt/ε)), where N is the system size, t is the evolution time, and ε is the allowable error. We then consider generic lattice Lindbladians with finite-range interactions and dissipation, and develop an algorithm for simulating time-evolved observables with gate count O((Nt)^(4/3) polylog(Nt/ε)) per sample with the sampling complexity Θ(ε⁻²). The gate count has the smallest known dependence on the system size among algorithms retaining polylogarithmic dependence on 1/ε. Our algorithms are based on two techniques that exploit locality: patching and merging. Patching decomposes dissipative dynamics into dynamics on subsystems with exponentially small error, generalizing a key idea underlying the Haah-Hastings-Kothari-Low algorithm for near-optimal Hamiltonian simulation. Merging absorbs reversed dissipative dynamics into other parts of the evolution, substantially reducing the overhead associated with quasi-probabilistic sampling. These results demonstrate that locality can be fully exploited to achieve fast quantum simulation of dissipative many-body dynamics, opening the way to applications such as predicting nonequilibrium phenomena and preparing desirable quantum states.

items.title: Real-Frequency Diagrammatics with Pole Representations
items.authors: Rayan Farid, Lei Zhang, Aiman Al-Eryani, Agnieszka Jażdżewska, Emanuel Gull
items.matched: Probing many-body dynamics on a 51-atom quantum simulator

Controlled ESPRIT-based recompression truncates pole count, avoiding pole proliferation in self-consistent GW and second-order Born (GF2) calculations.
items.question: Can real-frequency finite-temperature diagrammatics be evaluated self-consistently without grid discretization or numerical analytic continuation while controlling pole proliferation?
items.limits: Equilibrium Keldysh framework, weak-coupling conserving approximations without vertex corrections.
items.tools: Keldysh formalism · Prony-type approximation · ESPRIT signal processing · self-consistent GW and GF2 · Cauchy-Stieltjes transforms
items.caption: Pole counts for retarded self-energy, screened interaction, and spectral function versus compression tolerance ε (left) and iteration step (right) for GW on a half-filled Bethe lattice (U/t=2, βt=10). Recompression bounds the number of poles across self-consistency iterations.
items.abstract: Finite-temperature many-body theories are typically formulated in imaginary time, where they are amenable to efficient numerical treatment. However, the extraction of spectral properties from the imaginary axis is difficult and requires numerical analytic continuation, while a direct formulation on the real axis requires prohibitively expensive numerical quadrature. In this paper, we represent the objects of many-body perturbation theory using systematically improvable pole and moment expansions and develop the corresponding framework for evaluating diagrammatic contributions directly on the real axis. We introduce a controlled recompression procedure that prevents the proliferation of poles under algebraic and diagrammatic operations. We benchmark the approach on paradigmatic quantum impurity problems and apply it to self-consistent calculations of the uniform electron gas. The resulting spectral quantities converge systematically towards numerical accuracy. This work provides a practical framework for controlled and systematically improvable calculations of spectral quantities within diagrammatic many-body theories, including self-consistent conserving approaches.

items.title: Scaling of qubit coherence in quantum dot based Majorana chains: Rabi and Ramsey oscillations of Majorana qubits formed by four and six quantum dots
items.authors: Haining Pan, Sankar Das Sarma
items.matched: Quantum computation with quantum dots
items.result: Rabi and Ramsey coherence times do not improve universally when scaling from four-dot to six-dot artificial Kitaev chain qubits under realistic disorder. Six-dot qubits suffer from increased leakage during Ramsey rotations due to larger detuning needed to overcome suppression of energy splitting.
items.question: How do Rabi and Ramsey coherence times scale when expanding quantum-dot-based Majorana qubits from four dots to six dots?
items.limits: Theoretical simulations with modeled quasi-static disorder under three parameter regimes (small gap, large gap, experimental parameters); non-adiabatic transitions out of Majorana subspace included.
items.tools: Kitaev chain model · qubit rotation simulations · disorder averaging
items.abstract: We present a theoretical study of the Rabi and Ramsey coherence time of Majorana-based qubits formed by double N-site quantum-dot artificial Kitaev chains, following the recent experimental realization arXiv:2607.09511. We generalize the qubit to two chains of arbitrary length and compare the Rabi and Ramsey oscillations of the four-dot and six-dot qubits, simulated with realistic disorder for three sets of parameters: small and large superconducting gaps, and the experimental parameters. We find that, in the pristine limit, the Rabi oscillation is independent of the chain length, whereas the Ramsey oscillation of the six-dot qubit suffers from larger leakage, because the third site suppresses the unwanted energy splitting away from the sweet spot but at the same time makes the deliberate splitting difficult to achieve, which requires a larger detuning that could excite the bulk. In reality with disorder, neither coherence time improves universally with the chain length. The Rabi coherence is set by the competition of three dephasing channels, and the additional dots pay off only if the fluctuation of the interchain tunneling is suppressed; the Ramsey coherence is set by the fluctuation of the energy splitting during the σ_z rotation, which for the four-dot qubit is fixed by the sweet-spot disorder alone and does not depend on the mean splitting, whereas for the six-dot qubit the detuning that generates the splitting adds a fluctuation growing with the splitting itself, so the additional dots pay off only for small splittings. This implies that a longer chain is thus a better quantum memory but not necessarily a better qubit under manipulation. Although topological protection is expected in a longer Kitaev chain qubit, observing it in the current Rabi and Ramsey measurement protocols remains an experimental challenge.

items.title: Bias-driven circular currents in a quantum ring: Effects of electron-electron and electron-phonon interactions
items.authors: Moumita Mondal, Santanu K. Maiti
items.matched: Semiconductor spin qubits
items.result: Electron-phonon coupling g increases the effective interaction-to-hopping ratio u^eff/t^eff, enhancing bias-driven spin currents and transport spin polarization in asymmetric quantum ring junctions despite suppressing charge transport current.
items.question: How do electron-electron and electron-phonon interactions affect bias-driven circular charge and spin currents in an open quantum ring nanojunction?
items.limits: Tight-binding 1D ring, zero temperature, dispersionless out-of-plane optical Einstein phonons, acoustic phonon modes neglected.
items.tools: Hubbard-Holstein model · Lang-Firsov transformation · Hartree-Fock mean-field scheme · Non-equilibrium Green's function formalism
items.caption: Spin polarization coefficient plotted against bias voltage V across different electron-electron interaction strengths u and electron-phonon coupling strengths g. Increasing g enhances spin polarization at low bias, which collapses toward zero at higher voltages where transport windows overlap.
items.abstract: The phenomenon of bias-driven circular charge and spin currents in a ring nanojunction is investigated in the presence of electron-electron (e-e) and electron-phonon (e-ph) interactions within a tight-binding framework based on the non-equilibrium Green's function formalism. The Lang-Firsov transformation is employed to map the interacting system onto an effective electronic model, which is subsequently treated within the Hartree-Fock mean-field scheme. By exploring the interplay among e-e interaction, e-ph coupling, and electrode-ring interface sensitivity, several intriguing features emerge in both circular charge and spin currents that, to the best of our knowledge, have not been reported previously. In addition to bias-driven circular currents, charge and spin-dependent junction currents through the nanojunction are also analyzed. Selective spin transport is achieved, leading to a high degree of spin polarization. All four current components, two associated with circular currents and two with transport currents, are systematically inspected over a wide range of parameter regimes to assess the sensitivity of the results to the relevant system parameters. Our findings provide useful insights into charge and spin transport phenomena in interacting nanojunctions with single- and multi-loop geometries.

items.title: In-orbit operation of a programmable quantum photonic processor
items.authors: Simon Steiner, Peter Schiansky, Antonius Scherer, Riccardo Albiero, Mathias Dragosits, Zhenghao Yin, Martin Mauser, Patrik Zahálka, Raphael Pimenta, Cristóbal Melo, Cédric Léonard, Abhiram Rajan, Niki Di Giano, Antonino Caime, Roberto Osellame, Francesco Ceccarelli, Daniel Martínez, Tobias Guggemos, Iris Agresti, Philip Walther
items.matched: Semiconductor spin qubits
items.result: Demonstrated an in-orbit programmable quantum photonic processor operating on a nanosatellite, generating and manipulating two-photon states in a six-mode universal integrated circuit and observing two-photon Hong-Ou-Mandel interference.
items.question: Can quantum interference conditions (spectral degeneracy, phase stability, and optical alignment) be established and maintained on a programmable photonic circuit in space?
items.limits: Payload constrained to 10 W average power, 9.8 kg mass, and 15 x 15 x 45.3 cm volume; low-noise coincidence measurements restricted to ~30 min per 92 min orbit during Earth shadow due to sunlight leakage and radiation-induced detector noise.
items.tools: Type-II SPDC in ppKTP crystal · 6x6 reconfigurable universal photonic integrated circuit (uPIC) · Single-photon avalanche photodiodes (SPADs) · Custom FPGA System on a Module (SoM)
items.caption: Normalized two-photon coincidence counts plotted against the ppKTP crystal temperature, showing the characteristic Hong-Ou-Mandel interference dip observed during orbital operation across multiple days.
items.abstract: Quantum technologies promise computational capabilities beyond the reach of classical systems. A forward-looking application lies in satellite missions, which increasingly depend on onboard computing under stringent constraints on size, weight and power. Quantum photonics is particularly attractive here: photon interference can enhance the machine-learning models needed to process large onboard data volumes, at fixed hardware resources. However, harnessing this interference requires more than generating single photons, as they must remain mutually indistinguishable: a fragile condition that is hard to maintain within the technically demanding framework of a space mission, which includes a rocket launch, strong thermal drifts, and radiation. This is why quantum states of light, though already generated and transmitted in orbit for secure communication and fundamental tests, have never been used as a computational resource. Here, we report a programmable quantum photonic platform operating on a nanosatellite, processing two photons in a six-mode universal integrated circuit. By programming distinct unitaries and tuning the photons into indistinguishability, we observe two-photon interference, establishing the on-board generation, manipulation and detection of non-classical light. This extends space-based technologies towards in-orbit quantum-assisted computing, for instance local encoding of Earth-observation data, or nodes in a distributed quantum network.

items.title: Deterministic photon waveform adaptation for quantum connectivity
items.authors: Jeffrey Mohan, Jérémy Berroir, Filippo Borselli, David Libault, Ferhat Loubar, Kilian Müller, Jed Rowland, Félix Hoffet, Eleni Diamanti, Tom Darras, Tommaso Mazzoni, Julien Laurat

items.result: Cold-atom optical quantum memory achieves simultaneous temporal waveform adaptation across durations from 20ns to 30μs and average storage-and-retrieval efficiency η=90.4(1.6)% with conditional overlap I_c=97.9(2)%.
items.question: Can an optical quantum memory provide deterministic temporal pulse reshaping without sacrificing high storage-and-retrieval efficiency?
items.limits: Coherent pulses with mean photon number ≈1; memory lifetime limited by thermal atomic motion and residual eddy-current magnetic field gradients (10ms MOT preparation duty cycle).
items.tools: electromagnetically induced transparency (EIT) · laser-cooled elongated ⁸⁷Rb MOT · optimal control theory for control field waveforms · integrated 19-inch rack hardware platform (QDrive)

Demonstrates over three decades of continuously tunable bandwidth compression and stretching while maintaining near-constant high storage efficiency.
items.abstract: The scalability of quantum technologies will depend on the ability to interconnect independent quantum systems through photonic channels. However, heterogeneous quantum platforms emit and absorb photons with widely differing properties, severely limiting inter-node interference and modular connectivity. Here we demonstrate a cold-atom optical quantum memory that simultaneously achieves near-unity storage-and-retrieval efficiency and deterministic temporal adaptation of single photons between arbitrary and programmable input and output pulse waveforms. Operating at high optical depth and within a fully integrated architecture, the system can store photons with durations spanning over three orders of magnitude and reshape them arbitrarily without compromising efficiency, achieving compatibility with many current platforms. By augmenting the role of a quantum memory from a passive storage element to an active programmable photonic interface, our results establish a key building block for scalable entanglement-based quantum networks and modular quantum computing architectures.

items.abstract: We introduce cavity Rydberg quantum photonics as a novel platform for generating hybrid entangled states of optical photons. The system achieves world-record sizes of these states and has the potential to produce yet larger states in the future. In the hybrid entangled state produced here, a superposition of two coherent states is entangled with a polarization qubit carried by a photon in another beam path. We perform quantum state tomography of this hybrid entangled state and evaluate various key properties. By optimizing the decoherence we increase the size compared to previous hybrid entangled states, reaching a size of α²= 2.4. Besides the fundamental interest in Schrödinger cat states, this work is interesting because of potential applications in the field of quantum information processing.

items.title: Broadband Quantum Optical Storage with Chemically Engineered Molecular Eu3+ Complex
items.authors: Yisheng Lei, Senthil Kumar Kuppusamy, Idris Tlemsani, Suma Al-Hunaishi, Pengrui Jiao, Olaf Fuhr, Mario Ruben, Philippe Goldner, Diana Serrano
items.matched: Quantum information with Rydberg atoms
items.result: Realized Hole Anti-hole Grating Echo Memory (HAGEM) in chemically engineered molecular Eu³⁺(TMHD)₃(phen), demonstrating 14.9% quantum optical storage efficiency over a 200 MHz bandwidth.
items.question: How can broadband quantum optical storage be achieved in non-Kramers rare-earth ions with more than two hyperfine levels?
items.prior: Memory bandwidth in solid-state Eu³⁺ was restricted by narrow hyperfine splittings to a few MHz up to tens of MHz.
items.limits: Input pulse mean photon number must remain well below 1 to avoid saturation of the 45 ns dead time single-photon detector; tested at 200 MHz bandwidth.

items.abstract: Broadband quantum memory devices are essential elements for future quantum networks. Here we propose a broadband quantum memory scheme called Hole Anti-hole Grating Echo Memory (HAGEM) for rare-earth ions in solids. We provide a Eu3+ molecular complex with special hyperfine level structures of which the hyperfine level separations are in a specific mathematical correlation that can be obtained by harnessing chemical engineering. Using the memory protocol and material, we experimentally demonstrate a quantum optical storage efficiency of 14.9% and a memory bandwidth of 200MHz, which can easily be extended to a few GHz. With this demonstration, we show the first quantum application enabled by molecular engineering which cannot be achieved by any other existing Eu3+ solid-state materials. In addition, we provide a framework for the chemical engineering of solid-state materials with rare-earth ions for quantum applications consisting of material design, synthesis & characterization techniques, and analytical methods for the quantum properties of rare-earth (RE) ions in solids. This work establishes a new direction in which molecular rare-earth ions can be used for a wide range of quantum applications, which cannot be realized by existing solid-state materials. This will greatly facilitate the development of molecular quantum emitter systems for real world applications.

items.authors: Nikita Semenin, Ksenia Khabarova, Nikolay Kolachevsky

items.result: Derives analytical filter functions and error formulas for Mølmer-Sørensen gate fidelity under fast laser phase noise (at trap frequencies) and slow noise (order of 1/τ), giving a simplified error estimate ε_slow∼Δωτ.
items.question: How do fast and slow laser phase noise components quantitatively impact the fidelity of Mølmer-Sørensen gates across common beam geometries?
items.prior: was numerical simulations without analytical expressions for fast noise (Nakav 2023) and filter functions restricted to optical path fluctuations (Kang 2023)

items.abstract: High-fidelity two-qubit entangling gates are essential for the realization of useful quantum algorithms on quantum processors. The Mølmer-Sørensen (MS) gate has become a common choice for trapped-ion quantum computing due to its resilience to ion temperature and its demonstrated record fidelities. However, the spectral impurity of the driving laser field impacts gate performance, with phase noise influencing the qubit dynamics through mechanisms operating on different timescales. In this work, we present a comprehensive theoretical analysis of laser phase noise in the MS gate, identifying two spectral ranges which influence the gate fidelity the most: "fast" noise at frequencies near the motional mode spectrum, and "slow" noise at frequencies on the order of the inverse gate time. We derive the noise Hamiltonians for two common laser beam geometries and obtain analytical expressions for the average gate error in terms of the laser noise power spectral density and gate parameters. For slowly varying noise spectra, we provide simplified error estimates. In addition, we validate our findings against previously published numerical simulations.

items.authors: Guohui Dong, Yao Yao

items.result: Engineering a bright-dark coupling Δ creates equally spaced dressed-dark states, yielding at least a 20-fold increase in steady-state energy storage over the Rabi-split blockade channel and near-quadratic power scaling P_s ∝N² in the bad-cavity limit.
items.question: How can energy blockade and dynamical bistability in driven quantum batteries with level splitting be circumvented to enhance energy storage and charging power?
items.prior: Conventional Rabi-split design blocked continuous excitation and suffered from bistability, giving at least 20 times lower energy storage and scaling at most as ∼N^(3/2) without bad-cavity collective dissipation.
items.limits: Requires resonant condition ω_c = ω₀, bad-cavity regime κ≫γ, and operation within the superradiant window 1/C₀ ≪N ≪N_max = κ²/g².

items.abstract: Blockade, a phenomenon in which one particle hinders the transport of another, constitutes a core research topic in mesoscopic and microscopic physics. Benefiting from the unique single-particle characteristics, it underpins versatile applications spanning from quantum computation to quantum metrology. Nevertheless, in the context of quantum energy?storage devices, i.e., quantum batteries (QBs), blockade triggered by the intrinsic level splitting is in turn detrimental to energy accumulation. Here we propose an antiblockade charging protocol enabled by deliberately engineering a bright-dark interaction. Rooted in a manifold of equally-spaced dressed-dark states, this elaborate configuration opens up a new charging channel facilitating an antiblockade energy flow and outperforms the Rabi-split blockade design with at least a 20-fold enhancement in energy storage. Additionally, we further illustrate the achievement of superextensive (quadratic) charging characteristic by operating the system in the bad-cavity limit. In view of its inherent generality, our scheme offers a universal and feasible pathway toward high-performance quantum energy architectures.

items.title: Non-Hermitian Purcell Physics in Dissipatively Coupled Planar Photon-Magnon Systems
items.authors: Shubham Singh, Sachin Verma, Animesh Chakraworty, Abhishek Maurya, Biswanath Bhoi, Rajeev Singh
items.matched: cavity QED, atom-photon interfaces and quantum networks
items.result: Dissipative photon-magnon coupling in a planar inverted octa-ring resonator and YIG thin film produces Purcell factors F_P between 4.11 and 5.27 for coupling strengths g/2π from 40.7 to 46.1 MHz, entering the Purcell regime under (κ_m - κ_c)/2 ≥g > κ_c.
items.question: How do magnetic damping and saturation magnetization govern non-Hermitian spectral evolution and Purcell-enhanced cavity photon decay in dissipatively coupled planar photon-magnon systems?
items.limits: Numerical simulation and theoretical modeling without experimental data; magnetocrystalline anisotropy neglected; static field along the in-plane x-axis.
items.tools: CST Microwave Studio full-wave simulations · non-Hermitian coupled-mode theory · input-output formalism · inverted octa-ring resonator (IORR) planar geometry
items.caption: Plots effective cavity photon damping rate β against intrinsic Gilbert damping α, and Purcell factor F_P against coupling strength g/2π.
items.abstract: The Purcell effect has emerged as a powerful mechanism for controlling spontaneous emission and dissipation in cavity and nanophotonic systems; however, its realization in dissipative non-Hermitian hybrid platforms remains largely unexplored. In this work, we investigate the Purcell effect in a dissipatively coupled photon-magnon hybrid quantum system consisting of a yttrium iron garnet (YIG) thin film integrated with an inverted octa-ring resonator (IORR) in a planar geometry. To describe the underlying dissipative hybrid dynamics, we develop a quantum theoretical framework based on non-Hermitian coupled-mode theory combined with the input-output formalism. We also analyze the temporal decay dynamics of the photon-magnon system. Full-wave electromagnetic simulations demonstrate that the system can be engineered to operate in the level-attraction regime through dissipative photon-magnon coupling. By systematically tuning the magnon damping, we uncover the emergence of a Purcell regime in which cavity-photon dissipation is selectively enhanced through magnon-mediated loss channels. We further show that the saturation magnetization (Ms) provides an additional degree of control over the onset, tunability, and robustness of the Purcell enhancement. The combined modulation of magnon damping and Ms strongly influences the effective photon-magnon coupling, hybrid-mode evolution, and dissipation landscape, enabling precise control of hybrid quantum states. These findings establish a versatile strategy for engineering magnetization- and dissipation-controlled photon-magnon interactions in planar, chip-compatible architectures, opening new avenues for non-Hermitian cavity magnonics, tunable microwave dissipation engineering, and hybrid quantum information technologies.

items.question: Can a long-lived fluxonium control qubit and an on-chip planar resonator implement standalone bosonic quantum error correction?
items.prior: Bosonic QEC relied on 3D cavities controlled by fixed-frequency transmons with logical lifetimes limited by transmon T₁^q ≈200 extmu s.
items.limits: Demonstrated at half-flux sweet spot; storage-fluxonium dispersive coupling χ/2π≈23kHz.
items.tools: heavy fluxonium control qubit · on-chip Archimedean spiral resonator · echoed conditional displacement (ECD) control · measurement-free GKP error correction · pulsed fluxonium reset
items.caption: Logical state distinguishability decay versus time along three Pauli axes for corrected and uncorrected GKP states.
items.abstract: Bosonic quantum error correction (QEC) offers a hardware-efficient route to fault-tolerant quantum computing. To date, however, superconducting circuit implementations of bosonic codes have utilized centimeter-scale 3D microwave cavities controlled by fixed-frequency transmon qubits, with logical lifetimes limited by transmon bit-flip errors. Here, we realize bosonic QEC in a fully planar architecture by pairing a heavy fluxonium, whose 451 ±70~μs bit-flip lifetime exceeds that of any control qubit in previous demonstrations, with an on-chip Archimedean spiral resonator several orders of magnitude smaller in mode volume than prior 3D cavities. We prepare finite-energy Gottesman-Kitaev-Preskill (GKP) states and stabilize them using measurement-free error correction with rapid fluxonium reset, extending the logical lifetime by a factor of 1.59 ±0.05. These results provide the first demonstration of resonator control using a weakly coupled fluxonium and, with it, the first realization of standalone bosonic QEC in a fully planar superconducting circuit architecture.

items.title: A photonic integrated comb engine for ultracold quantum gases
items.authors: Wei Sun, Xiaoying Yan, Jinbao Long, Sanli Huang, Zhixin Duan, Zhenyuan Shang, Zeying Zhong, Jiahao Sun, Yue Hu, Shichang Li, Baoqi Shi, Yi-Han Luo, Shuyi Li, Hao Tan, Chen Shen, Zhichuan Niu, Shengjun Yang, Junqiu Liu
items.matched: Cavity-based quantum networks with single atoms and optical photons
items.result: Hybrid-integrated 780 nm microcomb engine achieves 100-kHz-level frequency drift over 2,000 s via ⁸⁵Rb modulation-transfer spectroscopy lock, provides 102 mW injection-amplified single-tooth output, and coherently controls ⁸⁷Rb BEC quantum states.
items.question: Can a fully chip-integrated laser microcomb deliver sufficient coherence, stability, and optical power to drive coherent quantum manipulation of an ultracold gas?
items.prior: Unstabilized self-injection-locked pump drifted by >200 MHz over 2,000 s.
items.limits: Demonstrated for a single ⁸⁷Rb BEC system; hold time limited by a 53.2 ms slow atom-number decay and spontaneous photon-recoil heating (0.556 μK/s minimum equivalent rate).
items.tools: III-V laser diodes (FP and DBR) · Si3N4 high-Q microresonators · Self-injection locking (SIL) · Modulation-transfer spectroscopy (MTS) · Injection-locking laser amplification
items.caption: Architecture and module comparison. Shows chip-scale generation of an atom-locked 780 nm platicon microcomb with injection amplification driving BEC Raman coupling and optical lattices, alongside packaged modules outperforming commercial Ti:sapphire setups in SWaP-C.
items.abstract: Cold atoms underpin quantum sensing, simulation and computation, but their coherent control demands highly stable optical fields whose generation, referencing and power scaling remain formidable integration challenges. While photonic integrated circuits have yielded compact visible lasers and high-Q microresonators have enabled chip-scale optical frequency combs, these crucial technologies have largely remained functionally fragmented. Consequently, the coherent manipulation of ultracold quantum gases using a fully integrated laser-comb source has yet to be realized. Here we demonstrate a scalable, hybrid-integrated microcomb engine at 780 nm that seamlessly bridges frequency synthesis, atomic referencing and power amplification to achieve quantum state control of a Bose--Einstein condensate. By self-injection locking of electrically driven III--V lasers to high-Q Si₃N₄ microresonators, we generate coherent platicon microcombs featuring 20- and 100-GHz mode spacings. Absolute referencing of the microcomb to an ⁸⁵Rb transition actively suppresses long-term frequency drift from over 200 MHz to the 100-kHz level across 2,000 s. A selected comb tooth is subsequently injection-amplified to 102 mW, entirely preserving the microcomb's pristine coherence and stability. We utilize this synthesized field to construct an optical lattice, drive coherent two-photon Raman transitions, and prepare stationary spin-orbit-coupled and Raman-lattice states within an ⁸⁷Rb condensate. By providing a synchronized optical grid, this atom-referenced microcomb allows multiple optical-control channels to scale without a proportional multiplication of independent frequency references. Our work establishes a transformative, fully integrated frequency-synthesis architecture essential for realizing deployable, large-scale atomic quantum systems.

items.title: Improved Transversal Non-Clifford Gates from Cup Products
items.authors: Louis Golowich, Itzhak Tamo, Guanyu Zhu
items.matched: High-threshold and low-overhead fault-tolerant quantum memory
items.result: Length-n quantum LDPC codes achieve distance d ≥n^((1-ε)/r) with constant stabilizer weight and support depth-1 transversal non-Clifford C^(r-1)Z gates on logical yield s ≥n^(1-ε) disjoint tuples for any constant r ≥3 and ε> 0. Yield-distance product surpasses ds ≫n, reaching magic state overhead exponent γ= log(n/s)/log(d) →0.
items.question: Can quantum codes with constant-weight stabilizers support transversal non-Clifford gates that achieve distance and logical yield with ds ≫n?
items.prior: All prior constant-stabilizer-weight qLDPC codes supporting constant-depth transversal CCZ had ds ≤O(n), requiring lim_(n→∞) γ≥1 (Zhu 2025, Lin-Li-Le 2026); beating this tradeoff previously required polylog(n) stabilizer weight (Golowich-Lin 2025).
items.limits: Asymptotic regime n →∞ with constant gate order r ≥3 and arbitrary constant ε> 0. Linear yield s = Ω(n) requires stabilizer weight and circuit depth n^ε.
items.tools: cup products · cochain complexes · classical Tanner codes · punctured tensor products · algebraic geometry codes
items.abstract: It is a major challenge in quantum fault-tolerance to obtain low-overhead protocols for performing non-Clifford gates. In this vein, we construct quantum codes with low-weight stabilizers that support transversal (i.e. low-depth) implementations of the non-Clifford C^(r-1)Z gate, for every constant r≥3. In particular, we obtain length-n quantum LDPC codes (with constant-weight stabilizers) of polynomial distance d≥n^((1-ε)/r) supporting transversal C^(r-1)Z gates on a close-to-linear number k≥n^(1-ε) of disjoint tuples of logical qubits, for arbitrarily small ε>0. Our construction is the first with constant-weight stabilizers that obtains dk≫n, and as a consequence achieves arbitrarily small magic state overhead exponent γ=log(n/k)/log(d)>0. Comparable prior constructions instead required at least polylogarithmic stabilizer weight. We also show how to obtain linearly many k=Ω(n) logical C^(r-1)Z gates, though with stabilizer weight and physical circuit depth n^ε. We show that our transversal gates also support addressing (i.e. targeting) of specific logical qubits. To obtain our codes, we develop a general transformation based on cup products that maps classical codes satisfying a multiplication property to quantum codes with transversal C^(r-1)Z. We apply this transformation to a new family of classical Tanner codes that we construct from punctured tensor products of algebraic codes.

items.title: Purely-logarithmic-time- and constant-space-overhead fault-tolerant quantum computation
items.authors: Zhengyi Han, Zi-Wen Liu
items.matched: High-threshold and low-overhead fault-tolerant quantum memory
items.result: Fault-tolerant quantum computation achieves constant space overhead with strictly logarithmic physical time overhead of depth O(Dlog(WD/ε)) using $O(W + F(n))$ physical qubits for adaptive Clifford+CCZ circuits.
items.question: Can constant-space-overhead fault-tolerant quantum computation achieve strictly logarithmic time overhead?
items.prior: was O(log^(1+o(1))(|C|/ε)) time overhead with constant space overhead (Nguyen and Pattison 2024)
items.limits: Holds below a constant physical error threshold under locally stochastic noise, with ideal all-to-all physical qubit connectivity, noiseless classical processing, and sufficiently large width W ≥C_F F(n).
items.tools: good quantum locally testable codes (qLTCs) · polynomial-subrank transversal logical CCZ gates · single-shot decoding · Hamming purification of Y states · recursive quantum Reed-Solomon magic-state distillation
items.abstract: We prove that constant-space-overhead fault-tolerant quantum computation can be achieved with provably strictly logarithmic time overhead, improving over the best known results with additional subpolylogarithmic factors. Our main construction uses polynomial-subrank transversal logical CCZ gates on good quantum locally testable codes to implement addressable universal computation by transferring batches of logical qubits between dense storage and active logical subspaces while reusing the same ancillary workspace. Logical CCZ gates are implemented directly by the transversal operation, so only stabilizer resource states require separate preparation. Furthermore, we give an alternative construction that also achieves purely logarithmic time overhead based on modifying the quantum Reed--Solomon magic-state distillation scheme of Nguyen and Pattison. Recursively applying a fixed distillation circuit protected by qLTCs of increasing block length eliminates the subpolylogarithmic time factor.

items.authors: Arda Aydin, Edwin Tham, Nicolas Delfosse, Min Ye

items.result: Soft beam search decoding based on cumulative belief-propagation iteration cutoff yields up to 580× logical error suppression at physical error rate 10⁻³ with 0.1% rejection in simulations, and more than doubles fitted logical qubit lifetimes on trapped-ion experimental data with 2.6%--5.6% rejection per round.
items.question: Can soft decoding confidence metrics be extracted directly from quantum LDPC beam search decoder execution without additional decoder invocations or likelihood calculations?
items.prior: Two-round logical-error criterion (2R-LEC) required multiple decoding passes and 1.5–3.1× higher mean belief propagation iteration counts; hard decoding on trapped-ion data achieved breakeven lifetime near physical qubit baseline of 3.84±0.48s (Tham 2026).
items.limits: Simulations assume circuit-level noise at physical rates p=10⁻³ and p=3×10⁻³; experimental validation performed via post-selection re-analysis of existing 1-to-6 syndrome cycle datasets.
items.tools: belief-propagation beam search decoder · iteration-cutoff post-selection · sliding-window streaming decoder · circuit-level noise simulations · trapped-ion experimental qLDPC dataset
items.caption: Logical bit error rate plotted against restart rate for sliding-window decoding of 4-round error-detected measurements in Q54 and Q70 codes at physical error rate 10⁻³. Tuning the iteration cutoff reduces error rate by up to 210× with 0.5 percentage points added restart rate.
items.abstract: The decoder is a critical component of a fault-tolerant quantum computer, computing corrections based on parity-check measurements performed throughout the computation. A soft decoder supplements its output with a confidence score which, when used alongside post-selection, can substantially improve logical performance. We introduce a soft beam search decoder for quantum low-density parity-check codes that uses internal decoder data as a confidence metric, removing the need for extra computation. We perform circuit-level simulations of five quantum LDPC codes relevant for superconducting and trapped ion architectures equipped with our global soft decoder and we obtain up to 580× logical-error suppression at a physical error rate of 10⁻³ while rejecting only 0.1% of shots. Then, we simulate an error detected measurement, which is a core logical operation of the walking cat architecture, using a streaming version of soft beam decoder and we achieve up to 210× error suppression while increasing the rejection probability by only 0.5 percentage points. Finally, we revisit recent quantum LDPC code memory experiments on trapped ions, demonstrating that our soft decoder doubles the logical qubit lifetimes at the price of a mean rejection rate of 2.6%--5.6% per syndrome round, bringing all five codes into the beyond-breakeven regime.

items.title: Near-optimal high-rate surgery from linear PCPPs
items.authors: Alexander Cowtan, Benjamin Ide
items.matched: High-threshold and low-overhead fault-tolerant quantum memory
items.result: Constructs a sparse high-rate surgery gadget of size μ^(1+o(1)) in polynomial time in μ to measure all t ≤k logical qubits in a subcode of size μ≤n of an arbitrary $[[ n, k, d ]]$ quantum LDPC CSS code, with phenomenological fault distance ≥d across d rounds.
items.question: How to design quantum LDPC surgery gadgets that measure large sets of logical operators in parallel while preserving code sparsity, maintaining fault distance, and minimizing auxiliary space overhead?
items.prior: Thickening required O(μd) ancillary space and O(n³) spacetime volume for good codes with t = Ω(k) (Cowtan et al. 2024), while parallel branching required tildeO(tw) space and tildeO(n³) spacetime volume (Cohen et al. 2024).
items.limits: Constants are unoptimized and practicality at finite blocklengths is untested; spacetime detectors are dense rather than sparse; measurement applies to predetermined subcodes rather than full arbitrary Pauli product addressability.
items.tools: linear Probabilistically Checkable Proofs of Proximity (PCPPs) · cochain complexes with relative cosystolic expansion · weight reduction via expander graphs · restriction of scalars
items.abstract: A central problem for surgery with quantum Low-Density Parity Check (LDPC) codes is the design of auxiliary systems which measure large sets of logical operators in parallel, while preserving sparsity and fault distance. We introduce a very general method for designing surgery gadgets which are 'high rate', meaning that the number of operators measured in parallel is large in comparison to the size of the auxiliary system. Given an arbitrary initial $[[ n, k, d ]]$ quantum LDPC Calderbank-Shor-Steane (CSS) code, and an arbitrary subcode of size μ≤n that contains t ≤k logical qubits, the method produces a sparse high-rate surgery gadget with size μ(logμ)^(O(loglogμ))=μ^(1+o(1)) which measures all t logicals in the subcode. The space overhead is asymptotically optimal up to subpolynomial factors, as the lower bound is Ω(μ). This gadget is produced in time polynomial in μ. When logical measurement is performed using these surgery gadgets, the phenomenological fault distance is at least d when performed for d rounds. Our main result comes from relating surgery gadgets with relative cosystolic expansion to linear Probabilistically Checkable Proofs of Proximity (PCPPs), which allow a randomised verifier to probabilistically verify the input to a linear circuit, using only oracle access to the input and a claimed proof.

items.title: Decoder-Prior Poisoning in Quantum Error Correction: Attacks and PriorGuard Defense
items.authors: Xinyi Li, Yifeng Peng, Juntao Chen, Ying Wang
items.matched: High-threshold and low-overhead fault-tolerant quantum memory
items.result: Poisoning 6.4% (k=100) of high-influence decoder-prior entries increases logical error rate by 3.35× without modifying syndrome streams. PriorGuard rejects evidence-inconsistent updates and restores near-clean error rates with 1.7 to 1.8 ms latency and under 0.31 MB auxiliary memory per update.
items.question: Can adversarial manipulation of the classical calibration-to-decoder prior-update path alter quantum error correction decisions, and can such attacks be defended against without modifying syndrome streams?
items.limits: Evaluated on rotated surface-code memory circuits with distances d ∈5,7,9, d syndrome rounds, and base circuit-level noise probability 0.0045; does not address adaptive diffuse poisoning.
items.tools: PriorGuard update gate · Stim rotated surface-code simulations · PyMatching decoder · Detector error model (DEM) single-edge ablation
items.caption: Logical error rate ratio and recovery ratio across different attack configurations, comparing PriorGuard with baselines including signed authentication, global clipping, and random monitoring.
items.abstract: Quantum error correction (QEC) protects quantum computations by repeatedly measuring stabilizer syndromes and using a classical decoder to infer corrections. Modern surface-code decoders are increasingly calibration-aware: they use recent device behavior to set priors such as matching-graph edge probabilities, and these priors directly shape the selected correction. We identify the prior-update path as an overlooked integrity-critical attack surface: a poisoned prior can change decoding decisions even when the syndrome stream, logical labels, and decoder implementation are unchanged. This makes prior poisoning different from ordinary syndrome anomalies and difficult for raw syndrome-anomaly tests to detect. We introduce PriorGuard, a lightweight semantic guard that checks proposed prior changes on high-influence detector-graph entries against private syndrome-derived evidence, accepts updates only when their log-odds movement is evidence-supported, and otherwise falls back to the last evidence-supported prior. We evaluate on Stim-generated rotated surface-code memory circuits decoded with PyMatching. Prior influence is highly concentrated, with the top 10 percent of entries carrying over 60 percent of positive logical-error influence; poisoning only 6.4 percent of decoder-prior entries can raise logical error rate (LER) by 3.35x. PriorGuard recovers most attack-induced loss with a low false-positive rate and modest update-boundary overhead of about 1.7--1.8 ms and less than 0.31 MB auxiliary memory per update.

PriorGuard rejects evidence-inconsistent updates and restores near-clean error rates with <math xmlns="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML"><mn>1.7</mn></math> to <math xmlns="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML"><mn>1.8</mn></math> ms latency and under <math xmlns="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML"><mn>0.31</mn></math> MB auxiliary memory per update.

items.title: Near-Optimal Bell Nonlocality with GKP and Entangled Cat States
items.authors: Özlem Erkilicc, Aritra Das, S. Nibedita Swain, Simon Devitt, Timothy C. Ralph
items.matched: High-threshold and low-overhead fault-tolerant quantum memory
items.result: Photon-number-resolving detection (PNRD) with Gaussian preprocessing and adaptive feed-forward yields near-optimal CHSH Bell inequality violations approaching the theoretical bound (S_max = 2√1+C², up to 2√2) in finite-energy GKP Bell states, cat-code pairs, and entangled coherent states without logical non-Clifford gates.
items.question: Are non-Clifford logical operations fundamentally necessary to access the Bell nonlocality of finite-energy GKP states?
items.prior: Homodyne detection with Gaussian operations and logical Pauli measurements yielded no CHSH violation (S ≤2), requiring costly non-Clifford magic state injection.
items.limits: Pure-state simulations truncated to finite Fock space (N_cut); numerical optimisation over continuous receiver parameters is non-convex and provides achieved lower bounds.
items.tools: finite-energy GKP Bell states · photon-number-resolving detection (PNRD) · Gaussian preprocessing (squeezing/displacement) · adaptive feed-forward · Löwdin orthogonalisation
items.caption: Maximum CHSH parameter S versus GKP squeezing (dB). Shows adaptive PNRD and squeezed-displaced PNRD approaching the unrestricted theoretical bound while beating the classical bound of 2 and bilateral homodyne detection.
items.abstract: Gottesman-Kitaev-Preskill (GKP) states are widely studied as a bosonic encoding for fault-tolerant quantum computing because small displacement errors can be identified and corrected through syndrome measurements. However, fault-tolerant operation requires substantially greater GKP squeezing than is currently available in optical platforms. It is therefore important to identify quantum-information tasks that can be realised with finite-squeezing GKP states. Here, we study Bell nonlocality in finite-energy GKP Bell states under experimentally motivated measurement constraints. Although finite-energy GKP Bell states support Bell nonlocality even at low squeezing, logical Pauli measurements alone cannot reveal it. Accessing the maximum CHSH violation supported by the state generally requires logical non-Clifford rotations. We instead show that the required non-Gaussian resource can reside in the measurement itself. Photon-number-resolving detection combined with Gaussian preprocessing and adaptive feed-forward closely approaches the maximum violation of the CHSH Bell inequality without implementing logical non-Clifford gates. The same measurement principle strongly enhances Bell violations for cat-code Bell pairs and entangled coherent states, demonstrating that its usefulness extends beyond the GKP lattice. Our results identify non-Gaussian measurements as a practical route to revealing Bell nonlocality in finite-energy bosonic states.

items.title: Bosonic Error Correction with Fluxonium
items.authors: Shantanu R. Jha, Shoumik D. Chowdhury, Gabriele Rolleri, Anaida Ali, Lev-Arcady Sellem, Réouven Assouly, David Pahl, Lukas Pahl, Junyoung An, Farid Hassani, Hung-Yu Tsao, Chia-Chin Tsai, Aranya Goswami, Jeremie Boudreault, Jeffrey M. Gertler, Michael A. Gingras, Bethany M. Niedzielski, Jeffrey M. Knecht, Mollie E. Schwartz, Kyle Serniak, Jeffrey A. Grover, Baptiste Royer, Max Hays, William D. Oliver
items.matched: Quantum error correction below the surface code threshold
items.result: Realized standalone bosonic QEC in planar architecture using heavy fluxonium (T₁^q = 451 ext extmu s) and Archimedean spiral resonator, extending logical GKP state lifetime by factor of 1.59 ±0.05.
items.question: Can a long-lived fluxonium control qubit and an on-chip planar resonator implement standalone bosonic quantum error correction?
items.prior: Bosonic QEC relied on 3D cavities controlled by fixed-frequency transmons with logical lifetimes limited by transmon T₁^q ≈200 extmu s.
items.limits: Demonstrated at half-flux sweet spot; storage-fluxonium dispersive coupling χ/2π≈23kHz.
items.tools: heavy fluxonium control qubit · on-chip Archimedean spiral resonator · echoed conditional displacement (ECD) control · measurement-free GKP error correction · pulsed fluxonium reset
items.caption: Logical state distinguishability decay versus time along three Pauli axes for corrected and uncorrected GKP states.
items.abstract: Bosonic quantum error correction (QEC) offers a hardware-efficient route to fault-tolerant quantum computing. To date, however, superconducting circuit implementations of bosonic codes have utilized centimeter-scale 3D microwave cavities controlled by fixed-frequency transmon qubits, with logical lifetimes limited by transmon bit-flip errors. Here, we realize bosonic QEC in a fully planar architecture by pairing a heavy fluxonium, whose 451 ±70~μs bit-flip lifetime exceeds that of any control qubit in previous demonstrations, with an on-chip Archimedean spiral resonator several orders of magnitude smaller in mode volume than prior 3D cavities. We prepare finite-energy Gottesman-Kitaev-Preskill (GKP) states and stabilize them using measurement-free error correction with rapid fluxonium reset, extending the logical lifetime by a factor of 1.59 ±0.05. These results provide the first demonstration of resonator control using a weakly coupled fluxonium and, with it, the first realization of standalone bosonic QEC in a fully planar superconducting circuit architecture.

items.title: The logical set of Gaussian states under the stabilizer subsystem decomposition
items.authors: Santiago Zamora, Kaustav Chatterjee, Ulrik Lund Andersen, Thiago Lucena de Macedo Guedes, Jonatan Bohr Brask, A. de Oliveira Junior, Rafael Chaves
items.matched: Surface codes: Towards practical large-scale quantum computation
items.result: Single-mode Gaussian states mapped into the square-lattice GKP logical subspace via stabilizer subsystem decomposition produce a convex XZ logical Bloch projection with boundary (X,Z)=bigl(A(V_pp),A(1/4V_pp)bigr), yielding an exact vacuum robustness of magic R⁽¹⁾(ρ_L^vac)=2A(1/2)≈1.160314. Squeezing cannot increase |X|+|Z| beyond this vacuum value.
items.question: What logical qubit states can Gaussian bosonic states produce when mapped into the GKP logical subspace via stabilizer subsystem decomposition, and what constraints does Gaussianity place on their non-stabilizerness?
items.prior: Numerical investigations found the vacuum mapped state had robustness of magic 1.160 and identified a maximum robustness of 1.303 at squeezing parameter r ≃0.26 (de Oliveira Junior et al. 2022).
items.limits: Applies to single-mode Gaussian states mapped under ideal square-lattice GKP extraction with discarded syndrome.
items.tools: Stabilizer subsystem decomposition (SSD) · Square-lattice GKP code · Navascués-Vértesi SDP hierarchy for prepare-and-measure scenarios · Tilted qubit witness optimization
items.caption: Z-component versus X-component of the logical Bloch vector. Shows the convex reachable XZ projection of all Gaussian inputs (left) and fixed squeezing levels r=0,0.5,1 (right), crossing the single-qubit stabilizer polytope boundary (red dashed diamond).
items.abstract: Universal quantum computation requires non-Gaussianity in continuous-variable systems and non-stabilizerness in discrete-variable systems. Yet, mapping a Gaussian state into the Gottesman-Kitaev-Preskill logical subspace can yield a logical qubit with non-stabilizer resources. To understand how the continuous-variable structure determines logical resources, we characterize the image of single-mode Gaussian states under the corresponding extraction channel, known as the stabilizer subsystem decomposition. Specifically, we derive series expressions for the logical Bloch vector and characterize the resulting reachable set, enabling an analytical treatment of the robustness of magic of the logical states. We then turn this geometric framework into a certification tool: by mapping a discrete-variable qubit witness to a continuous-variable squeezing witness, we obtain lower bounds on the squeezing of prepared states. We also show that ensembles of Gaussian states can violate both stabilizer and classical bounds. Violation of the stabilizer bound certifies the relational resource known as "set-magic," while violation of the classical bound enables the certification of cryptographic randomness at moderate squeezing.

items.title: Efficient learning of Clifford disentanglers and typical t-doped unitaries with exponentially more T gates
items.authors: Gerard Aguilar, Sofiene Jerbi, Jens Eisert, Lennart Bittel
items.matched: Hamiltonian Simulation by Qubitization
items.result: Disentangling Clifford unitaries and partitions for scrambled product states |ψ⟩= U_C bigotimes_i |ψ_i⟩ can be learned with poly(n) sample and computational complexity. For t-doped circuits, typical unitaries are properly learnable up to t = 2n non-Clifford gates.
items.question: Can unknown Clifford-scrambled product states and typical T-doped unitaries with extensive non-stabilizerness and entanglement be learned efficiently?
items.prior: was O(log(n)) T gates for efficient learning of T-doped circuits (Leone et al. 2024, Oliviero et al. 2024)
items.limits: Requires pure states with a stabilizer promise gap |⟨P⟩_ψ| = 1 or |⟨P⟩_ψ| ≤1 - η; t-doped unitaries require algebraic independence of rotated Paulis (fails for an exponentially small fraction at t ∼n, holds for a constant fraction at t = 2n).
items.tools: Bell sampling · quadratic Bell symmetries · simultaneous block-diagonalization · Choi state tomography · symplectic linear algebra over F₂

items.abstract: Highly entangled and highly non-stabilizer quantum states need not be hard to learn. We give efficient algorithms for testing and recovering hidden tensor-product structure in unknown pure state vectors of the form |ψ⟩= U_C bigotimes_i |ψ_i⟩, where U_C is an arbitrary unknown Clifford unitary. Although the Clifford can thoroughly scramble the visible product structure, we prove that the Bell distribution retains a characteristic family of quadratic symmetries. By simultaneously block-diagonalising these symmetries, our algorithms linearize the problem and manage to recover both a disentangling Clifford and the hidden partitions with polynomial sample and computational complexity. This may be viewed as an extension of the abelian StateHSP paradigm in which classical post-processing exposes genuinely quadratic structure. Applied to Choi states, the method yields efficient proper learning algorithms for typical t-doped Clifford unitaries in regimes containing exponentially more T gates than previously accessible: the required condition fails only for an exponentially small fraction of circuits when t∼n, and continues to hold for a constant fraction even when t=2n. Our framework also provides tools for compressing structured many-body Hamiltonians and suggests benchmarking protocols for encoded logical product states in the early fault-tolerant regime.

items.question: Can constant-space-overhead fault-tolerant quantum computation achieve strictly logarithmic time overhead?
items.prior: was O(log^(1+o(1))(|C|/ε)) time overhead with constant space overhead (Nguyen and Pattison 2024)
items.limits: Holds below a constant physical error threshold under locally stochastic noise, with ideal all-to-all physical qubit connectivity, noiseless classical processing, and sufficiently large width W ≥C_F F(n).
items.tools: good quantum locally testable codes (qLTCs) · polynomial-subrank transversal logical CCZ gates · single-shot decoding · Hamming purification of Y states · recursive quantum Reed-Solomon magic-state distillation
items.abstract: We prove that constant-space-overhead fault-tolerant quantum computation can be achieved with provably strictly logarithmic time overhead, improving over the best known results with additional subpolylogarithmic factors. Our main construction uses polynomial-subrank transversal logical CCZ gates on good quantum locally testable codes to implement addressable universal computation by transferring batches of logical qubits between dense storage and active logical subspaces while reusing the same ancillary workspace. Logical CCZ gates are implemented directly by the transversal operation, so only stabilizer resource states require separate preparation. Furthermore, we give an alternative construction that also achieves purely logarithmic time overhead based on modifying the quantum Reed--Solomon magic-state distillation scheme of Nguyen and Pattison. Recursively applying a fixed distillation circuit protected by qLTCs of increasing block length eliminates the subpolylogarithmic time factor.

items.title: The logical set of Gaussian states under the stabilizer subsystem decomposition
items.authors: Santiago Zamora, Kaustav Chatterjee, Ulrik Lund Andersen, Thiago Lucena de Macedo Guedes, Jonatan Bohr Brask, A. de Oliveira Junior, Rafael Chaves
items.matched: sampling-based quantum advantage and its classical spoofing
items.result: Single-mode Gaussian states mapped into the square-lattice GKP logical subspace via stabilizer subsystem decomposition produce a convex XZ logical Bloch projection with boundary (X,Z)=bigl(A(V_pp),A(1/4V_pp)bigr), yielding an exact vacuum robustness of magic R⁽¹⁾(ρ_L^vac)=2A(1/2)≈1.160314. Squeezing cannot increase |X|+|Z| beyond this vacuum value.
items.question: What logical qubit states can Gaussian bosonic states produce when mapped into the GKP logical subspace via stabilizer subsystem decomposition, and what constraints does Gaussianity place on their non-stabilizerness?
items.prior: Numerical investigations found the vacuum mapped state had robustness of magic 1.160 and identified a maximum robustness of 1.303 at squeezing parameter r ≃0.26 (de Oliveira Junior et al. 2022).
items.limits: Applies to single-mode Gaussian states mapped under ideal square-lattice GKP extraction with discarded syndrome.
items.tools: Stabilizer subsystem decomposition (SSD) · Square-lattice GKP code · Navascués-Vértesi SDP hierarchy for prepare-and-measure scenarios · Tilted qubit witness optimization
items.caption: Z-component versus X-component of the logical Bloch vector. Shows the convex reachable XZ projection of all Gaussian inputs (left) and fixed squeezing levels r=0,0.5,1 (right), crossing the single-qubit stabilizer polytope boundary (red dashed diamond).
items.abstract: Universal quantum computation requires non-Gaussianity in continuous-variable systems and non-stabilizerness in discrete-variable systems. Yet, mapping a Gaussian state into the Gottesman-Kitaev-Preskill logical subspace can yield a logical qubit with non-stabilizer resources. To understand how the continuous-variable structure determines logical resources, we characterize the image of single-mode Gaussian states under the corresponding extraction channel, known as the stabilizer subsystem decomposition. Specifically, we derive series expressions for the logical Bloch vector and characterize the resulting reachable set, enabling an analytical treatment of the robustness of magic of the logical states. We then turn this geometric framework into a certification tool: by mapping a discrete-variable qubit witness to a continuous-variable squeezing witness, we obtain lower bounds on the squeezing of prepared states. We also show that ensembles of Gaussian states can violate both stabilizer and classical bounds. Violation of the stabilizer bound certifies the relational resource known as "set-magic," while violation of the classical bound enables the certification of cryptographic randomness at moderate squeezing.

items.title: Simulation of a Battery Cell on Quantum Computers: Reactions & Transport
items.authors: Albert J. Pool, Michael Schelling, Birger Horstmann
items.matched: Probing many-body dynamics on a 51-atom quantum simulator
items.result: Hybrid quantum-classical implementation of the Feynman-Kitaev Hamiltonian solves non-linear transport and reaction PDEs, demonstrating the first quantum simulation of a battery cell using the Single Particle Model with electrolyte (SPMe).
items.question: Can non-linear partial differential equations modeling electrochemical battery transport and reactions be solved efficiently on quantum hardware?
items.limits: Demonstrated for the Single Particle Model with electrolyte (SPMe) approximation; tailored to divide non-linear PDE computational tasks for noisy quantum systems.
items.tools: Feynman-Kitaev Hamiltonian · hybrid quantum-classical algorithm · Single Particle Model with electrolyte (SPMe)
items.abstract: Simulations of electrochemical materials and systems accelerate technological progress, but are still limited by computational power. In particular, quantum computing offers prospects for higher resolutions, due to the exponential amount of data that can be stored in a quantum state. As current quantum computers are still noisy, we consider a hybrid quantum-classical algorithm, that divides the problem into smaller computational tasks. We describe how to implement such an algorithm for non-linear partial differential equations, the Feynman-Kitaev Hamiltonian, in a scalable way for an electrochemical system. We show how it can evaluate general electrochemical models and present a quantum simulation of the Single Particle Model with electrolyte (SPMe) as the first quantum simulation of a battery cell.

items.title: Influence of fast and slow laser phase noise on the fidelity of the Mølmer-Sørensen trapped-ion gate
items.authors: Nikita Semenin, Ksenia Khabarova, Nikolay Kolachevsky
items.matched: Probing many-body dynamics on a 51-atom quantum simulator
items.result: Derives analytical filter functions and error formulas for Mølmer-Sørensen gate fidelity under fast laser phase noise (at trap frequencies) and slow noise (order of 1/τ), giving a simplified error estimate ε_slow∼Δωτ.
items.question: How do fast and slow laser phase noise components quantitatively impact the fidelity of Mølmer-Sørensen gates across common beam geometries?
items.prior: was numerical simulations without analytical expressions for fast noise (Nakav 2023) and filter functions restricted to optical path fluctuations (Kang 2023)
items.limits: Assumes common laser source, white-noise approximation above cutoff frequencies of 10–100 Hz, equal intensities of bichromatic components, and finite measurement duration T₀.
items.tools: Hamiltonian perturbation theory · Filter function formalism · Spectral analysis

items.abstract: High-fidelity two-qubit entangling gates are essential for the realization of useful quantum algorithms on quantum processors. The Mølmer-Sørensen (MS) gate has become a common choice for trapped-ion quantum computing due to its resilience to ion temperature and its demonstrated record fidelities. However, the spectral impurity of the driving laser field impacts gate performance, with phase noise influencing the qubit dynamics through mechanisms operating on different timescales. In this work, we present a comprehensive theoretical analysis of laser phase noise in the MS gate, identifying two spectral ranges which influence the gate fidelity the most: "fast" noise at frequencies near the motional mode spectrum, and "slow" noise at frequencies on the order of the inverse gate time. We derive the noise Hamiltonians for two common laser beam geometries and obtain analytical expressions for the average gate error in terms of the laser noise power spectral density and gate parameters. For slowly varying noise spectra, we provide simplified error estimates. In addition, we validate our findings against previously published numerical simulations.

items.title: Certifying fermionic Gaussian states (and a little more) with optimal precision dependence
items.authors: Ninnat Dangniam, Laphas Premcharoen, Metrasit Sripech, Thiparat Chotibut
items.matched: Evidence for the utility of quantum computing before fault tolerance
items.result: Certifies any d-mode pure fermionic Gaussian state to infidelity ε and failure probability δ with N ≤lceil(d(d-1))/(ε) ln1/(δ) rceil copies, single-qubit measurements (only one adaptive per copy), and O(d³) classical runtime per copy.
items.question: Can every fermionic Gaussian state be certified with single-qubit measurements, optimal ε⁻¹ precision scaling, and efficient classical processing simultaneously?
items.prior: was O(d³ ε⁻²) with non-adaptive single-qubit measurements (Gluza et al. 2018) or O(d ε⁻¹) with adaptive measurements on all d-1 qubits and product-basis amplitude oracle access (Gupta et al. 2024)
items.limits: Pure states of definite fermionic parity. Exact worst-case bound holds on specific factorized states; random instances show better empirical scaling.
items.tools: quantum state verification · d ↔d-2 down-up Markov chain walk · entropy contraction and variance bounding · Pfaffian computational-basis sampling
items.caption: Spectral gap γ(L) of the certification walk versus mode count d on log-log scales across random Gaussian states, random Slater determinants, 1D spin chains, and theoretical lower bounds.
items.abstract: Fermionic Gaussian states are the workhorse reference states for qubit-based quantum simulation of fermionic systems, yet existing certification protocols either proceed via fidelity estimation, leading to suboptimal sample complexity in the target precision ε, only apply to Haar-typical states, or require adaptive measurements on a large fraction of qubits. We give an adaptive protocol that certifies any d-mode pure fermionic Gaussian state using O(d²ε⁻¹) copies, single-qubit measurements with only one qubit measured adaptively per copy, and O(d³) classical processing time per copy. The ε⁻¹ dependence is optimal for the certification problem, even among strategies using entangled measurements. The sample complexity is controlled by the spectral gap of a d↔d-2 down-up walk---a Markov chain studied in the theory of high-dimensional expanders, equivalent to a two-site Glauber dynamics in statistical physics---relating certification efficiency to relaxation time to equilibrium. The worst-case bound is tight for this protocol and is attained by physically relevant states, including ground states of the fully dimerized Su-Schrieffer-Heeger (SSH) chain and BCS pair states. In contrast, numerics up to d=14 suggest that O(d ε⁻¹) copies suffice to certify Haar-typical Gaussian states, a factor of d improvement over the worst-case bound. Finally, because the bound depends only on the target's computational-basis distribution, the protocol extends to efficiently phase-dressed states---states obtained by injecting an efficiently computable diagonal phase to Gaussian states---with the same sample complexity. The class includes a continuous family of four-mode non-Gaussian magic states for matchgate computation.

items.title: Quantum Simulation of Si/SiGe Devices with Experimentally Calibrated Micromagnet Effects
items.authors: Andrii Sokolov, Conor Power, Mathieu Moras, Claude Rohrbacher, Brian Malone, Sergey Amitonov, Agostino Apra, Amir Sammak, Nodar Samkharadze, Elena Blokhina
items.matched: analog quantum simulation of lattice models on cold atoms or superconducting ar…
items.result: Full-stack 3D device simulation incorporates Jiles-Atherton micromagnet hysteresis and semi-empirical parasitic charge screening, matching experimental qubit resonance frequencies across a 6-dot Si/SiGe array and reproducing microwave power chevron Rabi dynamics.
items.question: How can theoretical CAD models be calibrated to accurately reproduce experimental electrostatic screening, micromagnet hysteresis, and driven spin dynamics in multi-dot Si/SiGe spin-qubit devices?
items.limits: Model requires empirical calibration of electron affinities, discrete parasitic charge domains, and pre-magnetization history. Residual errors remain bounded by lithography, film thickness, and Co purity variations.
items.tools: QTCAD electrostatic solver · COMSOL Multiphysics with Jiles-Atherton hysteresis model · Rotating wave approximation time-dependent Schrödinger solver · 6-dot Si/SiGe heterostructure device
items.caption: Resonant frequency and magnetic field versus external field calibration (left) and comparison of experimental versus simulated resonant frequencies across all six qubits in the array (right).
items.abstract: Silicon-based spin qubits in Si/SiGe heterostructures are a leading platform for scalable quantum computing, yet bridging the gap between theoretical computer-aided design(CAD) models and experimental reality remains a significant challenge. Standard simulations often fail to capture critical physical phenomena, such as interface dipoles, parasitic charge accumulation, and the magnetic hysteresis of on-chip micromagnets. In this work, we present a comprehensive, experimentally calibrated 3D simulation pipeline for a 6-dot Si/SiGe device. We refine the semiconductor band alignment and introduce a semi-empirical classical charge screening model to accurately capture the formation of parasitic wells and their suppression of gate lever-arms. Furthermore, we apply the Jiles-Atherton model to account for the hysteresis and pre-magnetization of integrated cobalt micromagnets, successfully reproducing the experimental resonant frequencies across all six qubits. By coupling these calibrated electrostatic and magnetic profiles into a time-dependent rotating wave approximation (RWA) Hamiltonian, we reproduce experimental observables, including microwave power chevrons. This framework provides a robust foundation for predicting device behavior, evaluating microwave line losses, and optimizing future scalable spin qubit architectures prior to fabrication.
